papers.title: InitFree-SfM: When Initialization-Free Bundle Adjustment meets Learned Structure-from-Motion
papers.abstract: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.

The joint optimization of camera poses and scene landmarks, known as bundle adjustment (BA), is a central component of structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines [6]. In its traditional formulation [24], BA is used as a refinement stage, after suitable initial estimates of the camera poses and scene structure have been obtained, typically through a sequence of geometric steps such as relative pose estimation, rotation averaging, and triangulation.

A recent line of work [34, 10, 9, 17] challenges this paradigm by considering BA with random initialization. This setting, referred to as initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA), seeks to jointly optimize global camera poses and scene landmarks without requiring an initial estimate of either. To tackle this challenging problem, existing methods typically adopt a three-stage pipeline: (i) a surrogate Object Space Error (OSE), combined with regularization, is optimized using variable projection (VarPro); (ii) camera parameters and landmarks are refined by minimizing reprojection error; and (iii) a metric upgrade [20] is applied to recover Euclidean camera poses from relaxed camera matrices in ℝ3×4\mathbb{R}^{3\times 4}.

papers.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains coding agents directly against programmatic test suites (Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Unlike isolated function-level exercises, multi-module repositories bundle test fixtures, configuration plugins, equality comparators, and evaluation hooks alongside editable source files, while visible unit tests often cover only a few edge cases (Zhong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Gupta and Joshi, 2026). Once a policy discovers that preloading a workspace fixture, spoofing object equality, or overfitting to sparse test cases yields higher return than solving an algorithmic bottleneck, group-relative policy optimization amplifies that shortcut (Wang et al., 2026b) and transfers deceptive habits to downstream tasks (MacDiarmid et al., 2025).

When a detector flags suspicious trajectories during training, an alignment pipeline can intervene at the reward signal, the training data, or the evaluation environment, as shown in Figure 1(a). Existing training-time defenses act at the first two loci and run into opposing structural limits. Penalizing flagged outputs leaves the verifier open and fails on both error branches of an imperfect detector (Baker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Wong et al., 2026): false negatives still earn full reward and select for shortcuts disguised behind routine engineering rationales, whereas stripping reasoning context to inspect raw code or runtime flags causes false positives that zero out valid solutions and corrupt within-group advantages. Quarantining flagged tasks or masking flagged rollouts avoids step-level evasion gradients by withholding penalties (Wang et al., 2026b), yet induces inverse difficulty selection: because shortcuts beat genuine attempts earliest on hard repositories where valid solutions are scarce, task quarantine depletes the training pool while rollout masking leaves hard prompt groups with zero reward variance.

In this paper, we propose online environment repair (OER), a training procedure grounded in operant extinction that repairs exploited environments online without penalizing the triggering rollout. At each GRPO step, rollouts are scored unconditionally against the active environment version, removing any step-level incentive to conceal intent in reasoning traces or code comments. Passing rollouts that trigger execution invariants or intra-group differential fuzzing enqueue the environment for asynchronous repair by a Qwen3-32B agent while holding the problem specification fixed. A candidate patch replaces the environment on subsequent steps only if it clears three automated gates: specification integrity, exploit replay failure, and reference or benign solution preservation. Because no specification-preserving patch can cause a valid solution to fail replay while keeping equivalent reference solutions passing, the opposing gates cancel detector false positives without penalizing valid rollouts or corrupting environments, and enable structural propagation across sibling repositories without scaffold family labels or reference solutions.

papers.title: HS-OVSeg: Multi-Granularity Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation in Remote Sensing via Heterogeneous Supervision
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) enables flexible, text-driven mapping of remote sensing (RS) imagery beyond predefined categories. Despite advances in segmentation foundation models, RS-OVSS remains constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, semantically diverse datasets with accurate pixel-level annotations. Meanwhile, existing RS datasets contain abundant scene- and object-level annotations that offer valuable semantic information but lack precise pixel-wise supervision. To exploit these complementary sources, we propose HS-OVSeg, a unified training framework that integrates heterogeneous scene-, object-, and pixel-level supervision for RS-OVSS. Specifically, we generate pixel-wise pseudo-labels using SAM3, conditioned on scene-level class names and object-level class names with bounding boxes. Combined with ground-truth semantic masks, these pseudo-labels enable joint training across all three annotation granularities through LoRA-based fine-tuning of SAM3. Our unified training spans 20 RS datasets, including 3 scene classification, 4 object detection, and 13 semantic segmentation datasets, with 1,000 images from the 7 classification and detection datasets manually annotated for pixel-level evaluation. HS-OVSeg substantially outperforms existing RS-OVSS models across both the 20 training-source and 5 held-out datasets, demonstrating strong multi-granularity segmentation capabilities under heterogeneous supervision. The code will be publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: MAQR: Lightweight Memory-Aware Q-Routing for Fresh Status Delivery in Multi-Hop IoBNTs
papers.abstract: This paper proposes memory-aware Q-routing (MAQR) for fresh status delivery over history-dependent molecular links in multi-hop Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) networks. Repeated transmissions leave residual molecules, making link reliability history-dependent and fixed routing inefficient. Each link is calibrated from a spatial Markov model and approximated by three nonnegative decay modes. The resulting reduced memory state and packet bit composition provide an instantaneous link-success estimate. MAQR combines quantized memory and reliability descriptors with packet age, queue occupancy, and molecule reserve in a lightweight partially observable Q-routing heuristic. It is trained offline and requires only reduced-state updates and Q-table lookup during deployment. Across five independent training pairs and 20 shared evaluation seeds, MAQR reduces mean AoI by 46.9 % relative to memory-blind Q-routing at 0.30 packets/slot while improving molecular efficiency. Frozen-policy sweeps further show comparable performance under weak memory and an increasing MAQR advantage as channel memory strengthens.

The Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) envisions networks of bio-nano sensors, engineered cells, and bio-cyber interfaces for in-body sensing and actuation [1, 2]. Molecular communication (MC) provides a biocompatible means of exchanging information at such small scales [3]. Since the range of an individual molecular link is limited, decode-and-forward relays can extend communication coverage and enable multi-hop delivery of physiological status updates to a bio-cyber gateway [4, 5]. One biologically inspired example is bacterial nanonetworking, in which natural properties such as motility, chemotaxis, and conjugation can be exploited to transfer information through intermediate bacterial populations [6, 7].

A key challenge in such networks is that molecular-link reliability depends on recent transmission history. Diffusion, advection, and reversible reception produce long channel tails, leaving residual molecules that affect subsequent observations [8]. Repeated use of the same link can therefore degrade its instantaneous reliability, making a fixed shortest or average-reliability route inefficient. The resulting decoding failures and retransmissions increase molecule consumption and delay fresh status delivery. This is particularly important for monitoring applications, where the age of information (AoI) captures the freshness of the latest update available at the destination [9]. Point-to-point molecular channels already exhibit a direct tradeoff between update frequency, intersymbol interference, and AoI [10].

papers.title: Probing the Rung-Mott Insulator in Bosonic Two-Leg Ladders
papers.abstract: Mott insulators typically appear at integer densities, but certain lattice geometries or non-local interactions can stabilise Mott insulators at fractional densities. In this work, we study strongly interacting two-leg ladders using ultracold bosonic atoms around half-filling, and identify the rung-Mott insulating (RMI) phase through its characteristic rung occupation in site-resolved measurements. We probe its excitation spectrum via lattice modulation spectroscopy, and interpret the observed spectra using numerical simulations that include the driven dynamics, coupling to multiple excited states, and energy offsets. As with other Mott insulators, the RMI phase is characterized through its incompressibility, which we probe via a site-resolved analysis of densities and chemical potentials. Our results provide direct insight into the excitation dynamics of a strongly correlated ladder system, and pave the way for studying transport and further dynamical properties in low-dimensional quantum systems with programmable lattice geometries.

papers.title: RestPose: Canonicalization for Open Object Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: In object pose estimation methods, predicted poses are expressed with respect to a canonical frame, defined by a reference model of that object. In learning-based methods, an arbitrarily chosen modeling convention defines this canonical frame, which is then used to generate the ground-truth pose-annotations for training. Object pose estimation methods are therefore bound to such arbitrary conventions, restricting generalization. In this work, we propose that such a canonical frame can instead be derived for any object, and present RestPose, an approach towards open object pose estimation that does not require reference models or canonical frame conventions during training. From a single input image, we generate an object mesh and canonicalize it through a geometric and physical analysis of the object, then use foundation model-based dense matching to estimate the pose. We choose category-level benchmarks for our experiments, which contain instances across various object categories and enable us to measure the effectiveness of our canonicalization. Across HouseCat6D, NOCS, and Omni6DPose datasets, we improve on the supervised state-of-the-art methods by 18.3 points in absolute metrics and 13.8 points in scale-agnostic metrics, without requiring task-specific training. Code will be published.

Estimating the 6D pose of an object requires a defined canonical frame to measure against. In an instance-level setting [31, 17, 27, 13], the frame is defined by the object’s CAD model. Alternatively, when no CAD is available, the frame is often defined from a reference view, so that pose is expressed relative to one arbitrary image of the object [19, 47, 6]. In a category-level setting, neither is available at inference - in this setting, every instance of any category is assumed to be seen for the first time during inference, and thereby has no distinguished orientation (canonical frame) until one is arbitrarily chosen.

Different sources of a canonical frame in object pose estimation: Model based methods inherit it from the object models. NOCS-style methods declare a per category frame and train networks to predict object coordinates in it. Reference-based methods borrow the frame of an arbitrary view and report pose relative to it. RestPose generates the object’s mesh and derives the frame following a geometric analysis. A solution to this problem was established by NOCS [40] and was widely adopted by category-level object pose methods [38, 3, 25, 5, 26, 22, 35, 36]. NOCS proposes to declare that canonical frame once per category and render coordinate supervision from CAD models aligned into it. A network trained on those renders does not use the category’s CAD at test time, and it appears to have no dependence on that chosen canonical frame per category.

papers.title: Lattice Thermal Conductivity of MgO and the MgSiO$_3$ Polymorphs Bridgmanite and Post-Perovskite at Lower-Mantle Conditions Using Fine-Tuned MACE Potentials
papers.abstract: Heat flow across the core-mantle boundary (CMB) depends on the lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa_{\mathrm{latt}}$) of lowermost-mantle minerals, yet calculated CMB values for MgO differ severalfold, and high-temperature estimates of the conductivity increase across the bridgmanite-post-perovskite transition range from about 20 to 50%. Direct solutions of the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (LBTE) require thousands of density functional theory (DFT) force evaluations per thermodynamic state. Here we replace these evaluations with phase-specific, fine-tuned MACE potentials for MgO, MgSiO3 bridgmanite (Pv), and MgSiO3 post-perovskite (PPv). The potentials reproduce DFT energies, forces, stresses, pressure-volume relations, and compressed-state phonons for all three phases. For MgO at 0 GPa, replacing MACE forces with DFT forces in otherwise identical transport calculations changes $\kappa_{\mathrm{latt}}$ by 0.2% at 300 K and 1.9% at 2000 K. PPv is 44-55% more conductive than Pv at the same pressure and temperature and strongly anisotropic, with $\kappa_{[100]}/\kappa_{[010]}$ ranging from 1.7 to 2.1. The quasi-harmonic phase boundary has a Clapeyron slope of $(7.4 \pm 0.1)$ MPa/K and intersects a model geotherm at 116.2 GPa and 2660 K, where the transition raises the silicate conductivity by 47%, to 8.6 W/(m K). Heating in the basal thermal boundary layer lowers the MgO and PPv conductivities to 37.3 and 6.7 W/(m K) at the CMB, where Hashin-Shtrikman bounds of 9.5-11.4 W/(m K) for an Fe-free aggregate of 80 vol% silicate and 20 vol% MgO encompass the 10 W/(m K) used in earlier heat-flow estimates. The density-temperature parameterizations provide an intrinsic end-member reference for lower-mantle thermal models.

papers.intro:
Heat conducted across the core–mantle boundary (CMB) couples the thermal evolution of Earth’s core and mantle. It governs how fast the core cools and the inner core grows, how much energy is available to the geodynamo, and how strongly the lowermost mantle is heated from below. Converting the temperature contrast across the basal thermal boundary layer into a heat flux requires the thermal conductivity of lowermost-mantle minerals at pressures near 135 GPa135\text{\,}\mathrm{GPa} and temperatures up to about 4000 K4000\text{\,}\mathrm{K}. Measurements under such conditions are still rare. Thermoreflectance experiments on MgO have reached about 140 GPa140\text{\,}\mathrm{GPa} at 1950 K1950\text{\,}\mathrm{K}, and about 3170 K3170\text{\,}\mathrm{K} at lower pressures (Hasegawa et al., 2023). Recent work on bridgmanite and Fe-bearing post-perovskite has also extended to high pressures and temperatures, but not yet across the full range expected near the CMB (Edmund et al., 2024; Okuda et al., 2020). Atomistic calculations therefore remain central both to interpreting these experiments and to extending them to deep-mantle conditions. Here we consider only the lattice contribution to the thermal conductivity of the Fe-free end members MgO, MgSiO3\text{MgSiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}} bridgmanite, and MgSiO3\text{MgSiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}} post-perovskite. Radiative and electronic transport, chemical substitution, point defects, and grain boundaries must be added separately when the results are applied to natural mantle assemblages.

Isotopic disorder, oxygen vacancies, and Fe substitution lower the conductivity further (Chabane et al., 2025), so ideal MgO should be read as a high-conductivity end member, not as a model for natural ferropericlase.

papers.title: Compositional Reachset-Conformant Modeling for Managing Uncertainty in the Development of Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: The development of cyber-physical systems (CPS) proceeds through iterative design revisions, and compliance with safety requirements must be re-established after every revision, typically based on a system model. Conventional models, however, predict only the most likely behavior, leading to model-plant mismatch that often surfaces only during late-stage testing, when redesign is most expensive. This article presents reachset-conformant modeling as a framework for managing uncertainty throughout the development process: instead of a single trajectory, a reachset-conformant model predicts a set of behaviors, calibrated from data to conservatively enclose the true system behavior with a statistical guarantee. Safety properties established on the model therefore transfer to the realized system. Beyond a practical introduction to reachset-conformant identification and its benefits for CPS development, our main theoretical contribution is a closure result: reachset conformance is preserved under serial composition, parallel composition, and feedback interconnection, and hence under any architecture assembled from these primitives. Subsystem models identified independently from local measurements can thus be substituted into the system architecture, and the interconnected model inherits a coverage guarantee from the subsystem guarantees. We complement this result with update strategies that adapt the uncertainty sets after design changes without restarting the identification workflow. Experiments on an automotive brake-system test bench demonstrate that a) a single model covers all operating conditions and hardware variants, b) late-stage modifications are absorbed by uncertainty set updates, c) a black-box hydraulic unit is conservatively abstracted from input-output data alone, and d) independently identified subsystem models form a conformant model by construction.

papers.intro:
Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are rarely built in a single pass. Their development proceeds through a sequence of design stages—from requirements analysis through system, architectural, and detailed design down to the implementation—followed by verification stages in which units, integrated subsystems, and finally the complete product are tested against the specifications; this workflow is commonly visualized as the V-process shown in Fig. 1. Progress along the V is iterative: subsystem architectures, component realizations, parameters, and implementation technologies are repeatedly revised, and compliance with safety and performance requirements must be re-established after every revision. Abstract models make this feasible: derived from first principles or identified from data, they allow the system behavior to be predicted and checked against the specifications at every stage, before a concrete implementation exists. Conventional models, however, describe most-likely rather than guaranteed behavior: exact yet tractable representations of the true dynamics rarely exist, and CPS exhibit inherent nondeterminism arising from unmodeled couplings, parameter variability, and external disturbances. The resulting model–plant mismatch may conceal unsafe behaviors until integration or acceptance testing, where the cost of correcting a defect has grown by orders of magnitude: the defect propagates back through requirements, architecture, control logic, and implementation, forcing the costly redesign loop illustrated in Fig. 1(a)—precisely the cycle that early modeling is intended to prevent.

papers.title: Fuzzy vectors from first and second moments: Affine consistency, carrying and sparsest realizations
papers.abstract: When the probability law of a random vector cannot be identified, its mean and possibly singular covariance can often still be elicited. We consider fuzzy vectors with compact convex cuts as mathematically tractable representations of such a moment pair, and ask how they must be designed to rely only on this information. We postulate two modeling desiderata, independence of the choice of origin and basis, and invariance under embeddings into a higher-dimensional space. Under these requirements alone we show that, in every ambient dimension, every level set of the fuzzy vector must be a Mahalanobis ellipsoid centered at the mean. Its complete specification then amounts to the choice of a radial profile for each covariance rank. We call a fuzzy vector a carrier of the moment pair if at least one of its random-set selections has exactly the given mean and covariance. For an ellipsoidal fuzzy vector of rank $p\ge1$ with radial profile $\rho$, carrying is equivalent to $\int_0^1\rho(\alpha)^2d\alpha\ge p$, and equality characterizes the inclusion-minimal carriers within the fixed-shape Mahalanobis class. A discrete random vector with the same mean and covariance and the fewest equally weighted atoms has its atoms on a regular simplex in Mahalanobis coordinates. Completing this simplex under the rotations left free by the moments yields the minimum-volume crisp ellipsoid in the state space that carries them. The ellipsoidal representation also encodes interaction through the covariance matrix.

In many such settings the underlying probability law cannot be identified reliably, whereas its mean vector and covariance matrix can be estimated from data, assessed by experts, or reported as summary statistics. The covariance may be singular, for instance when there are more variables than observations. Our starting point is a principle of informational restraint. A representation based only on specified information should not depend on arbitrary features of its description. We formulate this principle as coordinate neutrality and ambient neutrality. The former requires a representation to transform with the moments under invertible affine changes of coordinates. The latter requires that adding deterministic coordinates leave the intrinsic uncertainty unchanged. Their joint mathematical expression we term affine consistency.

Turning partial probabilistic knowledge into possibility distributions is a long-standing theme of possibility theory. Dubois, Foulloy, Mauris and Prade [2] develop probability–possibility transformations based on probabilistic inequalities, including the case of a prescribed mean and variance. Baudrit and Dubois [3] compare representations of incomplete probabilistic knowledge. Universal transformations require domination of every compatible law. Carrying is an existential counterpart, built on the standard notion of random-set selection (Section 2.4). Related foundations include selection-based means and variances of imprecise quantities [4, 5], random sets as ill-perceived random variables [6], random-set theory [7, 8], and identification through selections in econometrics [9]. Couso and Dubois [10] contrast a crisp variance of a fuzzy random variable with a fuzzy interval of variances of the classical random variables it may represent, and propose an interval-valued variance within imprecise probabilities. Salamanca and Couso [11] give necessary and sufficient conditions for a random closed set in Euclidean space to admit a selection of minimal Kruse variance. papers.title: Enhanced spatial resolution and performance for N-body simulation of self-interacting dark matter
papers.abstract: Studying the implications of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) on astrophysical objects often requires simulations. N-body simulations are a standard tool but face a few challenges. One is resolving the mean free path in gravothermally collapsing halos. This is necessary to obtain accurate results and is achieved in state-of-the-art simulations by increasing the number of resolution elements. I aim to formulate a numerical scheme that gives an enhanced spatial resolution compared to those methods and allows increasing the resolution without changing the number of resolution elements. The novel scheme that I present is formulated by discarding the classic approach of using kernel functions and computing interaction probabilities. Instead, pairs of particles always interact if their distance is below a specific threshold. Importantly, this distance threshold depends on their relative velocity and the size of the time step. This new formulation no longer requires some of the computations in state-of-the-art schemes and thus helps to increase the performance. Through a variety of test problems with known solutions, I study the accuracy of the new scheme and demonstrate its advantages over state-of-the-art SIDM formulations. Notably, the scheme reduced the computational costs, making the SIDM computations typically much cheaper than gravity. As a consequence, a typical SIDM simulation of isotropic scattering requires only a few percent of its total computational cost for the self-interactions. In conclusion, the new scheme presents an improvement over previous schemes and helps to address current challenges. Besides the enhanced performance, it allows us to achieve a higher accuracy when simulating gravothermally collapsing SIDM halos.

papers.intro:
Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) is a class of particle physics models for dark matter (DM) that allows the particles to interact with each other in a non-gravitational way. This is in contrast to the cosmological standard model, Lambda Cold Dark Matter (Λ\LambdaCDM), where DM is assumed to interact only gravitationally; other interactions, if present, have a negligible effect. SIDM was proposed by Spergel and Steinhardt (2000) to address historical discrepancies between DM-only simulations and observations.11 1 There is even earlier work by Carlson et al. (1992) that considered DM self-interactions in a cosmological context. The non-gravitational scattering of SIDM holds the potential to explain tensions and discrepancies between observations of astrophysical small-scale structure, such as galaxies, and predictions of Λ\LambdaCDM (Tulin and Yu, 2018; Adhikari et al., 2025; Nadler et al., 2026, e.g.). Of particular interest are gravothermally collapsing SIDM halos, where the self-interactions give rise to an increasing central DM density by transporting energy outward. These halos could account for observations that hint at compact dark objects (Minor et al., 2021; Yang and Yu, 2021; Nadler et al., 2023; Ragagnin et al., 2024; Li and others, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Fischer and Yu, 2026; Kong et al., 2026; Yu, 2026; Gilman et al., 2026b, e.g.).

For the astrophysically interesting cross-sections, SIDM behaves as mildly collisional. As a consequence, it cannot be approximated as collisionless or treated as a fluid. Instead, the Boltzmann equation together with self-gravity needs to be solved to describe the evolution of SIDM. Several methods have been developed to solve the Boltzmann equation numerically, a problem that is relevant for various areas of physics (Dimarco and Pareschi, 2014; Akhlaghi et al., 2023, e.g.). To study the impact of DM self-interactions on galaxies and other astrophysical objects, N-body simulations are a common method. Here, a coarse-grained distribution of numerical particles represents the underlying physical DM distribution and evolves under the influence of gravity and self-interactions over time. The first simulation of that kind was undertaken by Burkert (2000) and substantially improved by Kochanek and White (2000). Interestingly, a similar approach in the context of Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (Bird, 1963; Bird, 1994, DSMC, e.g.) schemes had been developed by Olson and Christlieb (2008). As of today, these simulations have been further refined in terms of numerical fidelity and the variety of particle physics models that can be simulated (Fischer et al., 2026; Rosenlyst et al., 2026, e.g.).

One limitation of the SIDM NN-body simulations is that the mean free path needs to be resolved, i.e. the separation of the scattering particles should roughly not exceed the mean free path. This had been first noted by Koda and Shapiro (2011) and later also demonstrated by Fischer and Sagunski (2024); Fischer et al. (2025b). In this paper, I address this issue by deriving a formulation that minimises the interaction distance between the scattering particles and thus helps to resolve the mean free path.

This had been first noted by Koda and Shapiro (2011) and later also demonstrated by Fischer and Sagunski (2024); Fischer et al. (2025b). In this paper, I address this issue by deriving a formulation that minimises the interaction distance between the scattering particles and thus helps to resolve the mean free path.

To do so, I deviate from the traditional scheme that computes an interaction probability based on pairs of particles. This probability is replaced by an interaction distance. If the particles are closer than this separation, they interact; otherwise they don’t. Thus, I do not draw pseudo-random numbers to decide whether they interact, but instead assume that the distribution of the numerical particles itself is random. The scheme has similarities with the one introduced by Huo et al. (2020). They use a geometric interpretation of the cross-section to compute a distance within which their numerical particles interact. However, this distance is not adaptive; e.g. it is independent of the simulation time step and can be disadvantageous for the time stepping of the simulation. In contrast, my new formulation depends on the time step and thus, the time step of the particles can be better adjusted, allowing for an enhanced performance of the simulation. The traditional scheme that comes the closest to my new scheme in terms of how the interaction probability is computed might be the one by Robertson et al. (2017), as their interaction probability is independent of the separation of the particles as long as their separation does not exceed the kernel size. In detail, they use a one-sided top hat kernel. This is similar because within the interaction radius, I assume a constant interaction probability as well, but a larger one, namely unity. However, their formulation does not choose the kernel size in a way to minimise the separation of interacting particles; instead, it is either constant or adapted to the local density as done in many SIDM implementations (Robles et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2021a; Ebisu et al., 2022; Valdarnini, 2024; Zier et al., 2026, e.g.). At the same time, the other advantages of the SIDM formulation as presented by Fischer et al. (2026), such as the explicit energy and momentum conservation, are kept.

This is similar because within the interaction radius, I assume a constant interaction probability as well, but a larger one, namely unity. However, their formulation does not choose the kernel size in a way to minimise the separation of interacting particles; instead, it is either constant or adapted to the local density as done in many SIDM implementations (Robles et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2021a; Ebisu et al., 2022; Valdarnini, 2024; Zier et al., 2026, e.g.). In summary, one may view the new scheme that I present here to some extent as a combination and generalisation of the work by Robertson et al. (2017) and Huo et al. (2020) with the addition of an adaptive interaction distance that depends on the relative velocity and the time step size. At the same time, the other advantages of the SIDM formulation as presented by Fischer et al. (2026), such as the explicit energy and momentum conservation, are kept.

In addition to formulating this novel scheme, I demonstrate that it successfully reproduces test problems with known solutions. Furthermore, I simulate a gravothermally collapsing SIDM halo and highlight the advantages of the new scheme for the deep collapse phase. The new scheme allows us to increase the spatial resolution for DM self-interactions and to speed up the NN-body simulations. No shortcomings are found compared to commonly used methods for modelling DM self-interactions. Only the assumption that the particle positions need to be sufficiently random needs to be fulfilled. Lastly, I note that I implemented the novel scheme in the cosmological simulation code OpenGadget3 (Dolag et al., 2026). It is a successor of gadget-2 (Springel, 2005) that has undergone several extensions and improvements (Ragagnin et al., 2016, e.g.).22 2 The code can be retrieved from the public OpenGadget3 repository: https://gitlab.lrz.de/AstroCodes/OpenGadget3 The implementation will become public in the near future.

papers.title: Low-excitation molecular gas in a Ly$\alpha$-associated companion of the $z=4.7$ quasar in BR1202-0725
papers.abstract: Quasar companions at high redshifts are usually gas-rich star-forming galaxies whose molecular gas masses ($M_{\mathrm{mol}}$) are estimated from [C II], dust emission or a single mid-$J$ CO line. We detect CO(5-4) and [C I](1-0) with ALMA in LAE-2, a Ly$\alpha$-associated companion of the $z=4.7$ quasar in BR1202-0725, and CO(5-4) at the location near LAE-1, the Ly$\alpha$ emitter between the quasar and the submillimeter galaxy (SMG). With the CO(2-1) flux from the literature, LAE-2 has an $L'_{\mathrm{CO(5-4)}}/L'_{\mathrm{CO(2-1)}}$ ratio of $0.22\pm0.04$, as in high-redshift main-sequence galaxies but four times lower than in the quasar host and the SMG. A non-LTE model places the CO(5-4) excitation temperature only 4 K above the cosmic microwave background (CMB), yet the same gas would show an even lower ratio against the $z=0$ CMB. The CMB-corrected $M_{\mathrm{mol}}$ from [C I], $\approx9\times10^{10} M_{\odot}$, agrees with the independent [C II] estimate, whereas CO(5-4) gives a four times lower mass if assumed thermalized at 40 K with the same CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor. Combining our 3 mm measurement with archival far-infrared photometry, we find cold ($\approx25$ K) dust and main-sequence star formation, with a gas-to-stellar mass ratio of $\approx4$ and a depletion time of $\approx0.7$ Gyr. Its star formation can supply the far-ultraviolet field that the [C I], [C II], and CO lines require. Quasar companions can thus retain massive, weakly excited molecular gas reservoirs that mid-$J$ CO surveys can miss.

papers.intro:
Luminous quasars at high redshifts often reside in dense environments: many have gas-rich, star-forming companions within a few tens of kpc (Decarli et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2026), some of which are interacting (Kade et al., 2023). These companions hold part of the cold molecular gas that fuels the build-up of stellar mass in the group (Tacconi et al., 2020), and they are exposed to the quasar’s radiation. Quasar photoionization is seen in the ionized gas of a close companion (Decarli et al., 2024), but whether the quasar alters the condition of the molecular gas of its companions is open: in one system at z≈2.7z\approx 2.7, quasar radiation has reduced the molecular gas seen in absorption in a companion a few kpc away to small, dense cloudlets (Balashev et al., 2025), and companions inside the virial radii of z≈3z\approx 3 quasars have lower gas-to-stellar mass ratios than those outside (Ritter et al., 2026). Measuring both the molecular gas mass (MmolM_{\rm mol}) and the excitation of those companion galaxies is difficult. The former is often estimated from [C ii] (Aravena et al., 2024; Bakx et al., 2024, e.g.), dust emission (Scoville et al., 2016) or a single mid-JJ CO line, which requires an excitation correction (Ono et al., 2022, e.g.) besides the CO-to-H2 conversion factor, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}; the excitation ranges from sub-thermal in main-sequence disks to near-thermal in starbursts and quasar hosts (Daddi et al., 2015; Boogaard et al., 2020). At z≈4.7z\approx 4.7, the 15.5 K cosmic microwave background (CMB) also alters the excitation and the line contrast (da Cunha et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016). Multi-JJ CO lines constrain the excitation, and [C i] provides an independent MmolM_{\rm mol} estimate, but such data on quasar companions are rare (Pensabene et al., 2021, e.g.).

papers.title: Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole
papers.abstract: Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history. We present the discovery of EUCL J150452.291+625224.39 (J1504+6252), selected from Euclid Wide Survey imaging and spectroscopically confirmed as the first quasar at z > 8 through observations with Keck, HST, LBT, and JWST. J1504+6252 exhibits the defining spectral signatures of archetypal quasars at lower redshift, including a luminous blue power-law continuum and broad permitted emission lines, indicating a classical broad-line region. JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy yields a systemic redshift of z = 8.129 +/- 0.005, corresponding to 630 Myr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by about 39 Myr (6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch). From H-beta and Mg II, we measured intrinsic broad-line-region FWHM of 3160 +/- 270 and 3740 (+160/-170) km/s, respectively. A widely used single-epoch H-beta calibration gives a reference black hole mass of log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.56 +/- 0.43. Applying a range of calibrations to both Mg II and H-beta yields log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.33-8.89 and Eddington ratios of 0.12-0.44. Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth. The discovery of a mature, sub-Eddington quasar at z > 8 suggests that substantially more luminous quasars hosting similarly massive black holes may remain to be discovered. Conversely, previously known reionisation-era quasars may represent the rapidly accreting end of a broader population of already massive black holes spanning a wider range of accretion states.

Over the past three decades, the quasar redshift frontier has steadily advanced deep into the epoch of re-ionisation: from the first quasars beyond z≈5z\approx 5 (Fan et al., 1999; Fan et al., 2000; Stern et al., 2000), to z≈6z\approx 6 (Fan et al., 2001; Fan et al., 2003; Willott et al., 2007), to the first quasar beyond z≈7z\approx 7 (Mortlock et al., 2011), and, in rapid succession, three more at z≈7.5z\approx 7.5 (Bañados et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021). Most recently, Yang et al. (2026) pushed the frontier to z=7.77z=7.77, corresponding to only about 660 Myr after the Big Bang, with the discovery of EUCL J172902.75++641018.1.

First, extending the quasar redshift frontier to earlier times places increasingly stringent constraints on black hole seeding and accretion models. The discovery of massive SMBHs at a progressively higher distance (Onoue et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021; Farina et al., 2022; Bosman et al., 2025, e.g.) leaves ever less time for their growth through conventional assembly pathways (Inayoshi et al., 2020).

Beyond constraining SMBH growth, as luminous background sources, the most distant quasars provide some of the longest sightlines through the intervening intergalactic medium (IGM), enabling studies of re-ionisation-era IGM opacity and metal enrichment (Davies et al., 2018a; Tie et al., 2024; Hennawi et al., 2025; Kist et al., 2026, e.g.). Absorption features in their spectra, including damping-wing signatures and metal absorption systems (Rowlands et al., 2026, e.g.), constrain the ionisation state, enrichment history, and large-scale opacity fluctuations of the IGM during the final stages of re-ionisation.

Quasars further mark rare, highly biased peaks in the underlying matter distribution and therefore trace the densest regions of the early large-scale structure (Eilers et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026; Schindler et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026, e.g.). Observations in the sub-millimitre regime reveal compact, ≲2\lesssim 2 kpc dust-emitting regions, host dynamical masses of about 101010^{10}–1011​M⊙10^{11}\,M_{\odot}, and frequent companions (Decarli et al., 2017; Decarli et al., 2018; Venemans et al., 2020; Neeleman et al., 2021; Belladitta et al., 2026, e.g.), while imaging with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-Infrared Camera (Rigby et al., 2023; Rieke et al., 2023, NIRCam,) now enables direct stellar-mass measurements (Ding et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2024; Stone et al., 2024, e.g.). papers.title: From residuals to warps: Probing disk geometry with gas kinematics
papers.abstract: Evidence of shadowing among protoplanetary disks suggests that warped protoplanetary disks are widespread, making it crucial to constrain their three-dimensional shape in order to understand their dynamical evolution and origin. Yet, inferring this warp shape from observations is challenging, as the typical signatures of a warp, especially shadows, are often degenerate with the warp shape. Kinematics of disks may provide a method to recover the shape by interpreting the residuals from a Keplerian disk model as local changes in inclination and position angle. In this work, we test its applicability and limitations. We perform radiative transfer simulations of disks with a parametrized warp shape to create synthetic maps of $^{12}\mathrm{CO}$ rotational line emission at ALMA wavelengths and compare the fitted warp with the true warp shape. We find that the warp shape can be recovered for nearly face-on disks with small warp misalignments of a few degrees, even without knowledge about disk properties such as emission height. The overall warp shape remains traceable even at moderate spectral resolutions up to $0.8\,\mathrm{km/s}$. However, we identify regimes where the method breaks down, including disks with an inclination higher than $40^\circ$, a high emission height of the tracer, and sharp warp transitions. In addition, radial and vertical motions can introduce apparent warps and twists, motivating extensions of the method to account for these effects.

papers.intro:
Shadowing in scattered light observations is common among protoplanetary disks, which has been interpreted as indirect evidence that these disks frequently have a warped or broken geometry (Marino et al., 2015; Benisty et al., 2017; Benisty et al., 2018; Garufi et al., 2022; Pinte et al., 2023, e.g.,). This idea was investigated directly by Bohn et al. (2022), who probed the orientation of different disk regions independently with VLTI/GRAVITY observations for the inner regions and ALMA velocity maps for the outer disk orientation. Asymmetries in edge-on disks (Villenave et al., 2024) and frequent moderate warps proposed as explanation for kinematic residuals in the recent exoALMA survey (Teague et al., 2025; Winter et al., 2025) further support the high prevalence of warps.

This idea was investigated directly by Bohn et al. (2022), who probed the orientation of different disk regions independently with VLTI/GRAVITY observations for the inner regions and ALMA velocity maps for the outer disk orientation. Asymmetries in edge-on disks (Villenave et al., 2024) and frequent moderate warps proposed as explanation for kinematic residuals in the recent exoALMA survey (Teague et al., 2025; Winter et al., 2025) further support the high prevalence of warps.

Constraining the parameters of the misalignment from observations may reveal the dynamical origin and evolution of the warp. However, recovering the warp shape is challenging. While shadows can weakly constrain maximum misalignments (Min et al., 2017; Facchini et al., 2018; Kraus et al., 2020; Muro-Arena et al., 2020; Nealon et al., 2020; Kimmig and Villenave, 2025, see, e.g.,), the underlying warp shape is often ambiguous.

Theoretical models show that the shape of a warp is strongly dependent on both the origin and evolution. Different formation mechanisms can produce distinct radial profiles and amplitudes of warps, while the subsequent dynamical evolution can further modify its shape. There are multiple proposed formation scenarios for warped disks, including gravitational interaction with an inclined binary companion (Papaloizou and Lin, 1995; Foucart and Lai, 2013; Lodato and Facchini, 2013; Facchini et al., 2013; Deng and Ogilvie, 2022; Rabago et al., 2023; Young et al., 2023), an inclined stellar fly-by (Clarke and Pringle, 1993; Cuello et al., 2019; Kimmig et al., 2026), late-infall events (Dullemond et al., 2019; Kuffmeier et al., 2021; Kuffmeier et al., 2024), stellar magnetic fields (Foucart and Lai, 2011; Romanova et al., 2021), or shadow-induced warps (Zhang et al., 2025). It is yet to be determined, which of these scenarios is most common and which characteristic warp profiles are associated with each formation mechanism.

It is yet to be determined, which of these scenarios is most common and which characteristic warp profiles are associated with each formation mechanism.

The presence of a warp fundamentally alters the dynamical evolution of a disk. In the wave-like regime relevant to protoplanetary disks, where the viscosity often parametrized with α\alpha (Shakura and Sunyaev, 1973) is much smaller than the disk’s aspect ratio h=Hp/rh=H_{\mathrm{p}}/r (where HpH_{\mathrm{p}} is the pressure scale height), warps propagate as bending waves (Papaloizou and Lin, 1995; Lubow and Ogilvie, 2000; Martin et al., 2019). In the other limit, α≳h\alpha\gtrsim h, warp dissipation becomes relevant and the evolution transitions to the diffusive regime (Papaloizou and Pringle, 1983; Pringle, 1992; Ogilvie, 1999). This regime becomes relevant for thin, highly viscous disks, for example accretion disks around black holes. The warp evolution drives a variety of fluid motions (Ogilvie and Latter, 2013a; Ogilvie and Latter, 2013b; Dullemond et al., 2022) and can excite the parametric instability, a hydrodynamic instability arising from resonances of inertial waves in oscillating shear flows (Gammie et al., 2000; Deng et al., 2021; Fairbairn and Ogilvie, 2023; Held and Ogilvie, 2025). These dynamical effects play a significant role for the disk’s morphology.

As observed warp shapes may grant insight into the system’s dynamical past and connect to the warp origin, it is crucial to find a reliable method for retrieving the warp parameters from observed disks. Winter et al. (2025, hereafter W25) recently developed a method to determine the warp shape using the kinematics derived from emission line observations. This method interprets structures in the kinematic residuals as radial changes in observed inclination and position angle across the projected disk structure. A similar method was previously suggested by Casassus and Pérez (2019). These changes can then be translated into a warp shape. W25 applied this method to the molecular line observations from the exoALMA sample (Teague et al., 2025), finding that small warps of a few degrees may be common and could naturally explain a wide range of kinematic substructures.

It is well known that warps can leave characteristic signatures in kinematic observations. Juhász and Facchini (2017) were the first to investigate these signatures and showed that the integrated flux (Moment 1 maps) show deviations of the projected zero-velocity contour from a straight line at the disk systemic velocity for warped disks. This is because the orbital planes vary with radius, shifting the projected zero-velocity location for different radial regions. Such twisted contours are indeed observed in some disks, for example in HD 100546 (Walsh et al., 2017), J16042165-J130284 (Mayama et al., 2018; Fukagawa et al., 2026), HD 143006 (Pérez et al., 2018), and HD 142527 (Garg et al., 2021). We refer to Pinte et al. (2023) for a review. However, such wiggled zero-velocity contours can be degenerate with other physical effects such as planet-driven perturbations and fluid instabilities Pinte et al. (2023). In addition, Zuleta et al. (2024) showed that a radial flow (following Rosenfeld et al., 2014) can also lead to a bent zero-velocity contour, which appears very similar to the signature of a warped disk.

papers.title: Strain-enabled dynamical magnetoelectric coupling in BaFe$_{12}$O$_{19}$
papers.abstract: Optical excitation has emerged as a powerful tool for manipulating and creating non-equilibrium phases of matter. Yet, the pathways available for optical control are intrinsically limited by the symmetries and interactions of the equilibrium system. Here, we demonstrate that these pathways can be redesigned through atomic-structural engineering to access hidden dynamical properties. By combining resonant vibrational excitation with epitaxial strain, we realize a light-induced, room-temperature multiferroic state in strained thin films of the technologically relevant hexagonal ferrimagnet, barium hexaferrite (BaFe$_{12}$O$_{19}$, BaM). Time-resolved second harmonic generation and magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements reveal an enhanced ferroelectric polarization together with a weakening of the magnetic moment upon exciting mid-infrared phonons in strained BaM thin films, but not in the bulk material. Structural analysis and first-principles-based theory show that this effect is enabled by strain-generated displacement of Fe$^{3+}$ ions, which break the local symmetry and facilitate an emergent dynamical magnetoelectric coupling. Both the strong lattice excitation and strain-induced symmetry breaking are essential for enabling this dynamical coupling, promising an important template for designing otherwise inaccessible non-equilibrium phenomena.

papers.abstract: Broad absorption line (BAL) quasars offer a powerful view into the structure, kinematics, and feedback mechanics of active galactic nuclei. In this study, we track the dramatic behavior of intrinsic CIV outflows of the quasar SDSS J142129.40+522752.0 at z = 3.228. We analyze 199 high-signal- to-noise optical spectra collected over a 12-year baseline via the Sloan Digital Sky Survey III/IV Reverberation Mapping and the SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping programs. We quantify multi-year variability across two prominent absorption features: a primary high-velocity CIV BAL trough (Trough A) and a lower-velocity mini-BAL (Trough B). Both troughs exhibit rapid, significant variations in equivalent width and average depth, culminating in temporary disappearances during the 2022-2023 observing seasons before reappearing at their original velocities. We find that the behavior of the two troughs is highly correlated with both the g-band flux and each other, strongly indicating that the observed variability is driven by ionization state changes of the gas. The equivalent width of the mini-BAL Trough B is found to lag that of Trough A by ~4 days in the quasar rest frame, suggesting that the equilibrium timescales of the two absorbers are different and possibly indicative of different outflow densities or distances.

papers.intro:
Most massive galaxies host a supermassive black hole (SMBH) in their centers, and observations of strong correlations between the mass of the SMBH (MBHM_{\rm BH}) and various properties of their host galaxies suggest that the growth of these SMBHs is likely connected with the growth of the galaxy in which it resides (e.g., K. Gebhardt et al. 20, J. Kormendy & L. C. Ho 34). For example, strong correlations have been observed between MBHM_{\rm BH} and the stellar velocity dispersion within the host bulge (σ∗\sigma_{*}; known as the MBH−σM_{\rm BH}-\sigma relation; e.g., K. Gebhardt et al. 20, L. Ferrarese & D. Merritt 17), and the mass of the host-galaxy bulge (MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}, known as the MBH−MbulgeM_{\rm BH}-M_{\rm bulge} relation; e.g., J. Magorrian et al. 40, K. Gültekin et al. 25, J. Kormendy & L. C. Ho 34). Some SMBHs are actively accreting matter, releasing enormous amounts of energy in the accretion process; these are called active galactic nuclei (AGN), or quasars. AGNs provide a means for potential interaction between SMBHs and their galaxies through feedback (e.g., T. Di Matteo et al. 14, R. Moll et al. 43, A. King & K. Pounds 32). Some quasars have been observed to produce fast outflows that blow gas and dust into our line of sight and into the galaxy; if these outflows contain enough energy, they may produce feedback in the host galaxy and disrupt or induce the formation of stars. Quasar outflows can thus potentially have a significant impact on the host galaxy. Quasar outflows are thought to be launched from the accretion disk (e.g., N. Murray et al. 44, D. Proga 50, N. Higginbottom et al. 29) and/or from a dusty torus (C.-H. Chan & J. H. Krolik 11, H. Choi et al. 12) and appear along our line of sight as absorption lines in the observed spectra of quasars. Broad absorption lines (BALs) are defined as absorption features reaching a depth of ≤\leq 0.9 times the continuum-normalized flux, with a velocity width greater than 2000 km s-1 (R. J. Weymann et al. 61). Understanding the impact of these outflows on their host galaxies is crucial to understanding the effect a SMBH has on its galaxy.

In 2014, the SDSS Reverberation Mapping project (SDSS-RM; e.g., Y. Shen et al. 53) began monitoring a field of 849 quasars, accumulating a total of 90 epochs of spectroscopy over seven years as a part of the SDSS-III and SDSS-IV surveys (M. R. Blanton et al. 5). Kollmeier et al. 33) continued monitoring a subset of quasars in this field and has thus far acquired more than 100 additional epochs of spectroscopy over five more years (and continues to observe through 2026). SDSS has continued to monitor this quasar and has now accrued more than 200 epochs of spectroscopy that span more than 12 years. With these additional years of monitoring in hand, we decided to revisit this quasar to determine whether this dramatic variability continued and to characterize its behavior in more detail.

papers.title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. We develop an approach that follows citations, which often link case reports of similar patients. To determine what two linked cases share clinically, it prompts large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, and to match images by caption using the answers. Experts find the pairs highly accurate, and this question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning BiomedCLIP on PMC-PaIR improves retrieval in all modality, anatomy and diagnosis categories tested, for image-only queries and image queries with a short text naming the finding. We release the dataset and the automated pipeline, which can extend PMC-PaIR as new case reports are published.

papers.title: Bayesian Data Integration and Model Updating in Probabilistic Digital Twins
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data and behavior data, according to how observations relate to the digital state. Property data directly inform a subset of the uncertain model parameters and can therefore be incorporated using efficient dedicated Bayesian updating methods. Behavior data provide indirect information through the prediction model and require the solution of a Bayesian inverse problem. To reduce the associated computational cost, an active-learning-based surrogate strategy is introduced that evolves with the digital state and adaptively refines the prediction model in regions relevant to posterior inference. The framework is evaluated using an idealized cantilever beam example and a geotechnical case study of a canal wall subject to varying water levels and corrosion. The examples show how complementary data sources, including both equality observations and inequality information from observed system survival, can inform uncertain parameters and system reliability. The proposed surrogate-based updating scheme yields posterior estimates and prediction accuracy comparable to those of physics-based updating while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations. The proposed framework thus supports multi-source updating and reliability assessment in probabilistic digital twins of engineering systems.

papers.intro:
The growing availability of monitoring data throughout the lifecycle of infrastructure assets increases the interest in methods that systematically integrate observations with computational prediction models. Such methods have been developed in the context of system identification, where indirect measurements are combined with physical models to infer the underlying causes or states of a system (Smith, 2016). In structural engineering, Bayesian model updating has been used for several decades to include monitoring data in predictive models Beck and Katafygiotis (1998). Today, Bayesian updating and system identification find widespread application in Structural health monitoring (SHM) and related engineering fields (Vanik et al., 2000; Yuen et al., 2006; Goulet and Smith, 2013; Pasquier and Smith, 2015; Smith, 2016; Kamariotis et al., 2023, e.g.,). More recently, these methods have been included in the digital twin (DT) concept, which finds increasing application in architecture, engineering, construction, operations and management as a means to support data-driven decision-making. Despite its potential, several challenges still limit the widespread adoption of DTs in construction practice, including a lack of trust, difficulties in integrating heterogeneous data sources, limited predictive model accuracy, and scalability issues (Opoku et al., 2023; AlBalkhy et al., 2024).

More recently, these methods have been included in the digital twin (DT) concept, which finds increasing application in architecture, engineering, construction, operations and management as a means to support data-driven decision-making. Despite its potential, several challenges still limit the widespread adoption of DTs in construction practice, including a lack of trust, difficulties in integrating heterogeneous data sources, limited predictive model accuracy, and scalability issues (Opoku et al., 2023; AlBalkhy et al., 2024).

In traditional DT implementations, some of these challenges arise from the use of deterministic models and parameters. Achieving reliable predictions under such assumptions requires detailed physical models that accurately capture system behavior. In practice, however, model uncertainty is often substantial and is further compounded by uncertainties from material variability, environmental conditions, and measurement errors. Moreover, deterministic modeling frameworks do not naturally support model updating as new information becomes available. Instead, uncertainty is commonly addressed through safety factors. While safety factors can ensure a safe, conservative design, they cannot be combined with monitoring data that reflect the actual performance of the structures.

The Probabilistic Digital Twin (PDT) addresses these limitations (Kapteyn et al., 2021; Chaudhuri et al., 2023; Torzoni et al., 2024). In Cotoarbă et al. (2025) we propose a PDT for geotechnical design and construction. The PDT framework formalizes the observational method (Peck, 1969; Spross and Johansson, 2017; Bismut et al., 2024), which is a common design approach in geotechnical engineering and is incorporated into Eurocode 7 (CEN, 2004). It specifies the definition of contingency actions for deviations from acceptable behavior limits during the construction phase.

The PDT framework provides an explicit representation of uncertainty and uses probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference to update the system state as new data is observed. A central element of the PDT proposed in Cotoarbă et al. (2025) is the classification of observational data into two categories, which clarifies how different data sources contribute to the evolution of the digital state. The first category, referred to as property data, consists of measurements of material or physical properties and can be used to directly update the random variables corresponding to model parameters. The second category, behavior data, comprises data obtained by observing system response or performance, such as displacements or settlements, which can only be used to update model parameters through Bayesian inversion.

Bayesian updating with behavior data is more challenging than with property data, as repeated likelihood evaluations require a prediction model that is often computationally costly (e.g., a finite element model). To address this challenge, a range of sampling-based methods has been proposed, including Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (Hastings, 1970; Gilks et al., 1996; Gelman et al., 1995; Beck and Au, 2002; Neal, 2011), sequential Monte Carlo methods (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral et al., 2006; Cappé et al., 2007; Ching and Chen, 2007; Betz et al., 2016; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos, 2020; Kamariotis et al., 2023), and Bayesian Updating with Structural reliability methods (BUS) (Straub, 2011; Straub and Papaioannou, 2015; DiazDelaO et al., 2017; Betz et al., 2018).

These methods have also found increasing application in geotechnical engineering, where reliability assessment is often required under large epistemic uncertainties and limited data. High-fidelity geotechnical models are computationally expensive and therefore repeated evaluations within Bayesian inference are challenging. As a result, surrogate modeling approaches have been widely adopted for reliability analysis in geotechnical applications, including sheet pile walls in dyke bodies (van den Eijnden et al., 2022), monopile foundations (Depina et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2022), slope stability problems (Kang et al., 2015), and strip footings (Al-Bittar et al., 2018; Soubra et al., 2019). To improve the computational efficiency of training a surrogate model for high-dimensional problems, active learning strategies focus model refinement on regions of interest. The integration of active learning with sampling-based Bayesian updating methods, such as BUS, has been extensively studied in the context of reliability analysis (Wang and Shafieezadeh, 2020; Song et al., 2022; Rossat et al., 2022; van den Eijnden et al., 2022; Jiang and Lu, 2023; Prentzas and Fragiadakis, 2024; Prentzas and Fragiadakis, 2025; Huynh et al., 2025; Thompson et al., 2025; Pires et al., 2025, e.g.,). In this work, we investigate how active learning strategies can be systematically integrated within the PDT framework. By combining surrogate modeling, active learning, and Bayesian updating, both the digital twin and the surrogate model can evolve continuously and in parallel as new data is obtained. This enables accurate and computationally efficient inference over time, supporting the practical implementation of probabilistic digital twins for engineering applications.

papers.title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) provide effective interfaces to structured and unstructured data Li et al. (2024b); Gao et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024a). Location-aware applications extend this interface to questions such as “Which pharmacy is nearest to this address?”, “How far is the trip by bicycle?”, and “Which schools are within one kilometer of each neighborhood?” Answering these questions requires both language understanding and precise operations over geographic data.

Location-aware applications extend this interface to questions such as “Which pharmacy is nearest to this address?”, “How far is the trip by bicycle?”, and “Which schools are within one kilometer of each neighborhood?” Answering these questions requires both language understanding and precise operations over geographic data.

Street-level spatial queries expose a basic limitation of parametric knowledge. A model may associate a landmark with the correct city yet fail to place it within tens of meters, recover the nearby points of interest (POIs), or compute a route over the road network. Such errors are consequential because plausible coordinates and place names can be difficult for a user to distinguish from correct ones. Existing work likewise reports uneven geographic recall and spatial hallucination in LLMs Bhandari et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2025); Xie et al. (2025). However, spatial databases and routing engines already implement these operations precisely. The open question is how well LLMs perform without them, and which tool abstractions allow models to use them reliably.

We start with geocoding and reverse geocoding because they are primitive but essential operations. Geocoding converts the place named by a user into a spatial reference, while reverse geocoding converts a coordinate back into a human-readable place. Routing, directionality, proximity search, and spatial joins commonly require one of these resolution steps before spatial computation can begin. Figure 1 reports a preliminary ten-query probe per operation and model in four cities using GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 3.8 Flash, with low reasoning effort and temperature 0 for reproducibility. Even these primitive operations produce errors of hundreds of meters to several kilometers. Performance also varies by region, with West Lafayette and Indianapolis generally producing more errors than Chicago and New York City. This pattern is consistent with geographic data-availability bias in model pretraining, where less represented places are learned less precisely, and motivates explicit spatial grounding.

The workload varies locations across the study region, geometry types, distance scales, travel modes, requested cardinalities, and join semantics. This controlled design separates coarse geographic familiarity from the ability to retrieve and compute exact spatial relationships.

papers.title: Multi-vantage SO/PHI and SDO/HMI magnetic field observations of active region NOAA 13465
papers.abstract:
Context. Until the launch of Solar Orbiter, long term studies of active region magnetic fields were restricted to a single vantage point: that from Earth. What further restricted these studies were geometrical effects, such as foreshortening and projection, that plague magnetic field observations when the active region was away from the central meridian.
  Aims. To track an active region, in this case NOAA 13465, with Solar Orbiter during a perihelion pass and use co-observations made by SDO/HMI and SO/PHI-HRT from different vantage points to explore the systematics plaguing observations away from disc centre.
  Methods. We use the SHARP (Space-Weather HMI Active Region Patches) data series from SDO/HMI, and create similar datasets with SO/PHI-HRT observations. We compare and contrast the line-of-sight and the three heliographic magnetic field components. Finally we compare the unsigned radial flux, and unsigned totals of the northward and westward magnetic components using the SHARP masking method to select a common area.
  Results. We find that the instrument observing closer to the limb infers a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux compared to that observing at disc centre, with a maximum near approximately $45^\circ$. The plage displayed more susceptibility to resolution and projection effects than the active region's sole sunspot. In particular the deduced area of the solar plage drove the observed increase in flux near the limb. Thanks to its higher spatial resolution, the SO/PHI-HRT data showed a smaller effect compared to SDO/HMI near the limb, highlighting a dependence on instrument resolution. Finally, the ratio of the two instruments' vertical magnetic flux exhibits a strong positive correlation with the ratio of the cosine of the instruments' viewing angles.

papers.intro:
Active regions harbour the most intense magnetic fields found on the surface of the Sun, the photosphere. They typically contain at least one sunspot, seen as a dark feature in white light images, where strong magnetic fields suppress energy transport from below, resulting in a cool region relative to its surroundings (Solanki, 2003; Schmassmann et al., 2021). Active regions can last from a few days to months, undergoing several Solar rotations (van Driel-Gesztelyi & Green, 2015). They are also the source regions of the most energetic solar events, i.e. solar flares and coronal mass ejections (Fletcher et al., 2011; Webb & Howard, 2012).

Long term studies of individual active regions, until recently, have been restricted to a single vantage point along the Sun-Earth line. For long-living active regions, which survive several solar rotations, their evolution is hidden when on the far side of the Sun. Further restricting analysis is a geometrical problem. Due to the spherical shape of the solar surface, several effects plague the inference of the photospheric magnetic field when the active region is near the limb (edge of the visible solar disc). This further reduces the time span where one has reliable measurements of the magnetic field of active regions.

For long-living active regions, which survive several solar rotations, their evolution is hidden when on the far side of the Sun. Further restricting analysis is a geometrical problem. Due to the spherical shape of the solar surface, several effects plague the inference of the photospheric magnetic field when the active region is near the limb (edge of the visible solar disc). This further reduces the time span where one has reliable measurements of the magnetic field of active regions.

These include the projection effect, where one detector pixel near the limb spans a much larger area on the solar surface, decreasing the effective spatial resolution. Furthermore, most of the signal loss is due to the cancellation of Stokes VV signals due to opposite polarity fields within a resolution element (Krivova & Solanki, 2004, e.g.). These two effects lead to a much lower magnetic field being inferred with respect to the true value (Milić et al., 2024; Sinjan et al., 2024, e.g.). As the magnetic field is mostly organised into radial structures with respect to the solar surface, the polarisation signal near the limb is predominantly via the transverse Zeeman effect (perpendicular to the line of sight or longitudinal component). The transverse Zeeman effect intrinsically has lower signals compared to the longitudinal component, and is more sensitive to noise (Borrero & Kobel, 2011, e.g.). On top of this, due to the increased path in the solar atmosphere that photons near the limb must travel, more absorption takes places, increasing the height of formation of the spectral line. Because of the decreasing temperature with height in the photosphere (limb darkening), this increases the relative noise levels and because of the decreasing field strength with height, this further reduces the signal strength in Stokes Q,UQ,U. With highly inclined viewing angles, there are more gradients in the intensity and magnetic field along the line-of-sight. The impact of all these effects on the magnetic field inference has been investigated via simulations (Solanki et al., 1998; Centeno et al., 2023; Sinjan et al., 2024, e.g.), however there has been no focused study of these impacts on the magnetic field inference using simultaneous observations from vastly different vantage points.

With the launch of the Solar Orbiter mission in 2020 (Müller et al., 2020), carrying a magnetograph on board (Solanki et al., 2020, Polarimetric and Helioseismic Imager, SO/PHI,), a new vantage point out of the Sun-Earth line has been available for solar magnetic field measurements. At closest approach, Solar Orbiter reaches 0.280.28 au, while its aphelion lies near 1 au. The High Resolution Telescope of SO/PHI (Gandorfer et al., 2018, HRT,) enables high resolution magnetic field measurements at close approaches to the Sun from significantly different viewing angles, while the Full disc Telescope (SO/PHI-FDT) observes the entire disc, mostly outside these close approaches. Kontogiannis et al. (2025) and Finley et al. (2025) recently exploited far-side observations from SO/PHI-FDT in combination with Earth-based instruments to monitor active regions over multiple solar rotations.

This work represents a first step towards understanding the impact of viewing geometry on magnetic field inference, a topic that has not been thoroughly explored due to the lack of simultaneous observations from different vantage points. We seek to exploit multi-vantage co-observations of an active region by SO/PHI-HRT and the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (Pesnell et al., 2012; Scherrer et al., 2012; Schou et al., 2012, SDO/HMI,) to directly quantify how inferred magnetic field depend on viewing angles. We hope to achieve a systematic understanding of the viewing angles effects on the raw magnetic field measurements themselves, as they are used as inputs for many derived quantities of physical importance, such as the magnetic free energy, helicity and coronal magnetic field structure through extrapolations.
