papers.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
papers.abstract:
Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it.
  We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost.
  We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

papers.intro:
Rust guarantees memory and thread safety for programs that contain no unsafe code. Much of its ecosystem nevertheless rests on code that the compiler cannot check. Crates that wrap C and C++ libraries, such as OpenSSL, SQLite, and RocksDB, or the operating system’s interface, such as nix and socket2, call foreign functions through the foreign function interface (FFI) in unsafe blocks and expose them through an API that is marked safe [6]. Such a binding is sound if no program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior (UB) through it [23]. Since applications call these APIs on untrusted input, an unsound binding can turn a program written in safe Rust into one with a memory-safety vulnerability, and a single unsound function voids Rust’s guarantees for every program that uses it. The same holds for the safe abstractions on which Rust drivers in the Linux kernel are built.

Static analyzers detect instances of the patterns that they encode [8, 32], rarely model the foreign library [27], and report candidates rather than bugs. Sanitizers [37, 39] and Miri [24] report a violation only when an execution exhibits it, and a crate’s tests exercise its API as its authors intended. papers.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. papers.title: Multi-User Linear Precoder Optimization for Obfuscation-Aided Mixed Regular and Wiretap Coding
papers.abstract: Physical-layer security has attracted considerable research interest with the development of quantum computing. One prominent approach is wiretap coding, which exploits the channel advantage of a legitimate receiver over an eavesdropper to achieve secure communication. However, under unfavorable channel conditions, wiretap coding can significantly reduce the achievable rate compared to regular channel coding. Mixed coding alleviates this limitation by using wiretap coding to protect a short secret required for obfuscation, while the obfuscated payload is encoded using regular channel coding. In this work, we propose a generalized obfuscation-aided mixed-coding system based on the multi-user (MU)-linear precoding (LP) architecture that unifies existing approaches employing different obfuscation functions. We then formulate the corresponding precoder optimization problem, abstracting the obfuscation function through a minimum secrecy rate constraint. Numerical simulations using a geometric two-user line-of-sight (LoS) channel demonstrated how the minimum secrecy rate requirement determines the operating point of mixed coding between regular and wiretap coding. Subsequent beampattern analysis revealed a key synergy between mixed coding and precoding: Mixed coding enables individual beam shaping for the two coding layers. Finally, spatial analysis showed that mixed coding offers the largest sum-rate gains when users are positioned at similar angles.

Network traffic has become increasingly heterogeneous over the past decades due to the ongoing digitization. In recent years, this development has steadily expanded to include sensitive information, such as health records and authentication credentials. As this trend continues, ensuring the security of network traffic becomes ever more important. For decades, cryptography has provided the foundation for this security. However, advances in quantum computing pose a growing threat to existing cryptographic systems, particularly those relying on asymmetric cryptography [1].

However, advances in quantum computing pose a growing threat to existing cryptographic systems, particularly those relying on asymmetric cryptography [1].

These concerns have led to increased interest in physical layer security, which can be used to replace cryptography in various tasks, such as providing confidentiality, providing authentication, or generating keys [2]. In this work, we focus on the mechanism of WT (WT) coding, which can provide confidentiality against an eavesdropper with worse channel conditions than the intended user. Wyner showed in his seminal work [3] that, under these conditions, a stochastic wiretap encoder can utilize random dummy bits to overload the degraded eavesdropper channel, while the intended user can still reliably decode the message. However, sending dummy bits also reduces the rate available for data transmission. Therefore, relying on WT coding can significantly reduce the net data rate of the intended user if the channel conditions are not sufficiently favorable.

However, existing layered video coding is not designed to provide secrecy of the enhancement layers, which may therefore leak information about the original message. The common parts are combined into a single common message decoded by all users, while each private part is transmitted separately to its intended user. papers.title: Emergent Electric-Field-Tunable $p$-Wave Magnetism in Twisted Bilayer NiPS$_3$
papers.abstract: A perpendicular electric field can reorient a momentum-space spin texture without changing the local magnetic configuration. In this Letter, we investigate this mechanism in a $21^\circ$-twisted $\mathrm{NiPS}_3$ bilayer with zigzag order and coplanar, nonparallel layer N\'eel vectors. In the ideal nonrelativistic limit, an antiunitary in-plane half-translation enforces opposite-spin pairing at opposite momenta, while a layer-exchanging twofold operation pins the leading $p$-wave spin splitting to a crystallographic direction. A perpendicular layer bias lifts this orientational constraint while preserving the antiunitary symmetry, allowing a transverse component of the splitting vector. First-principles calculations show gate-dependent reorientation and deformation of spin-resolved isoenergy contours. Wannier-based linear-response calculations further reveal field-activated diagonal spin conductivities and a polarity-dependent tilt in the angular profile of the transverse spin-current response. The spin-texture axis, dispersion axes, and transport-response axis are distinct quantities governed by the same symmetry reduction. These results identify layer bias as a route to controlling odd-parity spin textures and spin-current anisotropy, provided that the coplanar magnetic state remains stable.

papers.title: Relaxation dynamics of Winfree oscillators on Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We study exponential relaxation to equilibrium for Winfree-type models on Riemannian manifolds. For the sphere model with entrainment point $p$ and canonical influence, we derive convergence to equilibrium, whenever no oscillator starts at the antipode $-p$. For the corresponding canonical model on $\mathrm U(d)$, we obtain the same convergence whenever no initial matrix has the eigenvalue $-1$. Both results hold above explicit coupling thresholds depending on the initial configuration and the frequency matrices. For a broader class of unitary influence functions, the same spectral condition yields exponential convergence for sufficiently large coupling strengths. Finite-time entrance into positively invariant stable regions and contraction estimates yield exponential convergence rates and equilibrium uniqueness within those regions. A finite symmetry construction on Lie groups realizes the unitary model and a special unitary analogue as invariant Kuramoto--Lohe subsystems, yielding local relaxation results. Finally, we formulate an abstract Winfree model on Riemannian manifolds and establish local exponential relaxation in a fixed coordinate neighborhood under quantitative attraction and regularity assumptions.

Synchronization can be roughly defined as a type of collective behavior in populations of interacting phase oscillators, in which phases or frequencies form a consensus. It appears across a remarkably wide range of physical and biological complex systems, from networks of neurons [14, 5] and cardiac pacemaker cells [11, 48] to Josephson junction arrays [45, 44] and flashing fireflies [41, 6, 7], with recent applications in signal recovery and alignment problems in data science [3, 4] and machine learning [49], etc. A central mathematical challenge is to develop rigorous qualitative and quantitative frameworks to understand when spontaneous synchronization occurs and how rapidly it sets in.

Related results concern locally coupled networks [18] and partial phase-locking [19, 36, 35]; in the latter group of works, synchronization is formulated through the control of phase differences and should be distinguished from convergence to a stationary equilibrium. In this work, we address the following questions:

“What are the natural high-dimensional counterparts of the classical 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-Winfree model (1.1)?”

“What are the natural high-dimensional counterparts of the classical 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-Winfree model (1.1)?”

“For such models, under what conditions on system parameters and initial data do they admit a unique equilibrium in a specified trapping region, and what does the relaxation dynamics look like?”

“For such models, under what conditions on system parameters and initial data do they admit a unique equilibrium in a specified trapping region, and what does the relaxation dynamics look like?”

These questions were already addressed in the literature. A high-dimensional realization of the Winfree model on the unit Euclidean sphere 𝕊d−1⊂ℝd{\mathbb{S}}^{d-1}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} was first studied by Park [37], where a sufficient framework for relaxation dynamics was established. Inspired by this, the authors of this paper further extended Park’s sphere Winfree model to the special orthogonal groups SO⁡(d)\mathrm{SO}(d) and not only established similar convergence phenomena but also developed a leader-follower mechanism [22].

The earlier sphere and special orthogonal analyses [37, 22] use localized influence functions and include leader–follower conditions requiring an oscillator initially near the entrainment point. Their admissible initial configurations can already include followers outside a hemisphere or with rotation angles exceeding π/2\pi/2. For the canonical influence functions considered here, we instead establish relaxation without requiring a nearby leader: every initial configuration avoiding the antipodal point, or the spectral value −1-1, respectively, converges for sufficiently large coupling depending on that configuration. There is also a need for a flexible theory of Winfree-type interactions on manifolds, allowing for many types of influence and sensitivity functions. Note that this was established in the one-dimensional, 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1}-setting by [24].

papers.title: Robustness of Transition Probabilities of Spectral Lines Deduced from Spatially Resolved Solar Spectra
papers.abstract: Atomic parameters are a key ingredient for the synthesis of spectral lines to model observed spectra and to extract meaningful physical information about the observed astrophysical object. We use quiet-sun observations to test the reliability of the atomic parameter inference from observed spectra. Our focus is on the transition probability of spectral lines, denoted as log(gf). We apply a spectropolarimetric inversion method to quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 $\mu$m from the GRIS/GREGOR spectrograph. We use the coupled method implemented in the globin inversion code, where atomic parameters are spatially coupled, and a single value of these parameters is determined for every spectral line over the entire field of view. We carry out tests to determine the sensitivity of the inferred log(gf) values to various atmospheric parameters and the data reduction fallibility. We find that our log(gf) values are weaker by 0.023 dex compared to the most recent study. This is most probably caused by the constraint imposed on the log(gf) parameter due to the spatial coupling, lifting the degeneracy between temperature and log(gf). We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to determine the uncertainty in the inferred log(gf) values. For the strongest lines in the spectral region, the uncertainty in log(gf) is 1-4 %, increasing to 12 % for weaker and blended lines. Our tests suggest that the log(gf) values inferred using the coupled method from globin are robust against any local contamination to the observed line profiles, such as spectral stray light, and return a reliable and unique set of log(gf) values for the strongest lines irrespective of the chosen atmospheric model and observation dataset. This result is valid as long as the underlying assumptions of line formation under local thermodynamic equilibrium and the completeness of the line list are satisfied.

papers.title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks
papers.abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

Sketching and imagery are basic forms of thinking, used for reasoning [27], ideation [81], and problem-solving [80]. Unlike language alone, they can express visuo-spatial structure directly [113]. An auxiliary line can simplify a geometry proof [44]. A spatial puzzle can become easier after mentally rotating an object [42, 35], and diagrams help tell stories and communicate scientific ideas. These visual representations are working states, not merely illustrations. They reorganize the problem and make later inference easier [41]. As multimodal language models mature, we increasingly ask them to solve math [53, 24], scientific [90, 33], and multimodal [25, 93, 109] tasks where people naturally rely on such intermediate visual reasoning.

This motivates interleaved reasoning: creating intermediate visual representations and using them to guide subsequent language-based inference. Unified models [17, 30, 60] support this exchange natively. However, coordinating visual and language steps requires training traces where intermediate images support the question being answered. Constructing these traces involves task-specific pipelines and data review [45, 68]. ThinkMorph, for example, designs interleaved traces around four tasks, each with tailored visual manipulations [30]. These pipelines can generate more examples, but covering new tasks often requires new designs, making interleaved supervision difficult to scale.

Our experiments show that instruction-free pretext practice makes subsequent instruction tuning more effective. With the tuning budget held fixed, this practice adds an average of 6.49 points in accuracy on three representative benchmarks, and its benefits generalize across unified backbones. Surprisingly, instruction-free traces still yield slightly better results than explicitly instructed ones, despite the added difficulty of inferring the task itself. Furthermore, the full two-stage recipe outperforms the baseline by 11.33 points on average across twelve benchmarks spanning three levels: basic visual perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. Improvements extend to nine benchmarks outside the instruction-tuning task families, supporting generalization to new tasks.

papers.title: X-ray induced structural and dynamical changes in supramolecular polymer networks
papers.abstract: Beam-induced effects are key considerations in X-ray scattering studies of soft matter. Because these experiments typically aim to probe the unperturbed system, the structural and dynamic changes induced by the beam often remain underexplored. In the study at hand, the influence of X-rays on metallo-supramolecular tetra-arm poly(ethylene glycol) (tetra-PEG) networks is studied in dependence of the dose rate. Based on their transient interlinkage, such materials have the ability to reconnect and self-heal mechanical damage. Here, wide- and small-angle X-ray Scattering were employed to understand the effect of X-rays on the micro- and mesoscale structure of such polymer networks. Dynamical effects were probed using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy. A restructuring of the polymer chains in the network is observed over several length scales, indicating a pre-crystallization step induced by the ionizing radiation, accompanied by expulsion of water from the network. In conjunction, a complex dynamical behavior is observed, consisting of an initial fast process, followed by an overall slow-down during the restructuring process. The two-time correlation functions exhibit an oscillatory behavior related to the development of multiple dynamic populations in the polymer network.

papers.intro:
Polymers and supramolecular networks with high water-content are ubiquitous in synthetic materials as well as in biological environments. Their collective molecular interactions give rise to a rich diversity of structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties. In particular, networks assembled by reversible non-covalent interactions provide versatile platforms for understanding and controlling the relationship between molecular organization, material properties, and emergent behavior. Supramolecular polymer networks consist of non-covalently cross-linked macromolecules.[13] Such transient links can be established by functionalized polymer building blocks. A particularly well-defined material platform to conduct such investigations are supramolecular networks formed from uniform star-shaped poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) building blocks with heterocomplementary interconnection,[1, 28] extending the tetra-PEG approach by Sakai and co-workers for model-network formation to transient interlinkage.[24] This can be achieved, for example, through the use of building blocks with ligands that complex to metal ions, bringing together slim and weak with strong and sterically demanding ligands. This combination favors a heterocomplementary connection to reduce the amount of primary loop formation.

X-ray scattering based experimental methods provide a range of useful tools to better understand the structure and dynamical behavior of such systems. However, radiation damage is an important issue when conducting experiments using X-rays, especially on soft matter. During X-ray scattering experiments radiation damage can manifest in various ways, such as heating due to X-ray absorption or the formation of radicals due to ionization.[3] These effects can lead to structural changes in the investigated materials and are therefore important to account for.[25, 7, 15] The problem is well know for a long time, in literature one can find e.g. reports going back to 1959 of X-ray induced crystallization of sucrose [25], as well as recent reports on long-range ordering of peptides [8] or X-ray induced structuring of nano- and gel particles, to name only a few.[27, 23] It has also been shown that the exposure to ionizing radiation can influence the mechanical properties of polymer systems, an effect that can also be made use of, for example, in radiation sensors.[29]

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing of Learned Spatial Surrogates for Transit Accessibility
papers.abstract: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.

Accessibility, the ease with which people can reach spatially distributed opportunities, is a long-standing objective and evaluation concept in transport and land-use planning (Hansen, 1959). A common operationalization is cumulative-opportunity accessibility, which aggregates opportunities reachable within a specified travel-time threshold (Tomasiello et al., 2023). Evaluating candidate bus networks requires multimodal routing and opportunity aggregation, often too costly to repeat throughout a design search.

A common operationalization is cumulative-opportunity accessibility, which aggregates opportunities reachable within a specified travel-time threshold (Tomasiello et al., 2023). Evaluating candidate bus networks requires multimodal routing and opportunity aggregation, often too costly to repeat throughout a design search.

Our solution is to pay this cost offline. For each sampled bus network, a routing-based accessibility calculation compares the same city with and without the candidate service. We call this the reference calculation. Its computed differences supervise a spatial model that predicts accessibility change from the candidate network and fixed rail and opportunity context. The trained surrogate then provides a fast approximation intended for repeated evaluation inside an optimizer (Figure 1). It does not predict routes, demand, or observed ridership.

papers.title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

papers.title: Dynamic tuning of anisotropy-induced quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum in liquid-crystal integrated dielectric metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Symmetry-protected quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) in all-dielectric metasurfaces can be excited either by introducing a geometrical asymmetry into the unit cell or by illuminating the metasurface under oblique incidence. To date, tuning the coupling strength of such qBICs to the continuum has mainly relied on control of the geometrical asymmetry. Here, we show that qBICs can also be induced in a symmetric dielectric metasurface by embedding the latter into an anisotropic birefringent medium, and that they can be actively tuned by either rotating the anisotropy axis of the medium or by varying the degree of anisotropy. We experimentally implement a corresponding system by embedding a highly symmetric silicon nanocylinder metasurface into a nematic liquid crystal (LC) cell. Importantly, the LC does not only provide the desired birefringence, but also dynamic control of its strength as well as of the orientation of its anisotropy axis in response to different external stimuli. Specifically, applying voltage across the LC cell, where the LC molecules are pre-aligned along one of the lattice directions of the metasurface, enables out-of-plane rotation of the anisotropy axis of the LC medium. Meanwhile, its birefringence can be tuned by changing the temperature. In our experiments, the coupling of the qBICs to the radiation continuum is first maximized by the application of 25 V across the LC cell at room temperature. We then systematically tune the temperature and show that the resonance depth of the qBIC modes, which is associated with their coupling strength to the continuum, of the qBIC modes increases monotonously with birefringence. Our findings establish anisotropy-induced qBICs in LC integrated dielectric metasurfaces as a promising platform for actively reconfigurable metasurfaces and their applications in displays, optical modulation and tunable photonic devices.

papers.intro:
All-dielectric metasurfaces are two-dimensional arrangements of subwavelength dielectric scatterers that enable unprecedented control over light beyond the capabilities of conventional optical components Chen et al. (2016); Liu et al. (2020b). Their functionality arises from the ability to engineer the optical response of individual scatterers, often called meta-atoms, by tailoring their geometry Kuznetsov et al. (2016); Decker et al. (2015), arrangement Rahimzadegan et al. (2019); Gutruf et al. (2016), constituent material Kuznetsov et al. (2016) and the refractive index of the surrounding environment Liu et al. (2020a); Xu et al. (2021). On the basis of their tailorable optical responses, optical metasurfaces have emerged as a versatile platform for realizing compact and highly functional flat optical devices. papers.title: Thermodynamics of complex crystals from a generalized mean-field bond model
papers.abstract: We extend our previously introduced mean-field bond model from unary fcc lattices to crystals with multiple chemical species and sublattices, accurately predicting finite-temperature thermodynamics without statistical sampling. Our generalization reformulates the model in terms of the Wyckoff positions of the crystal, representing each by one atom, and solving for the bond density of the reference bond of each of its neighbor shells. Bond-bond correlation functions are built from the zero-temperature force constants, allowing the deviation of every bond in the crystal to be expressed through linear functions of the reference bond of a shell. Thermodynamic self-consistency is enforced by requiring a single virial temperature for the whole crystal, and compatibility of average bond lengths with crystal volume. Model predictions are validated against molecular dynamics simulations of unary, binary, and ternary crystals using Morse-type bonding potentials, parametrized for each shell from the force constants of empirical interatomic potentials at several isotropic strains. In each case, the predicted bond densities and thermodynamics agree with the simulations to within their statistical uncertainty. We discuss strategies for combining the model with bonding potentials parametrized from first principles and foundation models to predict the finite-temperature thermodynamics of complex crystals at ab initio accuracy without statistical sampling.

papers.intro:
Many technologically relevant properties of materials, such as thermal expansion, heat capacity, and phase stability, vary with temperature, in large part through lattice vibrations [1]. In contrast to zero-temperature properties, for which a single relaxed configuration is sufficient, these properties are ensemble averages, conventionally evaluated over a large number of thermally sampled configurations [2]. Even with significant advances in modern high-performance computing, evaluating such averages with density-functional theory (DFT) [3, 4] remains prohibitively expensive, and finite-temperature thermodynamic properties are commonly computed analytically within the harmonic or quasiharmonic approximation (QHA) [5, 6].

Even with significant advances in modern high-performance computing, evaluating such averages with density-functional theory (DFT) [3, 4] remains prohibitively expensive, and finite-temperature thermodynamic properties are commonly computed analytically within the harmonic or quasiharmonic approximation (QHA) [5, 6].

Although the QHA captures the implicit anharmonicity due to the volume dependence of phonon frequencies, it neglects the explicit anharmonicity due to the underlying potential energy surface at each volume, the omission of which has been shown to lead to qualitatively incorrect thermodynamic trends at elevated temperatures [7, 8, 9]. In principle, explicit anharmonicity can be computed exactly using thermodynamic integration (TI), which integrates the ensemble-averaged energy difference between the target and a reference system along a suitable coupling path [10, 11]. In practice, however, every point along this path requires a converged ensemble average, and the number of sampled configurations needed grows with the difference between the potential energy surfaces of the two systems. Accelerating this convergence has motivated the use of intermediate reference systems that are cheaper to sample yet closer to the target potential energy surface, whose free energies can be upsampled to ab initio accuracy using free energy perturbation [12] by running DFT calculations on a small subset of their configurations [7, 13, 14, 15]. Alternatively, effective-harmonic methods, such as the temperature-dependent effective potential method [16, 17, 18, 19] and the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation [20, 21, 22], extract temperature-dependent force constants from forces on thermally displaced configurations and approximate thermodynamic properties using temperature-renormalized phonon frequencies. While these methods avoid the coupling path of TI, they still require sampling at each volume and temperature of interest.

Since every sampled configuration requires an evaluation of the forces on each atom, the computational cost of going beyond the QHA is determined by the number of such evaluations and the associated cost of each one. Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reduce the cost of each force evaluation while approaching the accuracy of the DFT data on which they are trained [23, 24, 25]. In contrast to the cubic scaling of DFT, MLIPs scale linearly with the number of atoms and offer a compromise between the efficiency of empirical potentials [26, 27] and the accuracy of DFT. MLIPs have since also evolved into universal potentials or foundation models [28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36] that are trained on databases spanning most of the periodic table [37, 38]. However, their accuracy relative to DFT for thermodynamic and vibrational properties has been benchmarked predominantly using quantities derived from the zero-temperature potential energy surface, namely formation energies and thermodynamic stability [39], harmonic phonons [40], and lattice thermal conductivities computed from second- and third-order force constants [41]. Assessing their accuracy for finite-temperature thermodynamics requires sampling for each crystal, volume, and temperature of interest, with the cost per force evaluation set by the architecture of the foundation model. Since this cost cannot be reduced without changing the model itself, the total computational effort can only be lowered by reducing the number of force evaluations.

papers.title: Stellar-evolution systematic biases on $^{12}\text{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\text{O}$ constraints from the primordial-black-hole mass gap
papers.abstract: The $^{12}\text{C}(\alpha,\gamma)^{16}\text{O}$ reaction determines helium-burning carbon-oxygen core masses and sets the pair-instability-supernova mass-gap boundary, which limits the maximum mass of stellar-origin primordial black holes. Gravitational-wave population analyses using GWTC-4 report a low-spin-black-hole upper cutoff at $68.5^{+19.8}_{-18.5}\,M_\odot$, implying a low astrophysical S-factor $S_{300}\approx 108.6\,\mathrm{keV\,barn}$, in tension with canonical nuclear-astrophysics evaluations. However, stellar-evolution systematic uncertainties from metallicity, rotation, and mass-loss prescriptions remain poorly quantified. Here we use the MESA stellar-evolution code to construct a three-dimensional parameter grid disentangling these coupled effects. We show that metallicity-dependent winds dominate helium-core retention; rotation suppresses carbon consumption via centrifugal cooling and meridional mixing; different mass-loss prescriptions produce $8$-$10\,M_\odot$ offsets in the black-hole-mass-gap edge. A parameter combination $Z\approx10^{-3}$, moderate rotation $\omega/\omega_\mathrm{crit}=0.4$, and optically-thin C15 winds reproduces the GWTC-4 inferred maximum primordial-black-hole mass for $S_{300}=108.6\,\mathrm{keV\,barn}$. The canonical $45\,M_\odot$ gap boundary represents an overlapping statistical intersection of black-hole-population distributions rather than a universal physical threshold. Our framework provides a pathway to jointly constrain nuclear-reaction rates, stellar-evolution physics, and gravitational-wave-source populations.

papers.title: SplatSeg3D: Efficient Zero-Shot 3D Segmentation via Point Cloud Surfelization and Splatting
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods rely on 2D foundation models applied to registered images captured alongside the 3D point clouds. However, such images may not be available in many cases, while direct 3D point cloud segmentation methods require semantic class supervision and are challenging to deploy in a zero-shot manner. To address these issues, we present SplatSeg3D, which segments a bare colored point cloud in an open-vocabulary manner without requiring the accompanying images, camera poses, class supervision, or instance mask proposals. To achieve this, we first surfelize the input point cloud and obtain oriented 2D Gaussians. We then render views of the scene by splatting, with a view selection strategy that maximizes scene coverage with as few views as possible. Next, we apply text-prompted segmentation on the rendered views, giving each 3D point a set of multi-view semantic cues, fused to produce a 3D segmentation of the scene. We evaluate SplatSeg3D on semantic segmentation and novel-class instance segmentation on 4 standard benchmarks: Scannet, Scannet++, Replica, and S3DIS. Our pipeline not only performs better or on-par with the state-of-the-art, but we also achieve these results efficiently across runtime and compute requirements. Code will be published.

papers.intro:
Open-vocabulary segmentation of 3D scenes has advanced mostly by leveraging 2D foundational features. Segmentation and vision-language models (VLMs) trained on billions of images [22, 36, 5] demonstrate strong open-vocabulary segmentation capabilities. Therefore, most methods in the open-vocabulary 3D segmentation literature perform lifting of multi-view image VLM and/or segmenter outputs onto the 3D point cloud [42, 18]. This imposes a strict requirement of posed image sequences or scene panoramas to accompany the point cloud. However, in practice, often only a 3D point cloud might be available, by design or by choice (e.g. from LiDAR or terrestrial scanner devices).

To tackle this challenge, SplatSeg3D (Fig. 1) synthesizes its own 2D image views directly from the input point cloud. However, a naive projection of raw points to get the image renders leads to insufficient quality for accurate image segmentation. Instead we propose surfelization of the point cloud, where at every 3D point we place a surfel [34], a flat 2D Gaussian disk that is aligned with the local surface normal. The surfels are computed in closed form and are standard 2D Gaussian splatting primitives [16].

When working with captured images of scans, flexibility in view selection is limited. In our case, a camera placement strategy is used to minimize the number of views while maximizing point cloud coverage, which is the main driver of efficiency in SplatSeg3D. We frame this camera placement as a depth-tested coverage problem over the point cloud, and design an automatic camera pose selector. Segmentation masks of the selected views can then be lifted to the point cloud’s 3D points. The final semantic labels of points then become the fused votes from the 3D lifted masks, and instances are the connected components of each semantic class, requiring no supervised 3D training or instance proposal network. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • SplatSeg3D, an open-vocabulary 3D segmentation method whose only input is a colored point cloud, without any images, camera poses, or trained instance proposals. Instead, SplatSeg3D renders its own virtual views through point cloud surfelization and splatting. • View selection algorithm for the splatted views, posed as a depth-tested view-coverage problem, minimizing the number of views while maximizing the point cloud coverage. • Zero-shot semantic and novel-class instance segmentation on four standard benchmarks, performing on-par with previous open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods, and exceeding all zero-shot baselines. • Efficiency in compute and runtime: SplatSeg3D performs 3D segmentation while requiring much lower GPU compute and runtime than other methods (Fig. 2). In combination with our zero-shot capability, the method is also more efficient to deploy.

papers.title: The majority game chromatic number for dense random graphs
papers.abstract: We show that for every fixed $2/3<p<1$ the majority game chromatic number of the Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi random graph $G_{n,p}$ is $3$ with high probability.

papers.intro:
Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite, simple graph. A (not necessarily proper) vertex colouring of GG is said to satisfy the majority condition at v∈Vv\in V if at most half the neighbours of vv have the same colour as vv. The majority colouring game, introduced by Bosek–Grytczuk–Jakóbczak [1] in 2019, is a two-player Maker-Breaker-type game in which the players alternately colour the vertices of GG from a fixed palette of colours such that the majority condition is maintained at every vertex at all times. The objective of the first player, Alice, is to get a colouring of all the vertices, which is called a majority colouring of the graph GG. The objective of the second player, Bob, is to prevent Alice from succeeding; that is, Bob tries to create a partial colouring where there is an uncoloured vertex for which every choice of colour violates the majority condition somewhere in the graph. We assume that Alice moves first. The minimum number of colours required for Alice to have a winning strategy for the majority colouring game on GG is called the majority game chromatic number of GG and is denoted μg​(G)\mu_{g}(G).

papers.title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.

papers.intro:
Demand for medical imaging has grown steadily over the past two decades1, and computed tomography (CT) use alone reached approximately 93 million examinations in the US in 20232. CT combines rapid volumetric acquisition and high spatial resolution with image intensities that represent the X-ray attenuation of tissue, linearly scaled to Hounsfield units3, making it essential for diagnosis across anatomical regions and clinical indications. Interpreting a single examination requires identifying abnormalities across thousands of images, involving multiple organs and disease processes, and the growing number of CT studies has substantially increased radiologist workload4. Missed abnormalities remain an important source of diagnostic error5.

Interpreting a single examination requires identifying abnormalities across thousands of images, involving multiple organs and disease processes, and the growing number of CT studies has substantially increased radiologist workload4. Missed abnormalities remain an important source of diagnostic error5.

Artificial intelligence (AI) systems can detect specific diseases6, 7 and generate reports from volumetric images8, 9. However, detecting a disease or producing a plausible report does not guarantee a thorough interpretation of an examination. Some important findings may be missed, and reported abnormalities may not have clear supporting evidence10, 11. A general-purpose CT model must therefore recognize a broad range of abnormalities across anatomical regions and examination types while linking individual findings to their locations in the scan.

However, detecting a disease or producing a plausible report does not guarantee a thorough interpretation of an examination. Some important findings may be missed, and reported abnormalities may not have clear supporting evidence10, 11. A general-purpose CT model must therefore recognize a broad range of abnormalities across anatomical regions and examination types while linking individual findings to their locations in the scan.

Research towards this goal has followed two largely separate directions. CT foundation models, including CT-CLIP12, Merlin13, RADAR14 and Pillar-015, have extended recognition beyond individual diseases16, 17, 18, but covering the whole range of findings encountered across CT examination types remains challenging. In parallel, CT2Rep8, CT-CHAT12, BTB3D19, RadFM9, MedMPT20 and NV-Reason-CT21 have advanced report generation from volumetric images. However, coherent reports do not ensure that all relevant abnormalities have been recognized or that each statement is supported by image evidence. Grounded report generation links statements to image regions22, 23, 24, but methods requiring manually annotated bounding boxes or segmentation masks25, 26 are difficult to scale to the diversity of findings in routine CT. Clinical reports have reduced the annotation burden for tumor segmentation27, 28, yet whether they can jointly supervise broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation remains unresolved.

Routine radiology reports usually describe findings for the whole examination, but they often do not specify exactly where these findings are located. Multiple-instance learning29, 30 can help identify which image regions support examination-level labels, so spatial evidence can be learned without needing lesion-level annotations. Radiological concepts also help connect images with language. Concept bottleneck models31 use clear, human-understandable concepts to guide later predictions. Multiple-instance learning29, 30 can help identify which image regions support examination-level labels, so spatial evidence can be learned without needing lesion-level annotations. Radiological concepts also help connect images with language. Concept bottleneck models31 use clear, human-understandable concepts to guide later predictions. Combining these concepts and their spatial evidence with visual features could guide report generation while preserving information beyond a predefined vocabulary.

Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts based on Radiopaedia32 and uses these concepts alongside visual features to generate radiology reports (Fig. 1). FORA combines a self-supervised three-dimensional visual encoder, attention-based multiple-instance learning and concept-guided report generation, with supervision from routine clinical reports and no manually annotated lesions. The CT cohort contains 28 acquisition protocol classes, grouped into 11 examination types and a mixed-examination category, yielding 12 categories for evaluation. papers.title: Weight Scale Rebalancing: Transferable Training Recipes for Transformers
papers.abstract: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $\sigma$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.

papers.intro:
Training a transformer well requires choosing a learning rate and a weight decay, and the right choice shifts with every architecture and every scale (Yang et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2025). Each new model therefore demands its own sweep, a cost that practitioners without large compute budgets cannot afford. Many works have studied ways to reduce this per-model sweep as much as possible. Hyperparameter transfer methods such as μ\muP (Yang et al., 2021) carry a configuration tuned on a small proxy model across width. The proxy configuration must nevertheless be re-established for each new architecture. The tuning is therefore relocated rather than removed. Layer reparameterizations such as weight normalization (Salimans and Kingma, 2016), spectral normalization (Miyato et al., 2018), σ\sigmaReparam (Zhai et al., 2023), and WeSaR (Nishida et al., 2024) stabilize training and in some cases reduce its sensitivity to hyperparameters. However, reduced sensitivity does not tell the practitioner which hyperparameter values to use. None of these methods provides a concrete configuration before training starts without a hyperparameter sweep on the target network. We show that a single reparameterization, UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), yields at negligible overhead a training recipe whose hyperparameters are determined by the shape of each layer. This recipe can therefore be fixed once and reused across architectures and scales.

Given any pair of dense layers with weights UU and VV​, UDVR inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix DD between them, yielding a U​D​VUDV block. It constrains each column of UU and each row of VV to a shape-determined norm and absorbs the residual scale into DD. This decouples direction from magnitude and keeps the forward gain of each block stable throughout training. Two hyperparameters are therefore introduced, the shape-determined norm scaler α\alpha and the corresponding learning rate constant CC. Their selection is extracted once, by a characterization sweep on small vision models, and this sweep is a one-off cost of establishing the rules, not part of deploying them. We highlight that the rules are reused unchanged across matrix shapes and across task domains, so deploying UDVR on any new model requires no sweep on the real network. UDVR thus achieves the goal of μ\muP, a configuration that transfers across scale. Unlike μ\muP, it does so through a fixed shape rule rather than a proxy configuration re-tuned for each new architecture.

papers.title: IMPACT-Seg: Consistent Anatomical Segmentation and Representation Learning Across CT, CBCT, and MRI
papers.abstract:
Computed tomography (CT), cone-beam CT (CBCT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide complementary representations of the same underlying anatomy, yet substantial differences in image appearance challenge consistent segmentation and deformable registration in adaptive radiotherapy. We investigate whether dense anatomical segmentation supervision can promote cross-modality correspondence without explicit feature alignment. We introduce IMPACT-Seg, which segments 126 structures across CT, CBCT, and MRI using shared network parameters. A collection of 8,290 volumes was assembled from public cohorts through label harmonization, model-assisted pseudo-label completion, iterative refinement, and 2,864 physics-based CBCT simulations with voxel-aligned CT labels. Unpaired images were used to jointly train 2.5D and 3D residual-encoder networks.
  On 139 real CBCTs, IMPACT-Seg 3D achieved a mean Dice of 0.842 versus 0.671 for the strongest comparator. On 497 voxel-aligned CT-simulated-CBCT pairs, the CT-to-CBCT Dice decrease was 0.022 versus 0.153-0.178 for competing methods. On independent pancreatic radiotherapy CBCTs, gastrointestinal Dice was 0.735 versus 0.634 for TotalSegmentator. Prediction agreement reached 0.881 on registered CT-CBCT and 0.790 on CT-MRI pairs. Adding MRI training data reduced CT-MRI encoder feature retrieval error from 36.8 to 3.2 mm. Registration pipelines incorporating IMPACT-Seg features ranked first on two multimodal Learn2Reg benchmarks. The 3D model segmented a whole-body CT in 15 s.
  These findings show that dense anatomical segmentation supervision can support consistent anatomical representations across modalities, with applications to both segmentation and registration. Code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/HEMONCedric/IMPACTSeg.

papers.intro:
Adaptive radiotherapy relies on repeated imaging to account for anatomical changes during treatment. Planning computed tomography (CT), on-treatment cone-beam CT (CBCT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide different representations of the same underlying anatomy, despite substantial differences in image contrast, quality, and artefacts. Although anatomical structures may change in shape and position between acquisitions, their identity and delineation conventions should remain consistent across modalities. Accurate and consistent delineation is essential for contour adaptation, dose evaluation, and longitudinal assessment. As manual delineation of numerous structures is impractical within the time constraints of online adaptation, automated segmentation and registration-based contour propagation offer valuable alternatives [37, 46]. Both approaches benefit from consistent anatomical identification despite differences in image appearance.

Existing segmentation tools provide broad anatomical coverage on CT, including TotalSegmentator [55], CADS [56], and VISTA3D [17]. Joint CT-MRI segmentation is supported by MRSegmentator [16] and NV-Segment-CTMR [40], while TotalSegmentator MRI [1] provides a dedicated MRI model. Differences in training distributions and label conventions nevertheless complicate their combined use in radiotherapy. CBCT adds scatter, noise, truncation, and motion artefacts, while dense annotations remain scarce. High accuracy on diagnostic CT or MRI therefore does not establish cross-modality consistency in the same patient.

papers.title: From Historical Schedules to On-Sky Control: Autonomous Scheduling on the 4-m Blanco Telescope
papers.abstract: The scientific efficiency of ground-based astronomical observatories relies on effective decision-making in a dynamic, multi-timescale environment with complex scientific rewards. Traditional observation schedulers are designed and tuned by domain experts to handle these considerations using heuristic rules based on models of the environment and observational system. Here, we leverage historical data to train an automated telescope scheduler using behavior cloning (BC). The BC scheduler is trained purely on historical datasets; it is not given expert scheduling heuristics nor an optimal scientific reward. It is then evaluated in order of increasing realism: first on expert states, then in closed-loop offline rollouts, and finally during autonomous operation with real-time feedback on the NSF's Victor M.\ Blanco 4-m Telescope. On expert states from holdout nights, the BC policy closely matches the expert distribution over airmass and Moon separation. During closed-loop rollouts on the same nights, we find that the per-observation data-quality metric, $t_{\rm eff}$, falls by $6.9 \pm 3.4\%$ relative to the expert's. During on-sky deployment, the policy scheduled $149$ exposures in $5.2$ hours with an average $t_{\rm eff} = 0.75 \pm 0.26$, consistent with closed-loop rollout evaluations. No additional degradation was observed when transitioning to real observing conditions. This represents the first real-world, real-time deployment of a learned autonomous scheduler on a leadership-class national observatory and establishes a path toward on-sky evaluation of reinforcement-learning-based schedulers trained on archival schedules augmented with counterfactual trajectories.

papers.intro:
Astronomical survey scheduling, i.e., deciding what a telescope observes and when, is a high-dimensional and multi-objective sequential decision-making problem within a partially stochastic environment. The problem is akin to the well-known traveling salesman problem, a combinatorial optimization problem that is known to be NP-hard [15]. Astronomical survey scheduling is further complicated by a changing environment (weather, sky brightness, target availability), high-priority interrupts, and long-term survey goals, which jointly impact the value assigned to each decision. Furthermore, since each decision changes the subsequent set of feasible observations, locally favorable decisions do not necessarily produce globally optimal solutions [22]. Traditional telescope schedulers [19, 6, 7, 9] address these challenges using iteratively tuned heuristic rules and priorities that are based on models of the environment and observing system. They generally incorporate human expertise, physical models, and explicit weighting of short- and long-term scientific objectives. Recent astronomical surveys provide extensive historical data capturing scheduling decisions and their consequences under real observing conditions, offering a foundation for learned schedulers that reduce reliance on computationally expensive simulations and human expertise.

Machine-learning (ML) approaches to astronomical scheduling have increasingly explored the use of simulated training environments, including reinforcement learning (RL) for resource allocation and cooperative scheduling across telescope arrays [27], target-of-opportunity and follow-up scheduling [25, 28], and autonomous target selection [23, 4, 26]. For the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) [14], Naghib et al. [17] explored RL and global optimization strategies to learn optimal weights for a set of expert-designed basis functions. While these studies demonstrate the promise of ML-driven scheduling, they do not jointly address the large action spaces, long survey horizons, real-time observing feedback, and iterative on-sky deployment considered here.

In this work, we train a model to directly learn scheduling behavior from archival scheduling data generated and executed by an expert-designed algorithm, obstac [19]. These data comprise six years of Dark Energy Survey (DES; [5]) observations obtained with the Dark Energy Camera (DECam; [10]) on the NSF’s Victor M. Blanco 4-m Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. This methodological approach anchors our algorithm in real observing conditions and reduces dependence on a fully synthetic and computationally expensive training environment, but also restricts coverage to trajectories only present in historical data. We use behavior cloning (BC) [2] to assess what imitation alone recovers, where it breaks down, and whether its performance differs when transitioning to on-sky deployment. We evaluate the scheduler in three increasingly realistic regimes: (1) single-step evaluation on expert states held out during training, (2) closed-loop policy rollouts on held-out test nights where each policy decision determines the next simulated environment state, and (3) real-time scheduling on the Blanco telescope. For this, we develop a modular, policy-independent framework that connects learned schedulers to real-time telemetry and the Blanco telescope control systems.

papers.title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
papers.abstract: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. papers.title: NEST: Uncovering and Nesting Unknown Objects in Open-World Object Detection
papers.abstract: Open-world object detectors aim to localize objects of classes not covered by their training annotations, but most label them only as "unknown". This label tells a system that an object is present but not what it is, while its broader category would allow a more informed decision. We therefore address both uncovering unknown objects and assigning them to the broader categories of a given class taxonomy. For uncovering, we find that most unknown objects are already localized and labeled "unknown" in our base detector, but are discarded during final top-k selection because background receives higher scores. To mitigate this, we propose a class-agnostic ranker that estimates how well each predicted box fits an object and uses these scores to select the final predictions. Across three benchmarks, our detector improves unknown recall by 3.8% to 195.1% relative to the strongest baseline in each task, while maintaining competitive known-class detection. For categorizing, we draw on Euler diagrams, in which the region of a category contains the regions of its members. Our categorizer builds each category's region from the known classes and learns how much room to leave for members it has never seen. On the same detections, it categorizes unknown objects more accurately than existing hierarchical methods. Code is available at https://github.com/TUM-AVS/NEST.

Detectors deployed in the real world may encounter objects outside their annotated training classes. Open-world object detection (OWOD) [15] aims to localize such objects and label them as unknown, while still recognizing the known classes. This label, however, treats all unknown objects alike. A broader category such as animal could help an autonomous system anticipate that an unfamiliar zebra may move on its own, unlike a fallen tree. We therefore argue that an open-world detector should answer three questions about each detection, namely (1) whether it is an object, (2) whether it belongs to a known class and (3) if not, to which broader category it belongs.

Only question (2) can be learned directly from known-class annotations. Questions (1) and (3) concern objects of unknown classes, which carry no annotations, so a detector must answer both by generalizing from the known classes. For question (1), existing OWOD methods generalize, for example, by pseudo-labeling unannotated regions [15, 11] or by learning a class-agnostic objectness score from known objects [43]. Question (3), which we term unknown object categorization, has been studied mainly in image classification, for example by HND [18] and ProHOC [35]. Most OWOD methods stop at the first two questions, and only a few detectors answer all three [42, 1].

One might expect that answering question (1) requires better localization of unknown objects. We find instead that final top-kk selection is the dominant bottleneck in our base detector. Most unknown objects are already well localized, but their detections are discarded because background receives higher classification scores. The first part of NEST is therefore a detector built around a class-agnostic ranker trained only on known-class annotations to predict box localization quality [14]. papers.title: Cell and nuclear shapes predict confined motility
papers.abstract: Cancer metastasis relies on an enhanced property of cells to migrate efficiently even through constrictions smaller than their nucleus. Both cell and nuclear morphology may influence this process. How these morphologies relate to the likelihood that a cell will transit through a constriction remains unclear. Here we combine microfluidic experiments with machine learning to predict whether MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells are able to transit through narrow constrictions. Cells migrate within vertically confined boxes, and may migrate into neighboring boxes by transiting through constrictions, requiring a deformation of the nucleus. Defining a set of 12 geometrical features derived from cell and nuclear contours, we find that their average values are not statistically indicative of whether or not a cell will transit. To overcome this limitation, we use trajectories to train classifiers and evaluate their ability to predict future transit events. We find that the cell area and cell circularity carry most of the predictive information and less circular cells are more likely to transit. Without retraining, the models also predict transit through narrower constrictions and in more adhesive substrates. Morphological features of cells about 30 minutes before a transit event proved most informative about future transit events occurring or not. Together, our results show that cell shape, readable from simple contour descriptors, contains a transferable but condition-dependent signature of imminent transit.

papers.intro:
The severity of cancer is closely related to metastasis, during which cancer cells migrate toward blood vessels and invade other organs by squeezing through confined spaces [38, 32]. This process has been studied extensively in the context of the epithelial to mesenchymal transition, where cells change phenotype from stationary epithelial, to highly motile mesenchymal state [35, 28]. Recent advances in microfluidics allow the use of precisely engineered geometries for the study of single-cell motility in complex environments [7, 30] with well controlled geometries [40, 8, 21, 37]. Furthermore, microfluidic studies indicate that the deformation of the nucleus during invasion may act as a rate limiting step [26, 10]. Although cellular and nuclear morphologies are important variables for the dynamics of invasion, their predictive role for efficient confined migration remains unclear.

This process has been studied extensively in the context of the epithelial to mesenchymal transition, where cells change phenotype from stationary epithelial, to highly motile mesenchymal state [35, 28]. Recent advances in microfluidics allow the use of precisely engineered geometries for the study of single-cell motility in complex environments [7, 30] with well controlled geometries [40, 8, 21, 37]. Furthermore, microfluidic studies indicate that the deformation of the nucleus during invasion may act as a rate limiting step [26, 10]. Although cellular and nuclear morphologies are important variables for the dynamics of invasion, their predictive role for efficient confined migration remains unclear.

Depending on the local geometry, migrating cells can adopt a variety of motility strategies. The mesenchymal mode of migration involves the formation of actin rich protrusions in the form of lamellipodia or filopodia, which bind to the environment with focal adhesions [3]. An alternative strategy is amoeboid motion, in which cells weakly adhere to the environment and move using acto-myosin contractility that generates protrusions known as blebs [13, 20]. Individual cancer cells often employ both strategies at once, or alternate between the two [5, 36]. Compared to the mesenchymal phenotype, amoeboid cells are rounder. These modes of migration, based on the dynamic organisation of the cytoskeleton, are very conserved among species, regardless of whether they possess a nucleus (eukaryotic cells) or not (prokaryotic cells) [33]. While cell morphology is a good indicator of the strategy employed for cell migration, the role of the nucleus during cell migration through confined spaces may not be as passive as initially considered. Indeed, the nucleus plays an important role in gene regulation, and also an impact on biomechanics [10, 2, 18]. As the stiffest organelle in the cell, it must be deformed as the cell moves through confined spaces, directly affecting migration dynamics [34, 47]. Nuclear plasticity may enable highly motile healthy cells such as neutrophils to navigate spaces [17]. Similarly, metastatic cancer cells can have highly deformable nuclei, increasing their migration efficiency under confinement [46]. Therefore, cell and nuclear morphologies are expected to be valuable sources of information pertaining to the state of the cell. They are thus fundamental for a mechanistic understanding of motility under confinement. While several works have used some morphological descriptors for theoretical modeling of cell migration [12, 6, 48, 29], a full description of the cell and nuclear contour dynamics could be a source of information on the ability of a cell to pass through constrictions. However, such an approach requires a large number of parameters which are difficult to measure experimentally.

Machine-learning (ML) methods are well suited for handling complex multivariate data for predictive tasks. ML has been used extensively on genomic data for predicting metastasis based on transcriptomics data [14], and in vitro assays [4, 44]. Recently, ML has been used to classify cell migration types based on raw single cell trajectories [19, 27], and contour-derived features to classify morphology types of cells migrating in extra-cellular matrix [9]. In another work, cell and mitochondria fluorescence images were used to extract features to predict the velocity of cells migrating under 5μ​m\upmu\mathrm{m} vertical confinement [50]. Here, we observe the morphology of motile cells and their nucleus in a microfluidic device made of flat boxes connected with narrow constrictions. A set of features are chosen to describe cell and nuclear morphology using their contours. This data set is then used to train a ML model capable of successfully predicting the transit probability. This model is based on a limited amount of features, and cell circularity, as well as area, are among the most predictive. The model is successfully transferred to other experimental conditions, on the one hand to smaller constrictions and, on the other hand, in enhanced cell adhesion conditions by coating the microfluidic surfaces with fibronectin. We extend the model to predict the time at which a given cell will transit, revealing a time scale of 30 minutes during which the model is most predictive.

papers.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
papers.abstract: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq

papers.title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.intro:
Realistic 3D scenes with fine-grained ground-truth annotations are essential for learning perception and action that generalize reliably to real-world settings. Perception models for inverse rendering, reconstruction, and scene understanding need dense ground truth, e.g., complete geometry, materials, and instance labels. Embodied agents need interactive environments that behave like the real world, so that navigation and manipulation can be both trained and evaluated in closed-loop settings.

Real-world scans [15, 86, 5, 13, 57] capture real appearance and layouts, but they are noisy and incomplete, and they cannot provide ground truth for albedo, roughness, lighting, unobserved geometry, or object parts. Synthetic scenes provide all of these by construction, but making them realistic at scale is hard. Procedural [17, 56] and agentic [84, 53, 79] methods scale well, but their realism is bounded by hand-crafted rules or by the quality of generated 3D assets [81, 82, 14]. Artist-created scenes [24, 58, 94, 39, 16, 34, 71, 51] are more realistic, but manual modeling limits their scale and scene types.

It covers a wide variety of indoor and outdoor scene types. papers.title: Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Five Agents
papers.abstract:
We study the envy-free cake-cutting problem, in which a divisible resource must be divided among a set of agents with heterogeneous preferences in a way that ensures that no agent envies the piece obtained by another. Remarkably, under some mild continuity assumptions on the agent valuations, it is known that an envy-free division where each agent receives a \emph{connected} piece of the cake is always guaranteed to exist.
  When the valuations are monotone, prior work has shown that a connected $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be obtained using $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries for up to four agents, leaving the case of five or more agents open. In this work, we develop a new simpler approach that yields such an efficient algorithm for five agents. Our algorithm uses $\mathcal{O}(\log^3(1/\varepsilon))$ queries and also yields a novel proof of existence for five agents that does not rely on any fixed-point theorems beyond the intermediate value theorem.
