papers.intro:
Social choice studies how collective decisions should reflect individual preferences. Within this area, fair division addresses the allocation of resources among nn agents whose preferences may conflict [21]. Even when a resource can be divided into equal physical shares, agents may disagree about which share is preferable: different locations in a plot of land or different periods of time need not be equally desirable. Fairness can be formalized in different ways. Proportionality, for instance, asks that each agent receive at least 1/n1/n of her value for the whole resource. Another natural requirement is envy-freeness: every agent should value her own share at least as much as anyone else’s.

Cake cutting is a fundamental problem in fair division that captures this question for a divisible, heterogeneous resource [26]. In this work, we focus on the model where each agent receives a single interval. Such connected, or contiguous, shares are natural when dividing land or allocating uninterrupted access to a resource, and use only n−1n-1 cuts for nn agents.

papers.title: Elastic rebound in viscous fluid: an efficient rigid--elastic splitting with an asymptotic gap model
papers.abstract:
We formulate and test a model for an elastic body that falls under gravity onto the bottom of a container filled with a viscous incompressible fluid and rebounds without topological contact. The body is a rigid body plus a small, quasi-static elastic deformation, represented by a fixed compliance operator. In the near-contact patch, the thin fluid film is described by a Reynolds equation with cavitation. This allows the use of coarse meshes that need not resolve the gap, enabling efficient simulation. The film is coupled implicitly to the elastic surface displacement and to the rigid normal motion. The bulk fluid is coupled monolithically to the rigid body. For the axisymmetric case with vertical translation, the coupled step reduces exactly to a small dense nonlinear problem for the film pressure, with the bulk eliminated through a $2x2$ affine map.
  The model is implemented in NGSolve and compared with the experiments of Hagemeier et al. (2021) and the Eulerian FSI simulations of Wahl et al. (2021a). For a PTFE ball the approach agrees with the Eulerian FSI to 1\%. For a soft rubber ball (St $\approx 120$) the purely elastic model gives about three times the measured rebound. Material damping is the most important missing effect: a Kelvin--Voigt compliance with loss factor $\tan\delta=0.6$ gives 4.0\,mm, against 4.4\,mm measured. A planar version of the model is compared with the recently published 2D benchmark of Corti et al. (2026).
  The radius of the film patch is the only numerical parameter of the splitting. It is fixed by one a-priori rule for all configurations, derived from a dry Hertz estimate of the approach, and the results depend only weakly on it.

papers.intro:
A smooth elastic body within a fluid-filled container is falling towards the bottom and bouncing off. This problem is easy to observe but its mathematical modeling and simulation is a hard problem. First of all, there is the no-collision result for the Navier–Stokes equations (e.g. [31, 24] among many others): if no-slip conditions act on body and bottom boundary, contact or release of contact is not possible. It must therefore be the elasticity of the solid body which explains the observation. An early hypothesis is a little fluid layer remaining in a gap between solid and boundary which transfers the forces, elastic energy being stored and released such that a rebound is possible without contact.

The numerical simulation of this problem has long been hindered by a missing formulation that is able to deal with elasticity and contact at the same time. The standard approach for fluid solid interactions (rigid as well as elastic bodies) is the mapping of the problem to a reference domain in Arbitrary Lagrangian Eulerian (ALE) coordinates [33, 40]. While being highly accurate, robust and reliable, ALE simulations of the falling ball must resolve the gap. Considering realistic parameters this is mostly not feasible. However, recent improvement in hardware and ALE remeshing techniques makes this possible, although at high cost [20]. An alternative to ALE is the Fully Eulerian approach [42], where the solid is mapped to the Eulerian system. The advantage is that this formulation is physically sound and that it does not need any artificial fields that might violate the numerical stability. Fully Eulerian formulations are able to model the elastic contact problem [42] and they are also able to cover physically relevant scenarios, see [49] and in particular [21]. However, the computational cost, mostly arising in the demanding solution of highly nonlinear systems, prevents the practical application.

papers.title: Measuring the tug-of-war between two nonlinearities in a monopolar plasma vortex
papers.abstract: From planetary atmospheres to magnetized plasmas, single-core vortices organize flows and transport heat and matter. Understanding their persistence requires identifying the nonlinear interactions that sustain a single core. The Charney--Hasegawa--Mima equation, shared by drift waves and Rossby waves, admits steadily propagating localized vortex solutions only in dipole form. Theories of monopolar drift vortices attribute the additional nonlinearity to either the electron-temperature gradient or density-profile curvature, but their respective roles remain experimentally unresolved. Here we show that the coupling sustaining a monopolar drift vortex results from the near cancellation of two much larger nonlinear contributions. We measure three-wave coupling among the vortex harmonics using simultaneous probe signals acquired around the full azimuth of a laboratory plasma and compare it with predictions of an extended drift-wave equation derived for the measured equilibrium conditions. The equation reproduces the sign, magnitude and triad dependence of the observed coupling without adjustable parameters, whereas neither contribution alone accounts for the measured coupling pattern. This coupling transfers fluctuation power from the linearly driven fundamental to damped harmonics, maintaining the single-core waveform. These results establish an experimental route to distinguishing mechanisms that produce similar vortex structures by resolving the nonlinear interactions within them.

papers.title: JWST/NIRSpec observations of AMORE6 suggest active Pop~III star formation in a self-polluted galaxy
papers.abstract: AMORE6 is a strongly lensed ($\mu\simeq78$), intrinsically faint galaxy at $z=5.725$, previously proposed as a metal-free candidate from the absence of [OIII]$\lambda$5007 in NIRCam slitless spectroscopy. We present deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of its brighter image, AMORE6-B. We detect HeII$\lambda\lambda$1640,4686, with HeII$\lambda$4686/H$\beta=0.080\pm0.015$ and EW(HeII$\lambda$4686)$=35\pm8$ {\AA}, weak [OIII] ($R_3=0.25$) and CIV$\lambda\lambda$1548,51, and no other metal lines. H and He lines give negligible attenuation, $T_e\simeq2\times10^4$ K, and $Y=0.226^{+0.022}_{-0.024}$. The oxygen abundance, $12+\log(O/H)\simeq6.08^{+0.24}_{-0.80}$ (0.04-0.4% $Z_\odot$, depending on the calibration), is the lowest at its stellar mass, while C/O is near or above solar. Photoionization models of different ionizing sources favour metal-free stars with a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF), as in the self-polluted phase of simulated Population III (Pop III) galaxies, or a metal-poor population with a luminous hard X-ray source; ordinary metal-poor populations, very massive stars, and accretion-based sources are disfavoured. A full SED fit in the fiducial self-polluted scenario gives $1.3\times10^5\,M_\odot$ of Pop III stars formed within the last 4 Myr, which ionize mildly enriched gas and leak 86% of their ionizing photons. The HeII-to-Balmer ratio constrains the slope $x$ and characteristic mass $M_{ch}$ of the Pop III IMF jointly, to $90x-268\lesssim M_{ch}/M_\odot\lesssim172x-330$ ($3\sigma$; $M_{ch}\lesssim70\,M_\odot$ for a Salpeter slope), excluding the most top-heavy IMFs allowed by near-field constraints. X-ray binaries are a possible alternative, but require either a metal-poor population too young (1 Myr) to host compact objects and an X-ray luminosity far above that of metal-poor galaxies, or $2\times10^6\,M_\odot$ of older Pop III.2 stars whose metals were mostly expelled.

papers.intro:
The first generation of stars, the so-called Population III (Pop III), formed out of gas composed exclusively of hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium produced in the Big Bang. In the absence of metals, cooling is inefficient and fragmentation is suppressed, so that Pop III stars are expected to be, on average, considerably more massive than present-day stars (KlessenGlover2023). Their extremely hot photospheres would produce copious hydrogen- and helium-ionizing photons, leaving a distinctive imprint on the nebular spectrum of their host systems, such as very large Balmer-line equivalent widths, strong He ii recombination emission, and the complete absence of collisionally excited metal lines (Schaerer2002; Schaerer2003). Although Pop III star formation is generally expected to peak at very early epochs, theoretical models predict that inefficient metal mixing can preserve pockets of pristine gas in which metal-free stars continue to form well into the epoch of reionization, and possibly down to z∼6z\sim 6 (Trenti2009; Venditti2023; Venditti2025). Finding such systems would provide a direct window on the conditions of the first star formation, on the primordial initial mass function, and on the first chemical enrichment of the Universe, whose imprint (e.g. super-solar C/O ratios in metal-poor gas) is now starting to be detected at z>7z>7 (Pollock2026; DEugenio2024gsz12; Nakajima2025).

Identifying a genuine Pop III system is, however, observationally challenging, because no single spectral feature constitutes an unambiguous signature (NakajimaMaiolino2022; Trussler2023). Strong He ii emission requires a hard ionizing spectrum, but this can also be supplied by very massive stars at non-zero metallicity (Schaerer2025), by stripped or binary stars (Eldridge2017), by X-ray binaries, or by accretion onto black holes, including direct-collapse black holes (NakajimaMaiolino2022); indeed, hard ionizing spectra producing strong high-ionization UV lines are not uncommon among metal-enriched galaxies in the reionization era (Topping2025, e.g.). Conversely, weak or undetected [O iii] emission does not by itself imply an extremely low oxygen abundance: the strength of the forbidden lines also depends on the ionization parameter (KewleyDopita2002; Kewley2019), on the shape of the ionizing spectrum (Gutkin2016; Steidel2016), on the gas density (through collisional de-excitation, which can mimic a low O/H in the dense nebulae common at high redshift; Harikane2025; Martinez2026; Moreschini2026; Hsiao2026), and on the geometry of the ionized region, e.g. in density-bounded nebulae leaking ionizing photons (JaskotOey2013; Zackrisson2013; Plat2019). In addition, the presence of metal lines does not by itself rule out Pop III stars, since galaxies hosting only metal-free stars can display metal emission once their gas has been polluted by the first supernovae (Rusta2025). Moreover, at the oxygen abundances of interest (12+log⁡(O/H)≲712+\log(\mathrm{O/H})\lesssim 7), metallicity diagnostics are largely uncalibrated and must rely on photoionization modelling or extrapolations (Morishita2024; Nakajima2022empress; Isobe2026mzr). A convincing case for Pop III-like star formation therefore requires the simultaneous combination of several independent constraints: a hard ionizing spectrum, the joint absence of lines from multiple heavy elements (O, C, N, Ne, S), and the quantitative exclusion of alternative explanations.

The JWST has dramatically advanced the search for such objects. Deep spectroscopy of strongly lensed sources has revealed star-forming complexes with oxygen abundances of only a few per cent of the solar value or less, such as LAP1 at z=6.6z=6.6, with 12+log⁡(O/H)≈6.512+\log(\mathrm{O/H})\approx 6.5–6.8 (Vanzella2023; Nakajima2025; Scholtz2026), while other extremely metal-poor systems have been reported both in lensed and blank fields (Willott2025; Cullen2025; Maiolino2026BHnearpristine; Li2026arXiv260924589L, e.g.). At the same time, spectroscopic follow-up has demonstrated how fragile these identifications can be: deeper NIRSpec observations of the GLIMPSE-D candidate detected [O iii] and ruled out a metal-free interpretation (Fujimoto2026). At higher redshift, a He ii emitter with no detected metal lines has been confirmed in the vicinity of GN-z11 at z=10.6z=10.6, with the pristine nature of the gas supported by deep limits on the metal lines and a Pop III interpretation favouring a top-heavy IMF, although non-stellar origins of its ionizing spectrum cannot yet be fully excluded (Maiolino2026; Ubler2026; Rusta2026). These results well illustrate both the relevance and the challenges of searching for Pop III galaxies: candidates are now being found, but their confirmation requires deep, multi-line spectroscopy and a careful treatment of the degeneracies between metallicity and other properties of the ionized gas.

papers.title: Learning to find cosmic filaments with graph neural networks
papers.abstract: Inferring the large-scale structure of the Universe from galaxy surveys is a fundamental challenge in cosmology. In particular, cosmic filaments form an extended and geometrically complex network whose underlying structure cannot be reconstructed from discrete galaxy catalogs without uncertainty. We investigate a generative approach to filament finding based on flow matching and graph neural networks. The learned model reproduces key statistical properties of the target filament distribution while generating a distribution over possible filament configurations, demonstrating its ability to model uncertainty. Our work provides a first step towards probabilistic inference of the cosmic web directly from galaxy surveys. More broadly, these results demonstrate the potential of conditional generative models for reconstructing filament-like structures from sparse observational tracers.

papers.intro:
On megaparsec scales, matter in the Universe is organised into the cosmic web: an interconnected network of clusters, filaments, walls, and voids produced by the gravitational collapse of the primordial density field (1, 2). Cosmic filaments are the elongated structures forming the backbone of this network, connecting high-density nodes and acting as preferential channels along which dark matter, gas, and galaxies are transported. They span a broad range of lengths, densities, and environments, from prominent bridges between galaxy clusters to tenuous structures extending into underdense regions (3, 4, 5, 6, e.g.). Despite their visual prominence, there is no unique definition of a cosmic filament. Existing approaches identify them through different representations of the matter distribution: local eigenvalues of the density, tidal, or velocity fields; multiscale Hessian-based morphology; topological skeletons and persistent homology; stochastic geometric models; or graph-based constructions (7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, e.g.). These methods broadly recover the most prominent structures but can differ substantially for weaker filaments and in their inferred extent, connectivity, and topology (10).

These methods broadly recover the most prominent structures but can differ substantially for weaker filaments and in their inferred extent, connectivity, and topology (10).

Obtaining robust filament catalogues is becoming increasingly important because the cosmic web is moving from a qualitative description of large-scale structure to a quantitative astrophysical and cosmological observable. Filaments regulate the environments through which galaxies acquire matter and can influence gas accretion, star formation, halo and galaxy spins, and the connectivity of galaxies to their surrounding matter distribution (13, 14, 15, 16, e.g.). At the same time, their geometry, abundance, matter content, and associated galaxy statistics contain information complementary to conventional two-point clustering and are beginning to be explored as probes of the growth of structure, dark matter, and gravity (17, 18, 6, 19, 20). With surveys such as DESI, Euclid, and Rubin-LSST delivering unprecedented three-dimensional maps of the galaxy distribution, the limiting factor is increasingly not the availability of data but our ability to extract filamentary structure consistently, reproducibly, and with well-characterized uncertainty. This makes filament identification a natural setting for modern machine-learning methods capable of learning complex geometric and topological structure directly from cosmological data.

The multi-scale nature of the cosmic web implies that there is no unique universal definition of filaments. Once we pick a scale, usually determined by the number density of galaxies in a given catalog, it is clear that a good filament definition should involve the total matter density and velocity fields. As these fields are not directly observable, the mapping from observed galaxies to underlying filaments is probabilistic and should be modeled as such. Generative neural networks are thus the natural approach to constructing the desired mapping.

As these fields are not directly observable, the mapping from observed galaxies to underlying filaments is probabilistic and should be modeled as such. Generative neural networks are thus the natural approach to constructing the desired mapping.

We use conditional generative modelling to solve this problem. Specifically, we use stochastic interpolants flow matching (21, 22) to learn a continuous transport from a simple particle distribution to a distribution concentrated around cosmic filaments. Starting from a set of particles sampled from a simple, galaxy-conditioned base distribution, our model learns a conditional flow that transports these particles towards a filamentary distribution. A representation of the filaments by discrete points is not ideal but it is a technical choice motivated by the results of a similar method [23]. The resulting model combines the flexibility of generative modeling with geometric and physical inductive biases appropriate for the cosmological setting.

In this initial study, we focus on a controlled problem in which the training targets are filaments identified by the deterministic DisPerSE algorithm [8] from the galaxy catalogs and not the dark matter field. This method is currently widely used in filament studies. This allows us to develop and evaluate the generative reconstruction method. Planned improvements are outlined in the conclusions. Our method avoids the detour of full field reconstruction (24, 25, 26, 27, 28).

papers.title: TESS discovers an eclipse of the Be star V1294 Aql (= HD 184279) by its not-so-small, low-mass companion
papers.abstract: In a single sector of observations with the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), an eclipse-like event occurred in the Be star V1294 Aql. The reality of the eclipse is corroborated by $UBV$ photometry from the Hvar observatory. The event occurred at phase 17.97 of the linear ephemeris by Harmanec et al. (2022) for the upper conjunction of this SB1 binary (P$_{\rm orb}$ = 192.9 d). Therefore, we conclude that the Be star was eclipsed by its companion. With this elimination of the uncertainty of the orbital inclination, the mass of the secondary is 0.99 to 1.17 M$_\odot$ for masses of the primary from 14 to 18 M$_{\odot}$. The depth of the eclipse of $\sim$6.0% (0.06 mag) is incompatible with a white-dwarf (WD) nature of the companion. At the implied radius of $\sim$25% of that of the B0.5 primary, the secondary is not a bona-fide sdO/sdB star, either, but it could be still in its contraction phase. The increasing number of such stars may lend support to model calculations according to which the timescale of the contraction can be not thermal but instead is governed by the much slower removal of a residual H-rich envelope. It is also possible the companion is on the pre-main sequence in which case the two stars have not yet interacted. Two new interferometric observations were obtained near orbital quadrature but the secondary star was not detected, nor was it detected in high-resolution high-S/N echelle spectra.

papers.intro:
Many classical Be stars (Rivinius et al., 2013; Rivinius and Klement, 2026) have acquired their ∼\sim 80% critical rotation and much of their mass from a formerly more massive companion (Pols et al., 1991; Shao and Li, 2014; Boubert and Evans, 2018; Klement et al., 2019). Given that even every single indirect detection through radial-velocity (RV) variations (Nazé et al., 2022) requires a fair amount of high-quality observations, a fraction close to 100% is not currently excluded for the earlier-B subtypes. Many of the directly detected companions are sdO stars (Wang et al., 2018). sdB stars (Klement et al., 2022) are less frequently observed. In some cases, the (now) secondary stars have not yet contracted to their equilibrium state (Frost et al., 2022; Rivinius et al., 2025). Gies et al. (2023) suggested that for the X-ray emitting γ\gamma Cas analogs the low-mass companions may be white dwarfs (WDs) that have undergone a second mass-transfer stage and are not generally within reach of present interferometers. Undetected companions in the observations by Klement et al. (2024) are consistent with this view, as is the recent confirmation that X-rays originate from a WD companion in the prototype of this class (Nazé et al., 2026). The orbital periods are typically between 1/4 and 1/2 yr. Even lower-mass stripped stars (≲\lesssim0.4 M⊙) may be unable to fuse helium and begin contracting towards a WD phase without lingering as an sdB star (Labadie-Bartz et al., 2025, e.g.).

Estimates of radii and masses of companions rest on flux ratios (which are extreme in the visible part of the spectrum), temperature estimates, and RV curves, all of which have significant uncertainties. A major obstacle is the paucity of inclination-angle measurements of the orbits, which require the combination of spectroscopy and interferometry (Klement et al., 2022, cf. ), or eclipses. Until the serendipitous discovery of an eclipse in V1294 Aql detailed below, only one other classical Be star has been reported to show eclipses (de Amorim et al., 2025, V658 Car;) with the companion being a post-interaction stripped star.

papers.title: Teaching Time Without Losing General Retrieval: Adapting Multimodal Embeddings for Time-Sensitive Video Retrieval
papers.abstract: In text-to-video retrieval, MLLM-based embedding models do well when the text describes the scene (general retrieval), but poorly when it describes actions and their direction (time-sensitive retrieval). TARA, a pioneering work, fine-tunes such a model on text triplets with temporal hard negatives; it improves time-sensitive retrieval but lowers general retrieval (mean R@1 over six benchmarks in our rerun on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B: 58.4->44.8), and its released model keeps general retrieval only when ensembled with Qwen3-VL-Embedding. Our goal is strong general and time-sensitive retrieval with one model and one vector per clip. Three findings lead to three simple components. Keep loss: general retrieval follows how far the output embeddings drift from the base model, not how far the weights move; we therefore keep them near the base model, which keeps most general retrieval even without general-domain data. Pair loss: the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close; we therefore widen the gap between the video embeddings of each clip and its reversed copy, in the direction of the difference between their two text embeddings. Middle-layer LoRA: frames are combined in the middle layers, and temporal information peaks in or just after them; we therefore train LoRA only on these layers, which nearly matches training all weights on most time-sensitive benchmarks with 0.15% of the parameters and keeps general retrieval better. General R@1 stays at 58.4, while R@1 with each clip's reversed copy in the gallery rises from 55.5 to 63.2; the gains carry over to unseen benchmarks and InternVL2-8B-RA. The keep loss is also a remedy for the TARA recipe (general R@1: 44.8->57.8), and ensembling TARA with Ours gives the highest scores on RTime and unseen CiA among the compared models.

On RTime [7], R@1 falls from 89.589.5 to 55.555.5 when the reversed copy of each clip (see Fig. 1a for an example) is added to the gallery. We call this RTime Hard.

Temporal information peaks in or just after them (L15–L28 on Qwen) and then fades. (H3) Training these layers gains more than training only the later layers.

Second, the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close. papers.title: Polar Streams through Active Condensation in Flocks
papers.abstract: Two of the most paradigmatic phenomena in active matter are flocking, where particles align to move collectively, and motility-induced phase separation, where self-propulsion causes particles to condense even without attractive interactions. Here, using experiments on self-propelled Janus colloid dimers, we show that flocks can phase separate to form polar streams. These structures are elongated dense clusters of particles that flock along the stream's long axis, in contrast to the well-known transverse bands that form close to the flocking transition. We use particle-based simulations and hydrodynamic theory obtained through coarse-graining to identify the underlying mechanism, which we call active nematic condensation: Denser regions of the flock develop stronger polar and hence nematic order, which leads to further particle fluxes into the dense region. These results reveal a generic mechanism whereby flocks can condense into streams. Our findings uncover that flocks can be shaped by nematic order, which is usually not accounted for in the standard Toner-Tu equations. More broadly, our work shows that collective motion and phase separation can not only coexist but also cooperate in active matter.

papers.intro:
Active matter exhibits striking non-equilibrium collective phenomena such as flocking [65, 35] and motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) [10], which both arise due to the interplay of self-propulsion and interactions between active particles. Flocking — the self-organized collective motion of active particles — appears in many systems across scales, ranging from bird swarms [11] and cell layers [56, 33, 8, 49, 47] to synthetic active systems like Quincke rollers [9] and carpets of cytoskeletal filaments [46]. Flocking is typically caused by polar alignment interactions between particles, as in the Vicsek model [64], but can also be due to other effects such as turn-away torques [17] and polarity-velocity self-alignment [56, 67, 30, 4]. Respectively, active phase separation can be caused by a decrease in motility of active agents in dense regions due to quorum sensing [57] or repulsive interactions [18], but also due to other effects such as turn-towards torques [74] or active nematic flows [6].

Respectively, active phase separation can be caused by a decrease in motility of active agents in dense regions due to quorum sensing [57] or repulsive interactions [18], but also due to other effects such as turn-towards torques [74] or active nematic flows [6].

While these phenomena are often studied in isolation by means of simple models, in experiments they were found to compete with each other [22, 63]. On the one hand, MIPS can cause flocks to jam and lose polar order [22]. On the other hand, polar alignment was shown to interrupt motility-induced phase separation [63]. Thus, it remains unclear to what extent flocking and MIPS can coexist [32].

Here, we show that flocks can undergo active phase separation to form polar streams, i.e., elongated dense clusters in which particles collectively move along the long axis of the cluster. We first observe polar streams in experiments with Janus colloid dimers. To explain this behavior, we develop and simulate a microscopic model of active particles that captures the emergence of streams through a flocking transition followed by phase separation into dense streams within a dilute flocking phase. To understand these transitions, we coarse-grain our model to derive a hydrodynamic theory, which explains the observations and allows us to identify the mechanism of stream formation. We show that streams are the result of phase separation caused by extensile nematic fluxes that condense the flock perpendicularly to its direction of motion — a mechanism that we call active nematic condensation. Our results uncover physical mechanisms that shape flocks: we reveal how flocking and phase separation can take place sequentially to cooperatively organize a flock into dense and dilute phases.

papers.title: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Defect-free industrial samples can vary considerably in appearance, texture, and geometry. In few-shot anomaly detection, this variability has to be modeled from only a handful of images. SubspaceAD showed that a single principal subspace of foundation-model patch features is a strong training-free model of nominal appearance. However, a single subspace has to cover all of the nominal data's variability, so a deviation that is anomalous for one semantic region can be within the nominal variability of another. We propose LocalSubspaceAD, which extends SubspaceAD from a single subspace to a mixture of subspaces, assigning each group of patches with similar features its own subspace. The set of patch-features is partitioned using k-means, one subspace is fit per cluster, and each patch is scored by the minimum of re-projection residuals over all subspaces. The proposed method requires no training and no EM refinement. On MVTec AD, VisA and Real-IAD with 1, 2 and 4 shots, it improves over a single subspace (SubspaceAD) on both evaluated backbones: by 1.2 to 1.8 points image AUROC on DINOv2, and by 1.4 to 4.4 points in image AUROC, pixel AUPR and AUPRO on DINOv3. The gains are most pronounced on objects with heterogeneous nominal appearance, such as multi-instance categories and PCBs. Ablations show that the gains stem from a finer-grained model of variability through locally oriented subspaces, rather than from the subspace offsets (cluster means). We further show that the gains do not stem from added capacity alone: the local subspaces appear to capture the structure of coherent clusters in feature space, and the model does not merely act as a compressed memory bank.

papers.title: Spin-Group versus Magnetic-Group Selection Rules for Nonlinear Photocurrents in Compensated Ferrimagnets
papers.abstract: Optical excitation offers a contact-free, ultrafast route to charge and spin currents, with symmetry determining which nonlinear photocurrents are allowed and whether they carry charge, spin, or both. Spin-group symmetry describes the limit without spin-orbit coupling (SOC), whereas magnetic-group symmetry accounts for SOC. We show that the two descriptions yield different selection rules for both charge and spin photocurrents in the multiferroic compensated ferrimagnet GaFeO$_3$. Without SOC, only linear shift and circular injection currents are allowed, with identical components for charge and spin, so every charge current is spin polarized along the moments. SOC leaves these charge currents nearly unchanged, activates magnetic linear injection and circular shift charge currents, and enables pure spin currents polarized perpendicular to the moments. Ferroelectric switching reverses the linear shift and circular injection charge currents and their spin polarization. These findings establish the importance of magnetic-group symmetry for a complete description of nonlinear charge and spin photocurrents in compensated ferrimagnets.

papers.title: Quadratic Wasserstein transport for elliptical distributions
papers.abstract: The quadratic Wasserstein distance between Gaussian distributions is given by the classical Bures-Wasserstein formula, which depends only on the means, the covariance matrices $\Sigma_0$ and $\Sigma_1$, and their interaction $K=(\Sigma_0^{1/2}\Sigma_1\Sigma_0^{1/2})^{1/2}$. The same formula holds for elliptical distributions with a common radial law. In this paper, we extend this representation to general elliptical distributions by identifying an additional transport cost $\Gamma$ that depends on the radial laws and the spectrum of $K$. We describe $\Gamma$ via a weighted quadratic transport problem involving Dirichlet distributions and show that optimal couplings preserve directions within the eigenspaces of $K$. When $K$ has a single eigenvalue, we obtain an explicit cost formula and an optimal Monge map. For general spectra, we derive remarkably tight lower and upper bounds for $\Gamma$ using nested spectral projections and Knothe-Rosenblatt couplings. The lower bound is based on one-dimensional integrals and can be computed fast. For Gaussian, Student-$t$, uniform ball, and uniform sphere distributions, the upper bound also admits computationally efficient representations via dynamic programming. Numerical experiments demonstrate that we reduce the gap between the previously known bounds by more than 80% in many settings, and by over 99.9% in certain scenarios, even in dimension $10^6$. These improvements are particularly valuable in high-dimensional or heavy-tailed settings, where accurate numerical computation of quadratic Wasserstein distances is challenging.

papers.title: Superconductivity with valley-imbalanced Fermi surfaces in thick rhombohedral graphene
papers.abstract: Superconductivity in spin-polarized metals challenges conventional opposite-spin pairing, particularly when a magnetic field strengthens rather than suppresses it. In graphene, the additional valley degree of freedom broadens the possible pairing channels, making the valley occupation of the parent metal central to understanding such superconductivity. Here we report in-plane-field-enhanced superconductivity in hBN-aligned 17-layer rhombohedral graphene. Normal-state quantum oscillations reveal unequal Fermi pockets consistent with a valley-imbalanced, spin-polarized parent metal. Calculations show that the parent electron pocket is predominantly localized on the bottom surface and largely preserved by electrostatic screening as additional Fermi pockets emerge. Superconductivity persists in this regime but is suppressed when carriers are polarized toward the hBN-aligned surface, where the parent bands undergo strong moire reconstruction. An adjacent nonlinear metallic response evolves continuously into superconducting critical-current features and persists above the superconducting transition temperature. The combination of valley imbalance and in-plane-field-enhanced superconductivity motivates a phenomenological magnon-assisted equal-spin intervalley pairing scenario. These findings provide experimental constraints on pairing in valley-imbalanced metals and open a route to testing magnetic pairing mechanisms through layer-selective control of the parent electronic states.

papers.title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.

papers.title: To Critic Or Not To Critic
papers.abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly important. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.

We argue that neither GRPO nor PPO is universally preferable. Instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, and we focus on three that shape the bias–variance tradeoff.

The first is batch size, the number of trajectories used per actor update. Larger batches reduce gradient variance but not bias, so the relative performance of PPO and GRPO can change with batch size. The second is critic reliance. GRPO avoids the critic entirely, while PPO’s GAE parameter λ\lambda controls how strongly its advantage calculation bootstraps from the critic. More bootstrapping typically lowers variance at the cost of bias from critic approximation error [3]. The third is task complexity, which we study through horizon and domain. Longer horizons increase our upper bound on gradient variance (Section 3.2). Domains differ in properties that may also raise gradient noise, such as the dimensionality of the state and action spaces and the diversity of trajectories relevant to learning [16, 17]. We find that both can make variance reduction more valuable (Sections 4.3 and 5).

papers.title: AVQ-Attention-2: Adaptive Vector-Quantized Attention with Exact Local Blocks and Linear-Cost Training
papers.abstract: Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in the number of tokens. Vector-quantized attention reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ by clustering the $N$ keys, attending to the $M$ codewords instead, and its adaptive form, AVQ-attention, concentrates codebook resolution where a query's attention mass actually falls. We present AVQ-Attention-2, a better design that merges it with exact local attention and attends to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword. We show three improvements: consistently better quality at comparable cost; training that now also costs $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$; and an approximation accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning. Across a variety of sequence lengths the result is competitive not merely with other approximate attention but with exact dense attention, running faster than FlashAttention at little to no loss in quality.

papers.intro:
Attention compares every token with every other, so its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024) removes the memory bottleneck of that computation but not its arithmetic: the quadratic term counts pairs of tokens, and an exact method has to look at all of them. Cheaper attention therefore has to decide what not to pay for, which leaves two alternatives: cut the pairs deemed less important and keep the rest exact, or keep every pair and approximate it.

Cheaper attention therefore has to decide what not to pay for, which leaves two alternatives: cut the pairs deemed less important and keep the rest exact, or keep every pair and approximate it.

In the first camp, local attention methods like windowed and neighbourhood attention (Liu et al., 2021; Hassani et al., 2023) restrict every query to a nearby subset of keys and evaluate those exactly. In doing so they lose global information, and at high resolutions the neighbourhoods have to grow in step to keep proportional coverage. Vector-quantized attention instead sorts the NN keys into MM clusters and attends over the clusters (Lingle, 2024), so every key still contributes, through a coarser stand-in; AVQ-attention (van den Dool et al., 2026) makes that resolution adaptive, spending a per-tile refinement budget on whichever key clusters receive the most attention mass.

In doing so they lose global information, and at high resolutions the neighbourhoods have to grow in step to keep proportional coverage. Vector-quantized attention instead sorts the NN keys into MM clusters and attends over the clusters (Lingle, 2024), so every key still contributes, through a coarser stand-in; AVQ-attention (van den Dool et al., 2026) makes that resolution adaptive, spending a per-tile refinement budget on whichever key clusters receive the most attention mass.

However, attention mass is often concentrated near the query. Local sparse methods build that prior in directly; AVQ-attention has to rediscover it from the data, and then spends part of its budget approximating keys that a local method computes exactly, and faster. papers.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
papers.abstract: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

Language models are increasingly deployed as agents that act in an environment over many steps to reach a goal, with the model running inside a harness that gives it tools, executes its actions and manages the history it sees (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). A coding agent, for example, explores a repository and runs shell commands, while a personal assistant calls the APIs of everyday applications on behalf of a user (Trivedi et al., 2024). In both cases the quality of the agent rests on its policy, that is, on the action it chooses given the task and everything that has happened so far.

The standard recipe supervises the full trajectory, which typically consists of a chain-of-thought (CoT), some visible commentary and an action such as a shell command or an API call.

papers.title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
papers.abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

Bandit convex optimization is a fundamental framework for optimizing an unknown convex function when gradient information is not available (Flaxman et al., 2005; Agarwal et al., 2011; Shamir, 2013; Lattimore, 2024). In the one-dimensional stochastic, fixed-confidence setting, at each time t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots a learner selects a query point Xt∈[0,1]X_{t}\in[0,1] and observes noisy evaluations YtY_{t} with mean f⁡(Xt)f(X_{t}). For a given confidence δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the learner’s goal is to output a recommendation x^\hat{x} as soon as it can guarantee a prescribed accuracy ε\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. The central measure of performance is the number of samples collected in this process, also referred to as sample complexity.

Classical minimax analyses characterize the worst-case performance over a given function class (Agarwal et al., 2011; Jamieson et al., 2012; Shamir, 2013; Akhavan et al., 2024). With the motivation that this may not reflect the true difficulty of the problem, we take an instance-dependent perspective and ask: Is it possible to adapt to the particular convex function ff being optimized? Are there “easier” convex functions to optimize than others? If so, what is this difficulty determined by? The answer depends on the notion of correctness. We consider two criteria. The first is simple regret, where a recommendation is correct if it is nearly optimal in value, i.e. f⁡(x^)−minx∈[0,1]⁡f⁡(x)≤εf(\hat{x})-\min_{x\in[0,1]}f(x)\leq\varepsilon (Bubeck et al., 2009). The second is minimizer localization, where a recommendation is correct if it is close to the minimizer in the decision space, i.e. |x^−argminx∈[0,1]f​(x)|≤ε|\hat{x}-\argmin_{x\in[0,1]}f(x)|\leq\varepsilon. Our results show that there is a stark contrast between these: minimizer localization admits instance-dependent guarantees on the sample complexity, whereas simple regret does not, in the sense that every instance requires a number of samples on the same order as the worst-case minimax rate.

Simple regret is a natural objective when the function’s value directly tells us about the goodness of a solution. As an example, this is the case when one wants identify a dosage xx of a drug with small negative efficacy f⁡(x)f(x), or find a hyperparameter configuration xx for which a machine learning model has small loss f⁡(x)f(x). However, when the final quantity of interest is the minimizer, simple regret does not necessarily provide a meaningful guarantee. Say we want to determine the location of a pipe buried in the ground. A scanner can be positioned at a horizontal location xx to measure the return time f⁡(x)f(x) of a reflected pulse. Assuming that the return time of the reflected pulse is minimized at the pipe’s true location x⋆x_{\star}, the minimizer localization objective allows us to find a location close to the pipe. On the other hand, a small return time f⁡(x)f(x) does not necessarily imply that the measurement location xx is close to the true location x⋆x_{\star}. The minimizer localization objective is suitable here, while simple regret is not. More generally, localizing the minimizer can be viewed as an inverse problem: we seek to infer the unknown location of the minimizer from noisy measurements of a response function.

papers.title: SetCon: Setup-Conditioned IMU-Language Learning from 3D Human Motion
papers.abstract: Aligning inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals with text enables zero-shot activity recognition across wearable devices. A worn device's signal depends on its setup, the combination of body site and mounting. Leading IMU-language models make their encoders invariant to the mounting, which also discards the device's orientation relative to the body, such as the direction of gravity that separates sitting, standing and lying. We introduce SetCon, which replaces full invariance with selective invariance. It estimates each device's mounting on its known body site from a few unlabeled windows and conditions its encoder on this estimate. Because the mounting stays nearly fixed while the device is worn, the moving body serves as a calibration target. Both calibration and representation learning are supervised by 3D human motion, since one movement can be simulated under many known sensor setups. At test time, a class is represented by its name or by an anchor, which averages the text embeddings of the name and of activity descriptions and needs no labeled window. A language model built on the frozen encoder also answers how and in what order a movement is performed. papers.title: MinPair: Measured Minimal Pairs for Fine-Grained Control in Text-to-Motion Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-motion generation has made great progress in capturing what action to perform, yet it remains limited in controlling how that action is executed. For example, when only the height word of a kick request changes, none of the tested state-of-the-art methods reaches all three of knee, waist and head height. The other words of a caption usually imply an attribute such as height, so neither the training loss nor the standard metrics require a model to use the word that states it. A model has to use this word only when it alone separates two otherwise identical captions. We introduce MinPair, which creates such caption pairs from real motion clips. It starts from rule-based motion descriptors that measure the 3D body motion of each clip. From these descriptors a language model writes MinPair captions, timed body-part captions that say how each body part moves. The same descriptors show in which attributes two clips of the same action differ. A measured minimal pair joins the true caption of one clip with an altered copy in which only one attribute takes the value measured in the other clip. A contrastive pair loss then requires a diffusion denoiser to reconstruct the clip more accurately from its true caption than from the altered copy. Training needs no synthetic motion and inference stays unchanged. Control is tested on 22 target tasks and on caption edits that each change one attribute. MinPair captions alone help motions reach their targets and improve the standard metrics M2M, R@3 and FID, yet a model trained on them still ignores most single-word edits. The pair loss raises the share of followed template edits from 11% to 60%, while the standard metrics do not improve further. With body-part captions, MinPair reaches more targets than state-of-the-art methods that were trained on up to 99 times more motion data.

papers.intro:
In text-to-motion generation [8], a request such as kick to head level should produce a kick that reaches the head. The action alone leaves open how high, how fast and how far a movement goes and how much it turns. We call such execution properties attributes. An animator who asks for a head-level kick or a robot operator who asks for three steps forward expects exactly that execution. Diffusion models have become the standard generator for this task [11, 35]. FrankenMotion [21] gives every body part its own timed track of sentences, which we call part captions. HY-Motion [37] and Kimodo [31] scale data and parameters. Yet when only the height word of a kick request changes, none of these state-of-the-art methods reaches all three requested heights (Fig. 1). Nothing in their training singles out the attribute word. Text labels [27, 8] rarely state how high, how fast or how far a movement goes, so part captions derived from them [21] rarely do either. Where captions do state it, the other words give it away. In captions written from measurements, a linear classifier recovers a masked tempo word from the remaining words of a held-out caption in 77% of cases against 41% for the most frequent tempo. The denoising loss and the standard metrics M2M, R@3 and FID all reward the complete caption, so a model can succeed from the context without using the attribute word. A model learns to follow a word reliably only once that word alone decides the outcome.

We introduce MinPair (Fig. 2). It measures every training clip with rule-based motion descriptors. From these a language model writes MinPair captions, which say how each body part moves in each phase. For a source clip whose caption places the wrist at shoulder height, a partner clip of the same action keeps it at hip height. We copy the source caption and change only this value to the partner’s. The copy is wrong for the source clip in exactly one attribute and serves as its negative caption [41]. The new words arise in one of two ways. In a template pair, the attribute word moves along a fixed word scale of the captions. In a free-form pair, a language model words the measured difference itself in one span of up to 4 words, which we check against the measurements. Because the partner is a real clip, no motion is synthesized and the negative describes an execution that really occurs. As in contrastive learning [36], a pair loss then requires the denoiser to reconstruct the same noisy copy of the source motion more accurately from the true caption than from the negative [17, 19]. Only the changed words can make this difference. Inference stays unchanged.

papers.title: CORALIE Radial Velocity Search for Companions around Evolved Stars (CASCADES) VI. Revised masses and homogeneous estimation of the stellar parameters of 583 red giants
papers.abstract:
Giant-star radial-velocity surveys allow us to study how the exoplanet population varies with stellar mass and evolution. However, obtaining accurate estimates of stellar masses for such stars is challenging, as methods like isochrone fitting are prone to large errors due to the degeneracy associated with the closeness of isochrones.
  We provide a homogeneous re-derivation of the stellar parameters of the CASCADES giant-star survey. This includes parameters obtained from spectral energy distribution fitting, as well as an update of the stellar masses using asteroseismology.
  We use TESS light curves to measure the frequency of maximum oscillation power, $\nu_{\rm max}$, for all the stars when applicable. We re-extract the stellar radii of the survey by fitting broadband photometry with ARIADNE, a spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting package, using priors from spectroscopy for the effective temperature, metallicity and $\log g$. By using scaling relations, we compute revised estimates of the stellar masses of targets with a $\nu_{\rm max}$ measurement.
  We obtain new estimates of mass for 583 out of the 640 stars of the survey. These revised masses are typically 15 to 20% lower (median difference of $-0.35\,M_\odot$) than the ones obtained by isochrone fitting, in particular for low-metallicity stars for which this effect is stronger. These new masses impact the overall mass distribution of the sample, whose median decreases from $2.11\,M_\odot$ to $1.65\,M_\odot$.
  These revised masses provide the basis for future occurrence-rate analyses aiming to study the link between host-star mass and planet occurrence. They also highlight the uncertainties associated with the determination of masses for evolved stars.

papers.intro:
With the increasing number of exoplanet detections, our understanding of exoplanet demographics has improved substantially. Exoplanets are now found over a wide range of periods, masses, and host stars. A question that remains of actuality is how the occurrence rate of exoplanets depends on host-star mass and metallicity (Johnson et al., 2010; Reffert et al., 2015). To answer this, one needs to find exoplanets around more massive hosts, for which planet occurrence remains less well constrained. Studying more massive stars, in the 1.5 - 5 M⊙M_{\odot} range, is however a challenging task for stars on the main sequence (Borgniet et al., 2019). Since they are hotter and rotate faster, achieving the radial-velocity (RV) precision to detect exoplanets orbiting them is particularly hard. Red giants, however, have a slower rotation rate and cooler surface, making them more suitable for RV surveys. Studying intermediate-mass giant stars, whose progenitors may have been A to F stars on the main sequence, is thus a proxy to study this population of stars. In this context, several surveys have been launched to look for exoplanets around these evolved hosts (Frink et al., 2002; Sato et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2011; Wittenmyer et al., 2011).

papers.title: An exponential-rate consensus-based algorithms for estimation from relative measurements: implementation and performance analysis
papers.abstract: In this work we address the problem of optimal estimating the position of each agent in a network from relative noisy vectorial distances with its neighbors. Although the problem can be cast as a standard least-squares problem, the main challenge is to devise scalable algorithms that allow each agent to estimate its own position by means of only local communication and bounded complexity, independently of the network size and topology. We first propose a synchronous consensus-based algorithm that is guaranteed to have exponentially convergence rate to the optimal centralized least-squares solution. We then extend this algorithm to more realistic asynchronous implementations via the use of local memory variables. We show that exponential convergence is still guaranteed under both uniform persistent communication and randomized persistent communication protocols. We finally complement the analytical results with some numerical simulations.

papers.intro:
The proliferation of relatively inexpensive devices capable of communicating, computing, sensing, interacting with the environment and storing information is promising an unprecedented number of novel applications throughout the cooperation of these devices toward a common goal. These applications include swarm robotics, wireless sensor networks, smart energy grids, smart traffic networks, smart camera networks. These applications also pose new challenges, of which scalability is one of the major ones. Scalability is intended as the ability for an application to continue functioning without any dramatic performance degradation even if the number of devices involved keep increasing. In particular, an application is scalable if it is not necessary to increase HW resources or to adopt a more complex SW algorithms in each device even if the total number of devices increases.

papers.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
papers.abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

The resulting evidence lower bound (ELBO) VAE-NLME algorithm replaces the MCMC step of SAEM by a neural network encoder trained by stochastic gradients. It is fast and is well-suited for AI applications, but it has never been analyzed mathematically. Moreover, it maximizes only the ELBO, so that its limit, if it exists, is a maximum of the ELBO instead of the maximum likelihood estimator. In PMX, however, the likelihood is the hard currency for the quality of a model, e.g., for model comparison [17]. Second, can it be extended to converge to the maximum likelihood estimator while keeping its gradient-based training?

papers.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.

papers.title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.

papers.intro:
Linear attention offers an efficient alternative to softmax attention by compressing the growing key–value cache into a fixed-size recurrent state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). This allows inference costs per token to remain constant with sequence length, making these architectures attractive for processing long contexts. However, their ability to use information from earlier in the sequence remains a persistent concern. Even when overall language modeling performance is comparable, linear attention models often underperform on associative recall (AR), where previously encountered information must be retrieved from a partial cue (Jelassi et al., 2024; Waleffe et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2023). This recall gap remains a major obstacle to the wider adoption of fully recurrent architectures and has motivated both changes to recurrent state updates (Yang et al., 2024b; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) and hybrid models that combine recurrent layers with softmax attention (Waleffe et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026).

Linear attention offers an efficient alternative to softmax attention by compressing the growing key–value cache into a fixed-size recurrent state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). This allows inference costs per token to remain constant with sequence length, making these architectures attractive for processing long contexts. However, their ability to use information from earlier in the sequence remains a persistent concern. papers.title: Modeling of Chemically Reactive Gas Flows for Multi-Scale Problems
papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of chemical reactions plays a key role in the investigation of high-temperature flows. The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method provides highly accurate solutions for such flows. However, its computational cost becomes prohibitive for low Knudsen regimes. Particle-based continuum methods employing the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) or Fokker-Planck approximations have gained increasing attention in recent years, improve computational efficiency in low-Knudsen regimes by modeling relaxation processes rather than binary collisions, while retaining the particle approach that enables straightforward coupling with DSMC. In the last years, different continuum-based models in the open-source particle code PICLas have been extended to simulate gas mixtures with internal energy modes. The present work focuses on modeling of chemically reactive gas mixtures in the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model. Model accuracy is assessed for two test cases of a reactive gases confined in a reservoir.

papers.intro:
Numerical results for flows over a wide range of Knudsen numbers are of utmost importance to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physical processes, in particular due to limitations in experimental investigations. The well-established Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method [1] is a highly reliable approach to simulate non-equilibrium gas flows, proven to produce accurate results. However, since the computational costs of DSMC increase significantly in the low Knudsen regimes, alternative approaches are required. In recent years, particle-based continuum methods, e. g. the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) [2] or Fokker-Planck (FP) [5] approximations, have gained increasing attention for simulating multi-scale problems, as they improve computational efficiency in low Knudsen regimes. Due to the same particle approach, a simple coupling with the DSMC method is possible, where DSMC is then used for the high Knudsen flow regions and BGK or FP for the lower ones. The BGK and FP methods are based on a relaxation process of the particle distribution function towards a specific target distribution instead of modeling binary collisions, leading to less restrictions on the time step and simulation particle number compared to DSMC.

This work focuses on the extension of the ESBGK model to include chemical reactions in gas mixtures, which is of great importance in particular for space applications such as spacecraft re-entry. Here, the flow is characterized by high temperatures, where chemical reactions such as the dissociation of molecular oxygen and nitrogen cannot be neglected. Previous work on the implementation of chemical reactions in the ESBGK model [9] is updated and extended by a presentation of the chemistry model. The theoretical basics of chemical reactions are briefly explained in section 2.1, while the extension of the ESBGK model and the subsequent implementation in PICLas are discussed in sections 2.2 and 3. For verification purposes, two different test cases of a reactive gas mixture confined in a reservoir are presented to demonstrate the functionality of the proposed model. The solutions of the simulations are compared to DSMC results in section 4.

papers.title: Band-Selective Coupling to Charge Density Wave Fluctuations in Kagome Superconductors AV3Sb5
papers.abstract: The kagome superconductors AV3Sb5 (A=K, Rb, Cs) host multiband superconductivity (SC) within an unconventional charge density wave (CDW) parent phase, yet the relationship between the two remains unresolved. Through time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (tr-ARPES) experiments on CsV3Sb5 and KV3Sb5, we observe coherent band oscillations driven by coupling to a low-energy CDW amplitude mode at 3.1 THz. We find this coupling to be highly band-selective, differing by a factor of over 2 even between bands with dominant V-3d character. We reproduce these results with frozen-phonon density functional theory calculations, offering insight towards the relation between differing Fermi surface characters and our observed band selectivity. Furthermore, we observe differences in coupling channels between KV3Sb5 and CsV3Sb5. These results establish CDW amplitude mode fluctuations as a band-selective low-energy coupling channel that intimately contributes to the interplay between CDW and SC in the AV3Sb5 compounds.

papers.title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models
papers.abstract:
Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss.
  As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.

papers.title: Analyzing Single-Bit Flips on LLMs and Their Backbone-Matched VLMs
papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) enable offline weight analysis and are reused as backbones in vision-language models (VLMs), increasing the risk of bit-flip attacks that manipulate stored weight bits to induce malicious model behavior. An adversary could identify vulnerable bits on a public LLM and later flip the same locations in a deployed LLM or its backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip is particularly practical in this setting because it is easier to achieve under hardware fault attacks than multi-bit flips. However, existing selectors are mostly limited to multi-bit flips, without in-depth analysis of single-bit flips. In this paper, we adapt representative data-free and data-based bit selectors to identify candidate bits. We evaluate each bit independently on source LLMs and at the same logical coordinates in backbone-matched VLMs (without re-search), considering both performance degradation and prediction patterns across multiple inputs. Results show impact of single-bit flips varies across selectors on LLMs and their backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip can make the model tend to produce a repeated output string across different inputs. Our robustness analysis reveals vulnerabilities in terms of performance and prediction patterns.
papers.intro:
Bit-flip attacks (BFAs) are a form of fault injection that induce malicious behavior by flipping a small number of bits in model weights stored in main memory [15, 3, 1, 5]. The increasing availability of open-weight large language models (LLMs) and their reuse as language backbones in vision-language models (VLMs) amplify the risk of bit-flip attacks across models. This paper is motivated by the concern that an adversary may identify vulnerable locations on a public LLM and later modify the corresponding locations in the same LLM that is deployed or in a VLM that uses the LLM as a backbone. Single-bit flips are particularly realistic in this setting because manipulating a single vulnerable bit may be easier to realize under hardware fault attacks than attacks that require manipulation of multiple bits. Single-bit attacks have been studied in DNNs under hardware fault settings [9].

Previous works have left three gaps in our understanding of bit-flip attacks. First, existing bit selectors are designed for attacks in which multiple selected bits are flipped together [15, 3, 1, 5]. Consequently, they do not characterize the effects of a single bit in the bit set identified by existing selectors. Prior work [7] studies single-bit faults but focuses on the one bit that maximizes the damage of the attack. Second, existing bit-flip studies focus on metrics that evaluate the outputs of the model. The patterns of impact on the model outputs induced by a bit-flip attack across multiple inputs have not previously been studied. These patterns might potentially either conceal or reveal the fact that the model has been attacked. Third, prior bit-flip studies typically identify and manipulate vulnerable bits directly on the LLMs or VLMs. This leaves open whether vulnerable locations identified offline on a public source LLM remain damaging when the same LLM architecture is reused as the language backbone of a VLM, without searching again on the VLM itself.

papers.title: Contact Geometry for Generative Models: An Unbalanced Optimal Transport Formulation
papers.abstract: Real-world generative problems in biology, medical imaging, or robotics, rarely come with perfectly paired source and target distributions. While unbalanced Optimal Transport (uOT) provides a robust framework to bridge unpaired datasets via minimum-length paths in probability space, existing formulations based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry introduce a structural bias toward high density regions, often triggering mode collapse. We introduce Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (CuOT), a novel uOT formulation grounded in contact geometry that decouples density transport direction from mass growth to eliminate structural bias. This allows CuOT to adapt sampling steps to the local data structure, naturally reducing step sizes in high-density regions to prevent overshooting and ensuring stable convergence. The result is a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver that consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.
