papers.title: Aerodynamic Collision Avoidance Manoeuvres in Very Low Earth Orbit: Exploiting Lift for Short Warning Times and Reduced Orbital Decay
papers.abstract: Very Low Earth Orbits (VLEO, below $450\,\mathrm{km}$ altitude) offer promising mission capabilities for future spacecraft, but increasing traffic and the presence of orbital debris create collision risks that pose a particular challenge for satellites without conventional propulsion. Aerodynamic drag, resulting from interaction with the residual atmosphere, has been shown effective for performing collision avoidance manoeuvres (CAMs). However, short warning times remain challenging, and current methods do not exploit aerodynamic lift forces that enable out-of-track manoeuvres, which could help enhance control authority and mitigate drag-induced orbital decay. This work addresses both gaps by developing and evaluating two complementary optimisation methods: a heuristic approach using reachable set analysis to determine minimum lead times, and a direct shooting method to limit the increase in orbital decay due to the manoeuvre. Analyses using data derived from real conjunctions show that achieving a sufficient reduction in collision risk in the considered scenarios is feasible with lead times lower than one orbital period. Results also show that lift-based manoeuvres outperform drag-only approaches, with modest lead time reductions and more pronounced benefits in limiting orbital decay. Performance sensitivity to variations in control authority due to the type of gas-surface-interaction, altitude, and the encounter geometry is characterised. The methods and results presented highlight the potential of aerodynamic CAM for short warning time scenarios, contributing to sustainable operations in the increasingly congested VLEO environment.

papers.intro:
The near-Earth environment has become progressively congested by space traffic and debris. Collisions pose a lethal risk to operational spacecraft and require actions in form of collision avoidance manoeuvres. Increasing launch traffic and large constellations accelerate the trend despite upcoming mitigation efforts and guidelines [17]. Very Low Earth Orbits (VLEO, below 450 km450\text{\,}\mathrm{km}) offer operational benefits with higher resolution in Earth observation, lower communication latency and improved link budgets. Although the faster natural decay aids the removal of debris, the rising spatial density due to constellations also affects the upper end of very low Earth orbit as captured by the European Space Agency’s MASTER population [18]. Consequently, collision risks and frequent conjunctions remain operational challenges even at very low altitudes.

Aerodynamic manoeuvres exploit forces from interaction with the residual atmosphere as a propellant-free means to change a satellite’s trajectory. Drag-based collision avoidance manoeuvres act primarily in-track and have been shown effective when planned several orbits ahead [9, 36]. However, short warning times and increased orbital decay due to the manoeuvre present open challenges that could be addressed by using lift forces acting perpendicular to drag. Advances in shape optimisation and surface materials promise an increase in achievable aerodynamic lift [21], enabling out-of-track control that is not possible with drag alone. This is especially valuable for late, just-in-time collision avoidance manoeuvres performed only a few orbits before the projected conjunction. Fresher tracking data reduces propagated uncertainty and helps avoid unnecessary manoeuvres [26].

This work develops methods to design aerodynamic collision avoidance manoeuvres that include lift and quantifies their benefits over drag-only manoeuvres. Two complementary solution methods are presented: a reachable set heuristic that is based on a backward sweep approach and identifies minimum feasible lead times, and a direct shooting approach that minimises the inevitable increase in orbital decay due to the manoeuvre. Problems of collision avoidance manoeuvre design are often solved using direct and indirect methods [28]. However, since the dynamics as well as the constraint on collision risk are nonlinear and, in general, non-convex, convergence to the global optimum is not guaranteed. The developed heuristic method builds upon recent work on time-optimal collision avoidance manoeuvres [16, 31] and extends them to manoeuvers with constrained control direction. It serves as an initial guess for further refinement using direct methods for minimising decay. The proposed tools operate directly on collision risk and track changes in time of closest approach due to the manoeuvre. Performance is evaluated across representative conjunction geometries, altitudes and surface properties.

papers.title: Automated Design and Evaluation Pipeline for Optimal Control Transcriptions in Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: The computational burden of Model Predictive Control represents a bottleneck limiting its widespread deployment in real-time applications. The selection of the optimal control transcription strategy for a given MPC formulation is a key driver of computational efficiency. Identifying performant MPC transcriptions requires significant effort and domain knowledge. We propose an automated pipeline for the design and evaluation of performant optimal control transcriptions for a given MPC formulation. Custom multi-objective design metrics, such as computation time or closed-loop performance, can be specified and are minimized by the pipeline. As a transcription method, a pseudospectral Legendre-Gauss-Radau method is employed. We show that it incorporates forward Euler integration and implicit collocation methods of low and high order in one formulation, leveraging the pipeline to evaluate both numerical approaches. Furthermore, different mesh configurations can be parameterized. To identify the optimal configuration of the transcription, a Bayesian Optimization framework is applied. The pipelines improvements in MPC performance are demonstrated through On-Orbit Servicing scenarios involving spacecraft motion planning and closed-loop control.

Model Predictive Control (MPC) is an established control methodology that repeatedly solves an optimal control problem (OCP) to determine the next control input. One of the limiting factors for the broader application of MPC is the computational cost [1]. The numerical scheme and the OCP formulation are key components in determining the computational complexity [2, 3], leading to the question of which OCP transcription best matches the specific performance metrics.

One of the limiting factors for the broader application of MPC is the computational cost [1]. The numerical scheme and the OCP formulation are key components in determining the computational complexity [2, 3], leading to the question of which OCP transcription best matches the specific performance metrics.

Direct methods are the default approach to solve the OCP in the context of MPC [4]. A numerical discretization scheme is used to transcribe the continuous OCP into a Nonlinear Program (NLP) [5]. Two prominent direct methods are Multiple-Shooting (MS) [6, 5] and collocation methods [7].

MS is a time-marching formulation that solves an initial value problem (IVP). The time domain is divided into several sub-intervals, and the IVP is solved simultaneously on each of them. The continuity of the solution trajectory is ensured by continuity constraints at the interval borders. The order of the integration scheme determines the solution accuracy. A common class of integration methods is explicit and implicit Runge-Kutta methods. In the MPC context, MS transcription is often used with explicit integration schemes, such as in automotive [8], aerospace [9] and robotics [10].

In the MPC context, MS transcription is often used with explicit integration schemes, such as in automotive [8], aerospace [9] and robotics [10].

Collocation methods enforce that the system dynamics match the derivative of an approximate state trajectory at given collocation points, resulting in an implicit formulation [7]. Thus, a system of equations must be solved in each iteration. A common approach is to use pseudospectral methods [11, 12, 13, 14]. The time domain is discretized using non-equidistant collocation points derived from the roots of an orthogonal polynomial [12]. Pseudospectral methods are often used for offline trajectory optimization. In recent years, pseudospectral transcriptions are employed more frequently in MPC formulations, e.g., in space applications [15], or in the automotive field [16, 17].

In application-driven MPC design, key decisions include choosing between explicit and implicit formulations, selecting the approximation order, and determining the mesh structure. Several surveys analyze and compare optimal control transcriptions, discussing their respective advantages and disadvantages in the context of MPC [2, 18, 19, 7]. However, general guidelines for selecting a suitable OCP formulation for custom MPC problems remain difficult to establish. This is primarily due to the strong interdependence between the system dynamics, the embedded constraints, the solver, and the accuracy requirements. Benchmarking these approaches is time-consuming, as it demands full implementation and scenario-based comparison for each parametrization. The question arises whether a general approach exists for finding the best-performing optimal control transcription for a given MPC scenario?

An automated design and evaluation pipeline for optimal control transcriptions (APOCT) is proposed to identify an optimized formulation for a given MPC problem, evaluated against custom performance metrics. This is enabled by the integration of a local pseudospectral Legendre-Gauss-Radau (LGR-LOC) [12, 14] method, which is proven to reduce, in a first-order parametrization, to an explicit multiple-shooting formulation with forward Euler integration. Furthermore, the transcription enables a variable local mesh structure by allowing the number of sub-intervals, the interval boundaries, and the prediction horizon to vary. This provides a high degree of flexibility in discretizing the OCP. The LGR-LOC is embedded in a Bayesian Optimization pipeline, shown in Fig. 1. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the integration of a flexible OCP transcription into a hyperparameter optimization pipeline for identifying performant MPC formulations is a novel contribution.

papers.title: On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys
papers.abstract: Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.

papers.intro:
Process mining applied to healthcare can unlock unprecedented insights and help improve both the quality of care and the systems designed to support it [1, 9]. Typically, process mining has been applied to healthcare data from a healthcare provider’s perspective. This perspective helps identify bottlenecks and inefficiencies in healthcare systems and improve their processes. However, it implicitly treats the patient as a “customer” of the process. This limits the scope of process improvement in three ways. First, it overlooks the patient’s own knowledge, even though patients often possess extensive knowledge of their clinical histories. Second, due to data availability, it often restricts the analysis to individual information systems (e.g., those of a single hospital), whereas patient care spans multiple systems, clinicians, and treatments. Third, the insights from these analyses often aim to improve the healthcare provider’s processes (e.g., those of a hospital). Such improvements may, of course, benefit patients. Nevertheless, the ultimate measure of the quality of care is what the patient experiences throughout their journey [10], which cannot be fully captured by analyzing only the data from information systems logs and must therefore be captured directly from patients themselves. However, such accounts are incomplete and may change, they are told in natural language, and they span a complex domain of conditions, treatments, and stakeholders. These three challenges make the data hard to model before analysis methods can be applied. Moreover, patient journeys involve several entities at once (e.g., patients, conditions, treatments). Object-centric event logs (OCELs) [3] are best suited to analyze all these perspectives at once.

In this paper, we identify challenges and requirements related to the creation of object-centric event logs from patient journeys. To address them, we propose a stepwise approach, starting from the data collection until the generation of an OCEL. Key features in our approach include the temporal and semantic resolution of the concepts extracted from the narrative of the patient. Our approach includes a mapping scheme to guide the creation of OCELs. This mapping scheme is based on general principles and can be applied to any patient journey to convert them to OCEL. We evaluate the approach on a synthetic cohort of patients.

papers.title: Protective-Design Pre-Emption in Child-Facing Generative AI
papers.abstract: Generative AI is adopted rapidly by children, yet unrestricted general-audience models dominate their usage. This paper presents the open problem of \emph{protective-design pre-emption}: Delayed market introduction, low access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption foster unrestricted AI model lock-in, leading children to bypass child-centric platforms. With first signs of lower adoption of child-centric platforms, we argue that this shift may reinforce existing AI risks such as exposing children to deepened parasocial dependencies, skill erosion, and misinformation. To address this problem, we propose interdisciplinary research directions to quantify pre-emption, understand its socio-technical drivers, and develop interventions ensuring child-centric AI is actively adopted, not just available.

papers.intro:
Multiple independent surveys across countries agree that children indisputably use AI tools for schoolwork, information retrieval, and leisure [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. A study of over 25,000 children aged 9 to 16 in the European Union finds that 72% used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in the last month [1]. We distinguish between two categories of AI tools children use. General-audience platforms (e.g., ChatGPT [6], Gemini [7]) are designed for a broad, mostly adult audience, with safety measures for minors retrofitted after launch, if present at all. Child-centric tools (e.g., Khanmigo [8]) are designed from the outset with age-appropriate content boundaries and child-specific safety guardrails.

A study of over 25,000 children aged 9 to 16 in the European Union finds that 72% used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in the last month [1]. We distinguish between two categories of AI tools children use. General-audience platforms (e.g., ChatGPT [6], Gemini [7]) are designed for a broad, mostly adult audience, with safety measures for minors retrofitted after launch, if present at all. Child-centric tools (e.g., Khanmigo [8]) are designed from the outset with age-appropriate content boundaries and child-specific safety guardrails.

There is a clear lag between the introduction of general-audience AI models with new capabilities and the introduction of safe and child-centric variants like Khanmigo [8]. In fact, OpenAI introduced parental controls in ChatGPT almost 3 years after its launch in 2022 [9] and only started predicting the user age at the beginning of 2026 [10]. This lag may lead to children using and getting used to popular but unsafe general-audience AI platforms, lowering the adoption of child-centric ones. We call this protective-design pre-emption: child-centric models are introduced later such that children come to prefer the unrestricted frontier models they are already using, strengthening a status quo bias. ChatGPT, as the most popular platform for children by far [2, 5], highlights the effect.

We argue that protective-design pre-emption reinforces the risks associated with GenAI usage that child-centric AI is designed to mitigate. Already, surveys show first signs of reliance on chatbots, with the Common Sense Media census reporting that 42% of children who use AI daily expect difficulty with not using it for a month [2]. Children place trust in AI summaries, with almost half of those who use them believing that they are always correct [11], highlighting the dangers of lacking AI literacy. Apart from schoolwork, many children have reported using AI for advice, to practise social skills, and to talk about feelings [2], opening up potential risks for children’s social development.

papers.title: HARI4D: Hand-Articulation Aware 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
papers.abstract: Reasoning about human-object interaction from RGB cameras is important for gaming, VR environments, and robot learning. Yet 4D reconstruction from a monocular RGB camera is challenging, especially when articulated hands are involved. Prior full-body works neglect hands during reconstruction, causing them to penetrate into, or float from the object. We present HARI4D, a hand-articulation-aware method for reconstructing spatially and temporally consistent 4D human-object interaction from monocular RGB video. We introduce a history-aware object tracker that provides robust and stable tracking. Based on these tracks, we improve the interaction configuration through coarse-to-fine reasoning that follows the order of object manipulation: ReachNet first brings the full body and arms to the object during contact, and TouchNet then finalizes hand articulation according to temporal context and local object geometry. On ARCTIC, unseen in training, our method reduces the object error by 56% and improves hand contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior art. Our method recovers accurate full body-object interaction with coherent hand articulations and applies to online videos. Our code and pretrained models will be released.

papers.intro:
Reconstructing human–object interactions from ordinary RGB videos can turn demonstrations into rich supervision for embodied agents. Beyond identifying which object moves, a robot must understand how the body approaches it, the arm positions the wrist, and the fingers establish and maintain a grasp. Metric 4D reconstruction of this process can support robot learning from human demonstrations [86, 21, 67], realistic digital humans for games [16], and interactive virtual and augmented reality content [42].

Recent full-body human–object interaction (HOI) methods have progressively relaxed their assumptions on the manipulated object: from template-based reconstruction [69, 84], to reconstructing unseen instances within specific categories [72, 9], and finally to category-agnostic reconstruction [73, 64]. Yet these methods represent the hands without detailed hand articulation, precisely where physical manipulation happens. Conversely, hand–object methods recover articulated hands from images [19, 79, 8, 36] or videos [20, 80, 13, 60], but typically leave out the supporting full-body pose. This separation is limiting: a plausible object manipulation not only depends on hand and wrist poses but also should be supported by the arm and full body.

Conversely, hand–object methods recover articulated hands from images [19, 79, 8, 36] or videos [20, 80, 13, 60], but typically leave out the supporting full-body pose. This separation is limiting: a plausible object manipulation not only depends on hand and wrist poses but also should be supported by the arm and full body.

Bridging these two scales is particularly difficult in monocular video. Depth ambiguity makes the relative placement of the human and object underconstrained, while their motion causes persistent and changing occlusion. The evidence also becomes progressively weaker toward the point of contact: the body occupies a large image region, but the wrist and fingers may span only a few pixels and are often hidden by the object during manipulation. A successful method must therefore reason jointly about body motion, object motion, and hand articulation, while using temporal context to recover what is invisible in individual frames.

Our key idea is to follow the natural hierarchy of manipulation: the body first approaches the object, the arm then positions the wrist, and the fingers finally form the grasp. We initialize the human pose and metric object shape with complementary foundation models, and obtain a stable object anchor with our history-conditioned object pose tracker. We then refine the interaction in a coarse to fine manner. ReachNet uses local object geometry, image-based contact cues, and temporal context to adjust the body, arms, and wrists. Given this holistic reconstruction, TouchNet reasons over the local object surface through time to refine wrist orientation and hand articulation. Because both refiners operate on local geometric relations rather than object-specific features, the resulting system generalizes to unseen objects, see Fig. 1.

papers.title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
papers.abstract: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.

papers.intro:
As many scientific disciplines become more and more data driven, the need for large datasets increases. However, acquiring several smaller datasets is often more feasible than a single large one. Unfortunately, separately recorded datasets regularly show structural differences. Such differences can be technical nuisances like varying measurement techniques or protocols employed, or signals like donors or donor sex, that are undesirable for the task at hand. We collectively call such structural differences batch effect and the different smaller datasets batches. Many methods have been proposed to remove the batch effect and to integrate batches (Luecken et al., 2022). These typically integrate the data in the original feature space or in a relatively high-dimensional latent space.

As a result, these general-purpose batch removal methods are not directly usable when the aim is to visually explore the data. Visualizing the data as 2D scatter plots, e.g., with neighbor embedding methods like t-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008), has become an important step in many exploratory data analysis pipelines (de Bodt et al., 2025). General-purpose batch integration excels at producing good representations for downstream analysis, which then can be visualized with tools like t-SNE. But when visualization is the primary aim, directly producing an integrated visualization is both conceptually simpler and can yield better results.

For this goal, we propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), a novel approach combining optimal transport (Peyré and Cuturi, 2019) and the popular t-SNE algorithm. Vanilla t-SNE lays the k-nearest-neighbor graph (kNN graph) out in 2D. In the presence of a strong batch effect, no kNN edge crosses from one batch to the other, leading to fully separated batches in the visualizations (Fig. 1a, c). The key idea of OT-tSNE is to augment this graph with explicit cross-batch edges before computing the layout. Many existing tools rely on cross-batch k-nearest neighbors, either mutual nearest neighbors, when both points are each other’s nearest neighbors (Haghverdi et al., 2018; Stuart et al., 2019; Hie et al., 2019; Barkas et al., 2019) or shared nearest neighbors, when at least one point is the nearest neighbor of the other (Polański et al., 2020; Jain et al., 2021). Nearest neighbors are inherently local as each point selects nearest neighbors separately. This can lead to hubs among the cross-batch edges, especially on the fringes of the batches (Lun, 2019, “kissing problem”), which can deteriorate the integration in the visualization (Fig. 1d,e). Instead, optimal transport computes the overall best association between both batches, while ensuring that each point contributes equally. This allows OT-tSNE to produce very well-integrated visualizations while retaining the structure of individual batches (Fig. 1b,f).

papers.title: (No) Separation of Concerns: Philosophical Concerns about Agent Ethics and Implications for SE Practitioners
papers.abstract: The use of AI agents in software engineering (SE) are commonplace, with differing levels of autonomy, a myriad of capabilities, and ability to perform a variety of tasks. Philosophers have begun to examine the ethics of such agents, and SE researchers or practitioners could benefit from them; on the other hand, SE practitioners currently explore most of these concerns through the lens of principlism. We bridge this gap by reviewing the philosophical literature on AI agents indexed in PhilPapers, and translating its ethical concerns into a research agenda for SE researchers and into implications for teams that use coding agents. A systematic mapping study of PhilPapers -- a major philosophy index and open access archive -- yielded 33 peer-reviewed papers by professional philosophers published since 2023. We coded these papers thematically, with cross-disciplinary review of the emerging themes, resulting in eight themes and 85 codes. From these, we derive seven research questions for SE, covering developers' reliance on agents, responsibility for agent-written code, ethical constraints in agent configurations, and benchmark design. For practitioners, we derive five implications: decide which choices an agent must refer to a human, keep agent-written pull requests small enough to review, pair configuration-file instructions with checks, watch for changes to tests, and record who approved what. We argue that ethical concerns cannot be separated from SE concerns into a module of their own: they arise inside code review, configuration, evaluation, and requirements work, and addressing them requires cross-disciplinary work.

papers.title: Net-Gain-Optimized Constellation Shaping for the 5G NR DFT-s-OFDM Uplink: Probabilistic, Geometric, and Joint Designs
papers.abstract: Constellation shaping improves the achievable information rate of coded modulation. On the single-carrier uplink waveform of 5G New Radio, discrete Fourier transform (DFT)- spread orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), the same shaping can also raise the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). A higher PAPR forces more power amplifier back- off and reduces the link budget. Prior work characterized this penalty for fixed probabilistically and geometrically shaped constellations, but did not turn the trade-off into a design objective. We optimize constellation shaping (CS) to maximize the net-gain, i.e., the sum of the communication gain and the PAPR gain, at the fixed spectral efficiency of 4 bits per channel use for 64-QAM. We apply it to probabilistic shaping (PS), geometric shaping (GS), and a joint scheme that combines both. As the coded block error rate cannot be evaluated inside a gradient loop, we use the achievable information rate as a surrogate for the communication performance and the PAPR surrogate as differentiable cost functions for the optimizer. The learned constellations are then validated on a complete DFT-s-OFDM link-level chain. Conventional Maxwell-Boltzmann PS yields a negative net-gain, but net-gain-aware optimization removes this deficit in every method. GS converts it into a substantial gain, as it not only improves the communication performance but also lowers the PAPR below the uniform 64-QAM reference, achieving the largest net-gain among the CS methods studied.

In 5G nr (nr) the dl (dl) employs cp (cp)-ofdm, whereas the ul (ul) additionally offers dft-spread ofdm (dft-s-ofdm), also known as sc-fdma (sc-fdma) [1]. As a multi-carrier waveform, cp-ofdm exhibits a high papr, so the pa (pa) must be operated with a large obo (obo) to remain in its linear region and avoid spectral regrowth and in-band distortion [2, 3]. This back-off lowers the mean radiated power the pa can deliver within its linearity limits, and hence the link budget, a penalty that is most severe on the power-limited ul. Since dft-s-ofdm is a single-carrier waveform with substantially lower papr, it is the preferred ul waveform for power-limited transmission. This benefit is usually associated with the lowest modulation orders, but dft-s-ofdm also supports high-order constellations, up to a maximum of 256-QAM [4]. Thus, any optimization technique applied to the waveform must be assessed not only by its communication performance but also by its effect on papr.

papers.title: Low-Power Spiking Neural Network Acceleration with Differential Time Representation: A Modular Hardware Framework
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer promising energy efficiency, making them well suited for energy-constrained applications. Much of their energy savings stems from the sparse encoding of spike trains. We show that spike trains can be represented more efficiently using Differential Time Representation (DTR), which requires fewer bits than Address-Event Representation (AER) or equidistantly sampled 1-bit spike trains. To support multiple input spike trains, we provide a rigorous proof that DTR sequences can be merged with low complexity. We also provide a set of modular hardware streaming components using this representation that can be flexibly connected to construct custom accelerator architectures for specific SNNs. Tailoring the hardware architecture to the selected SNN is streamlined by a Python framework combining the modular hardware components into a full SNN implementation. We use the framework to generate three accelerators for the Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD), Spiking Speech Commands (SSC), and PSMNIST benchmarks, each in a throughput-optimized parallel variant and a resource-reduced time-multiplexed variant. We report results for FPGA and ASIC implementations, the latter synthesized with a fully open-source flow targeting the predictive ASAP7 PDK. On the SHD dataset, the ASIC implementation reaches 92.46% classification accuracy, while sustaining $\approx{}$12,027 inferences per second at 20.37$\mu{}$J per inference, exceeding the neuromorphic Loihi processor by 109$\times$ in throughput and 1.8$\times$ in energy efficiency. The corresponding FPGA implementation achieves $\approx{}$6,023 inferences per second without using DSP blocks. Across all three datasets, the synthesized ASICs reduce energy per inference by 27-37$\times$ relative to their FPGA counterparts, demonstrating that competitive SNN accelerators can be realized entirely within an open-source design flow.

papers.intro:
The field of ai (ai) and more specifically ml (ml) is evolving, with a clear trend towards larger and more expansive network architectures, consequently leading to larger datasets and parameter spaces. While GPUs, faster memory and higher bandwidths can alleviate the impact of high memory requirements for server-side applications, large models present a significant challenge in embedded and edge applications where power efficiency and computational constraints are paramount. Accordingly, less computationally expensive architectures have gained interest in academia and industry in recent years. One of the approaches is to utilize snn instead of traditional ann, due to their improved power efficiency [1], sparsity characteristics [2] and, depending on the choice of the neuron model and spike encoding, decreased computational effort. This is especially important for embedded devices and edge applications, as these often impose hard limits on energy efficiency and inference time.

One of the approaches is to utilize snn instead of traditional ann, due to their improved power efficiency [1], sparsity characteristics [2] and, depending on the choice of the neuron model and spike encoding, decreased computational effort. This is especially important for embedded devices and edge applications, as these often impose hard limits on energy efficiency and inference time.

Notably, a significant part of the efficiency advantage that snn have over ann is due to the sparse nature of their inputs, as well as efficient data representation schemes used for these spike trains[3]. This representation is particularly important, since it not only influences the number of symbols used to encode a spike train, but also directly shapes the computation required to process these spikes. Therefore, we advocate for the use of dte (dte) [4] over other commonly used schemes such as the absolute time representation often employed by the aer (aer), as well as the equidistantly sampled 1-bit spike trains. We demonstrate that dte outperforms both aforementioned representations in terms of total number of bits required. Furthermore, we also highlight the fact that the differential time used for dte can be directly leveraged for computing neuron dynamics.

papers.title: Space-Time Point Defects as Probes of Criticality: Application to the Gross-Neveu-Heisenberg Transition
papers.abstract: At criticality, a local field acting at a single point in Euclidean space-time is irrelevant and induces a modulation in space and time that decays with twice its scaling dimension. This turns two-point correlation functions into one-point measurements: one operator insertion enters the Boltzmann weight, the other is measured. For the local magnetization the relation is exact at any source strength. Implemented in auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, the approach yields the static spin susceptibility and imaginary-time-displaced correlations with unprecedented precision. We apply it to the Dirac-semimetal to antiferromagnetic-Mott-insulator transition of the half-filled $\pi$-flux Hubbard model. This lattice model provides a regularization of the $N_f=2$ Gross-Neveu-Heisenberg universality class. A finite-size scaling analysis estimates the critical exponents as $ \nu=1.10(3)$ and $\eta_\phi=1.09(4)$, close to field-theory predictions of $\eta_\phi\simeq1$. Since $\eta_\phi>1$, the equal-time structure factor at criticality does not diverge with the system size. Hence, the equal-time structure factor at the ordering wave vector is dominated by background contributions and cannot be used for extracting critical exponents. Consistently, the spin dynamics at the transition is strongly incoherent and the quantum Fisher information remains bounded.

papers.title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
papers.abstract: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.

papers.intro:
Many tasks map a spoken or written conversation to a document with a fixed structure of sections and fields. This includes medical appointments, emergency calls, interviews, or further similar scenarios. Training or evaluating such a model needs conversations together with the filled-in record that they should produce. These pairs are hard to collect, annotating them consistently is slow, and in sensitive domains the conversations cannot be shared or sent to a third-party service. Annotating real conversations with an existing model would just result in distillation, and especially in a specific and difficult domain, finding a sufficiently good teacher model also becomes an issue.

Our approach is to build the data in the opposite order. We first sample a record, meaning a filled-in and schema-valid instance of the target form, then write a dialogue from that record, and optionally synthesize speech from that dialogue (Figure 1). No real consultation is recorded or annotated, and no real patient’s data enters the corpus, which is very beneficial for privacy and data protection. This is not enough to create useful data, though, because simply asking a language model to create a realistic conversation from a record will only produce small variations of one conversation. Section 3 describes the mechanisms we add against this, and they are also generally applicable to other schemas.

Now we have to verify whether those mechanisms work. Diversity is the most important property here, because a generator that writes the same conversation 452 times creates a corpus that is large but useless for training. The number of configurations a generator can reach is only an upper bound on this, so Section 5 measures the variation that arrives in the text. We embed each conversation, analyze the geometry of the resulting point cloud, and compare the full configuration against an earlier, narrower generation run and against two corpora of medical dialogue. These statistics depend on sample size, text length and language in ways that are easy to overlook, so we state each of these dependencies together with the numbers.

papers.title: Spectroscopic identification of z>7 quasars with Roman Space Telescope
papers.abstract: The Roman Wide Field Instrument grism will cover a large area over 1.0-1.93 micrometers, making it possible to search directly for Lyman-alpha breaks in quasars beyond redshift z = 7. We simulate quasars at z = 7.5-10 under HLWAS-like exposures with ESpRESSO, including PSF convolution, slitless dispersion, source and background Poisson noise, read noise, and Horne optimal extraction. Three Lyman-alpha equivalent-width (EW) prescriptions are used to bracket the uncertainty in line strength, and the extracted spectra are compared with M/L/T dwarfs and passive red galaxies using the spectral angle mapper. The Lyman-alpha-break completeness remains above 90% to J_AB approximately 23.7-24.1 and reaches 50% at J_AB approximately 24.3-24.7. Beyond J_AB approximately 25, the result depends strongly on the adopted EW distribution. In the fixed-redshift SAM test, the QSO recovery rate is TPR >= 0.982. None of the noisy brown-dwarf or red-galaxy test spectra is classified as a QSO. Because those test spectra are generated from the same finite parent libraries as the reference classes, this result measures the stability of the classification against noise within those libraries rather than an independently calibrated survey false-positive rate. At the faint end, the strongest astrophysical sensitivity in the present calculation is to the high-EW tail of the Lyman-alpha distribution.

papers.intro:
One of the central questions in cosmic-dawn astrophysics is how the first massive black holes formed and grew. Quasars at z≳6z\gtrsim 6 show that active supermassive black holes were already present within the first Gyr of cosmic history, while their spectra probe the ionization state of the intergalactic medium during reionization. The most luminous systems show strong Gunn–Peterson absorption blueward of Lyα\alpha, indicating substantial neutral hydrogen at z∼6z\sim 6–7 [9, 3]. Even more strikingly, billion-solar-mass black holes have been discovered at z≃7.5z\simeq 7.5 [2, 42], only ∼700\sim 700 Myr after the Big Bang. These objects prove that rapid black-hole growth occurred early, but they also expose a deeper limitation: the known quasars are only the rare, luminous tail of the population.

A key unknown is the faint end. A numerous population of faint quasars would change the inferred black-hole growth history, reshape the high-redshift AGN luminosity function, and set the possible AGN contribution to hydrogen reionization. An analysis at 4.5≤z≤6.54.5\leq z\leq 6.5 found that AGN could provide 31–75% of ionizing photons, conditional on its adopted galaxy escape fractions and other model assumptions [35]. Whether that contribution persists at z>7z>7 remains unmeasured. Only ∼70\sim 70 quasars are known at z>6.5z>6.5, and most have M1450<−25M_{1450}<-25 [38]. At fainter magnitudes, the challenge becomes both statistical and diagnostic. The sources are harder to detect, and the candidate lists become increasingly contaminated. At JAB≳24J_{\rm AB}\gtrsim 24, color-selection efficiency can fall below ∼20%\sim 20\% because high-redshift QSOs, late-type dwarfs, and red galaxies occupy overlapping color space once photometric scatter is included [38]. The faint-quasar problem is therefore not only a depth problem. It is a completeness–purity problem.

The first years of JWST have made this problem more urgent. Deep NIRCam and NIRSpec observations have uncovered a substantial population of compact red sources — the so-called “Little Red Dots” — many with broad Hα\alpha emission consistent with faint AGN activity [23, 11, 16]. JWST spectroscopy has also identified broad-line AGN at z>4z>4 with luminosities below the classical wide-field quasar regime [12, 18]. These sources do not simply extend pre-JWST quasar samples to fainter fluxes. Their apparent abundance, compact host morphologies, broad-line widths, and inferred black-hole masses have been argued to challenge simple extrapolations of pre-JWST luminosity functions and black-hole–galaxy scaling expectations. In particular, several candidates appear overabundant relative to conservative pre-JWST forecasts, have black-hole masses that may be high compared to their stellar masses, and occupy bolometric luminosities below those probed by classical wide-field quasar searches. At still higher redshift, GN-z11 hosts evidence for an accreting black hole at z=10.6z=10.6 [19], while UHZ1 is an X-ray detected quasar candidate at z≃10.1z\simeq 10.1 whose inferred black-hole and host properties have been argued to favor a heavy-seed origin [5, 28]. Together, these discoveries suggest that early black-hole growth may extend to lower luminosities and earlier times than classical quasar samples alone imply. However, they come from small survey areas. JWST can characterize faint AGN in remarkable detail; it cannot by itself measure the abundance of rare faint QSOs over the cosmological volumes needed for a luminosity-function census.

papers.title: Critical ocean physics on the edge of AMOC instability
papers.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is expected to weaken under global warming, but whether this signifies a transient response or a tipping transition remains unclear. Distinguishing between these cases requires a physical understanding of the boundary separating ocean states leading to AMOC recovery from those leading to collapse. In a global ocean model with 1{\deg} resolution, we compute an AMOC edge state -- an unstable saddle equilibrium that anchors this instability boundary. The edge state maintains weak overturning sourced by marginal deep water formation in the Nordic Seas. Analyzing the North Atlantic freshwater and heat balances that govern the edge state dynamics, we show that near the edge state, thermal and haline components of the surface buoyancy flux approximately compensate. Surface buoyancy loss (gain) coincides with AMOC recovery (collapse). Our findings support using the regional net surface buoyancy flux as an indicator for the onset of AMOC tipping.

Given its major role in the global ocean circulation and northward heat transport, a substantial AMOC decline would likely have large-scale climate impacts Jackson et al. (2015); Liu et al. (2020); Ben-Yami et al. (2024). However, it remains uncertain whether AMOC weakening under anthropogenic forcing represents a transient response with subsequent recovery or a tipping transition to a persistent collapsed circulation state Bonan et al. (2022); Guo et al. (2026); Drijfhout et al. (2025).

The tipping potential of the AMOC is supported by a hierarchy of climate models Dijkstra et al. (2026). Quasi-equilibrium hysteresis experiments imposing a slowly varying freshwater input over the North Atlantic consistently demonstrate a multistable AMOC regime in which a strong and a collapsed AMOC state coexist Stommel (1961); Rahmstorf et al. (2005); Hawkins et al. (2011); Van Westen and Dijkstra (2023). A key mechanism underlying this multistability is the salt-advection feedback Stommel (1961); Rahmstorf (1996); Dijkstra and Weijer (2005); Vanderborght et al. (2025), enabling self-sustaining AMOC change once a critical threshold has been crossed. Yet, distinguishing a tipping transition from transient weakening is difficult based on AMOC strength alone Börner and Dijkstra (2026). This distinction matters for understanding the stability and resilience of the AMOC, particularly its nonlinear sensitivity and reversibility under climate change scenarios.

The scenario of bifurcation-induced tipping Ashwin et al. (2012) forms the basis for statistical early-warning indicators based on critical slowing down, as applied to observational AMOC fingerprints Boers (2021); Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen (2023). Our results suggest that a vanishing BfluxB_{\text{flux}} correlates reasonably well with the separating boundary forming the stable manifold of the edge state. By linking dynamical systems ideas with oceanographic analysis, we hope to improve our understanding of the AMOC under present and future forcing.

papers.title: Instantiation of Human Values in Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models are increasingly embedded in everyday visual culture, yet little is known about how they translate abstract human values into visual scenes. We address this gap by introducing a framework, grounded in Schwartz's theory of basic human values, for studying value instantiation: the process by which ideals such as success, care, or freedom are visually realized. Using person-centered prompts from 70 positive and negative value items, we generate 28,000 images across four state-of-the-art T2I models. We identify visual prototypes, recurring combinations of subjects, actions, and settings, and use them to quantify how narrowly models instantiate these values and how this breadth compares with human descriptions of the same items. We then map these prototypes onto a taxonomy of social configurations spanning setting, sociality, mode of engagement, and social register, revealing what is systematically foregrounded or omitted. Our results show that T2I models produce far more concentrated representations than humans do when describing the same values. They default to a hyper-individualistic, adult-centric worldview, reproducing value-specific associations, such as achievement tied to formal institutional settings or hedonism rendered as affluent consumption, while marginalizing everyday labor, relational care, and non-adult perspectives. As a proof of concept, we show that these structural gaps can guide a steering method that diversifies outputs without modifying the original prompt.

papers.intro:
Text-to-Image (T2I) models have become powerful tools for generating high-quality images from textual prompts, with applications across art, education, and media (42). As these systems become embedded in everyday content production, their outputs circulate widely, making it important to examine not only what they generate, but also the social assumptions they reproduce. Recent work has documented demographic biases (14, 24), stereotypical portrayals (1, 6), and failures of cultural alignment (43, 30, 16). However, existing evaluations focus primarily on directly observable attributes, such as demographic representation, leaving underexplored how T2I models depict more subtle forms of social meaning, such as human values.

In AI research, values have been studied mainly in the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), especially through evaluations that infer value priorities from model-generated language (50, 38). These studies typically ask which values are most strongly expressed in model outputs: for example, whether responses give more weight to achievement than to benevolence across judgments, explanations, or hypothetical scenarios (50, 38). This priority-based framing, however, leaves open a different question: not which values are preferred, but which concrete realizations make a value recognizable in the first place. Cognitive and social psychology distinguish between values as abstract ideals (36) and their instantiations: the concrete behaviors, settings, and social contexts through which values are lived, expressed, and recognized (25, 19). Cross-cultural research shows that although people broadly agree on the importance of values such as success, they associate them with different situations, from career advancement and athletic achievement to familial responsibility or community contribution (18). This matters because values often become meaningful through concrete instantiations that shape which ways of realizing a value seem natural, recognizable, or legitimate (25).

This distinction is especially significant in image generation. While LLMs can, in principle, describe several possible ways a value might be instantiated in a single response, T2I models are forced to realize a value through a specific and coherent visual scene. Each output therefore specifies a subject, setting, activity, and set of social cues through which the concept becomes visually legible. For example, repeated depictions of success as an adult male in an elite institutional setting make one realization especially visible while underrepresenting other plausible instantiations of success. Despite these representational consequences, value instantiation remains unstudied in image generation.

papers.title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction
papers.abstract: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show that RECAP consistently outperforms the task-reward-only RL baselines on both environments, leading to an absolute improvement of 4.6% and 4.3% on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, respectively. Ablations further highlight the value of jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior for RECAP.
papers.intro:
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex tasks through reasoning, tool use, and multi-step interactions with their environments (Yao et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2021; Smith, 2025). Recent advances in post-training, particularly reinforcement learning (RL), have further improved agent performance in various challenging domains such as deep-research (Jin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), software engineering (Wei et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) and scientific discovery (Huang et al., 2026; Falck et al., 2026). However, as task horizons increase, LLM agents accumulate growing interaction histories that can exceed the context limit before task completion (Beltagy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2024). Thus, scaling LLM agents to long-horizon tasks requires effective management of the information retained in the context for subsequent decisions.

However, as task horizons increase, LLM agents accumulate growing interaction histories that can exceed the context limit before task completion (Beltagy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2024). Thus, scaling LLM agents to long-horizon tasks requires effective management of the information retained in the context for subsequent decisions.

Context compaction provides a straightforward approach to overcome context limits by consolidating an overlong interaction history into a compressed summary (Zhou et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). This simple yet effective mechanism allows agents to operate within a fixed context budget and has been widely adopted in various agent harnesses (Smith, 2025). In particular, earlier works have explored context compaction through carefully designed summarization prompts (Kang et al., 2025) or separately optimized compressors (Yi et al., 2026). More recent works focused on jointly training the agent policy and compaction through RL (Lu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). However, these approaches typically rely on final task rewards to optimize both compaction and task execution. In long trajectories, the effect of a compaction decision might propagate through many subsequent actions or later compactions, making credit assignment difficult. This raises a fundamental question: Is there a more direct learning signal for context compaction that can guide training long-horizon LLMs beyond task success?

In this paper, we introduce RECAP (REinforcement learning for Context compaction and Agent Policy optimization), a framework for training long-horizon agents with context compaction. Our key insight is that a useful summary should retain the information needed for subsequent decisions, thereby preserving the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the token-level KL divergence between the agent’s responses under compressed and original contexts. Here, the same policy conditioned on the original context serves as a self-teacher, specifying the behavior to be preserved after compaction.

We decompose the gradient of the distortion objective and show that it provides two complementary learning signals: (i) distortion-based reward for summary generation, and (ii) self-distillation for actions after compaction. The distortion-based reward assigns higher credit to summaries that induce less behavior distortion compared to the original context. The context self-distillation directly trains the subsequent actions using the full-context policy as the self teacher, providing dense token-level supervision to the same policy conditioned on the compressed context (Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). We combine these two learning signals with the task-success objective, jointly optimizing context compaction and the agent policy within a unified RL framework, which does not require any additional rollouts or environment interactions.

papers.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
papers.abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.
papers.intro:
Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly integrate evidence from multiple, potentially complementary technologies, including tissue profiling, targeted molecular assays, and genomic testing, among others. Within this landscape, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathology remains the most broadly available tissue readout in clinical practice, capturing morphological and architectural information at scale 1. In parallel, highly multiplexed spatial proteomics (Method of the Year 2024 by Nature Methods 2) extends H&E by quantifying dozens of proteins in situ while preserving spatial context. It enables molecularly specific readouts of cell identity, functional state, and microenvironment organization that complement morphology, including a more detailed characterization of the tumor immune microenvironment that impacts on immunotherapy response and resistance. Despite rapid methodological progress and clear translational promise 3, 4, 5, multiplex spatial proteomics is not yet part of routine clinical oncology due to cost, tissue requirements, operational complexity and the lack of a clear clinical framework for deployment. In addition, substantial variation in marker panels and acquisition protocols across studies and sites limits assay standardization and cross-site comparability, further hindering broad clinical deployment. Consequently, most patients are evaluated with H&E alone, and spatial proteomics is typically reserved for selected research cohorts, despite its complementary molecular specificity. This asymmetry creates a clear need for frameworks that can learn from cohorts with deep spatial readouts and transfer molecular and microenvironmental insight to routine H&E under the heterogeneous and partially observed conditions of clinical practice. Such a framework must address two coupled challenges: First, comprehensive tissue characterization increasingly requires integrating complementary modalities: H&E captures morphology and architecture, while spatial proteomics reveals molecular composition and cell state in their spatial context. Second, any clinically useful approach must translate insights from high-depth assays into tools that remain effective even when only routine histology is available.

These models learn general tissue representations that support diverse downstream tasks with minimal annotation, including prediction, stratification, and quantitative tissue phenotyping 8, 9, 10. However, most existing FMs are built for a single modality (unimodal), either H&E 8, 9, 11 or specific multiplex assays 10, 12, which limits their ability to learn how morphology relates to molecular cell states and microenvironment organization. This motivates a single multimodal FM that jointly learns from routine histology and spatial proteomics, so that specific molecular insights can inform standard analysis of slides while enabling unified inference when both modalities are available.

papers.title: A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations
papers.abstract: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nystr\"om approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.

papers.title: Anchoring VAE Fine-Tuning to Its Latent Diffusion Prior
papers.abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models are effective priors for transfer learning, from geometry estimation to physics simulation. Existing approaches fine-tune the diffusion backbone but freeze the encoder of the VAE to preserve the latent distribution. However, a frozen encoder may miss salient details in non-RGB inputs and is limited to three channels. We introduce Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), a regularizer applied during VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to steer latents toward the high-density manifold on which the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. We validate DPA across three image and video models (FLUX 3, LTX-Video, Wan2.2) and four tasks: monocular depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation, and surface normal estimation, where DPA lowers the prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE, 4.9% to decoder-only fine-tuning, and 4.0% to unanchored VAE fine-tuning. Its gain grows the further the target data lies from the RGB training distribution, from 3.3% on monocular depth estimation to 7.2% on complex-valued MRI. DPA also applies to modified VAEs, including pruned and multi-channel variants. With a four-channel VAE that encodes depth and surface normals, it lowers depth estimation error by 9.3%.
papers.intro:
Latent diffusion models pretrained on large-scale image and video collections provide powerful generative priors for transfer learning to downstream tasks. Fine-tuned on datasets far smaller than their pretraining corpora, they accurately estimate monocular depth and surface normals [29, 22, 46], simulate interactive environments in real time [60, 23], and serve as fast surrogates for physics simulations [47]. In each case, transfer learning exploits the structural prior that the diffusion backbone has learned in the latent space of a separately trained VAE [51].

Fine-tuned on datasets far smaller than their pretraining corpora, they accurately estimate monocular depth and surface normals [29, 22, 46], simulate interactive environments in real time [60, 23], and serve as fast surrogates for physics simulations [47]. In each case, transfer learning exploits the structural prior that the diffusion backbone has learned in the latent space of a separately trained VAE [51].

However, this paradigm rests on the assumption that the pretrained VAE accurately reconstructs the target domain. In practice, this confines adaptation to three-channel inputs and outputs that resemble natural RGB images or videos. In many domains of interest this assumption does not hold. Geometric maps, complex-valued MRI scans, and physical velocity fields share the spatial and temporal layout of natural images and videos, but fall outside the RGB pretraining distribution. Consequently, a frozen VAE reconstructs their pseudo-RGB encoding poorly. Modalities with more than three channels, such as joint depth and surface normals, cannot be encoded at all.

To unlock latent diffusion models for such domains one should adapt the VAE alongside the diffusion backbone. In current practice only the VAE decoder is fine-tuned, while the encoder is kept frozen [60, 46, 47] to preserve the expected latent distribution for the pretrained diffusion model. However, a decoder cannot recover information that the frozen encoder has not learned to preserve. Jointly updating both the encoder and the decoder might seem the obvious solution, except that fine-tuning the VAE solely for reconstruction is unconstrained with respect to the diffusion model. Latents thus drift away from the manifold on which the diffusion backbone was trained to denoise.

We propose Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), which regularizes VAE fine-tuning directly with the frozen diffusion model, via score distillation sampling (SDS) [48]. At each training step, an encoded latent is perturbed with noise, denoised by the frozen backbone, and pulled toward its clean estimate (, left). This steers the encoder toward latents that the pretrained prior recognizes and thus can denoise accurately, while the reconstruction loss preserves task-specific fidelity. DPA needs only forward passes of the diffusion model and adds no inference cost.

papers.title: ET: Efficient Transfer from Softmax to Hybrid Attention
papers.abstract: Converting pretrained softmax Transformers to efficient attention often causes substantial performance degradation, while recovery typically requires costly fine-tuning. We propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework for high-fidelity attention conversion with minimal optimization cost. ET combines exact local and shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating, achieving linear complexity in sequence length. To preserve pretrained knowledge, ET freezes pretrained weights and calibrates only newly introduced parameters through alternating least squares on a small set of unlabeled samples, without gradient updates. On ImageNet-1K, ET achieves 79.64% and 81.55% top-1 accuracy on DeiT-S and DeiT-B, respectively, within 0.25 percentage points of their softmax teachers. At $768\times768$, ET outperforms T$^5$ by 3.59 percentage points at comparable inference FLOPs, without gradient-based fine-tuning. On DiT-XL/2, ET achieves an FID-50K of 2.59 with only 250 LoRA updates. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ET matches the teacher's GenEval score at 1K resolution with just 0.73 A100 GPU-hours of gradient-free conversion and a 1.39$\times$ inference speedup.

In recent years, Vision Transformers (ViTs) [7, 28] have achieved remarkable success in image classification, visual representation learning, and image generation [13]. However, the quadratic complexity of softmax attention with respect to sequence length leads to substantial computational costs, particularly at high resolutions. Linear attention and other efficient attention mechanisms [5, 20, 33, 32] offer promising alternatives for reducing inference costs. Nevertheless, directly replacing softmax attention in pretrained Transformers often causes severe performance degradation, while training efficient architectures from scratch requires substantial computational resources. Efficiently transferring pretrained knowledge to alternative attention architectures, while preserving model performance and minimizing conversion costs, therefore remains an important challenge.

In recent years, Vision Transformers (ViTs) [7, 28] have achieved remarkable success in image classification, visual representation learning, and image generation [13]. However, the quadratic complexity of softmax attention with respect to sequence length leads to substantial computational costs, particularly at high resolutions. Linear attention and other efficient attention mechanisms [5, 20, 33, 32] offer promising alternatives for reducing inference costs. Nevertheless, directly replacing softmax attention in pretrained Transformers often causes severe performance degradation, while training efficient architectures from scratch requires substantial computational resources. Efficiently transferring pretrained knowledge to alternative attention architectures, while preserving model performance and minimizing conversion costs, therefore remains an important challenge.

Several studies have explored converting pretrained softmax Transformers into efficient attention models. For example, LiT [29] leverages pretrained weight initialization and knowledge distillation to convert Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) into linear attention models; T5 [23] introduces a Test-Time Training (TTT) architecture and recovers performance through fine-tuning; and LoLCATs [37] performs attention conversion through attention output matching and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [16]. These approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging pretrained knowledge to reduce the cost of developing efficient attention models. However, recovering performance after architectural conversion often still requires substantial gradient-based optimization. Meanwhile, gradient-free conversion methods [35] avoid expensive fine-tuning but can suffer considerable accuracy degradation when replacing all attention layers. These limitations highlight the need for an attention transfer framework that preserves pretrained capabilities with minimal optimization overhead while providing a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

In this paper, we investigate how to efficiently transfer pretrained softmax Transformers to hybrid attention architectures while minimizing performance degradation and optimization costs. Specifically, we address two key questions: (1) How can we design an efficient hybrid attention mechanism that preserves the essential interactions of the original softmax attention? (2) How can we leverage pretrained knowledge to recover model performance with minimal calibration and fine-tuning costs? To this end, we propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework that combines high-fidelity hybrid attention design with lightweight, gradient-free knowledge transfer.

Specifically, we address two key questions: (1) How can we design an efficient hybrid attention mechanism that preserves the essential interactions of the original softmax attention? (2) How can we leverage pretrained knowledge to recover model performance with minimal calibration and fine-tuning costs? To this end, we propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework that combines high-fidelity hybrid attention design with lightweight, gradient-free knowledge transfer.

Our core idea is to decompose attention into two complementary components: exact computation and efficient approximation (Fig. 2). Specifically, ET preserves exact softmax attention within local windows and over a small set of shared keys to retain important local and global interactions. For the remaining positions, ET preserves the exact mean of remote values and approximates only the query-dependent deviation through a scan-free global linear correction. Adaptive gating combines the exact and approximate branches, enabling efficient attention computation with linear complexity in sequence length. To transfer pretrained knowledge efficiently, ET inherits and freezes all original model weights and calibrates only newly introduced parameters through alternating least squares using a small number of unlabeled samples, without backpropagation or gradient updates. For challenging generative tasks, where approximation errors may accumulate across layers and sampling steps, the converted model further provides a high-quality initialization for lightweight LoRA recovery. ET thus integrates high-fidelity attention approximation and low-cost knowledge transfer within a unified framework.

papers.title: Open-OmniCoach: Evidence-Enhanced Trajectory Learning for Omni Video Agents
papers.abstract: Training capable omni video agents requires more than diverse question-answer pairs: agents must learn to reliably find, connect, and correct task-relevant evidence in omni-setting. However, we argue that existing data pipelines provide limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision for these capabilities. In this work, we present Open OmniCoach, a new framework for evidence-seeking omni video agents. It contains a high-quality dataset, OmniCoach-240K, and a new agentic reinforcement learning (RL) method, Step-Level Evidence-Guided Policy Optimization (SEPO). For the former, OmniCoach-240K comprises 248.2K interaction trajectories, including 230.7K multi-span trajectories and 17.4K reflection trajectories. We design a three-stage data pipeline by leveraging both fine-grained omni-evidence and the agent's own errors. Meanwhile, compared with other RL baselines, SEPO provides turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization. Applying both trajectory data and the SEPO method, we obtain Open OmniAgent models. The resulting models outperform the baselines across multiple video and audio-visual understanding tasks by significant margins, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Open OmniCoach framework. In particular, Open OmniAgent-30B improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks, with gains of 12.2 and 13.3 points on LVOmniBench and LVBench, respectively.

papers.title: Discovering Bandwidth-Efficient Prefetchers to Shrink the Cache Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.

papers.intro:
Over the past decade, last-level cache (LLC) capacity on server system-on-chips (SoCs) has grown rapidly to keep pace with demand, consuming an increasingly massive share of valuable compute silicon. For example, the shared 32 MB L3 takes roughly 44% of the eight-core AMD Zen 4 core complex and 37% of the full chiplet (Munger et al., 2023; Burd et al., 2024). This heavy reliance on large physical caches has run headfirst into a critical scaling barrier: while logic density continues to improve with each new technology node, high-density SRAM scaling has largely stalled (Yeap et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022). Consequently, server architects face a painful trade-off between cores and cache. They must either limit core counts to sustain sufficient cache capacity per core, or pack in more processing cores at the cost of drastically slashing the cache available to each (Burd et al., 2024; Amazon Web Services, 2026).
