This silicon tax raises a fundamental architectural question: how much on-chip cache capacity can a smarter data prefetcher replace without losing performance? In principle, a prefetcher can hide off-chip memory latency and match the performance of a much larger LLC. In practice, building one for a modern cache hierarchy without increasing bandwidth requirements is exceedingly hard (Srinath et al., 2007; Bera et al., 2021). A competitive prefetcher must coordinate across a multi-level cache hierarchy under strict metadata budgets (Wu et al., 2019; Pakalapati and Panda, 2020). Furthermore, it must not degrade performance when LLC capacity and DRAM bandwidth are scarce (Wu et al., 2011; Seshadri et al., 2015) and saturating off-chip memory buses (Lee et al., 2008).

Autonomous LLM agents offer a promising way to navigate the vast design space of multi-level data prefetchers. Recently, ArchAgent v2 (Gonzalez et al., 2026) showed that coding agents can evolve prefetchers that beat the championship-winning, hand-designed BertiGO (Singh et al., 2026) on single-core benchmarks. However, agentic hardware design hits a brutal bottleneck: cycle-level simulation is orders of magnitude slower than software benchmarks, with a full four-core (4C) evaluation taking over a day per design. This simulation wall severely constrains the search space that prior agentic systems can explore. ArchAgent v2 evolved only one cache level at a time on single-core and introduced multi-core configurations only in its final stage to save on simulation time. This cascaded approach leaves its design about 1.3% behind BertiGO under 4C shared-LLC contention while using 7% more 4C DRAM traffic (14% more than the baseline).

To scale agentic discovery beyond this simulation wall for multi-core systems, we introduce DuoArchitect. Building on the multi-fidelity paradigm of DuoDiscover (Agarwal et al., 2026), DuoArchitect dispatches fleets of sandboxed agents that co-evolve all three cache levels at once. Rather than waiting over a day for full simulation at every iteration, agents co-evolve prefetcher designs and fast local evaluators, called yardsticks, inside their sandboxes, substantially accelerating iterations while enabling joint multi-core optimization across all three cache levels. Promising candidates are then evaluated on a disclosed search set across a distributed simulation cluster before final evaluation on the full official set, which adds held-out workloads.

Over a ∼\sim13-day search, our flagship run (DuoArch-Nano) screened an estimated ∼\sim19,800 candidates on local yardsticks, evaluated 1,521 on the search set, and ran the official evaluation on only 22 new best designs. The resulting three-level prefetcher delivers a 9.2% overall geomean IPC speedup with the full-size DPC4 caches (Fig. 1a), with 9.6% at full bandwidth, 7.5% at limited bandwidth, and 10.5% on 4C (Fig. 6). papers.title: DesignEvo: Recovering and Tracking Repository-Level Implemented Design Systems Across Commits
papers.abstract: Modern frontend applications rely on design systems to maintain consistency across pages and releases. However, documentation and component libraries do not fully capture how interface patterns are implemented, reused, and adapted in practice. Existing UI analysis techniques focus on visual defects, interface structure, or element correspondences, providing limited support for automatically recovering and tracking implemented design systems at the repository level. To bridge this gap, we present DesignEvo, which combines screenshots, DOM structure, element geometry, and style values to recover functional UI groups. DesignEvo constrains vision-language model judgments to program-generated candidate regions, aggregates recovered groups and styles into repository-level records, and infers lifecycle states across adjacent commits. We evaluate DesignEvo on 10 open-source repositories comprising 317 page-version instances, 3,478 annotated functional UI groups, and 2,435 lifecycle-state labels. DesignEvo achieves an F1 score of 0.85 for group recovery and an overall lifecycle-state accuracy of 0.84, compared with 0.71 for the strongest lifecycle baseline. Ablations demonstrate the contributions of candidate constraints, functional categories, and style evidence. The resulting records provide structured, traceable evidence of recurring UI patterns and their evolution to support frontend maintenance and change auditing.

papers.intro:
Modern software user interfaces (UIs) are normally built on top of internal design systems: reusable component libraries, style values, and interaction conventions that encode the visual, structural, and behavioral rules the product’s UI is expected to follow (Google, n.d.). From a software engineering standpoint, a design system serves as the UI layer’s quality contract: an evolving specification that hundreds of pages and dozens of engineers are jointly expected to conform to. Its presence shapes downstream UI quality assurance, accessibility checking, cross-team governance, and long-term frontend maintenance (Yuan et al., 2025; Chiou et al., 2024; Mesbah and Mirshokraie, 2012; Mazinanian et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2024; zeroheight, n.d.). However, documented conventions do not always reflect how interface patterns are implemented and adapted in practice. As frontend applications evolve, locally modified components, inconsistent styling, and outdated patterns can accumulate across pages, making it increasingly difficult to understand and maintain UI consistency.

A design system is only partially documented. Its authoritative form lives in the frontend implementation—the components, class hierarchies, style tokens, and layout patterns actually rendered to users. The documented design system and the implemented design system are two artifacts that must be kept aligned, and in practice they routinely diverge. Engineers introduce a locally reasonable Card variant that never returns to the shared library; a color is hard-coded instead of referencing the shared token; a deprecated pattern lingers in three pages after the design system has retired it; a de facto convention emerges in code that the documentation has not yet acknowledged. We refer to all such gaps as design-system–implementation drifts. Some drifts are unintentional deviations that should be corrected; others are legitimate evolution signals that the design system itself should absorb (OverlayQA, n.d.). Distinguishing the two is a software quality-management decision that requires design-system-level evidence.

Second, design-system-level consistency is not the same as visual identity. Two regions may look different while following the same project convention, and two regions may look similar while relying on different structures or style values. We present DesignEvo, a cross-artifact approach that recovers repository-level implemented design-system records and tracks its functional UI group and family lifecycle states evolve across commits. Given selected repository versions, DesignEvo renders target pages and collects runtime evidence from screenshots, DOM hierarchies, UI-element boxes, and style records. It generates candidate regions from interactive containers, shared navigation targets, and DOM containers, and constrains a taxonomy-guided VLM to select, remove, or merge only these fixed candidates into functional UI groups. Finally, DesignEvo aggregates recovered groups and style values across pages into repository-level UI group families and their variants, and repository-shared style values. For every recovered family and functional UI group record, DesignEvo also infers a lifecycle state across adjacent commits—Reused, Changed, Introduced, Removed, or Ambiguous (Table 1)—giving human reviewers and downstream agents a design-system-level view of each change and a basis for deciding whether to absorb it into the design system or revert against it.

papers.title: Towards determination of intrinsic spin properties in MAPbI$_3$ crystals using spin noise spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Spin noise spectroscopy in back- and forward-scattering geometries is used to study the spin dynamics of charge carriers in a MAPbI$_3$ (MA = methylammonium) single crystal. The spectra reveal electrons and holes with different degrees of localization. At low temperatures ($T \approx 4$~K), hole spin relaxation is dominated by the hyperfine interaction with nuclear spins. The broadening of the spectra with increasing temperature can be attributed to thermally activated hopping of localized holes. From the thermal activation energies, we estimate hole localization lengths that are consistent with both the hyperfine-induced dephasing rates and the zero-field frequency shifts measured at low temperature. By contrast, the electron spin dynamics cannot be explained by the hyperfine interaction alone: even at the lowest excitation powers, it is affected by the probe light, and we observe a slowing down of spin relaxation with increasing power. Comparison of the back- and forward-scattered spin noise signals indicates that the spatial distribution of carriers is inhomogeneous: electrons are located preferentially near the crystal surface, weakly localized holes (characterized by slower spin relaxation) are found mostly away from the surface, and strongly localized holes are somewhere in between.

Methylammonium lead triiodide (MAPbI3) is one of the most studied hybrid organic-inorganic lead halide perovskites. The great attention that it has attracted was initially due to its photovoltaic efficiency [2]. Later on MAPbI3 has been reported to exhibit up to tens of nanoseconds long carrier spin lifetimes, positioning it as an attractive system for exploring spin coherence in a solution-processable semiconductor [31, 17, 21, 10, 26, 23, 18, 20]. However, despite extensive efforts, the nature of carriers and thus the mechanisms governing spin relaxation in these systems remain insufficiently understood.

Methylammonium lead triiodide (MAPbI3) is one of the most studied hybrid organic-inorganic lead halide perovskites. The great attention that it has attracted was initially due to its photovoltaic efficiency [2]. Later on MAPbI3 has been reported to exhibit up to tens of nanoseconds long carrier spin lifetimes, positioning it as an attractive system for exploring spin coherence in a solution-processable semiconductor [31, 17, 21, 10, 26, 23, 18, 20]. However, despite extensive efforts, the nature of carriers and thus the mechanisms governing spin relaxation in these systems remain insufficiently understood.

A central open question for this material is the microscopic mechanism that limits carrier spin relaxation in the orthorhombic, low-temperature phase. In conventional semiconductors two mechanisms are usually invoked. For free (delocalized) carriers, spin relaxation is expected to proceed via the Dyakonov-Perel (DP) mechanism, in which momentum scattering randomizes the spin precession in a kk-dependent effective spin–orbit field associated with local inversion-symmetry breaking [8]. While some experiments point out that DP spin-relaxation mechanism is inactive in MAPbI3 crystals with orthorhombic symmetry [20], other studies report Rashba-type spin splittings at low temperature in hybrid perovskites, attributed to low-symmetry domains, or local electric fields from defects [30, 25]. Whether such extrinsic or local inversion-symmetry breaking is strong enough to make DP relaxation relevant in MAPbI3 crystals remains an open question.

In lead halide perovskites HF coupling is much stronger for holes than for electrons [26, 21, 22], but for both types of carriers the resulting coherence times depend on the localization volume and eventually on the spin hopping rate [14, 12]. To make the picture even more complex, the presence of holes with different localization volumes (referred to as weakly (h1) and strongly (h2) localized holes) has been reported [21]. Remarkably, weakly localized holes have only been observed in single crystals of MAPbI3, but not in thin polycrystalline films [10, 26].

Spin noise (SN) spectroscopy is a powerful technique which has been extensively used to explore intrinsic spin properties of conventional bulk semiconductors [32, 14]. It relies on mapping of stochastic fluctuations of electron and/or hole spins at thermal equilibrium onto Kerr (Faraday) rotation and/or ellipticity fluctuations of the Raman-scattered light using continuous wave probe beam tuned below exciton resonance [32, 37]. Fourier spectrum of these fluctuations provides new insights into spin dynamics of electrons and holes, as compared to photo-induced Kerr (Faraday) rotation, and photoluminescence-based Hanle and polarization recovery experiments, in particular due to minimized density of photocarriers. Moreover, because the SN spectra of electrons and holes in MAPbI3 at non-zero magnetic field are centered at different frequencies, their individual contributions can be easily separated, in contrast to Hanle and polarization recovery experiments, where the magnetic field is scanned through zero and additional hypotheses are needed to separate electrons and holes [21, 26].

SN experiments in perovskites has been reported only recently [23, 24]. These first experiments, performed in forward-scattering geometry, identified a single Lorentzian SN resonance in MAPbI3 thick crystals. It was assigned to delocalized holes, with a spin relaxation time of several nanoseconds that decreases with increasing temperature, a trend the authors argued was inconsistent with a HF-limited mechanism and instead attributed to DP relaxation of delocalized carriers. This assignment — a different carrier population (delocalized rather than localized) relaxing via a different mechanism (DP rather than HF) — stands in direct tension with the picture built from reflection-geometry photoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved Kerr rotation measurements [20, 21, 17]. The discrepancy has been noted by the authors of Ref. 23 as possibly arising from the difference between forward and back-scattering geometries, i.e., from the possibility that each technique preferentially probes a different subset of the carrier population.

Our results bridge, at least partly, the gap between the observations made using these different experimental techniques. Relying on comparison of SN spectra with the Hanle and polarization recovery profiles measured via PL in similar samples [21], we suggest that these methods probe the same families of spin carriers. In addition, SN spectra detected at different energies in both forward- and back-scattering geometries indicate that spatial distribution of carriers is inhomogeneous. This is followed by the presentation of a typical SN spectrum and identification of its constituents in Section III. Probe energy, power and temperature dependencies are analyzed in Sections IV, V and VI, respectively. Section VII shows how a combination of back- and forward-scattering SN spectra allows us to uncover spatial inhomogeneity of the spin carrier distribution. Finally, in Section VIII we summarize the results and discuss our experimental observations in comparison with available data from the literature. Section IX presents the conclusions.

papers.title: Sub-Riemannian structure for Oriented Point Clouds
papers.abstract: Many frameworks dealing with 3D (oriented) point clouds define locality in the ambient Euclidean space: $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs and radius balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are critical to define which points are "close to one another" and should exchange information. This can unintentionally merge sampled surfaces that are close in space but geometrically distinct such as the two faces of a thin leaf. Then, features are more prone to leak across boundaries which hinder performance. To address this, we propose to define a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$: points are lifted to $(x,n)$ with $n$ a surface normal, and "motion" is constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution in which spatial velocity must stay in the plane orthogonal to the normal which can reorient at a cost. From this, we derive an explicit score, which locally approximate the distance, to compare oriented points for downstream tasks. We report improved segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contact when using the score as a drop-in change inside PointNet++ aggregation mechanism as well as reduced leakage when using it to simulate heat diffusion on oriented points.

To deal with unstructured 3D data, such as (oriented) point clouds, triangle soups and Gaussian splats (Kerbl et al., 2023), many networks (Qi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019), equivariant architectures (Thomas et al., 2018; Fuchs et al., 2020), and classical geometry processing algorithms (Taubin, 1995; Fleishman et al., 2003), define locality as Euclidean. Neighborhoods are kk-Nearest Neighbor (kkNN) sets or radius balls in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, and convolutions, message passing, or diffusions act over them.

One way or another, this encodes the assumption that points close in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} are more likely to exchange information. This assumption is challenged as soon as distinct pieces of surface pass near one another: two stacked leaves in a plant, a wall, or a sheet of metal are separated by a relatively small distance and angle (opposite or co-oriented) normals. A point near an acute angle has a kkNN ball encompassing both incident faces, folded and layered geometry stacks surfaces within any fixed radius. In all these cases Euclidean neighborhoods mix samples that should belong to distinct geometric semantic (such as for two parallel sheets). This can make denoisers merge distinct folds, segmentation labels may leak through thin structures. The standard workaround such as visibility heuristics, clustering the kkNN by normal, hand-tuned anisotropic neighborhoods, and others treat symptoms case by case depending on the task. To address this, some approaches starts from the Euclidean neighborhood and re-weight it by normal similarity (Fleishman et al., 2003; Guerrero et al., 2018), or add a normal term to the distance (Rusinkiewicz and Levoy, 2001) but these are limited for describing strong orientation anisotropy. Sub-Riemannian (SR) geometry offers a rigorous framework for this construction including in particular a strongly anisotropic metric to encode forbidden short-circuits mentioned earlier. We strongly advise the reader to read through Appendix A for a simplified background on sub-riemannian geometry and contact metric. This type of structure on roto-translation groups has demonstrated its interest for contour perception and crossing-preserving image enhancement (Petitot, 2003; Citti and Sarti, 2006; Franken and Duits, 2009; Duits et al., 2016; Boscain et al., 2014), and have recently powered equivariant PDE networks on images (Smets et al., 2023; Bellaard et al., 2023). Those constructions lift curves in images, aligning spatial motion along the orientation. Here, we propose to adapt this idea to surfaces described as unstructured (oriented) point sets rather than grids.

papers.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.

Coding agents have become capable of writing competent robot navigation code [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], but navigation still has open challenges [6, 7] and the research addressing them continues to advance, with scientific output growing by roughly 4%4\% per year [8]. Even a model trained on that research is unlikely to recall every relevant finding, or to think of applying it to the specific task in front of it. In particular, how reliably a model recalls a fact depends on how often it appears in its pre-training data [9, 10], and its effective knowledge cutoff often precedes the reported one [11]. Research literature could therefore complement the knowledge of a model in three ways. Firstly, novelty: findings published after the training cutoff cannot be recalled at all. Secondly, coverage: when asked plainly, a model tends to reproduce the few mechanisms most represented in its training data, while the literature contains a wide variety of alternatives. papers.title: AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly pay for data and computation through protocols such as x402 and AP2, but individually funded wallets idle and require asset transfers for every payment. We present AgentBank, a smart-contract banking layer that lets agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits. Internal payments update account balances without transferring assets, while pooled backing funds are allocated between reserves and yield-bearing strategies. We bound losses from compromised agent keys and analyze how correlated demand affects reserve requirements. Experiments show that AgentBank reduces idle liquidity by 52-77% relative to per-agent wallets and lowers gas costs for batched internal payments. Using historical DeFi liquidity data, we evaluate how reserve policies balance treasury returns against payment availability during market stress. We further examine the risks of automated bank runs and evaluate mechanisms to mitigate them.

On Base, x402 recorded 136.7 million settlements in 280 days, although most of this count is fictitious or operator-internal rather than independent demand [46].

These systems share one financial abstraction, the wallet. An agent’s payment capacity is the balance of a wallet funded for that agent, possibly guarded by spending policies [16]. This abstraction creates three costs. First, liquidity is fragmented. Each wallet must be prefunded for its own peak demand, and task-driven agent demand is bursty, so the sum of per-agent buffers far exceeds what aggregate demand requires. Second, prefunded balances are idle and earn nothing. Third, every payment, even between agents of the same ecosystem, transfers the settlement asset on-chain. In addition, a security concern arises that an agent manipulated through prompt or memory injection [52] can spend whatever its wallet holds unless limits are enforced below the model.

Banking resolves the first three costs by construction. A bank balance is a liability rather than ownership of specific assets. Payments between accounts reassign liabilities without moving reserves, and the bank holds liquid reserves only against net outflows, deploying the remainder productively [21, 39]. Tokenized deposits carry this separation onto programmable ledgers [25, 4, 8, 34]. The same transformation creates fragility: backing assets deployed into DeFi venues can become illiquid when they are needed most. After the KelpDAO exploit of 18 April 2026, the USDC market of Aave v3 on Ethereum remained at 99.87% utilization for four days, leaving suppliers of $1.89 billion unable to withdraw [45, 56]. Fractional reserves also invite runs [21, 28], and on-chain transparency is known to accelerate them [47, 2], a concern that sharpens when depositors are themselves automated agents.

Deployed agent-payment systems occupy two corners of a design space: a funded wallet holds a full reserve for each agent, and an agent that holds yield-bearing tokens invests its entire balance. This work presents AgentBank , a smart-contract banking layer for AI agents that occupies the interior, where pooled liabilities are backed by a reserve whose size is a policy choice, and studies the efficiency–resilience trade-off that this choice introduces. The problem joins stablecoin reserve design, delegated strategy management, and transaction ordering in a setting where both payers and depositors are machines. We make three contributions. 1.) We design AgentBank, a smart-contract banking architecture that allows agents to spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates with on-chain spending limits. Payments between accounts are settled internally, while pooled backing assets are allocated between a settlement reserve and approved yield-bearing strategies under on-chain reserve and haircut-adjusted coverage constraints. Uncovered external payments enter an expiring queue. Solvency-contingent redemption governs payouts after impairment. Extensions include forward pricing, epoch settlement, and liquidity fees. 2.) We prove balance-sheet conservation and bound losses from compromised agent keys. We show that pooled reserve requirements converge to a single-factor (Vasicek) limit under correlated demand, derive a granularity adjustment for finite pools, and establish why the conventional square-root law underestimates liquidity requirements. We further show that sequential redemption at par concentrates losses on depositors who redeem later, while solvency-contingent redemption eliminates this first-mover advantage after loss recognition, absent further losses or liquidation costs. 3.) We evaluate a Solidity prototype against EIP-3009 and ERC-4337 baselines to measure the gas cost of delegated payments. Using bursty, correlated agent demand and historical lending-pool data, we quantify idle-liquidity savings of 52–77% relative to per-agent wallets and attribute them to owner pooling, bank pooling, and payment internalization. We also characterize the trade-off between treasury returns and payment availability during the April 2026 liquidity freeze, estimate reserve requirements for Treasury-bill-only strategies, and measure how fast automated depositors exhaust reserves.

papers.title: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
papers.abstract: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

Trained on large and diverse video datasets, modern video foundation models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating complex human activities, coordinated movements, and interactions between people, objects and the environment. These capabilities suggest that their learned representations extend beyond visual appearance, capturing useful knowledge about human motion and the relationships that govern human behavior. This raises an interesting question: can the motion knowledge embedded in video foundation models be used to generate more natural and semantically meaningful 3D human motion?

papers.title: Cup products with volume classes in bounded cohomology
papers.abstract: Let $M$ be a complete Riemannian $n$-manifold, $n\geq 2$, and suppose that either $M$ is negatively curved, or that it is a locally symmetric space of non-compact type. Via integration over straight simplices, every top-degree bounded differential form $\omega\in \Omega_b^n(M)$ defines a bounded cohomology class in $H^n_b(M)$. We prove that every such class belongs to the annihilator of the cup product in the whole graded algebra $H^{\geq 1}_b(M)$. In the case of closed orientable surfaces, this generalizes a result of Marasco, and, via transfer, provides a new proof of the fact that the cup product of the bounded Euler class of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ with itself vanishes. Our result also applies to degree-3 bounded classes constructed by Soma and Farre, thus showing that, for surface groups and for free groups, the annihilator of the cup product is infinite dimensional also in degree 3.

papers.title: Generating Property-Based Regression Tests from Source Code Semantics
papers.abstract: Conventional unit tests (CUTs) check a method under test at fixed concrete inputs. A test can therefore miss a regression if its input produces the expected output despite a fault. Property-based testing (PBT) checks universally quantified specifications across many randomly generated inputs, but writing properties and input generators by hand is difficult. Existing approaches automate PBT creation by generalizing an existing or generated unit test suite. They either over-approximate concrete inputs across repetitive tests or apply single-path symbolic analysis along concrete test runs. This paper presents an approach that derives property-based regression tests directly from source code semantics via multipath symbolic execution (SE). For each explored path through a target method, the approach records a path semantics comprising the path condition, the symbolic return value, and the state change map. Each path semantics induces a Hoare triple that compiles into an executable property. Because SE leaves parts of a class unspecified, the approach complements the generated properties with search-based CUTs for the whole class. We evaluate our Java implementation against EvoSuite and the test generalization tool Teralizer on EqBench and on 11 projects from TOGBench. On EqBench, our approach keeps validated properties for 82.0% of all methods. Its mean mutation score of 63.8% exceeds the 55.2% of EvoSuite and the 60.3% of Teralizer. On TOGBench, target selection, SE limitations, and property validation restrict validated properties to 2.8% of all methods. The resulting mean mutation score of 48.6% falls below the 50.9% of EvoSuite and the 51.1% of Teralizer. Failures during test generation leave a few classes without effective tests and lead to this gap.

papers.intro:
Automated unit test generators such as EvoSuite [1] and Randoop [2] generate conventional unit tests (CUTs) that target structural coverage and assert the behavior observed at concrete inputs. High structural coverage, however, does not guarantee fault detection [3, 4]. When a change or mutant alters an operation along an executed path, a CUT still passes if the fault does not change the output for that test’s input. This failure to expose an executed fault is known as coincidental correctness [5, 6]. Figure 1, Step 1 shows an example of a test suite containing CUTs that achieve full branch coverage, but fail to detect the behavioral change of the method under test. Data-driven test parameterization merges similar CUTs or recorded calls into parameterized unit tests (PUTs), but still checks only a fixed list of inputs [7, 8, 9]. Property-based testing (PBT) [10, 11] instead pairs an input generator with a parametric assertion and checks the assertion across newly sampled inputs on every run, killing more mutants per test than CUTs [12].

However, property-based tests remain rare in practice [12, 13]. Developers struggle to state general postconditions without a reference implementation and to write generators that satisfy input preconditions [14, 15]. Manually converting existing unit tests into properties also requires rewriting test setup and oracle code [13]. Recent approaches therefore automate PBT creation by generalizing existing or generated unit tests [16, 17]. Peleg et al. [16] group repetitive test execution traces into scenarios and instantiate predefined abstraction templates over their concrete values. Because these templates over-approximate the observed examples, the generated properties can fail on valid code. Glock et al. [17] instead run single-path symbolic analysis along the concrete execution path of each CUT to extract a path-exact specification. However, starting from CUTs restricts generalization to execution paths that a CUT already traverses and to behaviors that its assertions explicitly check. Their tool Teralizer also requires mapping each assertion back to a single tested method call and supports only pure, non-void methods without field updates.

papers.title: MINDS: The mid-infrared spectrum of the disk, jets, and winds of DG Tau
papers.abstract: DG Tau is one of the best-studied young stellar objects in transition from a Class I protostar to a T Tauri star. It is no longer embedded in a dense molecular cloud, but still reveals features that are commonly seen in protostars at earlier evolutionary stages. DG Tau hosts a protoplanetary disk and two energetic jets that can be studied down to the immediate environment of the star and disk at optical, infrared, and X-ray wavelengths. We use the Medium Resolution Spectrometer of MIRI on the James Webb Space Telescope. DG Tau's mid-infrared spectrum consists of a very bright continuum with various silicate features, and lines of CO, H$_2$O, OH, H I, H$_2$, Ne$^{+}$, Ne$^{2+}$, Ar$^{+}$, Fe$^{+}$, and Ni$^{+}$. We find substantial grain growth to at least 2 $\mu$m at an early evolutionary stage. Lines of H$_2$O and CO are formed at extremely high temperatures (600-2000 K). The ratio of warm to hot water is the lowest among previous observations of disks with JWST. This and a very strong continuum point toward the relevance of the strong accretion of DG Tau and consequently strong stellar UV irradiation. The pair of jets reveals a rich spectrum of emission lines from ions, in particular producing forbidden lines of [Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], and [Ni II]. The forward jet shows a collimated structure as found previously, while the hitherto poorly described, receding jet is more widely dispersed on scales of several arcsec, showing a layered structure with the fastest components being the most collimated. The ionization of the jet gas cannot be reconciled with high-energy radiation from the star itself. Instead, we propose a unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model in which the previously studied X-ray jet plasma continuously cools, recombining ions until, at temperatures around $10^4$ K and below, metals at low ionization stages emit the observed ion lines.

papers.intro:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST; Gardner et al. 2023) has fundamentally changed our view on protoplanetary disks (PPDs), particularly with respect to their structure, evolution, and composition, thanks to its order-of-magnitude increase in terms of the spatial resolution, spectral resolution, and sensitivity, especially in the mid-infrared (MIR) range (Argyriou et al. 2023). Currently, PPDs are revealing very diverse chemistry and compositions, ranging from carbon-rich compositions with highly abundant hydrocarbon molecules (Arabhavi et al. 2025b) to disks where emission from water dominates (Perotti et al. 2023; Gasman et al. 2023; Banzatti et al. 2025; Temmink et al. 2025). It is not yet clear whether such differences are entirely related to stellar mass (e.g., Grant et al. 2025; Arabhavi et al. 2025a) or whether they might also reflect an evolutionary scenario (Mah et al. 2024; Houge et al. 2025; see Grant et al. 2025 for a discussion of the dichotomy seen among very low-mass stars and classical T Tauri stars [CTTSs]).

It has been empirically demonstrated that the mechanism of accretion through a disk is coupled to disk mass loss in the form of a molecular uncollimated wind or a collimated jet, often seen in forbidden lines of, for example, [O I] and [S ii] in the optical (e.g., Hartigan et al. 1995), [Fe ii] in the near infrared (NIR; e.g., Agra-Amboage et al. 2011; White et al. 2014a), or [Ne ii] in the MIR (van Boekel et al. 2009; Güdel et al. 2010). Models for the jet and disk-wind mass loss include magnetohydrodynamic, and in particular, magnetocentrifugal winds that can radially extend from ∼\sim0.1 au to tens of au in the youngest objects (Blandford and Payne 1982; Pelletier and Pudritz 1992; Ferreira 1997), including fast jets from the innermost disk region and slow winds in outer regions, revealing an “onion-like” velocity structure around the outflow axis (e.g., Bacciotti et al. 2000, see Pascucci et al. 2023 and Frank et al. 2014 for reviews). For more evolved CTTSs, thermally driven photoevaporative flows launched at typically 1−101-10 au from the star result in slow winds. These show velocities of a few km s-1 and may be important for the formation of disk gaps in the later evolution of a PPD (Ercolano et al. 2008; Gorti and Hollenbach 2009; Gorti et al. 2009; Owen et al. 2010).

The JWST guaranteed-time program MIRI Mid-Infrared Disk Survey (MINDS, PID: 1282, PI T. Henning, Henning et al. 2024) is addressing structure, composition, and dynamics of a large sample of protoplanetary disks covering a wide range of stellar masses and evolutionary stages. Apart from disks around CTTS, the sample includes brown dwarf disks, disks around Herbig stars, and debris disks. Focusing on observations in the MIR utilizing the Mid InfraRed Instrument (MIRI; Wright et al. 2015), the program is specifically tuned to characterize inner disks; it also includes some objects that are known to drive disk winds, jets, and outflows.

papers.title: Modified recombination or dynamical dark energy (or both)?
papers.abstract: Several recent analyses report a hint of modified recombination when the latest cosmic microwave background (CMB) and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data are jointly analysed. We examine whether this preference persists when allowing for departures in the late-time expansion history of the Universe. We fit a seven-parameter reconstruction of the free-electron fraction and a $w_0w_a$ dark-energy model, separately and jointly, to DESI DR2 BAO, a $5\times2$pt combination of galaxy clustering and CMB lensing, and three CMB likelihoods: P-ACT, Planck PR4 and Planck 2018. With a cosmological constant, our baseline data combination favours early recombination near last scattering, agreeing with previous analyses. Allowing for dynamical dark energy (DDE) removes this preference, while the constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$ change little when the recombination history is marginalised over. DDE has the lowest Akaike information criterion of the models we consider for every data combination, and adding recombination freedom to it raises the AIC by $5.1$--$11.7$ and is disfavoured by the Bayesian evidence. We interpret these results in terms of CMB predictions for the BAO distances: earlier recombination and DDE both shift these predictions towards the measurements, but only DDE also changes the redshift dependence of the late-time expansion, which anisotropic BAO measurements constrain. We support these conclusions using noiseless mock data, finding that fitting modified recombination to a mock Universe generated with DDE reproduces the apparent preference for modified recombination, whereas DDE cannot similarly reproduce the signatures of modified recombination. The preference for modified recombination found with a cosmological constant therefore reflects the discrepancy between the CMB and BAO, rather than independent evidence for departures from standard recombination physics.

papers.intro:
Baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements from DESI DR2 are in mild tension with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) when both are interpreted within Λ\LambdaCDM. This tension is a disagreement between the low-redshift distances that BAO measures, using the sound horizon as a standard ruler, and the values predicted for those distances from the CMB under an assumed model for the late-time expansion. Allowing the dark-energy equation of state to evolve reduces this tension. In addition, dynamical dark energy (DDE) changes the shape of the late-time expansion history, which the BAO measurements probe directly, and these measurements mildly prefer a shape that departs from Λ\LambdaCDM. Analysed together, the CMB and BAO favour DDE over Λ\LambdaCDM at 3.1​σ3.1\sigma, and at 2.82.8–4.2​σ4.2\sigma when type Ia supernovae are included, depending on the compilation (Abdul Karim and others, 2025a). Abandoning the cosmological constant would be a substantial revision of the standard model, and the claim has accordingly been scrutinised from several directions: whether it is driven by the supernova compilations and their calibration (Efstathiou, 2025; Colgáin and Sheikh-Jabbari, 2025), and whether the apparent frequentist significance is matched by Bayesian evidence (Ong et al., 2025). Furthermore, explanations that preserve the cosmological constant and instead reduce the tension in other ways have also been considered.

Finally, we ask how the conclusions change when the distance-ladder measurement of H0H_{0} is taken at face value and included in the analysis.

papers.title: 3D Tracking Any Point with Events and Frames
papers.abstract: Tracking a fast-moving point in 3D is prohibitive when RGB frames are blurred or too far apart to reveal its motion. Event cameras record brightness changes between frames, providing measurements inside these temporal gaps. We introduce TrackAnyMotion, which combines monocular RGB frames and events to track arbitrary points in 2D and 3D, including at times when no RGB frame is available. The motion expected for a static point, given scene geometry and camera motion, provides a reference for identifying independently moving objects. An independent-motion decoder combines geometric motion cues with event guidance and 2D tracks, feeding its predictions back into iterative 2D and 3D refinement. We also introduce HyperEvent, a synthetic RGB--Event dataset with high-frequency 3D trajectories, geometry, and independent-motion labels. At RGB frame timestamps on this benchmark, TrackAnyMotion reduces 3D and 2D endpoint errors by 70\% and 32\%, respectively.

papers.title: From Fermions to Vortices: Microscopic Simulations of Phase Ordering in a d-Wave Superconductor
papers.abstract: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian remains a formidable challenge. Here we develop a microscopic framework for this problem using the recently introduced adiabatic variational principle (AVP) and demonstrate its application to a two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductor. The central construction maps evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with the associated Lagrange multipliers determining the thermodynamic driving forces. This enables dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining its microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Starting from disordered pairing configurations, we resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework. The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

papers.title: Better-than-3 Approximation for 2ECSS Using the Primal-Dual Method
papers.abstract:
In the $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph problem (2ECSS), we are given an undirected multigraph whose edges have nonnegative costs, and the goal is to find a $2$-edge-connected spanning subgraph with minimum total cost. Two distinct approaches yield $2$-approximation algorithms: a reduction to the minimum-cost rooted $2$-arborescence problem and iterative rounding. Despite significant efforts, the best known approximation ratio using the primal-dual method has remained at $3$.
  Our main result in this work is a primal-dual algorithm for 2ECSS that achieves an approximation ratio of $\sqrt{3}+1 (\leq 2.74)$. The algorithm runs in a single phase and the approximation guarantee is relative to the natural linear relaxation, which requires the sum of the edge variables across every cut to be at least $2$. The algorithm follows the standard template of growing dual variables corresponding to minimal violated sets, albeit at non-uniform rates, until the dual constraint for an edge becomes tight, at which point the edge is temporarily purchased. Once feasibility is attained, redundant edges are dropped in the reverse order in which they were purchased.
  Our choice of dual growth rates is inspired by the single-phase $3$-approximation algorithm of Beyer, Chimani, and Spoerhase (COCOON 2020). As in their work, our algorithm maintains a forest of purchased edges by repeatedly contracting $2$-edge-connected subgraphs, and dual variables corresponding to leaves and isolated vertices of this forest are grown at a rate of $1$. Our main modification is to additionally grow dual variables corresponding to nontrivial connected components at rate $(\sqrt{3}-1)/2 \approx 0.37$, when the forest is disconnected.

papers.title: Integrated lasing and dual-band gain in neodymium-implanted silicon nitride
papers.abstract: Lasers at wavelengths near 1 micrometer are used in quantum technologies, precision metrology, and sensing. Rare-earth gain at these wavelengths in photonic integrated circuits can reduce the size and enable the scalable fabrication of these lasers. We fabricate neodymium-based integrated waveguide amplifiers and a ring laser using neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride. The photonic integrated circuits were fabricated on a 200 mm commercial wafer platform, and individual dies were implanted with neodymium ions. We show that the amplifiers provide gain in two bands around wavelengths of 920 nm and 1100 nm, and we show lasing in a ring resonator. This demonstrates that neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride is a suitable gain material for integrated lasers.

Since the first demonstrations of neodymium-doped glass (Nd:glass) lasers in 1961 and neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) lasers in 1964 [1, 2], Nd3+-based gain media have played a central role in solid-state laser technology. Both systems exploit the F3/24→I11/24{}^{4}F_{3/2}\rightarrow{}^{4}I_{11/2} transition of Nd3+, providing near-infrared emission at a wavelength around 1.06 µ​m1.06\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, typically under optical pumping at a wavelength near 808 nm808\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}. Nd:YAG combines a large emission cross section, favorable four-level laser dynamics, and excellent thermal properties, making it particularly suitable for efficient continuous-wave and high-power operation. Nd:glass, on the other hand, offers a broader emission bandwidth, favorable energy-storage properties, and greater flexibility in material composition and fabrication, establishing its importance in high-energy laser amplification and ultrashort-pulse systems [3, 4].

Despite their widespread use in industrial, scientific, and medical applications, conventional Nd-based laser systems often rely on bulk gain media and free-space optical components. Nd-doped fiber lasers offer a more compact alternative, benefiting from efficient optical confinement and improved thermal management. Meanwhile, the growing demand for compact and scalable photonic systems, largely driven by the telecom and datacom markets, has accelerated the development of silicon photonics, combining low-loss passive waveguides, high-speed modulators, and heterogeneously integrated light sources. In this context, rare-earth-doped waveguide amplifiers and lasers have emerged as promising candidates for integrating optical gain on-chip. In particular, erbium-doped waveguide amplifiers (EDWAs), the integrated counterparts of erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs), have been demonstrated through ion implantation into low-loss silicon nitride (Si3​N4\mathrm{Si}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4}) waveguides [5, 6]. In parallel, reactive co-sputtering of rare-earth-doped aluminum oxide (Al2​O3\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}) has enabled not only erbium-based integrated amplifiers and lasers but also other rare-earths such as thulium (Tm3+), and holmium (Ho3+), operating across different wavelength bands [7, 8, 9]. These developments (Fig. 1 (a)) highlight the versatility of rare-earth-doped materials for integrated optical gain, while the combination of low-loss silicon nitride photonics and ion implantation, both well-established in CMOS fabrication, offers a scalable, wafer-level approach to their integration.

papers.title: Self-Sensing Compliant Anthropomorphic Hand for Speed-Dictated Shared Force Control in Teleoperation
papers.abstract: In vision-based teleoperation of robotic hands, the operator receives no haptic feedback and therefore struggles to regulate the grasp force, while adding tactile sensors to the fingers increases wiring, cost and integration complexity. Compliant hands offer an alternative, as their mechanical compliance, usually treated only as a passive property for safe and adaptive grasping, can also serve as a source of information. Here, we show that the elastic transmission of a compliant, tendon-driven anthropomorphic hand can itself act as the sensor for shared-control telemanipulation. Series springs in the tendon routing are read by potentiometers in a forearm-mounted motor box, from which the hand estimates its joint states and finger forces without any external sensors. Building on this self-sensing, we develop a contact-aware shared-control framework for VR-based teleoperation. The robot hand is controlled through a mapping from the operator's hand kinematics until a contact is detected proprioceptively. Control then switches to a finger-level force controller whose set point is determined by the operator's grasping speed, and control authority can be allocated to individual fingers. Experiments validate the system's force estimation and increased grasp success rate compared with direct teleoperation for fragile and heavy objects. These results show that compliance can serve not only for passive adaptation but also as an intrinsic sensing resource for physical human-robot collaboration.

papers.intro:
Teleoperation allows human operators to guide robots through tasks in which full autonomy remains unreliable, and it has become the main route for collecting human demonstrations for robot learning [1, 2]. For multifingered anthropomorphic hands, the operator’s hand is commonly tracked with RGB-D cameras [3, 4], data gloves [5] or, increasingly, virtual-reality (VR) headsets that track the bare hand without tethered hardware [6, 7, 8]. These interfaces map human finger motion to the robot accurately in free space, but they are purely kinematic because the operator sees the scene but cannot feel it. Once the fingers touch an object, the operator has no direct means to regulate the grasp force, so that fragile objects are over-compressed and heavy objects might slip. This problem is further aggravated by self-occlusion of the fingers and by the kinematic mismatch between the human and the robotic hand [9, 10]. Improving such teleoperation therefore calls for ways to regulate the grasp that do not rely on complex haptic interfaces.

Shared control addresses this limitation by distributing control authority between the human and the robot, combining human reasoning and decision-making with the sensing and control capabilities of the robot [11, 12]. At the hand level, the operator provides coarse finger commands while the robot hand regulates the details of the contact, such as grasp force or finger stiffness [13, 14], which improves grasp success and reduces operator effort [15, 16]. A prerequisite of every such strategy is that the robot estimates its contact state reliably, both to know when to take over from the operator and to regulate the force once it has.

An alternative to tactile sensing is to infer the contact from proprioception, i.e., from the internal signals of the actuation. Compliant hands are particularly suited to this approach. Underactuated, tendon-driven designs with elastic elements conform passively to objects and tolerate imperfect commands [23, 20, 24], which makes them well suited for teleoperation [8]. Their compliant transmission deforms with finger-object interaction, and this deformation encodes the external load, much as Golgi tendon organs, placed in series between muscle and tendon, provide humans with a sense of muscle tension [25]. papers.title: Beyond Expected Value: PPO with Distributional Critics for Systematic Conservation Planning
papers.abstract: Systematic conservation planning must allocate limited protection budgets sequentially under ecological and climatic uncertainty. Static tools cannot adapt as conditions change, and policies optimised only for expected outcomes can fail on the worst-case trajectories climate change makes increasingly likely. CAPTAIN was the first framework to cast this as sequential reinforcement learning, but its gradient-free Evolution Strategies (ES) optimiser lacks per-timestep credit assignment. We replace ES with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) via a Plackett-Luce solution to CAPTAIN's non-differentiable action space, and replace its scalar critic with an Implicit Quantile Network (IQN) modelling the full return distribution. A matched-granularity comparison shows decision granularity, not the optimiser, drives most of the ecological gain, so the real contribution is training efficiency and extensibility to risk-sensitive objectives. On a New Zealand marine dataset, it matches or exceeds ES's outcomes at a fraction of the training cost, offering a template for future work ES's black-box design could not support

papers.intro:
Biodiversity loss is one of the most consequential and time-critical effects of climate change, and conservation planning to slow it is fundamentally a sequential decision problem [10]: which sites to protect, in what order, under a fixed and shrinking budget, while species distributions, disturbance regimes, and climate trajectories keep changing. Static prioritisation tools such as Marxan [1] and Zonation [8] compute one allocation for a fixed snapshot of the data and have no native mechanism for adapting that allocation over time. CAPTAIN (Conservation Area Prioritisation Through Artificial INtelligence) [16] was the first framework to cast this problem in a form that could be explored with Reinforcement Learning (RL), and showed a learned policy can substantially outperform Marxan. Its original optimiser, Parallelised Evolution Strategies (ES) [13], is gradient-free and evaluates whole episodes. It updates parameters proportional to the resulting return, with no mechanism to attribute that return to the specific decisions that produced it, and no representation beyond the expected outcome.

This second limitation matters specifically for climate applications. A policy optimised purely for expected biodiversity outcomes can still perform badly on the worst-case climate trajectories that conservation practitioners most need to plan for. Addressing this requires more than a better point estimate: it requires a policy that represents how outcomes vary across possible futures, so a risk-sensitive objective has something to act on. Distributional RL, which learns the full distribution of returns rather than only its mean [3, 4], offers a principled route to exactly this, and from there to a risk-sensitive objective such as Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) [12]. Whether this combination, gradient-based credit assignment plus a distributional, risk-aware critic, can be made to work inside an existing, large-scale conservation-planning framework had not been tested. PPO is a natural candidate for this setting: it pairs stable, sample-efficient policy-gradient updates [15] with Generalised Advantage Estimation for genuine per-timestep credit assignment [14], directly addressing the credit-assignment limitation of ES described above. A distributional critic is a natural complement: beyond enabling risk-sensitive objectives, learning the full return distribution has been shown to improve policy quality even without an explicit risk-sensitive objective [3], suggesting it may help here independently of whether CVaR itself proves useful.

papers.title: A comparative analysis of the presence of haze in sub-Neptunes observed with JWST
papers.abstract: Photochemical hazes have been proposed to explain the diversity of sub-Neptune transmission spectra, with early HST observations suggesting a temperature-dependent trend in aerosol opacity. However, JWST observations reveal a more heterogeneous picture. Here, we perform a consistent atmospheric retrieval analysis of eight moderately irradiated JWST-observed sub-Neptunes, LP 791-18 c, TOI-1231 b, TOI-732 c, TOI-270 d, GJ 1214 b, GJ 9827 d, GJ 3090 b, and TOI-421 b, using experimentally derived haze optical properties. We compare haze-free models with two experimentally haze analogues to assess haze evidence and spectral signatures. We find significant evidence for haze in LP 791-18 c, TOI-732 c and GJ 3090 b, while LP 791-18 c and GJ 3090 b evidences may be biased by TLS. Haze-favored solutions are primarily driven by short-wavelength spectral slope rather than characteristic infrared absorption features of the experimental analogues, except for TOI-732 c. We find no clear correlation between retrieved CH4 abundance and haze preference, suggesting that haze formation also depends on atmospheric composition and photochemical conditions. For TOI-270 d, the inferred haze properties vary with the MIRI inter-instrument offset and temperature parameterization without yielding significant evidence for haze, highlighting multidimensional retrieval degeneracies. Overall, our results do not support a ubiquitous haze trend across the JWST sub-Neptune sample, but rather a heterogeneous picture that could nevertheless evolve toward the HST trend with improved characterization of the host stars, more accurate TLS corrections and accounting for different haze types. Broader experimental haze measurements and multi-wavelength observations, including phase curves, will be essential to disentangle atmospheric aerosols from stellar contamination and other retrieval degeneracies.

papers.intro:
Sub-Neptunes are among the most abundant classes of exoplanets, yet have no counterpart in the Solar System. Their intermediate nature between terrestrial planets and gas giants makes them key laboratories for studying planetary formation, atmospheric evolution, and chemical diversity (Bean et al., 2021). Transmission spectroscopy has revealed a broad diversity of atmospheric spectra, ranging from prominent molecular features to nearly flat spectra (Madhusudhan et al., 2025). A leading explanation for this diversity is the presence of aerosols (Gao et al., 2021). Clouds produced by equilibrium condensation and hazes generated by disequilibrium photochemistry can both obscure molecular features and modify the apparent atmospheric scale height, but arise from different physical processes and therefore provide distinct insights into atmospheric chemistry.

Early HST transmission spectra suggested population-level trends in aerosol opacity, with warm sub-Neptunes generally exhibiting more muted spectral features (Yu et al., 2021; Estrela et al., 2022; Edwards et al., 2023; Brande et al., 2024). These results motivated the view that haze formation may be common in warm hydrogen-rich atmospheres and may depend on parameters such as temperature, metallicity, and composition. JWST observations have since revealed a more heterogeneous picture (Roy et al., 2026), raising questions about the prevalence of hazes and whether the HST trends may partly reflect observational limitations, retrieval assumptions, or simplified aerosol models. Haze formation is expected to depend on a complex interplay between atmospheric composition, irradiation, redox conditions, metallicity, and vertical transport (Yu et al., 2021; Lavvas and Arfaux, 2021; Gao et al., 2023; Drant et al., 2026; Lavvas et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Recent laboratory experiments further indicate that aerosols can form over a broader range of atmospheric conditions than predicted by conventional hydrocarbon photochemistry and that their optical properties can differ substantially from commonly adopted parameterizations (He et al., 2024; Drant et al., 2026).

Motivated by these results, we extend this approach to a homogeneous re-analysis of eight moderately irradiated sub-Neptunes observed with JWST: LP 791-18 c (Roy et al., 2026), TOI-1231 b (Sarkar et al., 2026), TOI-732 c (Rigby et al., 2025), TOI-270 d (Holmberg and Madhusudhan, 2024; Constantinou et al., 2026; Holmberg et al., 2026), GJ 1214 b (Schlawin et al., 2024), GJ 9827 d (Piaulet-Ghorayeb et al., 2024), GJ 3090 b (Ahrer et al., 2025), and TOI-421 b (Davenport et al., 2025). By analyzing this sample within a common retrieval framework, we aim to reassess the observational evidence for haze trends in the JWST era and evaluate whether a unified picture of aerosol formation in sub-Neptune atmospheres can emerge.

papers.title: Confinement-induced Transitions of Chiral Active Particles and Dumbbells
papers.abstract: We present a coherent framework for the stochastic description of a chiral Active Brownian Particle (cABP) and a chiral Active Brownian Dumbbell (cABD) in a harmonic trap. On the one hand, we employ the Martin-Siggia-Rose path integral formalism, using the passive Brownian motion as a reference state around which activity is accounted for as a perturbation series in the self-propulsion speed. This method is suited best to calculate the exact time-dependent correlation functions. On the other hand, we use the Fokker-Planck equation, which works best to obtain the steady-state probability distribution. We discuss in detail the transitions from a trap centered distribution for low activity/strong confinement to a ring-shaped distribution for high activity/low confinement and the effect of chirality, i.e. the active angular velocity. For the dumbbell, a series of such transitions occurs and the correlation functions yield information about the particle's conformation and orientation. This establishes the combined framework as a powerful tool to investigate stochastic active particle systems.

Here we use a combination of the MSRJD path integral formalism and the Fokker-Planck equation to thoroughly study the behaviour of chiral active Brownian particles and dumbbells trapped in a harmonic potential. This work is structured as follows: first, in section II we briefly describe both methods and how they are applied to the stochastic equations of motion of active particles. Then, in section III we study in detail the chiral Active Brownian Particle (cABP, also referred to as Brownian circle swimmer) with both methods. As results we give the exact relevant moments and the steady-state probability distribution as a series expansion, allowing to quantify its shape transition in the trap as a function of velocity, angular velocity and trap strength. papers.title: Read My Lips: Context-aware Lip Reading Using Language and Audio-Visual Models
papers.abstract: Real-world speech is often partially observable: audio may be missing or corrupted by noise and competing speakers, while the speaker's lips remain visible. Recovering speech requires combining what can be heard, seen, and inferred from context. We introduce RML (Read My Lips), a collaborative method combining a lip reader, a language model, and an audio-visual generative model. The lip reader provides articulation hypotheses, the language model uses context to resolve ambiguous or missing words, and the audio-visual generator reconstructs synchronized speech while preserving speaker identity. Since source reliability varies, RML generates multiple reconstructions and uses the available evidence to favor the most reliable ones. This allows RML to handle missing audio, strong interference, and poor visual evidence without manually defined thresholds. Quantitative and qualitative experiments across these conditions show the benefit of combining visual, acoustic, and linguistic signals.

Imagine trying to follow a conversation at a crowded reception. Several people are speaking at once, music and background noise overwhelm parts of the speech, yet the person in front of you is clearly visible. Even when their voice becomes difficult to hear, their lip movements and the context of the conversation still provide clues about what they are saying. Similar situations arise in video calls with dropped audio, recordings made in noisy environments, archival footage with damaged sound, and film or content production where corrupted speech needs to be restored. In all these cases, recovering speech requires using whatever information remains available across the audio, video, and surrounding conversation.

Background noise or competing speakers may obscure the audio, words may disappear due to recording or transmission failures, and the speaker’s mouth may be occluded or seen from a difficult viewpoint. We characterize these challenges along three dimensions, illustrated in Fig. 1: acoustic noise, from clean speech to severe noise or competing speakers; missing words, from isolated words to large portions of an utterance; and visual readability, from a clear frontal face to difficult viewpoints, occlusions, or animated and generated speakers. These dimensions can vary independently, creating conditions in which no single modality is consistently reliable.

Visual articulation provides information about the spoken sounds, but is inherently ambiguous because different phonemes can produce similar lip movements. Acoustic evidence, even when heavily corrupted, can provide cues about phonemes, timing, and speaker identity. papers.title: PointX: Multi-View Consistent Intrinsics by Querying Surface Points
papers.abstract: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/

papers.intro:
Inverse rendering decomposes an image into the inputs of a renderer: the albedo, normal, roughness and metallicity of every surface point, and the light that reaches it, its irradiance. With these intrinsic properties [2], a captured scene can be relit, its materials edited, or new objects inserted into it. However, the decomposition is ambiguous, since the same pixel color has several valid explanations: a wall that appears red may be white under red light or red under white light. While recent methods [52, 41, 103, 72, 6, 36, 67, 25, 104] achieve accurate single-view predictions, a scene is usually captured in several images, or a video. The same surface point appears in several of them, yet per-image methods resolve the ambiguity in each image independently, so the point receives a different decomposition in every view. Applications using these intrinsics across multiple views then inherit this disagreement: a relit scene flickers from view to view, an edit made in one image does not carry over to the next, and materials texturing a reconstruction show seams.

One line of work addresses this inconsistency by attaching the intrinsics to a 3D representation of the scene, fitted per scene [111, 31, 106, 23, 56, 65] or predicted by a network [53, 35, 73, 109], and rendering them into every view, so that all views show the same underlying intrinsics. However, every view then inherits the errors of this representation, and per-scene fits take minutes to hours. A second line of work drops the 3D representation. Multi-view networks [98, 54, 14] compute the features of each view from all images through cross-view attention, and video models do the same across frames [55, 20, 85, 104]. Their predictions are more consistent than those of single-view networks, but each view is still decoded independently, so corresponding pixels of different views can still disagree. A third line of work keeps the per-view predictions and reconciles them afterwards, through a multi-view consensus at test time [11] or a per-scene optimization [40], which has to resolve the disagreement of separately predicted views. Thus far, consistency has either required an explicit 3D representation, been encouraged through attention and training, or been enforced after the predictions are made.

We introduce PointX, a feed-forward model that takes one or several unposed images of a static scene and predicts the intrinsics of a query surface point using evidence from all views in which it appears. A multi-view transformer, initialized from a feed-forward reconstruction model [90], first computes a feature map for each image. Given a query point in 3D or pixel space, we then find its correspondences across the input images and sample the feature maps at these locations. A 3D point is projected into each image with cameras and depth, estimated by a frozen reconstruction model [90] or taken from any other source, and a pixel can also be matched across the images with a dense matcher [66]. We pool these features into a single representation of the surface point, weighting each view by the confidence that the point is visible in it, and small MLP heads decode the point’s intrinsic properties from it only once. The resulting prediction belongs to the point rather than to a view, making it consistent by construction. The same model can predict properties directly for the points of a reconstruction, without having to fuse separate per-view predictions, or produce per-view maps by querying every pixel, which then agree across views as far as their correspondences do. PointX also benefits directly from more accurate geometry and correspondences, such as those of a dense matcher, without retraining. In Fig. 1, PointX predicts the intrinsic properties of the points of a laser-scanned scene [74], so that a light placed once or a material edited once produces consistent results across the input views.

papers.title: Enhancing Sparse-View Gaussian Splatting with Feed-Forward Priors via Spectral Fusion and Distillation
papers.abstract: Gaussian splatting from sparse training views renders high-quality images near training views, but reconstruction quality degrades at distant regions, which are undersampled by the training set. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models use strong learned priors to resample the scene from substantially different viewpoints, but they take more than ten times as long to render and produce high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes. We propose a plug-and-play method that enhances an existing sparse-view Gaussian model with a pretrained feed-forward NVS model. We observe that the two are complementary in the frequency domain: the prior is more accurate at low frequencies, and the Gaussians at high frequencies. The reliability of the prior relative to the Gaussians is inversely proportional to the image frequency, so the optimal fusion weight is a first-order low-pass filter with one parameter that can be fitted. Our key idea is then to intelligently fuse the reliable part of each of the two methods. To remove the slow feed-forward model at render time, we use these fused images as teachers and distill them back into Gaussians, balanced with supervision from input views. Our method improves the quality of various sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed, and our analysis works on different prior models. Project page: https://linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs/

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [16] renders photorealistic novel views in real time [59] and is used in XR [20, 21, 24, 9, 34], streaming [32, 46, 12, 41], autonomous driving [47, 11, 4] and teleoperation [39]. However, with only a few input views, it overfits to the inputs and performs poorly at novel views. Sparse-view methods regularize the optimization with dropout [31, 45], depth [60, 18] or stereo priors [10, 49]. They stay sharp near the training views and break at views far from them. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models [15, 33] carry a prior learned from many scenes. However, they cannot replace Gaussians, because (1) they render more than 10×10\times slower, and (2) their results carry high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes (Sec. 3).

papers.title: Current-Dependent Meta-GGA and Local Hybrid Functionals for Relativistic NMR Shifts
papers.abstract: NMR chemical shifts are key for the characterization of novel compounds. Especially for molecules with heavy elements, the experimental data is often corroborated with computational studies in density functional theory (DFT). However, modern meta-generalized gradient approximations (meta-GGAs) and local hybrid functionals are not widely supported in relativistic calculations with quantum chemistry program suites. So far, their current-dependent generalization in the spirit of Dobson, Becke, and Tao was not presented at all. This generalization ensures gauge invariance and does not introduce artifacts--unlike the more popular field-dependent generalization of the kinetic-energy density. In non-relativistic and scalar-relativistic calculations, the first was shown to be superior but the current density only arises due to the magnetic field perturbation. In contrast, spin--orbit coupling also induces current densities in the preceding ground-state calculation and the DFT framework needs to be generalized to a current density functional theory (CDFT) for consistency with the current-dependent response equations. Herein, we present the two-component relativistic generalization of the current-dependent kinetic-energy density of a Kramers-restricted Kohn--Sham reference for meta-GGAs and local hybrid functionals in NMR calculations. The extension is invariant under a position-dependent phase and a position-dependent spin rotation of the spinors, or a local U(1)$\times$SU(2) transformation. Relativistic effects are considered with exact two-component theory using a superposition of atomic potentials to include the two-electron picture-change correction (SAP-X2C).

papers.title: Tornado4D: Physics-Guided 4D Gaussian Reconstruction of a Laboratory Tornado from Sparse One-Sided Videos
papers.abstract: Characterizing how tornadoes evolve over space and time is critically important for understanding and preparing for these highly destructive weather events. Towards this end, we develop algorithms capable of forming time-resolved 3D reconstructions of laboratory smoke tornadoes from sparse one-sided videos. Even in a controlled environment, reconstruction is severely underconstrained: appearance is view dependent, motion is non-rigid, and the unobserved volume admits many geometries. We present Tornado4D, a physics-guided 4D Gaussian framework capable of reconstructing laboratory tornadoes from sparse, one-sided videos. Tornado4D uses knowledge of the enclosure geometry to introduce rotational airflow field priors that constrain how the 3D structure evolves over time. These rotational priors allow us to reconstruct otherwise unobserved structure. We evaluate reconstruction accuracy by computing novel-view synthesis accuracy on a held out camera view: Tornado4D outperforms frame-by-frame 3DGS and video-based 4DGS by a considerable margin.

We use this existing dataset to study a different problem: recovering a time-varying 4D representation of the rotating translucent plume.
