papers.intro:
Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) integrates data transmission and environmental sensing through shared resources and hardware, offering improved spectral efficiency and reduced deployment cost for next-generation networks [1]. However, the same transmitted signals that support legitimate sensing can also expose environmental information to unintended receivers [2, 3]. Many ISAC systems reuse pilots or other known reference signals for sensing. These signals are accessible to authorized communication users and may also be intercepted by external eavesdroppers outside the system. This can further enable either receiver to perform unauthorized detection, localization, or tracking [4].

Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) integrates data transmission and environmental sensing through shared resources and hardware, offering improved spectral efficiency and reduced deployment cost for next-generation networks [1]. However, the same transmitted signals that support legitimate sensing can also expose environmental information to unintended receivers [2, 3]. Many ISAC systems reuse pilots or other known reference signals for sensing. These signals are accessible to authorized communication users and may also be intercepted by external eavesdroppers outside the system. This can further enable either receiver to perform unauthorized detection, localization, or tracking [4].

A further threat is passive direct–echo bypass sensing: Eve correlates an intercepted direct-path signal with target reflections without knowing the signal structure. Such sensing with non-cooperative illuminators is well established in passive radar, including performance analysis and experimental detection and tracking [5, 6]. However, its performance is highly sensitive to reference-channel quality and interference in the surveillance channel [7]. In urban environments, clutter and background radio interference from concurrent transmissions can further degrade echo detection. For a moving receiver, channel imbalances also complicate direct-path and clutter suppression [8], while sampling-clock mismatch degrades reference alignment [9]. Direct–echo bypass sensing is well established, but its performance depends on reference quality and surveillance-channel interference. We instead focus on less-explored informed coherent sensing attacks, where Eve exploits nominal-reference knowledge to reconstruct a coherent reference.

Sensing-security research adapts established Physical-Layer Security (PLS) tools, including beamforming and Artificial Noise (AN) [10, 11]. These designs aim to limit the target and environmental information available to unauthorized receivers while preserving legitimate sensing performance. Zou et al. [4] consider a communication user acting as a sensing Eve and design beamforming with AN to limit its sensing mutual information while preserving legitimate sensing and communication quality. Ren et al. [12] extend joint protection to cell-free ISAC, optimizing cooperative information and sensing beamforming against sensing eavesdroppers. Joint signal perturbation and beamforming also target sensing-signal indistinguishability [13]. Papanikolaou et al. [14] design robust transmit covariances to misdirect unauthorized angular sensing under Eve-angle uncertainty. However, spatial protection often requires Eve’s channel or location information, or a specified uncertainty region. Obtaining and maintaining this information is challenging for a passive, mobile Eve. These spatial and covariance-domain designs motivate waveform-level protection when spatial separation is unfavorable. A Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-mounted Eve can reposition to seek a strong Line-of-Sight (LOS) link and intercept energy intended for legitimate nodes; protection should therefore be assessed under favorable interception geometry.

Waveform-domain methods modify the signal available to unauthorized sensing receivers and can provide protection without knowledge of Eve’s geometry or reliance on spatial separation. Han et al. [15] engineer the ambiguity function to introduce artificial targets and increase Eve’s range ambiguity. Du et al. [16] develop a detection-oriented Kullback–Leibler-divergence metric accounting for mainlobe, sidelobe, and noise contributions, and optimize time–frequency amplitude and phase perturbations. Their analysis connects waveform shaping to the sensing-security and communication tradeoff. Erdem et al. [17] introduce artificial phase and Doppler shifts for passive Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) sensing protection and demonstrate cooperative compensation through measurements. Temiz et al. [18] combine index modulation and phase coding in frequency-modulated continuous-wave chirps to impair unauthorized detection and ranging. Zhang et al. [19] instead use ambient Internet of Things (IoT) devices as cooperative jammers and ghost targets, jointly designing transmit beamforming and device reflection modulations. Keskin et al. [20] study oscillator phase noise, showing that different phase-noise correlations in monostatic and bistatic reception create a tradeoff among legitimate ranging, unauthorized ranging, and communication performance. Unlike a generated phase key, this mechanism exploits an oscillator-induced asymmetry. These approaches illustrate that unauthorized detection and estimation can be impaired through waveform manipulation rather than spatial suppression alone.

However, waveform-domain protection faces two threats from an informed Eve. First, Eve may estimate and compensate for the waveform modifications. In ISAC, one countermeasure strategy is to disguise the sensing reference among communication signals. Phase keys and AN in [21] can prevent correct demodulation by Eve, thereby hindering her identification of similar underlying bit-sequence structures in the protected signals for coherent sensing. Second, with knowledge of the security design and reference-signal generation, Eve may bypass the protection using a specifically trained machine-learning model. This risk remains underexplored and increasingly relevant. Existing waveform-domain protections [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20] are evaluated against an Eve who lacks the protection parameters, or, as in [17], against a single heuristic phase-tracking Eve in one measured scenario. Security should therefore not rely on undisclosed design details or estimation complexity alone. We analyze what Eve can learn and reconstruct when waveform construction and key-generation rules are available; secrecy rests only on the burst-specific key shared over secure backhaul.

papers.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
papers.abstract: We prove that the following problem is \textbf{NEXPTIME}-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.

papers.title: ShapeQuest: Towards Granularity-Controlled Edit-Conditioned 3D Asset Retrieval
papers.abstract: Given a reference asset and an instruction such as "remove one armrest," a retriever must find variants that make the edit and preserve the other parts. This search is well established for images but remains underexplored for individual 3D assets. To study this problem, we introduce ShapeQuest and ShapeQuester, a new benchmark and model for edit-conditioned 3D asset retrieval. ShapeQuest's open-source pipeline edits textured meshes through part additions, removals, and material and colour changes. It controls edit granularity across five levels, defined by the fraction of the object's surface area each edit affects. It constructs multiple valid targets when an instruction leaves the choice of part open. A vision-language model judges each edit from views chosen to expose the edited parts, and human raters audit its judgments. ShapeQuest has 87,824 queries in 50 categories and a 50,919-shape gallery with competing edits. To distinguish these variants, ShapeQuester learns retrieval alongside reconstruction of the edited point cloud, with part masks supervising changed and preserved regions. With a frozen pretrained point encoder, ShapeQuester reaches 50.4 operation-macro mAP@10 on the test split, against 47.2 for the fusion baseline with the same inputs and 48.6 for the strongest baseline. Reconstruction adds 6.5 points on the validation split when the point encoder is trained from scratch, including 3.3 from part masks.

papers.intro:
A 3D designer furnishing a virtual office finds a chair with the right shape and upholstery, but its armrests keep it from sliding under the desk. A text-based search for “armless chair” leaves out the details that made this chair a good choice. With the chair as a reference, the designer can simply ask for “this one without the armrests.”

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
papers.abstract: Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-B\'enard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

papers.intro:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) model a wide range of physical phenomena, including fluid flow, heat transport, and the response of heterogeneous materials. Their numerical solution on fine grids can require substantial memory and computing time. Tensor-Train (TT) methods approximate the discretized solution by a chain of small tensors [1, 2]. The dimensions connecting these tensors, called TT ranks, determine the storage cost and the attainable approximation accuracy. Calculations can be carried out on the compressed representation, with potential savings when the ranks remain moderate. TT methods have proven beneficial in a wide range of high-resolution applications, including fluid dynamics [3, 4], kinetic plasma dynamics [5], simulations of the Gross–Pitaevskii equation [6, 7], structural mechanics problems [8, 9] and computational homogenization [10, 11, 12, 13].

Spectral methods offer a natural way to accommodate these conditions through basis functions adapted to the underlying boundary-value problem. For suitable operators on uniform Cartesian grids, discrete cosine and sine transforms diagonalize the corresponding finite-difference operators for homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet conditions, respectively. This allows the discrete equations to be solved in spectral space, although the appropriate transform depends on the grid arrangement and boundary discretization [19]. Such operators arise, for example, in pressure-correction equations for wall-bounded incompressible flow [20] and in computational homogenization with prescribed displacement or traction boundary conditions [21, 22].

papers.title: Stability and periodic switching in feedback systems with sector-bounded hybrid integrators
papers.abstract: We study stability of piecewise linear systems composed of the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator. Exploiting the observation that for such systems state-dependent switching sequences asymptotically exhibit periodic behaviour, we develop a spectral approach to stability analysis as an alternative to sufficient Lyapunov-based methods. We formulate a conjecture that asymptotic periodicity holds irrespective of the initial conditions and system stability, and provide a description of the limit system and propose an algorithm to obtain its parameters. We establish this rigorously for second-order linear-time invariant processes. Based on spectral properties of the resulting periodic limit system, we derive sufficient stability conditions. The results provide a novel viewpoint for accurate stability analysis of general state-based piecewise linear systems.

papers.intro:
Piecewise linear systems form a specific class of hybrid systems, characterized by a partition of the state space into regions where dynamics are governed by linear models. We consider a particular class of piecewise linear systems arising from the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant (LTI) process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator [16]. The latter has attracted considerable attention in recent years, partially owing to its potential of overcoming fundamental limitations in LTI control [15], and its successful application in various industrial settings [14, 1, 18]. Despite these promises, the important problem of establishing tight stability guarantees for system interconnections with hybrid integrators remains far from trivial, especially due to the discontinuous nature of the corresponding dynamics.

These Lyapunov-based stability conditions, however, can be conservative.

papers.title: A Systematic Construction of High-Corank Kac--Moody Algebras
papers.abstract: We form a hexagonal prism from two six-cycles and iterate a doubling construction with a fixed positive integer edge multiplicity, producing a family of indefinite Kac--Moody algebras. The prism's spectrum determines the exact corank of every algebra in the family. Along each nonvanishing parity class, the corank grows exponentially, while its ratio to the matrix size tends to zero. For the twelve-node algebra we identify the two central directions, describe the first two graded levels, and characterize the integral central charges of its unitary highest-weight modules.

Joining two copies of the cycle at corresponding vertices produces a hexagonal prism. Its Cartan matrix has order twelve, rank ten and one negative eigenvalue. papers.title: Large-time existence for the gravity water waves equations
papers.abstract: We provide a new well-posedness result on the gravity water-waves equations, i.e. the free-surface, incompressible and irrotational Euler equations, in the absence of surface tension. Our main contribution is to provide the existence of solutions, in high enough but finite Sobolev regularity, on a timescale that grows like the inverse of the non-linearity parameter. Our result is also uniform in the shallow-water parameter. The main difficulty is that we allow for the presence of a large (though not emerging) bathymetry.

papers.title: The Jupiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE) Mission: Post-Launch Status and Mission Overview
papers.abstract: The JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) is the first large-class mission in ESA's Cosmic Vision programme. Proposed in 2007 and selected in 2012, it was launched on 14 April 2023 from Kourou and is now en route towards Jupiter. After arrival in July 2031, JUICE will spend approximately four years studying the Jupiter system, performing multiple flybys of three of its Galilean moons, the icy moons Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto, before entering orbit around Ganymede for its final year. The mission will investigate conditions that may support habitable environments within the satellites, all of which are thought to contain subsurface liquid water oceans. Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System, is a prime target due to its internal structure and possible subsurface ocean, its unique intrinsic magnetic field, and its complex interactions with Jupiter's magnetosphere, offering a natural laboratory for studying the emergence, evolution and potential habitability of icy worlds around giant planets. JUICE will also conduct a global investigation of the Jupiter system as the archetype for gaseous giant planet systems: it will study Jupiter's atmospheric circulation, composition, and flow of energy from the cloud tops to the thermosphere and characterise the 3D structure of the magnetosphere and its coupling with the ionosphere and thermosphere. Interactions between the moons and the magnetosphere, as well as tidal and gravitational evolution within the Galilean system, will also be assessed. Additional science objectives include the innermost Galilean moon, Io and its neutral cloud and plasma torus, some small inner and irregular moons, and the ring systems. The payload includes 10 instruments and one experiment using the spacecraft's telecommunications system to connect with ground-based radio telescopes, plus an onboard radiation monitor.

papers.title: Near-Zero Forgetting Is Not Enough: Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Continual Learning of Pretrained VLAs
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.

papers.intro:
Vision-Language-Action models have emerged as the generalist approach for robot manipulation tasks. These models combine a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) with an action head. This structure allows the transfer of generalist semantic priors to robot control tasks, enabling powerful generalization capabilities across different embodiments, tasks, and environments [1, 2, 3]. To avoid the costly retraining of these policies in changing real-world scenarios, continual adaptation would be desirable. This is the domain of continual learning (CL) [4], where new tasks or domains are learned sequentially. One of the main challenges is catastrophic forgetting [5], where the performance of previous tasks degrades as new ones are learned. This is closely related to the stability-plasticity trade-off [6], which presents the tension between the model’s ability to learn new knowledge (plasticity) and retain previous knowledge (stability).

In some cases, forgetting is reduced to nearly zero or even replaced by backward transfer. If these results extend to deployment settings, they would represent a significant shift in what continual learning can achieve, potentially bringing lifelong robotic systems closer to practical deployment under changing environments.

papers.title: Global full-f gyrokinetic analysis of energetic-particle-driven Alfv\'en eigenmodes and their phase-space drive with GYSELA
papers.abstract: We investigate the linear stability of energetic-particle (EP) driven Alfv\'en eigenmodes and the wave-particle interaction in phase space, using the newly implemented energetic-particle module in the electromagnetic global full-f gyrokinetic code GYSELA. The coupled gyrokinetic-Maxwell system self-consistently evolves the EP species alongside thermal ions and kinetic electrons, retaining finite-orbit-width and global profile effects. To mitigate the relaxation of the initial distribution in global full-f models, a canonical Maxwellian initialisation is employed, which strongly reduces this relaxation and the associated change of the drive. The framework is verified against the ITPA-TAE and the reversed-shear NLED-AUG cases, including scans in EP temperature and density. The agreement with published multi-code results is quantitative for the ITPA-TAE case and qualitative for the NLED-AUG case, where a reversed-shear Alfv\'en eigenmode (RSAE) is found near $q_{\rm min}$. Beyond verification, we use a constants-of-motion (CoM) diagnostic to project the gyrocentre distribution and the local wave-particle power exchange ($P = -\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$) onto invariant space. This identifies the orbit classes and resonances that interact with the mode. For the ITPA-TAE, deeply co-passing orbits dominate the drive. For the NLED-AUG RSAE, counter-passing orbits drive the mode and co-passing orbits damp it, and the sign of the exchange follows that of the linear EP drive. These results provide a basis for future global full-f studies of nonlinear energetic-particle transport and mode saturation.

papers.intro:
Energetic particles (EP) produced by auxiliary heating systems and fusion reactions can resonantly interact with shear Alfvén waves, driving Alfvénic instabilities that significantly affect confinement and plasma performance [20, 13]. Toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes (TAEs) arise from toroidal coupling between adjacent poloidal harmonics, which opens frequency gaps in the Alfvén continuum and permits discrete eigenmodes within otherwise heavily-damped frequency ranges. In reversed-shear configurations, the safety factor exhibits a local minimum qm​i​nq_{min}, producing an extremum in the Alfvén continuum. This continuum structure allows discrete modes, known as reversed-shear Alfvén eigenmodes (RSAEs), to localise near qm​i​nq_{min} and exhibit characteristic frequency evolution distinct from standard gap modes. Since these modes reside in spectral regions with reduced continuum damping, the stability of these eigenmodes is governed by the interplay between resonant fast-ion drive and residual background damping mechanisms. The accurate prediction of energetic-particle-driven Alfvénic activity therefore requires a self-consistent description of the thermal plasma that supports the waves as well as the wave-particle interaction in EP phase space. Several numerical approaches have been developed to study energetic-particle-driven Alfvénic instabilities. Hybrid MHD–kinetic models such as MEGA[42], HMGC [6], HYMAGYC [44], NOVA-K [21], CAS3D-K [27], AE3D-K [41], VENUS [16], and XTOR-K [8] treat energetic particles kinetically while retaining a fluid description for the thermal plasma. Gyrokinetic and particle-in-cell approaches, including LIGKA [31], GYGLES [34], ORB5 [25, 4, 30], EUTERPE [26], TRIMEG-GKX [32], gKPSP [14], and GTC [45] have provided detailed insight into wave–particle interactions and finite-orbit-width effects. The gyrofluid code TAEFL [40] and FAR3D [43] offer an alternative reduced-model treatment of fast-ion closures. These tools have successfully reproduced many linear properties of shear Alfvén modes and have played a central role in benchmark studies. Most of these results are based on a δ​f\delta f approach, in which the “equilibrium” state is removed, and a Krook operator is used to control the departure.

Electromagnetic field perturbations cause guiding-centre drifts that redistribute particles in phase space. In toroidal geometry, a simple local Maxwellian that depends only on radius and energy is not an exact kinetic equilibrium, as conservation of canonical toroidal momentum leads to redistribution through finite-orbit-width effects [7]. This effect is particularly pronounced in full-ff simulations using a local Maxwellian for energetic particles and has been shown to reduce the linear growth rate by approximately 40% for 400400 keV energetic particles in the ITPA-TAE case [32]. To mitigate this effect, we initialise the plasma using a canonical Maxwellian consistent with the invariants of motion so as to reduce initial relaxation. However, a small degree of profile adjustment remains unavoidable in a fully kinetic treatment. In a full-ff simulation the EP distribution itself is evolved, and for energetic particles the dominant effect is their finite orbit width. An initial distribution that is not exactly a function of the invariants of motion is therefore redistributed along the wide EP orbits. The canonical Maxwellian removes most of this redistribution. The small part that remains comes from the numerical initial distribution following the invariants only approximately, and it is phase-mixed along the particle trajectories within one or two EP transit times, which shows up as a small early relaxation of the EP profile [32]. Furthermore, using the EPCoM framework [11, 9], we apply a constants-of-motion (CoM) phase-space diagnostic that projects the gyrocentre distribution and the wave–particle power exchange (P=−𝐉⋅𝐄P=-\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}) onto invariant space. This diagnostic identifies the orbit classes responsible for drive and damping, and shows that the sign of the exchange is set by the invariant-space gradients rather than by the radial density gradient alone.

papers.title: A consistent generalised kinetic equation for damped ocean waves
papers.abstract: Contemporary spectral wave models, including those used in operational wave forecasts and in coupled earth system models, assume damping and non-linear wave energy exchange to be independent. Here, we critically examine this assumption. Starting from the equations of weakly non-linear waves, we rigorously derive a governing equation that consistently couples damping and non-linear interactions. This consistent generalised kinetic equation does not lead to an appreciable change in total wave--energy dissipation, but compared to the standard additive damping approach there is a noticeable difference in the distribution of energy among the wave frequencies. This effect is particularly important for weak damping, and is a consequence of a memory effect retained in model. Even stronger differences are observed when damping is allowed to depend on wave frequency, as is characteristic of many wave processes of growing interest such as the interaction with other components of the earth system, e.g. the cryosphere. Compared to the purely additive formulation, our new damped generalised kinetic equation has improved numerical stability characteristics. The formulation presented therefore provides a possible basis for future operational wave modelling. While our results are for ocean waves, the derived generalised kinetic equation can be applied to other weakly nonlinear dispersive systems where external damping (or forcing) applies.

Ocean wave modelling has become one of the work-horses of modern marine science. Such modelling encapsulates the basic physics behind ocean surface waves, starting with their generation by the wind, through their nonlinear coupling, to their dissipation by white-capping or other processes, such as interaction with sea–ice or the sea–bottom. Today, wave models like WAVEWATCH III or SWAN are a key component of modern coupled Earth system models and an indispensable tool in weather forecasts, sediment transport studies, marine ecology, and a host of offshore operations (Cavaleri et al., 2007; Cavaleri et al., 2012; Kousal et al., 2026). Their products – such as significant wave height or mean wave period – are stochastic in nature, independent of individual wave phases, and valid over large spatial and temporal scales.

Such models are commonly referred to as spectral wave models, since they deal fundamentally with the averaged Fourier spectra of ocean waves. Indeed, the Fourier transform of the water surface can be directly related to the energy of the waves, already identified by Sverdrup & Munk (1947) as the key variable for wave forecasts. With the advance of digital signal processing, Pierson (1952) and others began to reformulate the forecasting problem in the language of Fourier analysis.

While significant mathematical advances in nonlinear waves were made in the second half of the 19th century, almost all of these dealt with steady, periodic wave motion. A first attempt to extend a higher-order theory of irregular waves – with multiple Fourier harmonic components – was made by Tick (1959), beginning an incredibly fruitful decade in nonlinear ocean wave research.

Work by Annenkov & Shrira (2001a) and Tanaka (2001) among others critically assessed these assumptions, and a first generalisation of the kinetic equation to account for near-resonant interactions operating on faster time-scales was made by Janssen (2003). Subsequent work by Annenkov & Shrira using direct numerical simulations of the primitive Zakharov equation highlighted the fact that near-resonant contributions are every bit as important as exact resonances in determining spectral evolution, and also proposed a generalisation of Janssen’s equation (Annenkov & Shrira, 2006). This was further extended in work of Gramstad & Stiassnie (2013) to include Stokes frequency corrections.

papers.title: On Semilocal Convergence of a Semismooth* Newton Method
papers.abstract:
We give conditions under which the semismooth$^*$ Newton method solves $0\in F(x)$ from a given initial point. At each step, we bound the distance from the corrected point $(x_{k+1},0)$ to the graph of $F$ by a function of the correction length. We also bound $\|A^{-1}B\|$ uniformly over the selected coderivative pairs $(A,B)$. Together, these bounds give a test on the initial graph residual and the radius of a prescribed ball. If the test holds, the iterates converge to a solution in that ball. If the decrease modulus tends to zero, every infinite run converges $q$-superlinearly.
  For mixed complementarity problems on a box, we assume that the smooth part has a Lipschitz continuous Jacobian and that every nonempty principal submatrix is nonsingular. We bound the error after one step for each regular pair. The bound is quadratic in the distance to a solution and depends explicitly on the norm of the correction matrix. For affine problems, we give a threshold on the norm of the vertical component of a graph point. Below this threshold, all regular pairs at that point give the same solution in one step, even when their rows come from different branches. Hence any run with vanishing graph residuals terminates in finitely many steps. For integer affine data, we give a test for an exact step using only the problem data and the current iterate.

papers.title: An $O(n^{-1/2})$ remainder for the Chow--Robbins stopping boundary
papers.abstract: We sharpen the asymptotic approximation to the optimal stopping boundary in the Chow--Robbins game, proving the inverse-square-root remainder conjectured by Elton. The proof combines an exactly harmonic integral for simple random walk with a Catalan first-passage renewal identity. Averaging the stopping defect over one spatial period removes its leading lattice dependence, and a coupling of states at equal depth transfers this cancellation to the renewal sum. Consequently, the explicit integer stopping rule can fail at no more than a constant times the square root of the number of observation times.

papers.title: Frieze's $\zeta(3)$ and the Avram--Bertsimas constant under Haar conjugation
papers.abstract: Let $H_d=U_d^*\Lambda_dU_d$, where $U_d$ is Haar unitary and $\Lambda_d$ is a deterministic real diagonal matrix, and put $\sigma_d^2=\mathbb E|H_{12}|^2$. For minimum spanning trees with edge weights $\exp(-s|H_{ij}|^2/\sigma_d^2)$, we prove that the normalized expected weights differ from those of the independent Gaussian model by a polynomially small error, uniformly for $0<s\le S$ with fixed $S>0$. The limit is the classical Avram--Bertsimas constant and includes Frieze's $\zeta(3)$ at $s=1$. For edge weights $|H_{ij}|^{-1}$, we approximate the normalized expected weight by an explicit one-dimensional integral with polynomial error, and obtain a divergent expansion in inverse powers of $\log d$. The assumptions require the spectrum, after centering and division by its standard deviation, to remain uniformly bounded. From Penrose's high-dimensional edge-length limit we derive $2-\gamma-\zeta(2)$ as the first correction to the high-dimensional Euclidean minimum spanning tree constant after normalization by the unit-ball volume. This correction is a logarithmic moment of the limiting distribution of MST edge weights; half of it is the first logarithmic correction for the reciprocal Haar weights. Here $\gamma$ is Euler's constant and $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta function.

papers.title: CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence
papers.abstract: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. papers.intro:
Language models are increasingly used as the planning layer of robots: a person states a task in natural language, and the model translates it into calls to the robot’s skills. Not every instruction should be carried out as stated. “Put a bolt in tray 1” is ambiguous in a cell that stocks three bolt types; an instruction that needs a tool, location or capability the robot lacks is infeasible; and one that breaks a safety rule, or comes from a person not entitled to give it, is unsafe. Each calls for a different response: a clear instruction should be executed, an ambiguous one should prompt a question, and an infeasible or unsafe one should be refused. The errors are far from symmetric. Executing an unsafe instruction can injure a person, refusing a clear one makes the robot useless, and an unnecessary question costs the operator time. Choosing among these responses is what makes such a robot an agent in the sense used here: it perceives an instruction and its scene, decides on its own whether to act, ask or refuse, and gathers missing information by asking.

A few recent systems choose among executing, clarifying and rejecting in one gate [6, 7, 8], but three properties limit their use in a new robot cell. First, their thresholds and rules are tuned or set by hand rather than derived from the consequences of errors, so a change in what an error costs requires re-tuning by hand. Second, none acts on a calibrated probability; because current proprietary models often expose no token probabilities, a usable confidence has to be built from repeated sampling or from probabilities that the model states. Third, none has been fitted in one domain and then evaluated unchanged in another. Telling the model the costs is not a reliable substitute: stated error penalties have been found to leave the abstention behaviour of language models almost unchanged [9] or to move it in the right direction but far from the optimum [10], and a stated cost ratio moved escalation decisions towards the cost-optimal rule mainly for models that reason [11].

Soft computing offers a principled answer to this kind of choice under uncertainty. Three-way decision theory derives acceptance, deferment and rejection regions from a loss function by Bayesian minimum risk [12, 13], and its sequential form treats deferment as a step that gathers information for a later decision [14, 15]. Execute, ask and refuse map onto acceptance, deferment and rejection, and the clarifying question is the information-gathering step. What the theory leaves open is where the probabilities come from. For a language model, this confidence is itself uncertain and only partly graded (graded: taking many values between 0 and 1, unlike a ten-sample vote, which is often unanimous), and its granularity determines how the three-way rule behaves: a coarse estimate collapses the decision regions into a fixed lookup from the model’s answer to an action.

This paper proposes CATWAY (Cost-sensitive Agentic Three-WAY decisions), a gate for language-model robot agents, intended as the layer that decides autonomously, before every skill call, whether the agent acts. The model is probed about an instruction; a confidence estimate turns its answers into a probability distribution over the four conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe); and a minimum-expected-loss rule over an explicit loss matrix chooses execute, ask or refuse, with a second, two-way decision after the person’s reply. The confidence estimate is the design question. We compare a vote over sampled answers, stated probabilities, token probabilities and fusions of several probes, together with alternative decision rules and label-free adaptations, and select the gate by one rule applied to calibration data only. Every fitted quantity is estimated on household instructions and frozen. The gate is evaluated on held-out household instructions, on two new robot domains prepared for this study (a production cell and a mobile robot) and on an external smart-home benchmark, TRUST-NAV [8], against prompted, rule-based, conformal, fuzzy and agent baselines (Section 4.3). By an agent baseline, we mean that the model writes the robot’s plan as skill calls and the decision is read from that plan.

papers.title: A Unit-Gradient Neural Variational Method for Anisotropic Eikonal Equations
papers.abstract: We develop a variational neural method for computing viscosity solutions of the anisotropic eikonal equation. Building on the vanishing-viscosity principle, we minimize an energy functional whose Euler--Lagrange equation is the viscous anisotropic eikonal equation and introduce an auxiliary variable for the gradient, enforcing the constraint through a penalty. A key challenge in this formulation is to handle nonlinearity of the functional while controlling the interaction between the viscosity and penalty parameters. To address this challenge, we impose a unit-norm constraint on the auxiliary variable exactly, as prescribed by the eikonal equation. This removes the gradient from the exponentially weighted part of the functional and allows the viscosity and penalty limits to be studied separately. We establish two convergence results. First, for each fixed viscosity parameter $\epsilon>0$, we prove convergence to the viscosity solution as the penalty parameter $\lambda\rightarrow\infty$. Second, for the distance function to the boundary of a convex or smooth domain, we prove convergence as $\epsilon\rightarrow0$ for any fixed $\lambda>0$. The latter result motivates our stable numerical strategy, which keeps $\lambda$ fixed while decreasing $\epsilon$ whenever the training loss stagnates. The formulation is implemented using a neural network that satisfies the unit-norm constraint by construction and a mesh-free approach that evaluates the singularly scaled functional at randomly sampled points without requiring mesh refinement as $\epsilon\to0$. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the method on diverse isotropic and anisotropic problems, including three-dimensional open-surface reconstruction from point clouds.

Classical numerical methods for the eikonal equation include fast marching and ordered upwind methods [39, 38, 29], fast sweeping methods [48, 35], semi-Lagrangian schemes [12], and vanishing-viscosity schemes [9, 46, 20]. These methods achieve high accuracy and efficiency on appropriately constructed meshes. However, mesh generation remains a major bottleneck in industrial simulations, particularly for complex geometries, and fully automated meshing and mesh adaptation remain challenging research objectives [41]. Anisotropic mesh adaptation, in particular, continues to receive considerable attention [1]. Moreover, on polyhedral meshes, which are commonly used for complex geometries [17], the upwind updates underlying classical eikonal solvers, typically derived for simplicial meshes, cannot be directly applied [20]. These challenges motivate mesh-free approaches that avoid explicit mesh generation. For surface reconstruction from the unorganized point clouds, the complexity lies in the data Γ\Gamma rather than Ω\Omega, and Cartesian-grid level-set methods also handle such data without unstructured mesh generation [47]; extending our approach to domains that require unstructured meshes remains a direction for future research.

papers.title: Perturbation of CO A1{\Pi} by a3{\Pi} should have been undetectable: detection, mechanism, and surprises
papers.abstract: A direct perturbation between the $a^3\Pi$ and $A^1\Pi$ vibrational levels of two electronic states that belong to the same electronic configuration of the carbon monoxide molecule should be unobservably weak because the vibrational overlap integral $\langle a^3\Pi,v' \mid A^1\Pi,v'' \rangle$ for their near-degenerate levels is extremely small. Yet level-shift and transition-intensity signatures of the $a^3\Pi(v = 13) \sim A^1\Pi(v = 2)$ perturbation are unmistakably present in the $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O}$ isotopologue. A detailed study of, among others, the $A^1\Pi$ - $X^1\Sigma^+(2, 0)$, $B^1\Sigma^+$ - $A^1\Pi(0, 2)$, and $C^1\Sigma^+$ - $A^1\Pi(0, 2)$ spectra, obtained by the VUV- and Vis-FT complementary techniques in the energy regions of the six crossing points ($e$- and $f$-symmetry, $|\Omega| = 0, 1, 2$) between the $a^3\Pi(v = 13)$ and $A^1\Pi(v = 2)$ states, reveal that the perturbation pathways are indirect, primarily facilitated by the $e^3\Sigma^-(v = 4)$ state, and that quantum mechanical interferences via its F1e and F3e components occur.

papers.title: The first moment of symmetric cube $L$-functions
papers.abstract:
We establish a power saving asymptotic formula for the first moment of symmetric cube central $L$-values over Hecke--Maass forms in short spectral windows. As applications, we prove quantitative non-vanishing, an almost-all Lindel\"of bound, and almost-all decay of cubic periods. We also prove the corresponding first moment asymptotic for central derivatives in the holomorphic weight aspect.
  Our proof begins with an application of the Kuznetsov formula, followed by a first Poisson summation and stationary phase analysis. The key observation is that a periodic cubic factor can be separated from the resulting oscillation and incorporated into the arithmetic sum, allowing a second application of Poisson summation to yield further cancellation.

Of particular interest are the symmetric power LL-functions attached to GL⁡(2)\mathrm{GL}(2) forms. The symmetric square lift is automorphic on GL⁡(3)\mathrm{GL}(3) by Gelbart–Jacquet [7], and its central values have been studied extensively; see, for example, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 21, 22, 23, 27, 28, 30, 32, 33, 35]. Among these works, Luo–Sarnak [33] established an early bound on the second moment in the Maass form spectral aspect. In the holomorphic weight aspect, Lau [30] obtained an asymptotic formula for the first moment, while Khan [22] established an asymptotic formula for the twisted second moment after averaging over the weight. By comparison, far fewer results are known for central values of symmetric cube LL-functions. The symmetric cube lift is automorphic on GL⁡(4)\mathrm{GL}(4) by Kim–Shahidi [25]. papers.title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
papers.abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

papers.intro:
A central goal of NeuroAI is to build computational models that not only solve tasks the brain solves, but do so with internal representations that match those of biological neural circuits (Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Schrimpf et al., 2020; Doerig et al., 2023; Sadeh and Clopath, 2025). The dominant empirical instrument for testing this match is the brain score: a measure of how well a model’s internal activations predict neural responses to a shared stimulus set, typically via a linear readout fit on a training split and evaluated on held-out data (Schrimpf et al., 2018, e.g.,). Since the first demonstrations that task-optimized CNNs predict ventral-stream responses better than hand-designed models, brain scores have proliferated across modalities: vision (Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2018; Cadena et al., 2019), audition (Kell et al., 2018; Tuckute et al., 2023), and language (Wehbe et al., 2019; Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2026; AlKhamissi et al., 2025). They have substantially improved as architectures and training data have scaled (Antonello et al., 2023; Gokce and Schrimpf, 2025).

They have substantially improved as architectures and training data have scaled (Antonello et al., 2023; Gokce and Schrimpf, 2025).

Brain scores should be measured relative to what is achievable. Neural recordings are noisy: trial-to-trial variability, measurement noise, and finite sampling all place a hard ceiling on the variance any deterministic model can hope to predict (Hsu et al., 2004; Sahani and Linden, 2002; Schoppe et al., 2016). This noise ceiling is what separates a model that has captured the stimulus-driven signal from one that has room to improve. Without it, absolute brain scores are hard to interpret, as they confound model quality with data reliability. The noise ceiling reframes the question from “how high is the score?” to “how much of the explainable variance has been explained?”, a quantity on which models can be fairly compared across datasets, regions, and recording modalities.

Estimating the noise ceiling, however, is harder than it looks. The literature contains multiple procedures. Sahani and Linden (2002) introduced the explainable signal power estimator (SPE) to measure the fraction of stimulus-related variance of neural responses captured by models. Hsu et al. (2004) introduced the normalized correlation coefficient C​CnormCC_{\text{norm}}, which expresses model performance as a fraction of an estimated upper bound C​CmaxCC_{\text{max}} computed via split-half reliability with Spearman–Brown correction. Schoppe et al. (2016) showed that C​CnormCC_{\text{norm}} is preferable over the SPE in certain settings, and derived an alternative way of computing C​CmaxCC_{\text{max}} from signal power without resampling, avoiding computational expenses of the split-half procedure. Lage-Castellanos et al. (2019) extended this analysis to fMRI, comparing Monte Carlo, split-half, and analytic noise ceiling estimators across noise structures and regularization regimes. Schrimpf et al. (2021) introduced an extrapolation procedure used in Brain-Score. van Bree et al. (2025) clarified a common misinterpretation of noise ceilings in model evaluation, showing that split-half reliability is often incorrectly treated as a maximum achievable correlation rather than a bound on explainable variance (R2R^{2}). They demonstrate that this confusion can lead to inflated or misleading scores for model performance.

In this work, we revisit the noise ceiling from the ground up. We review the main families of estimators, derive analytical expressions under a generative model of brain signals, and characterize the assumptions and failure modes of each. Empirically, we show the qualitative match between model predictions and noise ceiling estimates on fMRI and EEG data. We close with concrete recommendations for which estimator to use, with the aim of putting brain-score comparisons on firmer statistical footing.

papers.title: Gorenstein symmetry can fail for noetherian rings
papers.abstract: We construct a two-sided noetherian ring $A$ which has injective dimension $1$ as a left module over itself and infinite injective dimension as a right module over itself. This shows that Gorenstein symmetry can fail for two-sided noetherian rings. It is further shown that there is such an example over any field of characteristic different than $2$, that it has a dualizing complex, and that its derived category of right modules does not satisfy injective-generation in the sense of Rickard-Keller.

papers.title: Triangle-free planar graphs need not be POSH
papers.abstract: We show that a triangle-free planar graph need not be partial one-sided Hamiltonian. This disproves a conjecture of Felsner, Schrezenmaier, Schr\"oder and Steiner.

papers.title: Forms and polynomial covers in many variables
papers.abstract:
Let $F \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be a homogeneous form of degree $d \ge 2$, and let $\sigma$ be the affine dimension of the singular locus of $F = 0$. We prove that the hypersurface $F = 0$ satisfies the smooth Hasse principle whenever \[
  n - \sigma \ge 2^{d + 1} - 3. \] This is the first improvement in the order of magnitude of Birch's classical result. We also apply the method to the counting problem for polynomial covers $F(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = g(y)$, and give a condition on $n - \sigma$ under which Serre's conjectural upper bound holds and another condition under which the expected asymptotic formula holds.

papers.title: Realization of expanding dynamics by a finite horizon parabolic law response
papers.abstract: We study the discrete dynamical system generated by iterating an episodic response of a population density. In each episode, the running potential is frozen at the current density, agents solve a quadratic control problem, and the terminal density is passed to the next episode. For each prescribed positive horizon $\tau$ and each $C^k$ map $F$ of finitely many Fourier moments, with $1\le k<\infty$, we construct a finite mode interaction realizing $F$ at order $\varepsilon$. In scaled coordinates, the exact parabolic response satisfies $\|T^{(d)}_{\varepsilon,\tau}-(F,S(\tau)|_{\Es_d})\|_{C^k}\le C\varepsilon$. The estimate is uniform over a full bounded infinite dimensional Sobolev fibre and needs neither Fourier truncation nor an invariant manifold. For scalar targets with disjoint expanding branches that strictly cover their convex hull, this $C^1$ control and parabolic compactness yield compact invariant sets of the exact response. These sets factor onto the full one sided shift and contain periodic densities of every least period. Nondegenerate periodic orbits continue, and hyperbolicity requires a separate strict multiplier condition. We also prove a derivative cost obstruction for nonaffine microscopic realization, a susceptibility weighted criterion for population energy designs, and the failure of exact scalar closure under nontrivial rank one feedback. The results concern designed frozen law responses, not Nash consistent mean field game equilibria or finite player limits.

papers.intro:
We study the dynamical system generated by iterating a frozen law optimal control response. At the start of each episode, a running potential is evaluated at the current population density and held fixed until the terminal time τ\tau. Agents then solve the resulting quadratic-control problem. This is a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman/Fokker–Planck pair, which the Cole–Hopf transformation reduces to linear parabolic equations. The terminal density becomes the input of the next episode. The structure is that of quadratic mean field games [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], where individual optimality is coupled to an evolving population law. Here, however, no equilibrium condition couples the running cost to the evolving law inside an episode. Agents optimize over a finite horizon against a frozen snapshot of the population law, so the response is not a Nash consistent forward–backward equilibrium. The iteration of this response map is the dynamical system studied here.

Agents then solve the resulting quadratic-control problem. This is a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman/Fokker–Planck pair, which the Cole–Hopf transformation reduces to linear parabolic equations. The terminal density becomes the input of the next episode. The structure is that of quadratic mean field games [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], where individual optimality is coupled to an evolving population law. Here, however, no equilibrium condition couples the running cost to the evolving law inside an episode. Agents optimize over a finite horizon against a frozen snapshot of the population law, so the response is not a Nash consistent forward–backward equilibrium. The iteration of this response map is the dynamical system studied here.

papers.title: Operationalizing Quantum Machine Learning for IoT Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased networked systems' exposure to cyber threats, making Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) essential for securing heterogeneous environments. While Deep Learning (DL) has shown strong performance in traffic analysis, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has recently gained attention as an alternative approach to learn complex traffic patterns. We assess QML's practical applicability to intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT scenarios. We present a hybrid quantum-classical NIDS and evaluate it on three recent IoT security datasets, under operationally relevant conditions. Beyond detection accuracy, we compare QML with a classical DL baseline across five operational perspectives: (i) performance under data scarcity, (ii) transferability through cross-domain evaluation, (iii) resilience to temporal constraints, (iv) robustness to quantum non-idealities across multiple noisy backends, and (v) prediction trustworthiness through calibration analysis. Experiments on binary and multiclass misuse detection show that DL generally outperforms QML under ideal and noisy conditions. However, QML remains competitive in data-scarcity and domain-shift scenarios and can outperform the DL baseline under temporal constraints.
papers.intro:
The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) enables a broad range of services such as remote monitoring, smart infrastructures, and safety-critical applications [15]. The increasing number of interconnected devices, including wearables and smart home systems, has significantly expanded both the volume and heterogeneity of network traffic.11 1 https://www.ericsson.com/en/reports-and-papers/mobility-report/reports/november-2025 However, the highly distributed and heterogeneous nature of IoT environments also enlarges the attack surface available to malicious actors. Cyberattacks targeting IoT systems may lead to severe consequences, including privacy breaches, financial losses, service disruption, and threats to human safety [6]. Consequently, significant research efforts have focused on developing solutions that detect cyber threats in a timely and reliable manner. Among them, Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) are designed to distinguish legitimate network activities from malicious traffic and identify the specific type of attack carried out by the adversary. However, traditional approaches often struggle to cope with the increasing complexity, scale, and encryption of modern network traffic. Machine Learning (ML) and, more recently, Deep Learning (DL) techniques have become central to modern NIDSs, especially in IoT scenarios, where the proliferation of connected devices considerably expands the attack surface. Quantum Computing (QC) represents a promising frontier in information science, emerging as a powerful response to the continuous growth of IoT traffic data volumes, with the ability to provide theoretical speedups on large-data processing and more accurate computational results. The intersection of QC paradigm with ML has given rise to Quantum Machine Learning (QML). QML combines quantum mechanics principles with AI-driven approaches [3, 13], offering a new way to capture non-linearity phenomena in complex data and a potential solution for pervasive security in IoT environments. Despite the surging interest in this field, practical quantum advantage remains an open issue [13], with empirical performance gains mostly limited to small-scale evaluations on synthetic or outdated datasets. Inherent quantum hardware noise affects circuit measurements and, consequently, QML outputs [14, 7]. QML-based NIDSs also face training data scarcity, domain transferability challenges, and timing constraints. Lastly, it remains unclear whether the confidence scores associated with classification decisions accurately reflect the actual predictive performance [11].

papers.title: The Borel Topos
papers.abstract: We construct a topos for Borel mathematics: statements which are true in Borel mathemaics correspond in a precise way to statements which are true in the internal logic of this topos. We investigate several other properties of this topos, including proving that it satisfies a Borel analogue of the Church-Turing thesis: the statement that every function on a standard Borel space is Borel. We also show that an earlier construction of a similar "Borel topos" by van Osdol does not suit these purposes because of an error in that paper.

Descriptive set theory, or more precisely Borel mathematics, is the study of the properties of mathematical objects built out of standard Borel spaces (see §2.5) using only Borel operations and relations. For example, Borel graph combinatorics is the study of graphs whose set of vertices form a standard Borel space and whose set of edges is a Borel subset of that space (see §4.2 for further examples).

Descriptive set theory, or more precisely Borel mathematics, is the study of the properties of mathematical objects built out of standard Borel spaces (see §2.5) using only Borel operations and relations. For example, Borel graph combinatorics is the study of graphs whose set of vertices form a standard Borel space and whose set of edges is a Borel subset of that space (see §4.2 for further examples).

One reason for interest in Borel mathematics is that on the one hand, Borel sets have many useful properties (for example, all Borel subsets of ℝ\mathbb{R} are Lebesgue measurable) and on the other hand, many of the mathematical constructions which one ordinarily performs do not take one outside the world of Borel mathematics.

The apparent robustness of Borel constructions suggests the existence of a self-contained “Borel mathematical universe” in which all mathematical constructions are in fact Borel constructions. We are thus led to the following two related questions: (1) Can we find a model for set theory which satisfies precisely those statements which are true in Borel mathematics? (2) Can we (at least partially) characterize the theory of this model? I.e., can we find a list of axioms which exactly characterize the constructions which are allowed in Borel mathematics? The purpose of this paper is to give an answer to (1). We also make some progress towards (2), although—despite this question being a large part of our motivation—we do not provide a definitive answer to it.

papers.title: SPARK: Spectral Preconditioned Analytic Residual Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for incompressible Navier Stokes equations
papers.abstract: We propose Spectral Jet KAN (SJ-KAN) to reduce the cost of differentiation and the network complexity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations. The input coordinates are embedded through Chebyshev bases whose spatial derivatives are known in closed form, and all differentiation matrices are computed once for the collocation points before training. A single linear layer compresses the Chebyshev bases into a few latent features, and a single nonlinear Chebyshev Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (CKAN) layer maps these features to the physical variables. Because the basis derivatives are known in advance and the compression is linear, the spatial derivatives in the NS equations are carried through the network analytically by a fixed sequence of matrix products and elementwise operations. Automatic differentiation (AD) is used only in backpropagation, to compute the gradients of the loss with respect to the network weights. We examine three variants of SJ-KAN (JetKAN, JetKAN-F, JetKAN-H), which differ in how the output layer maps the latent features to the physical variables. All variants are tested on the Taylor-Green vortex and on the lid driven cavity at Reynolds numbers Re = 100, 1000, 5000 and 10,000. The results are compared with a KAN that uses AD (PIKAN) and with a standard PINN. The SJ-KAN variants reach comparable or better accuracy than both, with up to 47 times fewer parameters and up to 8.2 times faster training per epoch. SJ-KAN also solves the lid driven cavity flow at Re = 10,000 without any reference data and with fewer than 9,000 trainable parameters. These results show that analytic derivative propagation, a small spectral input layer and a single KAN layer give a faster and simpler solver than methods based on AD, also for flows at high Reynolds numbers.

First, the conventional PINN implementations evaluate the required spatial derivatives using nested reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) [4].For second-order coupled systems like the Navier–Stokes equations, the AD cost scales with both network depth and derivative order [49], as shown in Equation 2. This cost grows with the network depth and the number of collocation points. [60] proposed the Spectral-Informed Neural Network (SINN), which operates entirely in the Fourier spectral domain and replaces high-order spatial derivatives with algebraic multiplications in frequency space, substantially lowering memory use and training time. In addition, Huang et al. [22] replaced AD with Chebyshev differentiation matrices (CD-PINN), cutting computation time by up to 86%86\%. Yin et al. [59] constructed neurons from Chebyshev basis functions (CSNN) that satisfy boundary conditions by construction, removing the boundary-penalty term from the loss.However, the computed derivatives are still evaluated through A​DAD. Chen et al. [10] combined Chebyshev spectral differentiation with Sobolev regularization (CS-PINN), addressing both derivative cost and solution regularity. Xiong et al. Among these spectral formulations, those that replace A​DAD with spectral differentiation retain fixed activation functions in the underlying network [60, 22, 10]. Second, the standard PINN architecture is built on a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with fixed activation functions that tend to learn low-frequency components first [40]. This property, known as spectral bias, makes it difficult to resolve the sharp gradients present in fluid flows [47, 44]. Efforts to address these issues include Fourier-feature embeddings [47] and adaptive loss-weighting strategies [52]. These works have partially alleviated spectral bias but do not, by themselves, remove the need for A​DAD-based derivative evaluation. Studies characterizing training failures in PINNs [29] have improved convergence in specific settings but again do not change how the residual derivatives are evaluated. Recently, Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) [36] have been developed to offer a structurally different alternative to MLPs. Instead of learning weights that multiply fixed activation functions at each node, a KAN places a learnable univariate function on every edge, a design motivated by the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem [28]. Training a KAN with a physics-informed loss yields a Physics-Informed KAN (PIKAN) [53]. For example, separable PIKANs (SPIKANs) [24] reduce cost further by assigning each spatial dimension its own KAN. However, this formulation requires a factorizable grid of collocation points [24]. Feature-enriched KANs (FEKANs) [38] accelerate convergence by augmenting the input with fixed nonlinear transformations, without adding trainable parameters.

KAN-based architectures can match or exceed MLP accuracy but exhibit distinct gradient pathologies during training. In the original KAN architecture, the B-spline parameterization was computationally expensive and sensitive to the number of collocation points [44]. Replacing the B-spline basis with low-order orthogonal polynomials such as Chebyshev, Legendre [44] and Jacobi [1] functions substantially improved both accuracy and training speed on the reported benchmarks. Chebyshev-basis PIKANs in particular proved faster and more accurate than B-spline PIKANs across a range of benchmark problems [44], including the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations [21, 13]. Despite these advances [39], polynomial-based PIKANs evaluate a learnable polynomial and thus increase the number of floating-point operations per edge [44, 21]. Furthermore, differentiating through these polynomial evaluations makes A​DAD even more expensive per parameter than in an equally sized MLP [44, 13]. Currently, the theoretical understanding of PIKAN training dynamics and their extension to coupled multi-output systems has received increasing attention [44]. To date, systematic studies of how architectural choices, such as network depth, polynomial degree, and basis type, affect multi-output accuracy and training stability on canonical fluid benchmarks remain limited.

papers.title: Quasifibrations in \'etale homotopy theory
papers.abstract:
We study quasifibrations in \'etale homotopy theory and prove a criterion for a morphism of schemes to be a quasifibration in terms of its (higher) direct images for sheaves of sets and (possibly non-abelian) groups. This allows to generalise Friedlander's formula for the homotopy fibre of geometric fibrations to the case of an arbitrary qcqs base scheme that is not necessarily normal.
  Among the applications to geometric fibrations are (1) specialisation is an equivalence on the pro-$\Sigma$ completed profinite \'etale homotopy types of geometric fibres, (2) a long exact sequence of \'etale homotopy groups in characteristic 0, and (3) a partially $\Sigma$-completed exact sequence of \'etale homotopy groups in low degree terms in general.

papers.title: The evolution of discs and the epoch of formation of giant planets around low-mass stars
papers.abstract: Large-grain depletion in the inner discs of young stellar systems provides a potential observational signature of dust filtration by forming giant-planet cores. In a previous study, we found that $0.50\pm0.10$ of prominent protoplanetary discs around solar-type stars ($0.7$--$1.5$~\Msun) with ages of 2--8~Myr show evidence for a depletion of large grains inside the snow line. Such a depletion may arise when a sufficiently massive planetary core acts as a barrier to the inward drift of large grains, filtering them from the inner disc. If this interpretation is correct, the frequency of dust-filtration signatures should decrease towards lower stellar masses, in accordance with the lower occurrence rate of giant planets around low-mass stars. Extending our analysis to lower-mass stars, we found that only $0.09\pm0.09$ of discs around stars with masses of $0.30$--$0.58$~\Msun, corresponding to the progenitors of main-sequence early M-type stars, show evidence of grain filtration. This fraction is lower than that measured for solar-type stars and is consistent with the lower frequency of giant planets around M-type stars. We also found that discs exhibiting evidence of filtration tend to have relatively massive outer dust reservoirs, with dust masses exceeding $20$~\MEarth. Conversely, the absence of filtration signatures in lower-mass discs suggests that Neptune-mass and lower-mass planets, despite being common around low-mass stars, may generally be unable to filter large grains efficiently.
papers.intro:
Planet formation and disc evolution are closely related. The disc provides the raw material from which planets form and acts as the birthplace of planetary systems. The formation of planets may sculpt the disc, modifying its properties. It is generally thought that there are two main mechanisms for planet formation: disc instability (Boss, 1997; Kratter & Lodato, 2016) operating on a timescale of a few thousands years, and core accretion (Safronov, 1972; Pollack et al., 1996; Mordasini et al., 2012; Armitage, 2020) operating on a slower timescale of millions of years. Disc instability is a top-down process and is expected to produce high mass companions at wide separation. Although the separation may change due to later migration to closer orbits, it is difficult to produce planets with mass ratios q≤0.001q\leq 0.001 with respect to their host stars through the disc instability process (Kratter & Lodato, 2016). For this reason, core accretion is the favoured mechanism for the formation of giant planets in the Solar System and for exoplanets, too.

The formation of planets may sculpt the disc, modifying its properties. It is generally thought that there are two main mechanisms for planet formation: disc instability (Boss, 1997; Kratter & Lodato, 2016) operating on a timescale of a few thousands years, and core accretion (Safronov, 1972; Pollack et al., 1996; Mordasini et al., 2012; Armitage, 2020) operating on a slower timescale of millions of years. Disc instability is a top-down process and is expected to produce high mass companions at wide separation. Although the separation may change due to later migration to closer orbits, it is difficult to produce planets with mass ratios q≤0.001q\leq 0.001 with respect to their host stars through the disc instability process (Kratter & Lodato, 2016). For this reason, core accretion is the favoured mechanism for the formation of giant planets in the Solar System and for exoplanets, too.

A peculiar feature of the core accretion mechanism is that once the cores of giant planets have formed (1–2 Myr after the initial formation of the stars), the inward drift of large grains (Weidenschilling, 1977) from the outer to the inner (long living) disc is likely inhibited, creating two separate reservoirs of grains (Paardekooper & Mellema, 2006; Rice et al., 2006; Kalyaan et al., 2023; Drążkowska et al., 2019; Houge et al., 2026). This process is called dust filtration. The segregation between non-carbonaceous and carbonaceous chondrites in the Solar System may be a manifestation of this phenomenon (Kruijer et al., 2017; Kleine et al., 2020). Weber et al. (2018) showed that only particles larger than a certain size can effectively be stopped from moving inward for a given diffusivity. Their calculations indicate that an appreciable effect occurs for rgrain≥0.03r_{\rm grain}\geq 0.03 cm and is related to a planet to star mass ratio q≈5×10−4q\approx 5\times 10^{-4}, which is about half of the Jupiter mass for a solar type star. On the other hand, dust grains undergo continuous collisions, leading to fragmentation (break-up) and coagulation (sticking) of the interacting particles, depending on the material properties and collision velocities (Birnstiel, 2024). Following these phenomena is then important to establish the ability of a planet gap to affect the size distribution of grains in the inner disc (Zhu et al., 2012). Updated hydrodynamical simulations investigating dust filtration by planet-induced gaps are presented by Pfeil et al. (2025). These authors performed two-dimensional multifluid hydrodynamic simulations of planet–disc systems that include dust coagulation and fragmentation. They showed that the efficiency of dust filtration is highly sensitive to grain evolution and, consequently, to disc properties such as turbulent diffusivity. Their results indicate that a planet with a mass of 0.6 MJup likely produces a significant depletion of large grains in the inner disc. In contrast, for planets with masses of 0.1 MJup – comparable to the expected mass of Jupiter’s core after (1–2 Myr) – dust filtration is generally insufficient to overcome grain coagulation, which continuously replenishes the population of large grains in the inner disc. Additionally, the impact of dust coagulation was also investigated by Drążkowska et al. (2019) who employed 2D hydrodynamic simulations of protoplanetary disks, showing that significant leakage of small grains can occur if fragmentation operates at the outer gap edge.

A peculiar feature of the core accretion mechanism is that once the cores of giant planets have formed (1–2 Myr after the initial formation of the stars), the inward drift of large grains (Weidenschilling, 1977) from the outer to the inner (long living) disc is likely inhibited, creating two separate reservoirs of grains (Paardekooper & Mellema, 2006; Rice et al., 2006; Kalyaan et al., 2023; Drążkowska et al., 2019; Houge et al., 2026). This process is called dust filtration. The segregation between non-carbonaceous and carbonaceous chondrites in the Solar System may be a manifestation of this phenomenon (Kruijer et al., 2017; Kleine et al., 2020). Weber et al. (2018) showed that only particles larger than a certain size can effectively be stopped from moving inward for a given diffusivity. Their calculations indicate that an appreciable effect occurs for rgrain≥0.03r_{\rm grain}\geq 0.03 cm and is related to a planet to star mass ratio q≈5×10−4q\approx 5\times 10^{-4}, which is about half of the Jupiter mass for a solar type star. On the other hand, dust grains undergo continuous collisions, leading to fragmentation (break-up) and coagulation (sticking) of the interacting particles, depending on the material properties and collision velocities (Birnstiel, 2024). Following these phenomena is then important to establish the ability of a planet gap to affect the size distribution of grains in the inner disc (Zhu et al., 2012). Updated hydrodynamical simulations investigating dust filtration by planet-induced gaps are presented by Pfeil et al. (2025). They showed that the efficiency of dust filtration is highly sensitive to grain evolution and, consequently, to disc properties such as turbulent diffusivity. Their results indicate that a planet with a mass of 0.6 MJup likely produces a significant depletion of large grains in the inner disc. In contrast, for planets with masses of 0.1 MJup – comparable to the expected mass of Jupiter’s core after (1–2 Myr) – dust filtration is generally insufficient to overcome grain coagulation, which continuously replenishes the population of large grains in the inner disc. Additionally, the impact of dust coagulation was also investigated by Drążkowska et al. (2019) who employed 2D hydrodynamic simulations of protoplanetary disks, showing that significant leakage of small grains can occur if fragmentation operates at the outer gap edge.

Pressure bumps leading to dust filtration might actually be present even in the absence of forming planets (see Chang et al. 2023). For instance, Charnoz et al. (2021) found that when the vertically averaged viscosity index is a decreasing function of the surface density, then the release of water vapour at the snow line decreases the sound velocity, and a pressure bump may appear given a constant inflow of icy pebbles with a ratio of the pebble influx to gas influx >0.6>0.6 for a power-law disc with a 1% ice-to-gas ratio, and >1.8>1.8 for a disc with an ice-to-gas ratio ∼0.3\sim 0.3%. On the other hand, dust traps may favour the formation of giant planets (see, e.g., Izidoro et al. 2022). Then they may still be related to the phenomenon of dust filtration.
