On the other hand, dust traps may favour the formation of giant planets (see, e.g., Izidoro et al. 2022). Then they may still be related to the phenomenon of dust filtration.

For several reasons, the region around and just beyond the snow line is considered a particularly favourable site for giant-planet formation (Drążkowska & Alibert, 2017). Tracking the evolution of the dust size distribution both within and beyond the snow line is therefore crucial to quantify the efficiency with which planetary gaps filter dust grains. In a previous paper (Gratton & Rigliaco 2026, hereafter Paper I), we investigated the properties of dust grains in the inner and outer regions of protoplanetary discs, separated by a boundary approximately corresponding to the snow line. We performed a simultaneous modelling of the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and ALMA dust-continuum images for a sample of 33 protoplanetary discs around solar-type stars, with stellar masses ranging from 0.7 to 1.5 M⊙ . The sample was selected to include systems for which accurate stellar ages could be derived from dynamical masses and evolutionary tracks. We found that the grain size distributions in the inner (interior to the snow line) and outer regions of the disc are statistically indistinguishable for systems younger than 2 Myr. In contrast, among discs with ages between 2–8 Myr, approximately half exhibit a significant depletion of large grains in the inner disc. As mentioned above, this is the expected consequence of the existence of cores with several tens of Earth masses whose formation requires 1–2 Myr (Paardekooper & Mellema, 2006; Rice et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2018; Weber et al., 2018; Pfeil et al., 2025). In contrast, the lack of evidence of dust filtration in very young discs would need a specific explanation for alternative mechanisms. Although the sample we considered is biassed because we selected stars with prominent long-living discs, the fraction of long-living discs showing evidence for grain segregation agrees with the frequency of Jupiter-like planets observed in young associations, which are the likely progeny of the sparse star forming regions in the Solar neighbourhood.

papers.title: On the unirationality of anticanonical weighted complete intersection surfaces: the infinite families
papers.abstract: Anticanonical weighted complete intersection surfaces fall into finitely many sporadic families and four infinite families. We prove that the anticanonical surfaces lying in the infinite families are unirational over their field of definition. Over a Hilbertian field, we further prove that a Hilbert subset of members consists of nonrational surfaces.

papers.intro:
Every log del Pezzo surface over a field of characteristic zero is geometrically rational. However, over a field that is not algebraically closed, geometric rationality does not imply rationality. The exceptional curves on the minimal resolution may form nontrivial Galois orbits, and a conic bundle may not admit a rational section even when it has a rational multisection. Log del Pezzo surfaces that arise as weighted complete intersections have the advantage of coming with explicit projective equations, which can be used in birational constructions to establish rationality properties.

Log del Pezzo surfaces that arise as weighted complete intersections have the advantage of coming with explicit projective equations, which can be used in birational constructions to establish rationality properties.

In this paper we work over a field KK of characteristic zero that is not algebraically closed and study anticanonical weighted complete intersection log del Pezzo surfaces over KK that belong to infinite families. These surfaces exhibit both phenomena described above. We prove that every such surface is unirational over KK. When KK is Hilbertian, we also prove that the members parametrised by a Hilbert subset of the parameter space are not rational over KK.

papers.title: Eccentricities and inclinations are decoupled in super-Earth systems
papers.abstract: Recent work on the longterm evolution of the inner Solar System has shown that the inclination contribution to the Angular Momentum Deficit (AMD) is almost constant even though inclinations and eccentricities are highly coupled in expansions of the perturbing function. We wish to characterize the conservation of the eccentricity AMD and inclination AMD, respectively describing the average eccentricity and mutual inclination of planetary orbits, beyond the case of the Solar System. We aim at showing that this conservation is a general feature of the stable planetary systems dynamics, in particular, in the context of low mass multiplanetary systems. We perform a series of numerical simulations using both N-body and secular codes to study the dynamics over billions of orbits. Taking as a template four equal mass Super-Earth with non uniform orbital spacing, we consider sets of systems with different AMD and use the orbital elements evolution to assess the conservation of inclination and eccentricity AMD components. For stable systems, the inclination AMD and eccentricity AMD relative variation is typically below 1%, making them quasi-integrals of motion. At low AMD, despite short Lyapunov timescales, the secular diffusion is confined and the dynamics almost quasi-periodic. As the AMD increases, the emergence of large scale secular chaos only weakly affects the conservation of the quasi-integrals, which breaks when systems become fully unstable. The eccentricity and inclination evolution (as measured by the variation of their AMD contributions) are largely decoupled for low mass multiplanetary systems. Combined with the weak diffusion of the Laplace-Lagrange modes at low AMD, these findings paint a picture where the secular dynamics are not necessarily ergodic. The uncovering of these quasi-integrals opens a new path to relate the observed planetary architecture to its formation.

papers.intro:
Since the very first discovery of an exoplanet by Mayor and Queloz (1995), the astrophysics community has been actively looking to discover more and more exoplanets. In this scope, many transit space-based missions have been completed (see e.g. Auvergne et al., 2009; Borucki et al., 2010, for the CoRoT and Kepler missions) and many more are undergoing, as TESS (Ricker et al., 2014) and, in preparation, as PLATO (Rauer et al., 2025). Radial velocity surveys have also allowed a large number of exoplanet discoveries, using for instance the spectrographs SOPHIE (Bouchy et al., 2013) and HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011; Bonfils et al., 2013; Mignon et al., 2024) or via the California Legacy Survey (Rosenthal et al., 2021). With no less than 6,451 confirmed exoplanets discovered to date11 1 As of October 15, 2026, according to the NASA exoplanet archive available at https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/., understanding their dynamics has been a focus. There have indeed been major advances in our understanding of exoplanet population distributions and the structure of planetary systems. It has become clear that the Solar System is highly atypical and does not follow the common architecture of planetary systems. Indeed, many systems seem to be formed of closely-packed, similarly massive planets (Weiss et al., 2018) and have very low mutual inclinations (≲5∘\lesssim 5^{\circ}) (Tremaine and Dong, 2012) and eccentricities (≲0.1\lesssim 0.1) (Winn and Fabrycky, 2015; Xie et al., 2016; Johansen et al., 2012).

The dynamical study of the Solar System has always been an active field of research and the first longterm simulations of the Solar System have shown its chaotic nature (Laskar, 1989; Laskar, 1990). As a result, it is impossible to accurately predict its evolution beyond about 60 million years (Myr). For longer timescales, it is still possible to make predictions, but through a statistical approach (Laskar, 2008). In Laskar and Gastineau (2009), the probability that Mercury’s orbit might cross the path of Venus was found to be about 1%1\% in the next 5 billion years. This apparent discrepancy between the long stability timescale and the short Lyapunov timescale of only 5 Myr found by Laskar (1989) hints to more complex dynamical features. Recent studies on the inner Solar System dynamics (Mogavero et al., 2023) have shown that the ergodic assumption (under which the entire phase space of the system may be explored) is not verified for the secular chaos, with quantities being almost conserved over planetary systems lifetime. In particular, an unexpected result was found by Mogavero et al. (2023) regarding the longterm evolution of the Angular Momentum Deficit (Laskar, 1997; Laskar, 2000, hereafter AMD\mathrm{AMD},). The AMD\mathrm{AMD} is the difference between the norm of the angular momentum of a coplanar and circular system with the same semi-major axes and the norm of the angular momentum. The AMD can be seen as, approximately, a weighted sum of the squared mutual inclinations and squared eccentricities of the planetary orbits. Mogavero et al. (2023) found that the part of the AMD\mathrm{AMD} originating from the inclinations (AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}}) is almost conserved in the inner Solar System22 2 The inner Solar System AMD\mathrm{AMD} is not conserved due to the forcing caused by the outer system inducing variations of AMD\mathrm{AMD} originating from the eccentricities (AMDe\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{e}}).. The conservation of AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} in the inner system is a possible explanation for the discrepancy between the Lyapunov timescale and the collision probability mentioned above. In fact, a conservation is a very unexpected result since the variables are strongly influencing each-other and exchanges occur for very inclined systems, for instance, through the well known Kozai-Lidov oscillations (Kozai, 1962; Lidov, 1962).

The amount of AMD acts as a dynamical temperature and determines the possibilities for planets within a system to suffer from close encounters. Having the AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} constant limits the pathways through which the system could evolve into an unstable configuration. Thus, systems tend to be more stable when the AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} is perfectly conserved than when it is not. Generalizing the conservation of AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} beyond the Solar System could be a new probe for understanding exoplanet formation conditions. We know from the work of Stewart and Wetherill (1988), Ohtsuki et al. (2002), and Stewart and Ida (2000) that, during instability phases, scattering of planetesimals in the disk tends to excite eccentricities faster than inclinations. If the conservation of AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} found by Mogavero et al. (2023) in the case of the Solar System is valid for exoplanetary systems, the current state of systems could be related to formation conditions within disks, and thus, for instance, provide insights into instability phases. Finally, this conservation has an implication for understanding how exoplanetary systems evolve over long timescales but also constrains the occurrence rate of multi-planetary systems. Indeed the detection capabilities of such systems are strongly impacted by the mutual inclination distribution (in particular in the case of the transit technique).

The amount of AMD acts as a dynamical temperature and determines the possibilities for planets within a system to suffer from close encounters. Having the AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} constant limits the pathways through which the system could evolve into an unstable configuration. Thus, systems tend to be more stable when the AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} is perfectly conserved than when it is not. Generalizing the conservation of AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} beyond the Solar System could be a new probe for understanding exoplanet formation conditions. We know from the work of Stewart and Wetherill (1988), Ohtsuki et al. (2002), and Stewart and Ida (2000) that, during instability phases, scattering of planetesimals in the disk tends to excite eccentricities faster than inclinations. If the conservation of AMDi\mathrm{AMD}_{\mathrm{i}} found by Mogavero et al. (2023) in the case of the Solar System is valid for exoplanetary systems, the current state of systems could be related to formation conditions within disks, and thus, for instance, provide insights into instability phases. Finally, this conservation has an implication for understanding how exoplanetary systems evolve over long timescales but also constrains the occurrence rate of multi-planetary systems. Indeed the detection capabilities of such systems are strongly impacted by the mutual inclination distribution (in particular in the case of the transit technique).

The results obtained in the 90s and 2000s, but also the recent work of Mogavero et al. (2023), were all made possible by a specific approach to the dynamics. Outside Mean Motion Resonances (MMRs) active regions, the motion of planets around massive objects like stars is dominated by the slow deformation of their orbits while keeping a constant semi-major axis. It is thus possible to simplify the system’s physics and drastically reduce the computation time of longterm evolution simulations. These dynamics, called secular, are known since Laplace and Lagrange’s times.

papers.title: An expert consensus on identification likelihood in NeuroImaging data
papers.abstract: Guidelines on the anonymity of neuroimaging data help manage research data, inform institutional legal and governance frameworks, and support data-sharing workflows. The question of identifiability is particularly salient in human brain imaging because such data are not only potentially personal (i.e., related to an identifiable person) but also sensitive and thus require extra precautionary and protective processes. The identifiability of brain imaging data is also salient for emerging legal and ethical frameworks regarding rights that emphasise the special status of brain data as closely linked to personal identity, mental privacy, and autonomy. Using a combined nominal group technique and Delphi process, we obtained expert consensus ratings of re-identification and singling-out likelihood across 34 neuroimaging data types, spanning multiple imaging modalities and processing levels, from curated research data to maps, matrices, and summary tables. Expert ratings suggest that 38-67% of the assessed neuroimaging data types could be shared with minimal restrictions based on their intrinsic re-identification likelihood, subject to contextual safeguards. The resulting classification enables researchers to engage with relevant legal teams to guide the appropriate and safe release of data, and to determine the appropriate level of protection (licensing, access controls, governance) in line with domestic and international legal requirements, with the ultimate goal of facilitating international data exchange. A website (https://brainimagingprivacy.github.io/) has been created to facilitate the dissemination of these findings and related evidence among relevant parties.

papers.title: An intrinsic kinematic wave model with conservative fluxes for overland flow on curved terrain
papers.abstract: Kinematic wave models, the simplest surface flow models, route overland flow by gravity alone and there is no pressure or inertial term to redistribute flow when the resulting velocities misroute it. Computed from piecewise-linear elevation data, this velocity jumps across the edges of the mesh: two neighboring cells can push water into each other, and the scheme can hold water in ponds that the terrain does not contain, or concentrate it where the data do not. We formulate the model intrinsically on the bed surface, with the depth normal to the bed as unknown, and obtain a single-valued edge velocity, in the unique edge frame of the intrinsic geometry, by correcting the raw cell field with the star-based conservative flux of Larson and Niklasson. Because the field is derived from data rather than from a Galerkin solution, the local problems are solvable only with a compatible load, the weak discrete divergence of the field being corrected, which for the slope is a discrete mean curvature of the terrain. With a Neumann boundary, every element is conservative, and the corrected field reproduces the cell average of the nodal divergence of the raw field, plus the divergence resolved inside the curved cells. Since any single-valued flux conserves mass, the correction is about consistency and robustness: the steady state of the upwind scheme solves an M-matrix system exactly when every cell drains to an outlet, and spurious ponds are closed classes of a transfer directed graph, computable before any simulation. Four rainfall tests, from a plane to a real catchment, are designed to verify the difference in storage and timing between the intrinsic and the classical form, the effect of the mesh on the consistency of the edge velocity, the robustness at a degenerate stationary point, and the application to terrain data.

papers.intro:
Surface runoff is modeled in practice using mainly three approaches belonging to the same family: the Shallow Water (SW) equations, the Diffusive Wave (DW) approximation, and the Kinematic Wave (KW) approximation. The SW equations are a consistent two-dimensional depth-integrated approximation of the Navier-Stokes equations, with the DW approach being derived from SW by dropping the inertial terms. A further approximation, at the basis of the KW model, neglects the pressure terms so that the flow is driven by gravity and with a direction that follows the steepest descent. These three models are used by different communities and their domains of validity are neither always clear nor analyzed with the appropriate mathematical rigor. Classical applicability criteria exist in one dimension on uniform slopes [53, 41], while for two-dimensional flows over curved terrain the question is largely open. Thin-layer models in topography-fitted coordinates, with the depth measured along the normal to the bed, are classical for granular and debris flows [44, 16], and were derived for shallow water over variable topography by [6, 19, 2]. A geometrically intrinsic formulation of the shallow water model was presented by [2]. Here the bed geometry enters the model through a local curvilinear coordinate system anchored on the bed. Further approximations of the Intrinsic Shallow Water Equations (ISWE) can produce corresponding intrinsic versions of the diffusive wave and kinematic wave equations. Our long term goal is to analyze these models, the importance of the geometry, and their validity in different scenarios, and the current work is a first step in this direction.

The KW approach is the natural entry point and the focus for this work. It is the simplest member of the hierarchy and the one most sensitive to geometry. Without inertia and pressure, the terrain slope is its only driver, so the discrete velocity field arising from the terrain gradient determines the flow paths, and no term of the model can redirect a flow that these velocities misroute. This is the central idea here: on a triangulated terrain, the consistency of the discrete model with the elevation data and its robustness are largely decided, before any water is moved, by the way a single-valued edge velocity is constructed from the data. We start by deriving the model on the bed surface itself as the zero-inertia and zero-pressure limit of the ISWE, and we discretize it with a first-order finite volume (FV) scheme built on the intrinsic geometry [2]. Despite its simplicity, the KW model and its discretization have requirements that are rarely stated explicitly. The first concerns the terrain: the topography must be KW-admissible (i). Without a pressure term, both a closed depression (pit) and a flat region trap water forever, and a boundary segment towards which the flow is directed must be an outflow. Real Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) violate these requirements, and the usual remedies, obtained by filling [24, 39] or breaching [30] of the depressions, modify the elevations and can introduce new artifacts, such as flats and parallel flow paths. The other two requirements concern the numerical scheme. An FV-based transport solver needs a single-valued and locally conservative normal velocity on every edge (ii), a condition violated by a velocity field computed directly from the surface mesh. Indeed, the tangential gradient of a piecewise-linear approximation of the height function describing the topographic surface, and hence the kinematic field built from it, is piecewise constant and jumps across edges and is generally not locally conservative. On a curved surface, single-valuedness also requires a common reference frame on each edge (iii), since the two cells sharing an edge have different tangent planes. For this study, we assume requirement (i) to be satisfied by the input. Requirement (iii) is met by the unique edge frame of the intrinsic FV scheme [2], while requirement (ii) is one of the main subjects of this work. We obtain the single-valued edge velocity feeding the finite volume scheme by a locally conservative correction of the piecewise-constant kinematic field, and we analyze what this construction imposes on the velocity field and what it implies for the robustness of the scheme.

This correction is the discrete counterpart of a situation well known in porous-media flow, where a continuous Galerkin (CG) velocity must be made compatible with a transport scheme. Local post-processing techniques recover, from the CG solution, edge fluxes that are single-valued and conservative on every element [28, 49, 12, 35, 15]. A global alternative, a constrained least-squares projection of the 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} gradients onto the ℛ​𝒯0\mathcal{RT}_{0} mixed finite element space with element-wise conservation, was proposed for particle tracking in [46]. In hydrological practice, overland flow on terrain meshes often bypasses the velocity field altogether. Flow-routing algorithms on grids and triangulations assign transfer fractions between neighboring cells directly from the elevations [43, 20, 50, 51, 36]. More recent approaches have focused on the identification of surface flow paths and the preservation of topographic features controlling drainage [36, 32]. In particular, in [32] the authors proposed the extraction of thalweg and ridge networks from unaltered elevation data as a basis for terrain partitioning. Such approaches address the representation of DEM-consistent terrain features and drainage pathways, but do not provide a consistent velocity field for a PDE-based surface routing model. On surfaces, locally conservative discretizations exist, but conservation is obtained by changing the discretization rather than by post-processing a CG field: hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (DG) and mixed methods, including surface Raviart-Thomas spaces [11], interior-penalty DG [13], cut DG for the Laplace-Beltrami operator [8], conservative discontinuous cut finite element method (FEM) for coupled bulk-interface problems, with conservation on macro elements [29], and finite volumes [25, 21]. The absence of flux recovery on surfaces is also visible in a posteriori error estimation, which for surface FEM is, as far as we could find, residual-based [14, 4]. An equilibrated (Prager-Synge type) estimator, which would require precisely a conservative flux recovery, has not been reported, whereas on flat domains such estimators are built from vertex-patch problems with a compatible load [7, 18].

papers.title: A robust Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume scheme for intrinsic shallow water equations with wetting-and-drying transitions on locally discontinuous beds
papers.abstract: In this work, we extend the Intrinsic Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume method for the Intrinsic Shallow Water Equations (ISWE) to account for localized topographic discontinuities that influence flow patterns. The ISWE formulation is modified to incorporate these bottom perturbations without altering the global structure of the system. The numerical discretization is based on a Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Volume scheme within an intrinsic geometric framework and consists of a Lagrangian evolution step followed by an Eulerian remapping onto a fixed reference grid. The combination of the intrinsic nature of the ISWE formulation and the dual Lagrangian-Eulerian structure of the proposed discretization yields a numerical method that naturally satisfies the three key properties essential for stability, accuracy, and robustness: well-balancing for preservation of the lake-at-rest equilibrium over irregular bathymetry; wetting-and-drying, enabling robust tracking of moving fluid boundaries; and hyperbolicity guaranteeing consistency with the system wave propagation and stability constraints. Numerical experiments on curved two-dimensional surfaces with localized bottom discontinuities demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the method, including accurate long-time velocity computations in near-dry conditions and transitions between wet and dry states.

papers.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

We consider solving nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems of the form: min𝒙∈ℝd⁡f⁡(𝒙)=𝔼𝒫​[F⁡(𝒙,ξ)],s.t.c⁡(𝒙)=𝟎,\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}\left[F(\bm{x};\xi)\right],\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c(\bm{x})=\bm{0}, (1) where f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} denotes the stochastic objective function, F⁡(⋅,ξ):ℝd→ℝF(\cdot;\xi):\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} denotes its realization with sample ξ∼𝒫\xi\sim\mathcal{P}, and c:ℝd→ℝmc:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} denotes deterministic equality constraints. Problem (1) arises in a broad range of applications spanning machine learning, statistics, and scientific computing. In statistical learning, it naturally appears as a constrained parameter estimation problem (Geyer, 1991; Hansen, 1982), where ξ\xi represents an observed data sample and f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) denotes the expected population loss or negative log-likelihood. Similar constrained stochastic optimization problems also arise in portfolio allocation optimization (Du et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2012), where the objective measures the expected performance of weighted random asset returns, while the portfolio weights must satisfy structural constraints such as budget, risk, or exposure conditions. Related formulations have further emerged in scientific machine learning, including physics-informed neural networks (Raissi et al., 2019) and stochastic PDE-constrained learning problems (Kouri et al., 2014), where the constraints encode physical laws or governing equations. These diverse applications motivate the development of efficient stochastic optimization algorithms for solving (1) and conducting valid statistical inference on the resulting primal–dual solutions.

papers.title: The Kelvin--Hicks Formula from the Energy--Casimir Principle
papers.abstract:
The classical Kelvin--Hicks formula expresses the propagation speed of a thin vortex ring in an incompressible ideal fluid in terms of its circulation, distance from the symmetry axis, and core radius. In this paper, we rigorously derive this formula from a variational principle based on Arnold's energy--Casimir method, without prescribing any of these geometric or physical quantities a priori. We introduce a scale-invariant variational principle involving the energy, impulse, and $L^p$ Casimir invariants. For $1 < p < \infty$, we construct orbitally stable energy-maximizing vortex rings and investigate how their geometry depends on the Casimir exponent $p$. For sufficiently large $p$, the vortex rings have cores homeomorphic to a ball and converge to Hill's spherical vortex as $p \to \infty$. In contrast, as $p\to1^+$, the energy-maximizing vortex rings concentrate onto a circular filament of radius $e^{1/3}$, uniquely selected by the variational principle. After suitable translations and rescalings, their vortex-core profiles converge to an optimizer of the logarithmic Hardy--Littlewood--Sobolev inequality.
  Introducing an effective core radius $\epsilon_p$ determined by the entropy of the vorticity distribution, we establish the Kelvin--Hicks formula \begin{align*} W_p = \frac{\Gamma_p}{4\pi R_p} \left(\log\frac{8R_p}{\epsilon_p}-1+o(1)\right) \quad \textrm{as}\ p\to1^+, \end{align*} where $W_p$, $\Gamma_p$, and $R_p$ denote the propagation speed, circulation, and effective ring radius, respectively. In particular, the constant correction $-1$ is obtained for nonuniform vortex-core profiles without imposing any prescribed core structure.

The propagation speed WW of a thin axisymmetric vortex ring translating through an incompressible ideal fluid is described by the Kelvin–Hicks formula [52, art. 163 (7), p. 241], [64, §10.2 (1)], [42, (1.3)]: (1.1) W=Γ4​π​R​(log⁡8​Rϵ−14+o⁡(1))as ​ϵR→0,\displaystyle W=\frac{\Gamma}{4\pi R}\left(\log\frac{8R}{\epsilon}-\frac{1}{4}+o(1)\right)\quad\text{as }\frac{\epsilon}{R}\to 0, where Γ\Gamma is the circulation, RR is the major radius of the vortex ring, and ϵ\epsilon is the radius of its cross-sectional core; see Figure 1. papers.title: The 2026 iron meteorite fall near Zadzim (Poland) and atmospheric ablation of iron meteoroids
papers.abstract: Understanding the process of penetration of cosmic material through the Earth's atmosphere is important for linking the atmospheric and ground effects with the properties of original bodies. It has been shown previously that the main process affecting the fate of stony impactors is atmospheric fragmentation. Much less is known about iron impactors,mainly because the scarcity of data about actual iron meteorite falls. Here we present the trajectory, dynamics, light curve, spectrum, and orbit of a fireball which occurred on April 17, 2026, over Poland and was observed by the European Fireball Network and the Skytinel Network. Based on the fireball observations, single 2.9 kg iron meteorite was recovered in the municipality of Zadzim. Analysis of the fireball data revealed no fragmentation although the body suffered a relatively large dynamic pressure of 5.2 MPa. Fitting the light curve needed luminous efficiency 3 times larger than for stony meteoroids. The initial mass was about 19 kg, corresponding to an effective size of 17 cm. We fitted the light curves of 7 other fireballs produced by iron meteoroids with sizes of 2.5 - 13 cm. The ablation coefficient reached enormously high values of about 1 kg/MJ in small meteoroids causing the material to be exhausted and the fireball to end suddenly high in the atmosphere. In the present case, the value did not exceed 0.08 kg/MJ and relaxed to 0.023 kg/MJ towards the end, enabling part of the meteoroid to survive as meteorite. We conclude that the fate of iron meteoroids strongly depends on their size. The reason probably is the high thermal conductivity of iron which leads to complete overheating and easy melting of smaller meteoroids. The orbits of 44 iron fireballs are also provided.

papers.intro:
Meteorites are broadly divided into stony, iron, and stony-iron. Iron meteorites are of interest because their high density and strength can lead to significantly larger ground damage produced by large impactors in comparison with stony projectiles of similar sizes (Luther et al., 2026). There are 18 known craters or crater fields on Earth produced by irons in the past, the largest being the 1.2 km Barringer crater in Arizona (Luther et al., 2026, and references therein). Most meteorites are, nevertheless, stony. The Meteoritical Bulletin Database11 1 https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meteor/metbull.php of The Meteoritical Society lists 49 witnessed iron meteorite falls as of July 15, 2026, which represents less than 4% of all 1278 witnessed meteorite falls. Stony-irons are even rarer with only 11 witnessed falls. In total, the database contains 1440 iron meteorites found on Earth and 11 found on Mars.

Iron meteorites have been divided into 13 groups and many ungrouped meteorites according to their composition (McSween Jr. and Husse, 2010). All of them are dominated by metal Fe with typically 5 – 20% of Ni, and small amounts of Co, P, S, and some other minor siderophile elements (Mittlefehldt et al., 1998). The average bulk density of fresh iron meteorites is 7500±2007500\pm 200 kg m-3 and both compressive and tensile strength can reach 400 MPa (Ostrowski and Bryson, 2019). While the compressive strength is comparable to stony meteorites (namely ordinary chondrites), the tensile strength of irons is much higher in comparison with stones (Pohl and Britt, 2020). Heat capacity of irons (∼\sim200 J kg-1 K-1) is less than half of that of stones and thermal conductivity (∼\sim40 W m-1 K-1) is an order of magnitude higher (Ostrowski and Bryson, 2019).

While observed iron meteorite falls are rare, numerous small iron meteoroids which completely ablated in the atmosphere have been identified by meteor spectroscopy (Halliday, 1960; Ceplecha, 1966; Borovička et al., 2005; Vojáček et al., 2015; Vojáček et al., 2020; Mazur et al., 2024). Meteors produced by mm-sized irons are often characterized by sudden onset of brightness, low beginning height, and short trajectory (Borovička et al., 2005; Mills et al., 2021). The light curves were successfully explained by a model considering iron melting, immediate removal of liquid iron from the surface in form of a cloud of droplets, and their subsequent vaporization (Čapek et al., 2019). The fragmentation into droplets was later directly imaged (Mazur et al., 2024).

At low brightness and low speeds (<<15 km s-1), iron meteors represent about 20% of all meteors (Mills et al., 2021). Among bright meteors (fireballs), irons were found to represent about 4% of sporadic fireballs on asteroidal orbits (Borovička et al., 2022b). Iron fireballs (with peak brightness between magnitudes −6-6 and −10-10) have a less steep brightness increase than faint iron meteors. On the other hand, they are characterized by very sudden drop of brightness at the end (Ceplecha, 1966; Vojáček et al., 2020). The trajectories are still quite short and when classified according to the end height with the PEP_{E} criterion (Ceplecha and McCrosky, 1976), they come out as weak bodies with PEP_{E} values similar to cometary dustballs (Vojáček et al., 2020; Borovička et al., 2022b). From those observations, it appears that it is very hard for iron material to reach the ground, unless, probably, the initial body is very big.

Until recently, only one iron meteorite fall was observed instrumentally. On November 7, 2020, an exceptionally bright fireball occurred over Sweden. The country was covered by clouds at that time, nevertheless, the fireball trajectory and orbit could be computed using four distant video records, three from Finland and one from Norway (Kyrylenko et al., 2023). Dark flight was also simulated and one 13.8 kg iron meteorite was finally recovered near Ådalen in early December (Moilanen et al., 2026). The fireball was also detected by spaceborne U.S. Government sensors22 2 https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/fireballs/, which measured the total radiated energy to be 8.5×10108.5\times 10^{10} J. The released light curve covering the brightest phase of the fireball shows a broad maximum peaking at ∼5\sim 5 GW ster-1, corresponding to visual magnitude of about −19-19. We detected the bright part also by radiometers in the Czech Republic, at a range of 1000 km. The fireball terminated at the remarkably low height of 11 km (Moilanen et al., 2026) but no details about the atmospheric deceleration and full light curve are available, except the recent sketch by Jenniskens et al. (2026).

papers.title: Understanding the Importance of Massive Activations through Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: A common occurrence in Large Language Models (LLMs) is the emergence of so-called massive activations. This phenomenon is well known in the literature and has been connected to attention sinks, representational compression, as well as signal propagation. However, the reasons and consequences for their appearance are not yet well understood. In this paper, we explain the role of massive activations in deep learning by showing that they are connected to the region migration phenomenon in delayed robustness. Under the spline theoretic interpretation of deep networks, we show that massive activations push the representations away from the nonlinearity boundaries of the network, decreasing the complexity of its input-output map around data points. Furthermore, we uncover for the first time that this phenomenon is not unique to transformers and actually appears in a number of common architectures performing simple supervised learning tasks. We validate this connection through extensive experiments on a diverse set of architectures including residual MLP, ResNet18, Vision Transformers and GPT and datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, Imagenette and Shakespeare Text. We consistently observe that massive activations and region migration co-occur with adversarial robustness. Furthermore, we illustrate that this connection holds in the large-scale pretraining of LLMs by showing that the rise of massive activations in LLMs closely tracks the adversarial accuracy of the model under perturbations of the token embeddings.

papers.intro:
Despite their remarkable success, the inner workings of neural networks remain poorly understood, giving rise to surprising phenomena that challenge our understanding of how they learn. One such phenomenon that recently gained traction in the context of LLMs is the so-called massive activations (Sun et al., 2024). These are a few activations in the hidden representation of neural networks that grow multiple orders of magnitude larger than the others. These activations rise in early layers and persist through the network via the residual stream, until disappearing near the output. Recent work has linked massive activations to attention sinks and pre-norm architectures (Sun et al., 2026b), traced their formation to interactions between normalization and feed-forward layers (Shi et al., 2026), and interpreted them as structural bias vectors (Chen et al., 2026). Related work on activation outliers has also implicated normalization, signal propagation, and optimization in their emergence (He et al., 2024). However, their broader functional role remains poorly understood.

papers.title: On the potential of widening the band of X-ray polarimetry
papers.abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) has made X-ray polarimetry a routine astrophysical diagnostic, but its sensitivity is confined to the 2-8 keV band, where the photoelectric effect in a gas is most efficiently exploited. Several of the questions raised by its results, as well as some classical goals of high-energy astrophysics, require polarimetry below 2~keV, to reach the thermal emission of neutron stars, black-hole discs and blazars, and above 8~keV, where reflection, cyclotron lines and the non-thermal emission of supernova remnants, pulsar wind nebulae and magnetars can be isolated. Following a recent review of the subject, we discuss the scientific case for extending the band over roughly 0.1-80 keV and beyond, and the techniques that can deliver it: Bragg diffraction on graded multilayers, photoelectric gas imagers read out by pixel ASICs with time-of-arrival capability, time projection chambers and focal-plane Compton polarimeters, including their combination in stacked focal planes. We then summarise how these techniques are being implemented, or could be, in REDSoX and GOSoX, eXTP, XPP, WXPT and in EXPO and PHEMTO, proposed to the ESA M8 call, as well as in the wide-field transient polarimeter POLAR-2, and we discuss the trade-offs that will drive the design of a wide-band polarimetry mission.

papers.title: Design, Testing and Calibration of the GAPS Experiment Si(Li) Tracker Readout ASIC: From the First Flight Campaign Toward the Second Mission Upgrade
papers.abstract: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is a balloon-borne experiment designed to perform three long-duration flights from Antarctica to search for low-energy cosmic antinuclei, in particular antideuterons, as an indirect signature of dark matter. Its detection method relies on the formation and decay of exotic atoms, identified through the emission of characteristic x-rays and the subsequent annihilation into secondary particles. At the core of the instrument is the silicon tracker, composed of lithium-drifted silicon detectors operated at -40{\deg}C and read out by a custom application-specific integrated circuit, SLIDER32, implemented in 180 nm CMOS technology. This thesis reports on the integration, calibration, and validation of the SLIDER32-based tracker readout electronics. Laboratory characterization of a tracker module with an Am-241 source and cosmic muons was complemented by calibration and testing of the full tracker in flight configuration, leading to the first x-ray spectrum acquisition from a Cd-109 source. These activities were part of the integration and testing phase for the first flight, culminating in the complete instrument assembly and validation during the 2024 Antarctic campaign. Building on this experience, the work presents the design and characterization of ANTARES4, a prototype integrated circuit in 65 nm CMOS technology conceived as an upgrade to SLIDER32. The chip integrates eight analog channels up to the shaping stage and implements dynamic signal compression based on dynamic-threshold MOS transistors, together with an improved detector leakage current compensation circuit at the preamplifier input. Its characterization provides a first validation of these design choices, laying the foundations for the next-generation tracker readout to be adopted in the second flight of the experiment.

papers.title: AI-Generated Code Issues: A Taxonomy from Repository Histories, AI Conversations, and Developer Interviews
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate source code, yet the quality issues in such code remain only partially understood. Understanding these issues can help developers adapt quality assurance practices, such as code review and testing, to better detect problems that may be more common in AI-generated than in human-written code. We study how quality issues in AI-generated code manifest in real software development activities through a mixed-method empirical study that draws on evidence from three complementary sources. First, we mine GitHub commits whose messages explicitly attribute a fix to a problem in AI-generated code, and we manually inspect the 914 matched commits to remove false positives and classify the quality issue being corrected. Second, we collect developers' shared conversations with AI tools, identify conversations including source code and textual signals of model mistakes, and manually analyze 299 of them to classify the underlying quality issue. Third, we interview 20 practitioners and researchers who use AI coding tools to enrich and validate the obtained catalog of quality issues. From these analyses, we derive a taxonomy of 87 types of developer-attributed quality issues in AI-generated code, going beyond functional bugs. Our findings contribute an empirically grounded taxonomy and implications for the design and evaluation of AI coding assistants and agents.

Large language models (LLMs) and AI coding assistants have become part of the software development process [1]. While these tools may increase productivity [2], they can also produce code that is incorrect [3, 4, 5], insecure [6, 7, 8], inefficient [9], and difficult to maintain [10]. Recent industry reports also suggest that these risks are not merely hypothetical: according to the Financial Times [11], internal Amazon material linked a recent trend of high-impact outages in part to “Gen-AI assisted changes” and to “novel GenAI usage for which best practices and safeguards are not yet fully established”. In this context, understanding the kinds of quality issues that arise in AI-generated code is increasingly important, as it can help in designing new quality assurance practices or adapting existing ones (e.g., code review, testing) to better detect issues in AI-generated code.

papers.title: The Poissonian limit of a model inspired by the one-dimensional ERAP, and its application to satellite data
papers.abstract: We consider a model of particle tracking in one dimension studied by Quarck in which $n$ independent random points of the interval $[0,1]$ are shifted by i.i.d. noise at a common scale $\varepsilon_n>0$. We prove that, if $\varepsilon_n=\alpha n^{-2}+\mathbf{o}(n^{-2})$ for some $\alpha>0$ when $n\to \infty$, then in the latter limit the total number of consecutive swaps in the shifted sample w.r.t. its order statistics converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with a parameter depending explicitly on the product of $\alpha$, the mean absolute difference of the shifts and the $L^2$-norm of the density of points. We compare the statistical criterion implied by this theorem to numerical simulations based on real terrain maps, and discuss both its usefulness and limitations.

papers.title: Topological Inference for degree-Cech complexes
papers.abstract: We study topological inference for the degree-Cech bifiltration from noisy samples of a manifold. Under a model combining uniform sampling on the manifold with uniform noise, we show that suitable choices of the radius and degree parameters recover the homotopy type of the underlying manifold with high probability. The analysis explains how the degree parameter suppresses sufficiently distant outliers while the radius scale captures topological signals. Our results provide theoretical support for the common intuition that degree bifiltrations carry meaningful topological information in the presence of noise.

papers.title: Learning Inelastic Homogenization with Memory: Deep Material Networks and Discrete Adjoints
papers.abstract: Deep material networks (DMNs) provide mechanically structured surrogate models for computational homogenization. Traditionally, they are identified from elastic data and subsequently extrapolated to inelastic responses. This procedure leverages highly efficient linear solvers and provides robust extrapolation to different inelastic constitutive laws. However, selecting the appropriate linear elastic training data for a given inelastic constitutive behavior is non-trivial. In this work, we identify the DMNs directly from macroscopic stress-strain trajectories. Applying automatic differentiation to such problems with history entails a huge memory demand, excluding most practically relevant problems. To mitigate, we derive a path-consistent discrete adjoint that avoids propagating parameter-wise state sensitivities by treating equilibrium and internal variable evolution over the complete loading history as coupled constraints. For a short-fiber composite with an elastoplastic matrix, the adjoint approach reproduces the sensitivities obtained by direct differentiation and by an independent automatic-differentiation implementation, while it requires only one backward solve of the linearized state equations per time step and avoids the parameter-wise propagation of state sensitivities. Inelastic training also improves predictive accuracy: A rank-$5$ DMN trained on inelastic trajectories outperforms a deeper rank-$8$ DMN trained on elastic homogenization data for different loading paths. This advantage is retained under perturbations of the constituent inelastic material parameters. The resulting inelastic trained DMNs preserve the same formulation for online deployment and remain several orders of magnitude faster than the full-field homogenization solver.

papers.intro:
Computational homogenization provides physics-based constitutive models that account for the material microstructure without resolving the heterogeneities throughout the macroscopic structure, which would be prohibitively expensive [1]. It solves the microscopic equilibrium problem on a representative volume element (RVE) and assigns the resulting effective response to a material point of the macroscopic body [2, 3, 4]. For linear elastic materials, the microscopic and macroscopic problems can be decoupled: The effective properties of a given RVE may be computed in advance, stored, and subsequently used in a homogeneous structural analysis. By contrast, the close relation between macroscopic inelastic behavior and the evolution of the microscopic constituents, for example, between macroscopic plastic strain and crystallographic slip [5], necessitates a coupled or nested two-scale formulation. In this concurrent setting, the microscopic internal variables evolve through the solution of a nonlinear cell problem at every macroscopic material point and load increment. Mature numerical techniques, most notably the finite element method (FEM) [6, 1, 7] and FFT-based solvers [8, 9, 10], see also Refs. [11, 12, 13] and the review [14], are commonly employed as high-fidelity microscopic solvers in FE2\mathrm{FE}^{2} [15, 16] and FE-FFT frameworks [17, 18].

Although cheaper than a fully resolved simulation, the repeated solution of nonlinear RVE problems remains computationally demanding, which limits concurrent multiscale simulations at the industrial scale and motivates reduced microscopic homogenizers that retain the fidelity of full-field models, particularly for inelastic materials. In the transformation field analysis (TFA) proposed by Dvorak [19], the microstructure is partitioned into subdomains within which the inelastic strain is assumed to be uniform. Consequently, a fine partition may be required to achieve satisfactory accuracy [19, 20]. To alleviate this limitation, Michel and Suquet [21] introduced the nonuniform transformation field analysis (NTFA), in which the spatiotemporal inelastic strain field is represented by spatially heterogeneous, time-independent modes and time-dependent activity coefficients. NTFA was applied to nonlinear composite structures [22, 23], extended to linear viscoelastic composites [24], and improved by mixed variational formulations [25] and series expansions [26]. In a similar spirit, Liu et al. [27, 28] proposed self-consistent clustering analysis, which approximates the Lippmann–Schwinger equation through kk-means clustering combined with a self-consistent scheme in the spirit of Hill [29]. Schneider [30] provides a detailed account of the mathematical connections among these reduced-order homogenization methods. As noted by Michel and Suquet [26], these approaches identify reduced bases for the internal variables, rather than for the displacement or velocity fields as in conventional projection-based model reduction. The latter category includes, for example, the proper-orthogonal-decomposition model of Yvonnet and He [31], as well as subsequent hyper-reduction techniques [32], such as the empirical cubature method [33, 34] and the empirically corrected cluster cubature [35, 36, 37], Hashin–Shtrikman-type reduced finite element formulations [38], and laminate-based reduced models on regular grids [39].

Neural networks emerged as versatile surrogates for inelastic material behavior and were already used in the 1990s to map strain sequences to stress sequences [40, 41, 42]. More recently, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and variants designed specifically for sequential data, such as long short-term memory networks, were employed to represent path-dependent material responses [43, 44, 45], where self-consistency [46] and thermodynamic structure [47] were identified as important ingredients. Neural ordinary differential equations with internal state variables [48] and history-aware neural operators [49] pursue related goals, building upon general operator-learning architectures [50, 51]. In computational homogenization, neural networks constructed from high-dimensional model representations were also used to replace full-field microscopic solvers at small [52] and finite strains [53, 54], to accelerate reduced-order models of woven composites [55], and Fourier neural operators were identified as universal linear elastic homogenizers [56].

More recently, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and variants designed specifically for sequential data, such as long short-term memory networks, were employed to represent path-dependent material responses [43, 44, 45], where self-consistency [46] and thermodynamic structure [47] were identified as important ingredients. Neural ordinary differential equations with internal state variables [48] and history-aware neural operators [49] pursue related goals, building upon general operator-learning architectures [50, 51]. In computational homogenization, neural networks constructed from high-dimensional model representations were also used to replace full-field microscopic solvers at small [52] and finite strains [53, 54], to accelerate reduced-order models of woven composites [55], and Fourier neural operators were identified as universal linear elastic homogenizers [56].

Neural-network architectures are commonly adapted to the structure of the problem at hand. In image processing, for example, convolutional neural networks use local kernels that reflect correlations among neighboring pixels [57]. Similarly, prior knowledge or inductive biases underlie the design of rotation- and translation-invariant networks [58] and equivariant transformers [59]. The same principle motivated physics-informed and physics-constrained architectures for micromechanical homogenization. Liu et al. [60, 61] introduced the deep material network (DMN), which approximates the heterogeneous RVE response through a hierarchy of laminates which serve as mechanistic building blocks. For each block, inelastic homogenization problems may be solved semi-analytically and thus cheaply, and the hierarchy of blocks progressively produces the effective response. Supervised training identifies the parameters - the volume fractions and rotated frames of each laminate - from constituent properties and effective stiffness or compliance tensors obtained by linear homogenization. The resulting network may then be applied to nonlinear and inelastic material behavior of the phases. Such rotated DMNs were extended to transfer learning [62], to thermomechanical [63, 64] and damage problems [65, 66], and to uncertainty quantification [67], while alternative network constructions were proposed to improve their accuracy [68, 69, 70], for instance graph-enhanced [71] and micropolar [72] variants. Rotated DMNs were also deployed for short fiber-reinforced composites in industrial settings [73, 74]. Comprehensive overviews and comparisons are provided in Refs. [75, 76, 77].

papers.title: Deterministic Distributed Graph Connectivity Sketching: Beating the Naive Sketch
papers.abstract:
In the distributed graph sketching model, each vertex in the graph is considered as a separate processor. Each vertex is given access to its neighbourhood, and is then responsible for composing a message to a central referee, with the goal being minimising the length of these messages. Classic problems in this model include computing spanning forests, connected components and connectivity of the full graph.
  In the case where the vertices have to act deterministically, it has long been suspected that the correct upper-bound for computing spanning forests, connected components or connectivity would be the naive method of reporting every edge, which can be done with per-vertex message length of $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ bits. In this paper we show that this is not true for connected components and connectivity, by presenting a protocol that only requires $n/3 +3\log_{2}n$ bits per vertex for $n\geq 13$.
  We also show that in this setting connected components and connectivity are closely related in the required message length of the vertices. Letting $C_{cc}(n)$ be the minimum required message length in bits per vertex to compute the connected components in a graph with $n$ vertices and letting $C_{conn}(n)$ be the minimum message length to compute if the graph is connected, we show that $C_{cc}(n) \le C_{conn}(2n)$ with a multiplicative blow-up in the error probability of $(n-1)^2$.

papers.intro:
Graph sketching asks how much information about a graph must be retained in order to recover a prescribed global property. We study the distributed graph-sketching model, closely related to the linear graph-sketching framework of Ahn, Guha, and McGregor [AGM12a, AGM12b]. The input is a simple undirected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E). Each vertex vv is viewed as a separate player that knows only its own neighbourhood NG​(v)N_{G}(v). Without communicating with the other vertices, every player sends a single message to a central referee, and the referee must compute the desired property of GG from the labelled collection of messages. The cost of a protocol is the maximum message length, measured in bits, over all vertices and all possible local inputs. Equivalently, this is a simultaneous-message protocol specialised to graph inputs; it is also closely connected to one-round algorithms in the broadcast congested clique [Yu21, Rob23].

papers.title: The Recycler: In-Transit Machine Learning on High-Fidelity Data from Simulation Campaigns as an Optimized Approach for Building Frontier Models
papers.abstract: We report on the first realization of in-transit machine learning using data streamed from multiple simulations running in parallel to the training on the same exascale high performance computing system. This workflow can be commonly applied to a broad variety of scenarios in which simulation campaigns play an important role. Unlike single simulations, campaigns run several simulations in parallel. This is interesting for finding an optimum operation point of a machine like a particle accelerator or a fusion reactor, quantifying the variation in model predictions e.g. in climate research, or discovering new capabilities e.g. in materials or drug design. Such campaigns produce huge amounts of high-fidelity data at high rates. File system bandwidth and capacity prohibit retaining all of that data, usually requiring orders of magnitude in reduction before it can be stored. We demonstrate a workflow that streams the data from multiple simulations to train a frontier model in parallel, thereby maximizing data throughput. We demonstrate that this can use a much larger amount of high-fidelity data as training data for the model compared to storage in files, essentially replacing file IO by in-transit training of large-scale frontier models. This will allow to create AI-informed feedback loops to steer simulation campaigns while reducing the overall computation time needed and provide high-fidelity frontier models for reuse by the scientific community.

Exascale simulations produce high-fidelity data at unprecedentedly high rates that exhibit dynamical features central to the understanding and control of complex systems. Applications include modeling weather, predicting materials properties or finding optimal operation points of fusion reactors. In this work, we take the example of LWFA as an advanced accelerator technology for producing brilliant, high-current electron beams. We demonstrate how to retain information contained in high-fidelity data streaming from multiple simulations for in-transit machine learning to predict critical operation data based on the plasma dynamics.

papers.title: FocusAnchor: Zero-Shot Metric Depth by Anchoring a Depth Foundation Prior to Focus Cues
papers.abstract: Existing depth-from-focus methods can struggle with weak focus cues, new cameras, or fewer focal slices. We present FocusAnchor, a recurrent model that uses focus-volume lookups to refine metric depth and repeatedly aligns a relative depth prior from a frozen foundation model to the current depth estimate. The aligned prior guides subsequent refinement in a feedback loop, carrying metric scale recovered from textured regions into regions where focus cues are weak while preserving scene structure. To support transfer across cameras, we synthesize training stacks with randomized camera parameters and focus distances. However, stack synthesis blurs existing image noise differently across slices, creating artificial depth cues even on textureless surfaces. We add independent per-slice noise to suppress these cues. We also introduce variable-stack training to improve robustness with fewer focal slices and support more practical mobile capture. Compared with FOSSA ViT-B, FocusAnchor reduces AbsRel by 36% on NYU Depth V2 and by 9% on DDFF-12 after fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation, FocusAnchor and its variable-stack variant, FocusAnchor-flex, achieve the two lowest AbsRel values on all five benchmarks. On ZEDD test, FocusAnchor achieves 9% lower AbsRel than the best competing method, FOSSA ViT-B, while FocusAnchor-flex achieves lower AbsRel with 40% fewer focal slices on ZEDD validation.

papers.intro:
Metric depth estimation predicts the distance from a camera to visible surfaces in meters. The metric depths are useful because they enable applications such as augmented reality to correctly scale and position virtual objects [7], and help robots judge distances for obstacle avoidance and manipulation [22]. Camera focus can provide a metric cue because surfaces appear sharpest when focused at their distance. Capturing the same scene at several known focus distances produces a focal stack, with each image called a focal slice. Depth-from-focus (DFF) models [17, 27, 30, 29, 8] estimate metric depth from sharpness changes across slices and their known focus distances. However, changes in sharpness are not equally informative across the image. Textured regions often provide informative focus cues, while smooth walls and other textureless surfaces can look similar across slices, making their depth difficult to determine.

HybridDepth [8] aligns a monocular depth estimate with a focus-based estimate and refines the result. FOSSA [34] adapts a pretrained depth model to focal stacks, demonstrating zero-shot transfer to new cameras and scenes.

We introduce FocusAnchor, a recurrent DFF model built around a feedback loop between depth refinement and prior alignment (). Given a focal stack, its focus distances, and an all-in-focus image, FocusAnchor maps a frozen foundation model’s relative depth prediction onto the focus range. A recurrent network refines this estimate through lookups in a focus volume, which stores learned scores across focal slices at each pixel. After initial scale adjustment, each refinement step fits the frozen prediction to the current estimate using a confidence-weighted local scale and shift. The aligned prior and focus evidence guide the next update, carrying metric scale recovered from textured regions into regions where focus cues are weak.

Following FOSSA, we synthesize focal stacks with randomized camera parameters and focus distances. However, during the synthesis process, blurring a captured RGB image also smooths the sensor noise already present. At each pixel, this noise is smoothed least in the slice focused at the surface’s depth, creating an artificial depth cue even on textureless surfaces. A model can therefore learn to locate the in-focus slice from residual noise rather than scene detail. This shortcut does not reflect real capture, where sensor noise is introduced separately in each exposure rather than blurred with the scene. We therefore add independent random noise to each rendered slice to suppress this shortcut. papers.title: Local Thermodynamic Reconstruction of Impurity Entropy
papers.abstract: Resolving the thermodynamic entropy associated with a local impurity in a spatially extended interacting quantum bath remains a numerical challenge. We develop a Local-Maxwell approach that reconstructs the impurity entropy from local observables in worldline quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. By integrating their temperature responses along the impurity coupling, the method avoids separate estimates of extensive entropies. For nonnegative worldline expansions with bounded local couplings, we establish bath-size independent bounds on all factorial moments of the impurity vertex count. For even vertex counts, the Maxwell estimator variance remains bounded as the coupling approaches zero. The transverse-field Ising benchmark reproduces exact free fermion results, while an interacting XXZ chain demonstrates up to several hundredfold improvement in statistical efficiency over conventional extensive thermodynamic integration. In a three-channel XXZ impurity junction, we reveal entropy recovery upon cooling and a nonmonotonic coupling dependence of the finite-temperature entropy contrast. These results establish local thermodynamic reconstruction as an efficient approach to impurity entropy in interacting quantum baths.

papers.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
papers.abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

papers.intro:
Most chess engines are built to play as strongly as possible. A different goal is to play like a human: reproducing the distribution of moves a player of a given strength would choose, including their mistakes. Such models power realistic sparring partners and bots. They also drive coaching tools that show a learner the kind of move a player at their level would make, and cheat-detection systems that flag games too strong to be human. From a player’s perspective, believability matters as much as raw accuracy, an opponent that feels human keeps players engaged, while one that plays robotically breaks the experience.

The behavioral cloning paradigm in chess was first established by Maia [1] with per-rating convolutional networks, which were later unified into a single skill-conditioned model [2]; Allie [3] moved to a text-based transformer over the move transcript, with search; and Maia-3 [4], built on the Chessformer architecture, returned to a spatial representation, treating the 64 squares as tokens in an encoder-only transformer. However, each of them discards the clock. Remaining time does not condition the policy, so none of these models can learn how a human’s move choices shift as time runs out.

Research on the speed–accuracy trade-off in chess shows that time restriction shifts the balance between recognition-based and calculation-based play, changing which moves a human is likely to choose [5]. Human decision quality falls sharply as the clock runs down, which we quantify in Section V-B. A model blind to the clock is forced to learn a single averaged policy that conflates comfortable and time-pressured play. This averaging is most damaging in critically time-pressured play, where human behavior diverges most.

papers.title: Three-phase contact lines as distinct molecular adsorption environments
papers.abstract: In wetting and multiphase systems, three-phase contact lines form where liquid, solid, and gas phases meet, creating effectively one-dimensional boundaries with distinct molecular environments. Despite their ubiquity in droplets, liquid menisci, capillary bridges, porous materials, and confined multiphase systems, molecular adsorption at these lower-dimensional boundaries has remained largely unexplored. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to show that the contact line on a hydrophobic substrate is not merely the geometric intersection of two interfaces but a distinct thermodynamic adsorption environment with a substantially stronger affinity for amphiphilic molecules than either neighboring interface. The investigated amphiphiles of different molecular structures exhibit a common scaling relation between line and surface adsorption in the dilute regime, while their behavior becomes molecule-specific at higher concentrations. Furthermore, contact-line affinity increases exponentially with alkyl-chain length, leading to crowding at progressively lower concentrations and making contact lines extraordinarily sensitive to trace amphiphilic impurities. Because line, surface, and bulk populations scale differently with system size, contact-line adsorption becomes increasingly important at small length scales, where it can substantially alter molecular partitioning. Contact-line enrichment is predicted to reduce the line tension by an amount comparable to its intrinsic magnitude, with potentially substantial consequences for heterogeneous nucleation. Our results establish molecular adsorption as a fundamental property of three-phase contact lines with implications for wetting and multiphase systems across length scales.

Whenever a liquid partially wets a solid in the presence of a gas, a three-phase contact line is formed. Such contact lines are ubiquitous, occurring in droplets, bubbles, porous media, evaporation fronts, capillary bridges, and biological wetting phenomena. Although often viewed simply as the geometric boundary between two interfaces, they constitute lower-dimensional objects with their own excess quantities and thermodynamic relations, analogous to the surface excesses and surface thermodynamics of interfaces De Gennes (1985); Drelich and Miller (1992); Drelich (1996); Schimmele et al. (2007).

(2007).

Yet, what determines the molecular affinity for contact lines, how this affinity compares with adsorption at the neighboring interfaces, and how it influences macroscopic phenomena remain poorly understood.

Amphiphilic molecules provide a particularly useful model system with which to address this question. Their adsorption at liquid–vapor, liquid–liquid, and liquid–solid interfaces has been studied extensively for more than a century Rosen and Kunjappu (2012); Aveyard (2019), owing to its central role in colloid science, chemistry, biology, and engineering. In contrast, far less is known about adsorption at three-phase contact lines.

Resolving this question has important implications. On the one hand, preferential adsorption at the contact line may locally amplify the concentration of specific molecular species and thereby influence reaction pathways, transport processes, or nucleation kinetics. On the other hand, molecules that preferentially accumulate at one-dimensional interfaces act as line-active agents, also referred to as linactants (also spelled lineactants) Trabelsi et al. (2008). The concept of lineactants is well established for line boundaries separating coexisting domains in two-dimensional systems (e.g., lipid membranes and Langmuir monolayers) Schäfer and Marrink (2010); Palmieri et al. (2014); Bischof et al. (2015). The role of lineactants at three-phase contact lines, however, has received little attention despite occasional theoretical proposals Law et al. (2017); Bey et al. (2021). By adsorbing at the contact line, these molecules contribute directly to the excess free energy of the contact line and are therefore expected to modify the line thermodynamics, analogous to the way surfactants modify surface thermodynamics through interfacial adsorption. Consequently, line adsorption may influence line tension, wetting behavior, contact-angle hysteresis, and nanoscale partitioning.

papers.title: Simultaneous Waring problems for binary forms and the geometry of rational curves
papers.abstract:
We investigate the simultaneous Waring problem for binary forms and its geometric applications to rational curves. By analyzing the minimal free resolution of the simultaneous annihilator, we establish formulas for both simultaneous Waring ranks and border Waring ranks including explicit computations for binary monomials.
  As a geometric application, we explicitly describe parametrizations of rational curves up to projective equivalence. We determine the minimum dimension of a rational normal scroll containing the curve as a section of its ruling in terms of the minimal generators of the corresponding simultaneous annihilator. For rational curves lying as divisors on rational normal surface scrolls, we characterize their smoothness and describe the generators of their defining ideals.

The polynomial Waring problem is a classical subject in algebraic geometry, seeking to determine the minimum number of linear forms required to express a given homogeneous polynomial of degree dd as a sum of their dd-th powers. papers.title: Tensor powers of the Steinberg character of $GL_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$, zonotopal algebras, and quiver varieties
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the $m$-th tensor power ${\rm St}^{\otimes m}$ of the Steinberg character of $GL_n(q)$. To do that we use the connection between tensor products of unipotent characters and the cohomology of certain quiver varieties for star-shaped quivers \cite{L2}\cite{LRV}. We prove that the cohomology ring of the quiver variety associated to ${\rm St}^{\otimes m}$ is generated by its tautological classes. We use this to prove that this cohomology ring is isomorphic to a central zonotopal algebra. We then deduce a combinatorial formula for the multiplicities of unipotent characters in ${\rm St}^{\otimes m}$. This formula has been conjectured by the second author when $m=2$.

papers.title: Slipstream: nonlinear beam dynamics in PyTorch
papers.abstract: Slipstream is a PyTorch package for nonlinear beam dynamics in storage rings, linacs and photoinjectors. It provides CPU and GPU particle tracking, field-map injector models with space charge, and automatic differentiation along supported tracking paths. Comparisons with elegant, ASTRA, GPT and other codes assess accuracy and computational cost for nonlinear ring tracking, optics matching and photoinjectors. Ring tunes agree with elegant to $10^{-9}$. For the tested ring workloads with tens of thousands of particles, GPU tracking in float32 is hundreds of times faster than the single-threaded CPU implementations compared here. Automatic differentiation reduces the time for 24-parameter optics matching by an order of magnitude compared to finite differences. Using a high-brightness photo-injector as an example, final horizontal emittances agree with ASTRA to about 1% at 20 and 100pC and differ by $\approx$4% at 250pC. For $2^{18}$ macroparticles, Slipstream's faster default settings take 14s on an RTX 3050 GPU and give emittances within 2% of that of ASTRA. Additional tests examine coherent synchrotron radiation, dynamic aperture and resistive-wall impedance. The package was developed predominantly by AI coding assistants under human direction. These comparisons identify where its models, GPU execution and derivatives are useful for repeated simulations in scans, fits and optimisation.

papers.intro:
Accelerator design, commissioning and optimisation often require beam-dynamics calculations to be repeated over many machine settings. Digital-twin applications place similar demands on simulation [15, 35, 23, 24]. The calculation must be fast enough for a scan or fit while retaining the physical effects that determine the observable of interest. A linear transport model can meet this need for some optics tasks, whilst non-linear ring dynamics and space-charge-dominated injectors require more detailed models.

Existing codes combine these capabilities in different ways, and GPU execution is available in several of them. Cheetah is a PyTorch code for differentiable beamline transport [33]; its linear models can be reduced to efficient transfer maps, and recent releases add the nonlinear element options used in the comparisons below, as well as space-charge kicks [19]. Here, we use differentiable to mean that the tracking is implemented with operations supporting automatic differentiation (AD), so that exact gradients of an output with respect to all inputs can be obtained by back-propagation through the simulation, at a cost that does not grow with the number of inputs (it grows with the number of outputs) and is small compared with the many forward runs needed by finite differences (FD). SciBmad and JuTrack (both Julia) and the linac framework HELIX (PyTorch, developed for the PIP-II hadron linac, with a particle-in-cell space-charge solver) also provide differentiable tracking, using different element models and space-charge treatments [52, 57, 44, 42]. Xsuite and ImpactX are established tracking codes with nonlinear maps and collective effects, designed for both CPU and GPU execution [30, 28, 38]. Because these choices are implemented differently, the same nominal lattice need not represent the same numerical map in every code, which matters when comparing both accuracy and speed.
