We distinguish between protocols that break the global ${\mathbb Z}_2$ symmetry by coupling to the order parameter and those that preserve it. These two classes of driving exhibit distinct scaling behaviors, with power-law exponents determined by the RG dimensions of the corresponding perturbations. We verify the proposed dynamic scaling theory through numerical simulations of both smooth single-frequency and discontinuous square-wave periodic drivings.

papers.title: Fractional minimality of the Simons cone for $s$ close to $1$
papers.abstract: We prove that the Simons cone in $\mathbb R^8$ minimizes the fractional perimeter $P_s$, under compact perturbations, whenever $s$ is sufficiently close to $1$.

papers.title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
papers.abstract: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.

authors.name: Alejandro Moreo
authors.institution: Istituto di Scienza e Tecnologie dell'Informazione "Alessandro Faedo"

authors.name: Fabrizio Sebastiani
authors.institution: Istituto di Scienza e Tecnologie dell'Informazione "Alessandro Faedo"

authors.name: Domenico Tortorella
authors.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

papers.title: A catalog of Gaia DR3 luminous blue variables and candidate luminous blue variables
papers.abstract: Galactic LBVs are rare, evolved massive stars whose defining evidence is long-term spectroscopic and photometric instability, including S Doradus-type cycles, and, in exceptional cases, giant eruptions. Candidate LBVs (cLBVs) share LBV-like spectra and/or circumstellar nebulae; however, they lack long-term observational datasets that would detect their long-term variability and confirm their classification as bona fide LBVs. Modern time-domain surveys provide homogeneous light curves for many Galactic massive stars, but each survey has its own limitations in terms of depth, temporal coverage, and observing cadence. Using confirmed Galactic LBVs as a control sample, we aim to test what Gaia DR3 and complementary photometric surveys can and cannot establish about LBV-type variability. We assembled a vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and cLBVs with near- and mid-infrared photometry from 2MASS, MSX, WISE, GLIMPSE, and MIPSGAL. The infrared material was used to validate identifications, evaluate source confusion, and place objects in a circumstellar-dust context. We then constructed light curves from Gaia DR3, the Bochum survey, the ASAS SN, and the ZTF, and analyzed large-amplitude and periodic cases with Lomb-Scargle (LS) and phase dispersion minimization (PDM) methods. Gaia DR3 matches are available for 67% of the sample and 76% are reported as variable. We identify high-amplitude variables and periodic systems that may be binaries rather than classical LBVs. Six confirmed LBVs and five candidates show variations larger than 0.6 mag in the Gaia RP filter. Their light curves are examined and three periodic variables are identified. The light curves of OMN2000 LS1 and DWC2011 140 show primary and secondary minima, strongly suggesting eclipsing binary systems. OMN2000 LS1 has a well-constrained period of 80.29 d, and DWC2011 140 of 95.07 d.

papers.title: Super-Eddington Neutron Star Accretion Columns: Comparing GRRMHD Simulations with Spectral Models
papers.abstract: The geometry and structure of neutron star accretion columns affect the X-ray emission in super-Eddington accreting systems. We perform four axisymmetric general relativistic radiation magnetohydrodynamic simulations of super-Eddington accretion onto magnetized neutron stars with the maximum surface magnetic fields ranging from $3\times10^{10}$ to $1\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{G}$. We measure the column width and estimate the characteristic radiation shock heights from the flow velocity and velocity gradient. Across the four models, the angular width decreases from approximately $0.14$ to $0.07\,\mathrm{rad}$, while the estimated shock height increases from $1.95$ to $3.89\,\mathrm{km}$. We then compare our solutions to the best-fit values derived from spectral modeling of super-Eddington Be/X-ray binary outbursts. We calculate area-equivalent column radii that vary between 5.2 and 3.2 km, three of which fall within the upper part of the range inferred from spectral results using the \texttt{bwcycl} model.

papers.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

authors.name: Michael Bader
authors.institution: Helmholtz Association of German Research Centres

papers.title: Internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental evidence in a quantum neurosecurity framework
papers.abstract: This article presents a technical and theoretical assessment of the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework intended for privacy-preserving, quantum-secure, AI-powered, multimodal healthcare data analysis, introduced by Ben Othman and Ali (2025). They claim QENSSF is a first-in-class framework with provable privacy and security guarantees, support these with theorems and proofs, report an experimental evaluation on IBM's quantum Eagle processor, report a real-world quantum key distribution (QKD) test, and claim use of real-world multimodal datasets (ADNI, UK Biobank, and MIMIC-IV). Our examination of quantitative support for these claims identified various concerns. Most importantly, the security criterion of a central guarantee (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied given the risk formulation and relevant constraints, which, along with calculation errors in the proof, directly undermines the claim of provable security. Furthermore, insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation limit verification of the experimental claims and overall reproducibility. QENSSF identifies a real need: ensuring privacy and security of healthcare data while patients benefit from AI-powered analysis. This need is particularly pressing for sensitive neural data, including the neuroimaging data available through sources such as ADNI. Privacy concerns also extend to wearable EEG data, for which reidentification risks can persist despite deidentification. However, QENSSF's foundational inconsistencies need resolution before it could be considered in the neurosecurity domain.

papers.title: Harmonic multi-valued $1$-forms and deformations of branched covers of special Lagrangians
papers.abstract: This article introduces the notion of a non-degenerate multi-valued $1$-form on a manifold $X$ in terms of immersed submanifolds of $T^*X$ and develops a deformation theory extending Donaldson's work on harmonic non-degenerate $\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z}$ $1$-forms. More precisely, the universal moduli space of harmonic non-degenerate multi-valued $1$-forms is shown to be a tame Fr\'echet orbifold whose projection onto the space of Riemannian metrics is a submersion and whose fibres are locally parametrised by their periods. The proof relies on H\"ormander's subelliptic estimates and the Nash--Moser submersion theorem. As an application of this analytic framework, harmonic multi-valued $1$-forms on a special Lagrangian are shown to control deformations of its branched covers, extending work of He for multiplicity two.

papers.title: Energy as a Service-Level Objective: Transaction-Level Energy Attribution
papers.abstract: Service engineers assess every change against functional requirements and qualities such as reliability, performance and availability. Energy is rarely part of this assessment. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.

papers.title: Semi-local Zariski-van Kampen theorems
papers.abstract: Zariski-van Kampen theorems are meant to constitute a complement to Lefschetz-Zariski theorems which, in turn, generalize the classical Lefschetz theorem on hyperplane sections to quasi-projective varieties or to the corresponding local case. Semi-local Zariski-van Kampen theorems are developed here as a tool which is useful both in the local and in the global case.

papers.title: Major progress on hamiltonian saturation in hypergraphs
papers.abstract:
For $1\leq \ell< k$, an \emph{$\ell$-overlapping $k$-cycle} is a $k$-uniform hypergraph in which, for some cyclic vertex ordering, every edge consists of $k$ consecutive vertices and every two consecutive edges share exactly $\ell$ vertices.
  A $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ is $\ell$-\emph{hamiltonian saturated} if $H$ does not contain an $\ell$-overlapping Hamilton $k$-cycle but every hypergraph obtained from $H$ by adding a new edge does contain such a cycle. For $n$ divisible by $k-\ell$, let sat$(n,k,\ell)$ be the smallest number of edges in an $\ell$-hamiltonian saturated $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. In the case of graphs Clark and Entringer showed in 1983 that, for sufficiently large $n$, sat$(n,2,1)=\lceil \frac{3n}2\rceil$. By ad hoc methods, the present authors proved previously that sat$(n,k,\ell)=\Theta(n^{\ell})$ for some rather narrow and scattered ranges of $\ell$. In this paper we present a unified proof of this equality for all $k$ and $\ell>k/2$.

authors.name: Andrzej Zak
authors.institution: Wrocław University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Joint Classification and Generation on Tabular Data: an Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Many applications of machine learning on tabular data need both a classifier and a generator of realistic records. The default is to train two separate models, whereas a single joint model promises both from one set of weights. Several families of tabular deep learning models can be turned into such a joint model, which raises the question of which joint model is preferable at which computational budget. In this empirical study, we introduce and compare joint models based on four state-of-the-art tabular data modeling families (energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models and tabular diffusion models) against measured FLOPs and wall-clock time, on 29 classification datasets. Methods are evaluated based on two defined aggregate scores that take into account different aspects of prediction and generation. We then also compare these joint models with every pair of a separate classifier and generator at different computational budgets, to see when a joint model may be a defendible choice against the regular practice of keeping a separate classifier and generator. We find that the best joint model is a probabilistic circuit at the smallest budgets and, beyond that, a tabular foundation model that generates column by column using a regressor (TabICL). Compared with pairs of separate models, this study finds a joint model is rarely preferable but often very close to the best pair, without the hassle of training and maintaining two separate models.

papers.title: First-principles phase diagram of monolayer CrS$_2$ polymorphs under biaxial strain and its sensitivity to the Hubbard U parameter
papers.abstract: In correlated two-dimensional magnets the balance between competing electronic and magnetic phases is often set by the strength of the on-site Coulomb interaction, so that the predicted ground state can hinge on a parameter that is not uniquely defined. Monolayer CrS$_2$ lies squarely in this regime, hosting several energetically close polymorphs whose character ranges from non-magnetic semiconducting to magnetically ordered metallic. We therefore investigate, using DFT$+U$ within the generalized gradient approximation, the structural, magnetic, and electronic properties of the 1H, 1T, 1T$'$, and 1T$''$ polymorphs of monolayer CrS$_2$ under varying Hubbard interactions ($U=0$--$8$~eV) and biaxial strain ($-10\%$ to $+10\%$). The 1T-derived structures remain metallic and magnetic throughout, with $U$ acting mainly as a spectral renormalization. The 1H phase behaves differently, passing from a non-magnetic semiconductor through an antiferromagnetic semiconducting regime before metallizing, so that the gap closes as $U$ increases while the local Cr moment grows monotonically. Biaxial tensile strain at fixed $U$ induces a similar sequence of transitions. Along both tuning pathways, the two inequivalent nearest-neighbor Cr--Cr exchange channels progressively separate and cross, with the parallel-spin channel becoming dominant, accompanied by a breathing-type bond disproportionation. Independent calculations with a localized-orbital implementation reproduce the overall evolution but yield shifted critical values of $U$ and of strain, demonstrating the robustness of the phase diagram while highlighting the implementation dependence of the transition thresholds.

papers.title: Photometric Characterisation and Evolutionary State Investigation of the Low Mass-Ratio Contact Binary FASTT 1558
papers.abstract: Contact binaries with low mass ratios, as potential progenitors of stellar mergers, offer important insights into the physical processes governing mass and energy transfer. In this work, we present the first spectro-photometry based evolutionary investigation of FASTT 1558, a totally eclipsing, low mass-ratio contact binary. We combine TESS and ASAS-SN photometry with phase-resolved spectroscopy obtained with the 3.6m Devasthal Optical Telescope. The lightcurve modeling with PHOEBE shows that the system has an exceptionally low secondary-to-primary mass ratio of $q=0.1544\pm0.0013$, with a deep contact degree of $f=0.61\pm0.01$. Our analysis yields a total system mass of $1.92\pm0.31\,M_\odot$, while the distance to the system is estimated to be $648.45\pm29.85$ pc. Analysis of long-term eclipse timings reveals an apparent orbital period decrease of $\dot{P}=-(3.03\pm0.26) \times 10^{-7}$ ${\rm day\,yr^{-1}}$, which may be associated with mass-transfer from the primary to the secondary on a thermal timescale. The spectra show phase-dependent H$\alpha$ and CaII equivalent widths, indicating a dynamically evolving chromosphere. Binary evolution calculations with MESA terminates through L2 overflow before reaching the observed low mass-ratio. Despite its extreme mass ratio, the system is presently Darwin stable, with $J_{\rm spin}/J_{\rm orb}=0.15\pm0.02$. FASTT 1558 therefore provides a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of low mass-ratio contact binaries.

authors.name: Kuntal Misra
authors.institution: Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences

papers.title: On the Capabilities and Limitations of Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Cloud Segmentation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language foundation models have enabled open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) without task-specific training, offering new opportunities for Earth Observation (EO) applications. However, their capabilities for cloud detection remain insufficiently explored. In this work, we evaluate twelve OVSS approaches across six publicly available EO datasets in a zero-shot setting, i.e., without fine-tuning or adaptation to the target data. We investigate both binary cloud detection and multiclass segmentation, distinguishing between thick clouds, thin clouds, cloud shadows, and background. Our results show differences in performance across models and datasets, with SegEarth-OV3 achieving the highest binary cloud detection performance on four of the six datasets. While several approaches demonstrate promising performance in binary cloud detection, multiclass segmentation remains more challenging, particularly when distinguishing between fine-grained cloud categories. Furthermore, our controlled prompt sensitivity analysis reveals model-dependent responses to alternative textual descriptions, with appearance-oriented prompts benefiting certain approaches while degrading the performance of others. Overall, our findings demonstrate both the potential and current limitations of zero-shot OVSS for cloud detection, establishing a comparative benchmark for future research on generalisable cloud segmentation. Code will be available at: https://github.com/josesosajs/zero-shot-cloudovss.

papers.title: Any2Act: Scaling In-Context Robot Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Robot in-context learning (ICL) enables a policy to perform unseen tasks by following contextual demonstrations, without task-specific fine-tuning. This is increasingly valuable as large language models reasoning at low frequency can specify tasks through demonstrations and delegate high-frequency execution to such a policy. However, methods conditioned on human videos are bounded by scarce human-robot pairs, while those conditioned on robot demonstrations accept only one or two source types at limited scale. We present Any2Act, a foundation model for robot ICL. Our key insight is that a demonstration should be expressed in the camera layout and action space of the robot that performs it (the executor), not of whoever provided it (the demonstrator). This unified embodiment-grounded representation decouples learning to follow from admitting a new source. Any2Act learns to follow once, from robot-to-robot pairs that already take this form in 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks. Human videos, simulation, UMI, and other robots are then translated into this representation, and source-routed adapters trained on only a few hundred pairs each absorb the residual gap while the pretrained model stays frozen. For long horizons, a training-free tracker feeds only the demonstration window around the executor's progress, bounding the context and rolling back to redo failed steps. From a single demonstration, Any2Act achieves 57.5% success on unseen tasks without fine-tuning, exceeding VLAs fine-tuned on 50 demonstrations per task; other demonstrators retain 74-91% of the success achieved with the executor's own demonstrations.

papers.title: Critical Eddington luminosity and photon cooling of compact spherical stars
papers.abstract: Context. Relativistic corrections to the luminosity have been used for neutron stars of radius greater than $3MG/c^2$ in studies of X-ray bursts. However, there is no fundamental limit that excludes the existence of more compact massive objects with a physical surface, fluid or solid. Aims. We aim to discuss critical "Eddington" luminosity for spherical stars that have a surface within the sphere of unstable circular photon orbits (photon sphere). Methods. We use standard analytical ray-tracing formulae in the Schwarzschild metric. Results. We find that for stars within the photon sphere, the Eddington condition for balance between radiative force and gravitational attraction is fundamentally altered by photons returning to the surface. The equilibrium is non-local and requires stationarity on timescales of photon fall-back. As a result, spontaneous symmetry breaking is possible, leading to non-uniformity of emission across the photospheric surface. Conclusions. For a fixed intrinsic luminosity, the photons returning to the surface decrease the cooling rate of stars inside their photon sphere. At the same time, the returning photons increase the value of the critical luminosity that would balance gravity. One and the same redshifted formula applies to the critical luminosity, as seen by a distant observer, for any radius of the star. In the X-ray burst literature, for stars with radius less than 3 gravitational radii a different formula has long been accepted that missed the essential physics of the photons emitted in directions outside the escape cone.

papers.title: Quasiperiodicity breakdown and homoclinic bifurcations in the forced librations of a parametric oscillator
papers.abstract: Above its instability threshold, a parametrically excited oscillator settles into one of two phase states. The response of these states to a second, much slower modulation of the same stiffness is investigated. In the rotating frame, this modulation periodically varies the detuning and drives the phase librations. When the modulation is slow compared with the libration frequency, the phase states follow adiabatically. As the two frequencies become comparable, this approximation breaks down and the driven libration resonates with the intrinsic one. This nonadiabatic regime is examined for a Duffing oscillator with nonlinear damping. The averaged equations describe a periodically perturbed planar system with integrable unperturbed dynamics, whose homoclinic loop is derived in closed form. The phase states persist as invariant tori supporting quasiperiodic motion. Their stability and period-doubling bifurcations are captured by a damped Mathieu equation, in which the modulation contributes to both parametric stiffness and parametric damping. A Melnikov analysis yields explicit thresholds for separatrix splitting and the onset of homoclinic intersections, which are corroborated by numerical computations of the invariant manifolds. Numerically it is revealed that these intersections arise well before sustained chaotic motion develops. The fate of the parametric oscillation depends markedly on the resonance condition: modulation at the libration frequency destroys the invariant tori and quenches the oscillation, whereas modulation at twice the libration frequency leaves it intact.

papers.title: Mixed local and fractional laplacian problems with $(\alpha,\beta)$-Neumann conditions
papers.abstract: The existence of non-constant solutions to a mixed local-nonlocal elliptic problem with $(\alpha,\beta)$-Neumann conditions, critical exponent, and parameter $\lambda>0$ is established for any $\lambda$ large enough. Proofs exploit both mountain-pass-type arguments and appropriate boundary Sobolev inequalities patterned after those of [19].

papers.title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.

authors.name: Michael Arbel
authors.institution: Centre Inria de l'Université Grenoble Alpes

papers.title: LATEC: Learned Axial TEnsor Compression for High-Dimensional Scientific Data
papers.abstract: With the growing scale of scientific simulation and infrastructure, part of the burden has shifted from producing scientific data to analyzing and storing it. Compression is a key step to expanding storage capacity, but requires dedicated techniques to enforce user-specified pointwise error bounds that ensure the validity of downstream scientific workflows. To further push the limits of compression, novel learned codecs have been developed, in particular for images and videos, but these methods often optimize for aggregated distortion and fail to meet error bound standards. Moreover, these methods often target fixed field dimensionality, failing to account for many scientific data use cases, or at the expense of large adaptation or retraining costs. In this work, we introduce the Learned Axial TEnsor Compression (LATEC) method, an error-bounded codec with a dimension-agnostic learned predictor based on a GNN architecture. LATEC is pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields, and evaluated with and without domain fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D. Results show that LATEC is consistently competitive with SZ3, achieving an 18.1% average improvement and greater consistency across all domains than other compressors. These results demonstrate that a shared learned predictor can serve as a single error-bounded codec across tensor dimensionalities, competitive with specialized compressors, while retaining pointwise error guarantees.

papers.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
papers.abstract: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.

papers.title: Majorana flat bands from mirror-particle-hole antisymmetry
papers.abstract: Majorana flat bands, zero modes across the whole edge Brillouin zone, usually rest on chiral symmetry. We show that a fully gapped class-D superconductor can host such a flat band without chiral symmetry or time reversal, provided its superconducting gap is odd under a mirror and translation along the edge is preserved. Combined with particle--hole conjugation, the mirror forms an antiunitary antisymmetry that squares to $+1$ and preserves the momentum along the edge, so it fixes the Kitaev index of every slice of fixed edge momentum. In a gapped bulk, this slice index cannot change with the edge momentum, and the edge zero modes form a band across the whole edge Brillouin zone. We construct a four-band model with exactly these symmetries, a helical $p$-wave superconductor with Rashba coupling in an in-plane exchange field, from which no term can be removed without restoring an additional symmetry. On the mirror lines, its two mirror sectors are exact Kitaev chains. This yields a closed-form phase diagram. Besides the flat band, the model hosts a phase with two Majoranas at each end of a wire, although its class-D index is trivial, and a second-order phase with Majorana corner modes. The spectral localizer detects all these indices in real space, directly on finite-size samples as relevant for experiments. On open rectangular flakes of two widths, it reproduces the phase diagram even though translational symmetry is broken. In the nodal regions, its reading depends on the flake size, so they are left unread. The readings persist under disorder several times the bulk gap. Without translation along the edge, the symmetries protect no more than Majorana parities, and we quantify the signatures that remain specific to the antisymmetry. A minimal model of magnetic adatoms on a triplet superconductor realizes the flat-band and second-order phases.

papers.title: Contribution to the GdTe$_3$ magnetic phase diagram from electronic transport measurements
papers.abstract: Magnetic phase diagrams of the three antiferromagnetic (AFM) transitions of GdTe$_3$ that occur at zero magnetic field at $T_{N1}=12$ K, $T_{N2}=10.5$ K and $T_1=7$ K are investigated by means of resistance measurements in a magnetic field oriented along the three crystallographic directions. With the magnetic field applied in the basal plane we found re-entrance of an intermediate phase which may be a result of the coupling between the $T_{N2}$ AFM and the charge density wave with possibly a ferroaxial order. A spin flop transition is also observed at a temperature that presumably converges towards a triple point in vicinity of 2.5-3.0 T and $T$ between $T_1$ and $T_{N2}$. Our results help complete a complex phase diagram of GdTe$_3$ and advance a method for investigating magnetic ordering via transport measurements -- a technique applicable to many other compounds.

papers.title: Convex computation of cost bounds for data-driven nonlinear optimal control
papers.abstract: The paper addresses the optimal control problem of an input-affine polynomial system with an unknown (state-dependent) input matrix affecting the control effectiveness. Under assumptions on the existence of a data set and the Lipschitz continuity of the unknown part {of the dynamics}, an uncertainty set is constructed and used to adapt the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation towards a data-driven formulation. We solve it for the best-case scenario, thus giving a lower bound on the best cost achievable by means of a feedback control policy. After relaxing it into a moment-SoS hierarchy of semidefinite programs, a control law is extracted from the primal on moments and compared with other benchmark methods in a numerical application.

papers.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

papers.title: First-Hit Photoconsistency for Neural Surface Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.

authors.name: Jean Ponce
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: SHARPnP: Self-Supervised and Plug-and-Play Hyperspectral Super-Resolution from Real Noisy Unaligned Camera Measurements
papers.abstract: Affordable snapshot hyperspectral cameras capture spectral images in a single exposure but suffer from limited spatial resolution and sensor noise. Low-cost RGB cameras provide fine visible details to guide NIR reconstruction, but introduce spatially varying cross-camera misalignment. Supervised fusion methods require relatively large datasets of clean, high-resolution hyperspectral images, are sensitive to sensor noise, and generalize poorly across new sensors. We introduce SHARPnP, an interpretable, flexible framework coupling registration and reconstruction for RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution from noisy, unaligned measurements without clean references. We adapt a pretrained registration model via a cross-view loss backpropagated through a fixed plug-and-play fusion module. Temporal and recorrupted pairs enable reference-free self-supervision on noisy inputs. At test time, we calibrate cross-camera radiometry and refine alignment. Plug-and-play fusion employs sequential three-band denoising. On the REAL benchmark, SHARPnP outperforms supervised fusion baselines at $4\times$, $8\times$, and $16\times$ on clean inputs and at $4\times$ under Gaussian noise ($\sigma=5/255, 10/255$). On native RGB-HSI snapshot measurements, it reconstructs all 51 VIS-NIR bands, beyond the conventional 31-band VIS setting, without high-resolution references.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
papers.abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.

papers.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
papers.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.

papers.title: Rich\'ard Wiegandt's theory of M\"obius products revisited
papers.abstract: In a 1959 paper Rich\'ard Wiegandt defined a general notion of M\"obius product of functions on arbitrary locally finite posets, and determined when this product is commutative and associative. He gave an example showing that not all locally finite posets allow such a M\"obius product. Here we characterize those posets of height 3 that can be equipped with a commutative and associative M\"obius product.

authors.name: Peter P. Palfy
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Electron processing of glycine: evidence for peptide-forming condensation reactions
papers.abstract: The discovery of amino acids on asteroids, including samples returned from asteroid Bennu, and the detection of glycine on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko support the hypothesis that glycine can form in extraterrestrial environments. Laboratory experiments show that glycine can form through both energetic and non-energetic processing of interstellar ice analogues. In the interstellar medium, glycine is exposed to various forms of energetic processing, including cosmic rays and the secondary electrons they generate, which have been shown to produce complex organic molecules, including peptides. This work investigates whether peptide-forming chemistry is a general consequence of energetic processing. Films of glycine and glycine-d3 were grown in two ultrahigh-vacuum chambers and irradiated with 1-2 keV electrons. The irradiated samples were subsequently characterised using infrared spectroscopy, temperature-programmed desorption, and vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy. Peptide formation through condensation reactions would produce water as a secondary product, and spectra obtained following irradiation of glycine-d3 showed evidence of D2O formation, supported by TPD measurements, which revealed H2O formation for glycine and H2O, HDO, and D2O for glycine-d3. VUV spectra of irradiated glycine showed the formation of decomposition products, including CO and CO2, as well as H2O. Following heating, a non-volatile residue remained on the surface. Electron irradiation of glycine produces reaction products similar to proton irradiation, suggesting that the resulting chemistry is not strongly dependent on the energy source. These findings support the possibility that larger organic molecules can form in a wide range of extraterrestrial environments. Such molecules may subsequently be incorporated into small bodies and delivered to planetary surfaces, potentially contributing to the emergence of life.

papers.title: A characterization of almost everywhere convergence of subsequences of Walsh--Fourier partial sums
papers.abstract:
We characterize the increasing sequences $(
u_j)$ in the set of positive integers $\mathbb N$ along which the Walsh--Fourier partial sums $s_{
u_j}(f)$ of every integrable function $f$ converge almost everywhere to $f$. This resolves a problem that Konyagin posed in his invited address at the 2006 International Congress of Mathematicians~\cite{K06}. The criterion concerns the binary expansions of the integers $
u_j$. Divide each $
u_j$ by $2^k$. Convergence holds if and only if, for some $K\in\mathbb N$, the number of distinct positive quotients whose remainder has binary variation larger than $K$ is bounded independently of the scale $k$. This is also equivalent to the weak type $(1,1)$ inequality for $\sup_{j\in\mathbb N}|s_{
u_j}(f)|$, and if the criterion fails, then the partial sums of some integrable function along $(
u_j)$ are unbounded at every point. The criterion contains the bounded variation condition and Konyagin's condition for separated spectra, and we give examples, for convergence and for divergence, that are not covered by the earlier results.

papers.title: On unique realisations of graphs under symmetry constraints
papers.abstract:
Global rigidity asks whether a realisation of a graph is uniquely determined, up to Euclidean congruence, by its edge lengths. In this paper, we study global rigidity of bar-joint frameworks under finite point-group symmetry constraints. A framework is called forced-symmetric globally rigid in $d$-space if every realisation of the graph in $\mathbb R^d$ with the same edge lengths and the same prescribed symmetry is congruent to it. We establish symmetric extensions of two fundamental results on global rigidity.
  Our first result extends Hendrickson's necessary condition to the forced-symmetric setting. For symmetry-generic frameworks with an arbitrary finite point group acting freely on the vertices and with at least $d+2$ vertex orbits, we prove that forced-symmetric global rigidity implies forced-symmetric redundant rigidity.
  Our second result extends the classical characterisation of generic global rigidity for body-bar frameworks due to Connelly, Jord\'an and Whiteley. For the symmetric body-bar model considered here, we show that forced-symmetric global rigidity is a generic property and obtain a combinatorial characterisation in every dimension.

papers.title: The Zero Enrichment Rare Objects (ZERO) Survey I: Photometric Calibration of NB395 and Metallicity Estimation
papers.abstract: We present the first results of the Zero Enrichment Rare Objects (ZERO) survey, a narrow-band photometric survey targeting metallicity-sensitive narrow bands using the Hyper Suprime-Cam on the Subaru Telescope. This paper outlines the scientific goals, survey strategy, current observational status, photometric calibration, and metallicity estimation. The current ZERO footprint comprises 21 pointings, covering approximately 35 deg$^2$ along the celestial equator in the NB395 band, reaching NB395 $\sim$ 24.5 mag (10$\sigma$) in one hour, significantly deeper than typical comparable narrow-band Ca H\&K surveys. The NB395 photometry is calibrated using corrected Gaia BP/RP spectra and the recalibrated SDSS Stripe 82 catalog, achieving a typical zero-point precision of $\sim$0.3 per cent and flat-field precision better than 1 per cent on spatial scales larger than 8$^\prime$. Under typical conditions (three repeats; total exposure time $\sim$1 hour), the photometric precision reaches $\sim$1.1 per cent at NB395 $\approx$ 12, $\sim$1.5 per cent at 20, and $\sim$10 per cent at 24. We estimate [Ca/H] using a Physics-constrained Stellar Locus Fitting Method. The resulting [Ca/H] precision is better than 0.18 dex for sources brighter than NB395 $\sim$ 20, spanning a wide metallicity range from metal-rich to the very metal-poor regime ($-3 \le$ [Ca/H]$\le +0.5$). We further show that NB395 traces [Ca/H] more directly than [Fe/H]. The final catalog contains one million sources with NB395 photometry, including 379,216 repeatedly observed and 61,845 with [Ca/H] estimates. These results provide a solid foundation for future ZERO survey, including photometric calibration, stellar parameter determination, and investigations of Galactic structure and chemical evolution.

papers.title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator
papers.abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.

papers.title: A concave-convex approach to bit depth allocation for linear MMSE estimation in wireless sensor networks with correlated noise
papers.abstract: Nodes in a wireless sensor network (WSN) are generally powered by batteries, and therefore energy efficiency is crucial. The bit depth used to quantize the sensor signal samples heavily influences energy consumption, as it strongly impacts the amount of information to be transmitted between the sensor nodes. Bit depth allocation problems seek to assign a bit depth to each sensor signal to optimize network resources, such as energy or bandwidth, together with algorithmic performance. We study a general bit depth allocation problem for linear minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimation in WSNs with spatially correlated noise and a communication energy model depending linearly on the sensor bit depths. This model follows from common configurations in digital communications with orthogonal multiple-access schemes. After relaxation to real variables, we formulate the resulting non-convex problem as a difference of convex (DC) problem, and develop an algorithm based on the concave-convex procedure (CCP) to find a local optimum. We show that the convex problem involved in each CCP iteration can be efficiently solved with a worst-case complexity that is linear in the number of sensors. Additionally, we show that our approach is more computationally efficient than previously proposed bit depth allocation algorithms and generic optimization methods, and it achieves significant energy savings.

papers.title: A Morphological Approach to Inverse Lithography
papers.abstract: Lithography is a critical step in the manufacturing of chips that works by projecting light through a patterned mask and subsequently focusing it onto a photosensitive layer on top of a wafer. The task of finding a mask that prints a desired pattern on the wafer is called inverse lithography technology (ILT). The design of the mask is complicated by the fact that it must satisfy a set of constraints in order to be manufacturable. In this paper we provide a mathematical characterization of these constraints. Next, we develop a scoring function that allows us to measure whether a given mask satisfies the manufacturing constraints and if not, how badly the constraints are violated. Since our scoring function is (sub-)differentiable it can be used as the regularizer in a gradient-based inverse problem solver. We show that the resulting MorphILT algorithm that we developed can generate manufacturable masks that have nearly the same print quality as the (unmanufacturable) masks obtained from unconstrained inverse lithography.

papers.title: FlashQLA: Efficient Context Parallelism for Gated DeltaNet
papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.

papers.title: On the Effectiveness of Resampling for Supervised Graph Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Class imbalance and scarce anomaly labels motivate oversampling in supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), but its benefits across detectors and benchmarks remain unclear. In the low-label setting of GADBench, with 20 labelled anomalies and 80 labelled normal nodes, we compare class weighting and up to six oversampling strategies in ten detector configurations from three families: graph neural networks (GNNs), tree ensembles on neighbourhood-aggregated features, and tabular foundation models, on 17 datasets. On the eight datasets with organic anomalies, no strategy has a statistically resolved average gain in any configuration, and which nodes are labelled matters as much as the strategy. On the nine datasets with injected anomalies, Gaussian-noise oversampling (ROSE) gains up to 5.2 AUPRC points in four of the six tree and tabular foundation model configurations, and in all six only on attribute-swap anomalies; in four GNNs its gain is not distinguishable from zero. This gain depends on the injection recipe, which gives swapped nodes an atypical feature norm: it is no longer distinguishable from zero when the swap uses a single random donor or preserves the norm, although most detectors then also stop detecting the swaps. Over the 17 datasets, tuning the tree detectors adds about three points, as much as ROSE, and cuts ROSE's gain by about half or more. With the same source nodes and class weight, sampled graph views are not distinguishable from plain copies of those nodes. We recommend tuning baselines, repeating labelled splits, reporting organic and injected anomalies separately, and checking label-free degree and feature-norm baselines.

papers.title: Diving Deeper into Dense Keypoint Localization in Object Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: 6D pose estimation of rigid objects is a fundamental and challenging task in computer vision. Recent dense semantic keypoint-based methods employ binary encoding for efficient global keypoint localization, delivering strong performance in object pose estimation. Nevertheless, the discontinuous nature of binary encoding hinders effective training at high resolutions, while its inherent discrete and quantization errors lead to significant localization uncertainty. We propose GHLAPose, a global-to-local framework that synergizes hybrid Gray-binary (HGB) encoding with local-aware refinement (LAR). Specifically, HGB encoding first alleviates discontinuity to achieve accurate initial global keypoint localization. To further address intrinsic encoding errors, the LAR module estimates uncertainty and refines keypoint localization. This synergy enables a precise global-to-local strategy by aggregating global and local features. Extensive experiments on LM, LM-O, YCB-V, and TUD-L datasets demonstrate that GHLAPose surpasses state-of-the-art methods, particularly on fine-grained metrics. On LM-O, it outperforms the second-best method by 1.4% and 1.9% on ADD(-S) 0.02d and 0.05d respectively, and on YCB-V by 1% on ADD(-S) 0.1d. The code will be available at GHLAPose.

papers.title: A short proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture
papers.abstract: We give a short alternative proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture, recently proved by OpenAI. Our proof combines their reduction with a different argument showing that every nontrivial oriented graph $G$ contains a nonempty set $X$ such that $X^+\ne V(G)$ and $|(X^+)^+\setminus X^+|\geq|X^+\setminus X|$, where $X^+=N_G^+[X]$.

papers.title: Hybrid AI for AI-Native RAN Control: A Functional Perspective
papers.abstract: AI-native radio access network (RAN) control involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales. Understanding how AI and conventional methods can jointly support these decisions requires a common basis for comparing their functional roles. This survey introduces a technique-agnostic taxonomy of RAN decision-making organized around four complementary capabilities: Representation and Reasoning, Prediction and Simulation, Adaptive Control, and Decision Synthesis. These capabilities are defined by their roles in the control process, independently of the techniques used to implement them. Through this perspective, we examine representative AI and model-based approaches, including foundation models, world models, reinforcement learning, and optimization. We then apply the taxonomy to representative RAN control solutions across slow, medium, fast, and cross-timescale applications to identify which capabilities they implement and how these capabilities are combined in hybrid AI systems. We also review datasets, benchmarks, simulators, digital twins, and experimental platforms according to their support for the decision-making process and reproducible evaluation. The review highlights a gap between the availability of resources for closed-loop experimentation and the standardization of tasks, metrics, and evaluation protocols needed for meaningful comparisons.Finally, we identify research directions for hybrid AI in AI-native RAN, including capability integration, multi-agent and cross-timescale coordination, constraint handling, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation. A curated list of surveyed works and evaluation resources is available at https://github.com/pegahani/Hybrid-AI-RAN-Survey.

papers.title: Flagging Batch Shift in Flow Cytometry using Jeffreys Divergence between Gaussian Mixtures
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for clinical flow cytometry are usually evaluated on data drawn from their training distribution. In routine practice, however, acquisition conditions and reagents may change, potentially making predictions unreliable without warning. We propose a model agnostic criterion for prediction reliability based on a notion of distance from the training distribution: each patient sample is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, and its Jeffreys divergence to a reference fitted on the training data is estimated using Monte Carlo integration. We illustrate our approach on real-life shifted cohorts of acute myeloid leukaemia patients, using a classifier trained to predict NPM1 mutation status. First, we show graphically and statistically that pairwise divergences capture acquisition cohort structure. We then calibrate a rejection threshold on a subset of shifted cohort samples and evaluate it on held-out subjects. Across 20 runs, the misclassification rate of rejected samples was 2.5 times larger than for retained samples. These results suggest that input divergence can help identify unreliable predictions, providing a strong candidate component for abstention frameworks, along with quality control measures and classifier confidence.

papers.title: Visual Thinking: Training-Free Active Perception for Counting and Localizing Hard-to-Find Objects
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models can precisely segment objects based solely on a text prompt. However, they struggle to recover objects that are small, occluded or whose appearance is poorly captured by the original textual description. Vision language models can examine the image and its context, they can propose richer descriptions of the objects to be detected. But these models struggle with precise segmentation and localization. We introduce Visual Thinking, a training-free framework that combines a vision-language model with Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) through an iterative active perception loop. At each iteration, the VLM proposes short noun phrases using the image, candidate crops and history from past iterations. A controller ranks these phrases using embedding similarity between the original prompt and the proposal, an entropy-based verification priority and the novelty of the prompt. Next, SAM 3 uses prompts to detect objects in the image. We associate detections across iterations and update each object's confidence score using a weighted mean of scores obtained from SAM 3 with a larger weight for detections using narrower prompts. We supply confident detections as positive visual exemplars for SAM 3, and incorporate image tiling to recover small objects in cluttered images. We evaluate counting and localization on CARPK, FSCD-147, PixMo-Count, and OmniCount (Fruits). Compared with SAM 3, Visual Thinking reduces the counting mean absolute error (MAE) by about 18 on FSC-147 and about 8 on CARPK. It improves box average precision (AP) by more than 12 on FSCD-147 and CARPK. Visual Thinking, with fixed or no tiling, performs on par with Claude Opus 5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort, while running on single desktop GPU in about 5.91 seconds per image, compared to about 46.53 seconds per image for Claude through its API.

papers.title: Relaxation dynamics of the impurity momentum in a one-dimensional Fermi gas
papers.abstract: We consider a single mobile impurity coupled by a repulsive contact interaction to a gas of free spinless fermions of equal mass in one dimension. Using the determinant overlaps between the interacting eigenstates and free-fermion states, we derive closed determinant formulas for the matrix elements of the impurity momentum operator and of its square between arbitrary Bethe-ansatz eigenstates of a finite system. At infinite coupling we prove a selection rule: both operators have vanishing matrix elements between distinct eigenstates that share the same rapidity, and every eigenstate carries the per-particle share of the total momentum. For an impurity injected into the Fermi sea we have the following: at infinite coupling the average impurity momentum relaxes completely in the thermodynamic limit, while at finite coupling relaxation remains incomplete. The closed-form matrix elements turn the spectral representation of the average impurity momentum into explicit finite sums over eigenstates. We evaluate the post-injection dynamics, resolve the quantum-flutter oscillations and the approach towards the diagonal-ensemble value, and map the stationary momentum as a function of the injection momentum and the coupling. Finally, we analyse the thermodynamic limit and its asymptotics as an integral over Fredholm determinants.

papers.title: Packing the Bragg sphere: complete three-dimensional photonic band gaps at the refractive index of polymers (1.55)
papers.abstract: Complete 3D photonic band gaps have so far been found only at refractive-index contrasts of about 1.9 and above, reached by rod-connected diamond lattice structures. Reciprocal-space design of quasiperiodic structures recently achieved considerable emission attenuation at much lower contrasts [L. Maiwald et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 10, 2100785 (2022)]. Here we implement systematic search and reciprocal-space design of periodic 3D structures with complete band gaps, solving a discrete optimization problem on an integer lattice. A gap above a high band needs the strongest Fourier components of the dielectric close to the Bragg sphere of that band. Crystals with large cells, started from Fourier peaks at the vertices of a polyhedron on this sphere and optimized against densely refined band edges, open complete gaps down to an index contrast of 1.55, that of common polymers against air. A rational approximant of an icosidodecahedron gave the most efficient location of the Fourier peaks among the polyhedra tested. Numerical calculations confirm the gaps over a resolution series, with band edges searched over the whole Brillouin zone. The best designs are connected porous networks, suited to a microwave test with printed polymer. A rigorous bound, valid for any structure, does not exclude gaps at lower index, and the next rational approximants of the icosidodecahedron, whose Bragg zones match bands 576 and 2440 almost exactly, point to where gaps at even lower contrast may be sought.

papers.title: TokenJoule: Energy Modeling for Distributed Training and Inference of LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) scale, energy dictates operating cost, cooling, and cluster capacity across training and inference. Early hardware design-space exploration (DSE) requires predicting energy before silicon exists, yet performance models miss hidden component work while prior energy predictors calibrate to deployed GPUs. We present TokenJoule, an open-source analytical tool that derives device kernel sequences, tiled compute, shared-memory staging, cache residency, and collective traffic, pricing activity directly with component energies. With zero workload fitting, TokenJoule achieves 3.3-6.6% activity error (151 A100/H100 runs) and 3.0-6.8% A100 energy error, guiding parallelism, memory packaging, and 3D-DRAM chip co-design.

papers.title: Adaptive Robust Optimisation for Frequency-Constrained Market Clearing Problem
papers.abstract: This paper formulates the day-ahead market clearing as a two-stage adaptive robust optimisation problem in which the first stage determines unit commitment, energy dispatch, and reserve procurement, while the second stage represents worst-case balancing actions under simultaneous uncertainty in renewable generation, load, and HVDC converter outages. Frequency security is enforced explicitly through inertia and fast frequency response constraints at the synchronous-area level, with HVDC lines allowed to provide emergency power support within their available headroom. The resulting min--max--min problem is solved by a column-and-constraint generation algorithm and applied to an eight-country North Sea test system comprising three synchronous areas, sixteen onshore bidding zones, and five offshore wind farm hubs connected through a meshed HVDC grid. We compare the Home Market (HM) and Offshore Bidding Zone (OBZ) designs on this infrastructure across different uncertainty scenarios. The results first demonstrate the value of robustness, where deterministic solutions that ignore uncertainty are severely vulnerable to worst-case realisations. Comparing the two designs, we find that OBZ's offshore zone boundaries make line congestion visible to the day-ahead market, enabling targeted reserve procurement that raises day-ahead costs but substantially reduces real-time load shedding, yielding a net reduction in total system cost that grows with the severity of localised offshore uncertainty. When both designs face the identical worst-case contingency, HM cannot distinguish an offshore converter trip from normal operation and thus fails to hedge against it, while OBZ considers the risk at the day-ahead stage. This advantage can be seasonal, scaling with the ratio of offshore wind output to HVDC line capacity and diminishing when onshore generation dominates the supply mix.

papers.title: CSC-Mamba: Bridging multimodal convolutional sparse coding and state space models for multi-contrast MRI super-resolution
papers.abstract: Multi-contrast MRI super-resolution accelerates clinical protocols by reconstructing high-resolution (HR) target modalities from low-resolution (LR) inputs, guided by easily acquired reference contrasts. While purely data-driven deep neural networks achieve strong performance via rich representation capacity, they rely on heuristic fusion mechanisms (e.g., naive concatenation or black-box cross-attention) that lack theoretical grounding. Alternatively, model-based deep unfolding networks enforce principled cross-contrast fusion through explicit priors, yet their unrolled steps remain constrained to shallow convolutions, lacking modern deep blocks to capture global context. To bridge this gap, we propose CSC-MAMBA, unifying deep-unfolded multimodal convolutional sparse coding with the Vision Mamba state-space backbone. By fusing common structural priors from the guidance modality via unfolded sparse coding and globally refining contrast-specific representations with a Mamba back- bone, our approach benefits from interpretable, model-guided fusion and long-range spatial context. Experiments on the IXI dataset demonstrate that CSC-MAMBA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality, achieving up to a 0.62 dB gain in PSNR while remaining computationally efficient.

papers.title: Pando: Noise-Coupled Parallel Draft Trees for Efficient Edge Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract:
Autoregressive (AR) decoding emits one token per forward pass, reloading the full model each time, so LLM inference on edge devices is memory-bound while the compute units sit idle. Speculative decoding puts that idle compute to work by verifying several drafted tokens in a single pass. State-of-the-art parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark propose an entire block of draft tokens in one forward pass, which makes drafting compute-efficient. However, they are deployed with draft chains whose length is capped by the block size they are trained for, leaving most of the computational budget for verification unused.
  To tackle this problem, we propose Pando, which builds dynamic draft trees on top of a parallel drafter and thereby removes this cap. Pando employs noise-coupled pruning, which draws the target model's sampling noise before drafting and ranks candidate branches under that noise, so the tree retains the branches the target will actually sample. Noise coupling is lossless and requires no retraining or additional model pass, yet increases acceptance length by up to $8.4\%$ on Qwen3-8B. To optimize and evaluate Pando configurations across hardware, we normalize an operator-level roofline to AR decoding, reducing every platform to its ridge point. On a representative edge device, a 16-node Pando tree attains $5.3\times$ speedup and $4.2\times$ energy reduction over AR decoding: $25\%$ faster than DSpark's released chain, and $27\%$ faster and $72\%$ more energy-efficient than an EAGLE-3 tree. The best configurations remain memory-bound on every edge device we model, so added compute capacity does not reduce their latency.
