papers.title: Bayesian approach to the Student's t-test based on the B-FBST
papers.abstract: This article proposes an exact Bayesian formulation of the B-FBST Student's t-test applied to the one-sample Student's t-test. The method relies on constructing an exact posterior distribution of the standardized parameter, then calculating the e-value to measure the evidence against the null hypothesis. To improve the stability of the procedure, posterior densities obtained from bootstrap samples are aggregated using random weights. A Monte Carlo simulation study was then conducted to compare the B-FBST Student's t-test with the classical Student's t-test and the bootstrap Student's t-test. The results, obtained from 100 Monte Carlo replications and 200 bootstrap replications, show that the B-FBST Student's t-test exhibits favorable overall performance, with an average of 71.0% correct decisions, compared to 65.5% for the classical test and 70.7% for the bootstrap test. The proposed method thus appears to be a robust alternative, particularly in several situations where the classical assumptions of the Student's t-test are compromised.

papers.title: Group classification of a class of systems of nonlinear diffusion equations. I
papers.abstract: We study the Lie symmetries of a class of systems of (1 + 1)-dimensional nonlinear diffusion equations. The equivalence algebra and the kernel of the maximal Lie invariance algebras of this class are found. We prove that there exist exactly nine inequivalent subclasses of this class for which the corresponding diffusion systems admit Lie symmetry extensions. We also carry out the exhaustive group classification of the systems of nonlinear diffusion equations from the first subclass.

papers.title: ModernELECTRA: Replaced-Token Detection with Boundary-Window Reconstruction for Compact Encoders that Classify and Embed
papers.abstract: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary "original vs. replaced" signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.

papers.title: On optimal packing of Minkowski spheres
papers.abstract: A method has been developed for the optimal packing of a continuum family of one-dimensional Minkowski spheres in the real plane. By applying this method to the problem of packing one-dimensional Minkowski spheres in the plane, an optimal lattice packing for a continuum family of such spheres has been obtained for the first time. Expressions for these optimal packing lattices have been derived, and their validity has been proven. Formulas for the packing density corresponding to these lattices have also been obtained.

papers.title: Open-Set Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification with Feature Fusion and Vision Transformer
papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) is a promising device authentication technique for the Internet of Things (IoT) that leverages hardware impairments to uniquely identify devices. However, most existing RFFI systems operate under a closed-set assumption and lack the ability to detect rogue devices, which poses significant security risks. In this paper, we propose an open-set RFFI approach that jointly performs rogue device detection and legitimate device classification. Specifically, we designed a multi-task RFFI system that integrates an autoencoder (AE) for rogue device detection and a fully connected (FC) layer for classification. To enrich the feature representation, we generated two channel-independent spectrograms (CISs) with distinct window lengths from the I/Q signals, capturing complementary time-frequency characteristics. These CISs were processed in parallel by two Vision Transformer (ViT) networks, and their outputs were fused via feature concatenation to construct a device fingerprint for both tasks. We built a testbed involving ten legitimate LoRa devices and five rogue devices. We conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation and compared our approach with several benchmark algorithms. Experimental results show that our fused feature multi-task RFFI consistently outperformed the baselines in both legitimate device classification and rogue device detection. Our proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 91.1% and an area under the curve (AUC) of over 0.72 in a realistic wireless scenario where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was 20 to 30 dB.

papers.title: HuluOPD: Unifying Heterogeneous Medical Specialists into One Lightweight Model with Unlabeled Prompts
papers.abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.

authors.name: Yitian Tang
authors.institution: First Affiliated Hospital of Xinxiang Medical University

papers.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

authors.name: Fucheng Niu
authors.institution: China University of Mining and Technology

papers.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.

papers.title: On the solving degree and complexity of Gr\"obner Basis computation over finite fields
papers.abstract:
Solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields is a central problem in algebraic cryptanalysis, commonly approached using Gr\"obner basis algorithms. The complexity of Gr\"obner basis computation depends on the algorithm employed and is governed by the solving degree, defined as the maximum degree of the polynomials processed during the computation. Estimating this quantity is therefore crucial, and several bounds in terms of the degree of regularity have been established in the literature.
  In this work, we investigate the effect of Buchberger's criteria on the elimination of redundant pairs, and prove that the solving degree of a Gr\"obner basis algorithm combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original algorithm is bounded above by the degree of regularity defined by the leading forms of the involved polynomials. This result provides a rigorous justification for using the degree of regularity in complexity estimates for Gr\"obner basis algorithms, thereby supporting a common assumption in algebraic cryptanalysis.
  We refine the complexity analysis by establishing bounds on the number of pairs that must be processed. These bounds improve upon published complexity estimates, with particularly significant gains in certain parameter ranges.

papers.title: A Bernstein-Type Variance-Adaptive PMW Mechanism for DP Query Release
papers.abstract: Private Multiplicative Weights (PMW) is a central mechanism for the differentially private release of adaptive linear statistics over a finite universe. Its classical analysis uses a fixed multiplicative-weights learning rate and does not exploit the local variance of the current hypothesis. This paper presents PMW-Bernstein, a variance-adaptive refinement in which the update step is determined by the relationship between the privately estimated query error and the variance under the current hypothesis. The mechanism retains the standard PMW privacy architecture based on Sparse Vector screening, Gaussian numerical measurements, sequential composition, and post-processing. Through a potential-based analysis, we prove a one-step progress bound that yields a global weighted energy bound, recovers the classical $O(1/{\alpha}2)$ update regime in general, and establishes an $O(1/{\alpha})$ update regime under a Bernsteintype condition on updated rounds. Controlled simulations over synthetic finite-universe distributions and query workloads show that the adaptive rule reduces the number of updates in the low-variance regime, remains competitive in the high-variance regime, and succeeds within the prescribed update budget in the heterogeneous regime where the fixed-step baseline fails.

papers.title: Classifying exact local-equilibrium solutions of the Boltzmann equation
papers.abstract: We provide a complete classification, in a \(d\)-dimensional Euclidean space, of all hydrodynamic states and external forces for which a local equilibrium distribution constitutes an exact solution to the Boltzmann kinetic equation. We demonstrate that the temperature \(T\) must be spatially uniform, that the velocity field is the sum of a rigid translation, a radial expansion or compression, and a rigid rotation, and that the external acceleration must be conservative, though time-dependent within a reference frame that translates and rotates along with the fluid. The density profile is then determined by the external potential, while its temporal dependence is governed by any temperature function \(T(t)\) that can be generated through an appropriate adjustment of the external acceleration. We recover the classic ``harmonic breather'' and obtain solutions involving static forces that exhibit algebraic cooling, similar to Haff's law, despite the occurrence of elastic collisions. Our classification identifies the exceptional circumstances under which local equilibrium is exact and provides rigorous criteria for evaluating kinetic and hydrodynamic approximations.

papers.title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses
papers.abstract: Two laws share a common component after each discards a fraction $\alpha$ of its mass, a trimming, exactly when their total variation is at most $\alpha$, so the contamination level $\alpha^\star = \mathrm{TV} (P,Q)$ is the share of each population without counterpart in the other. We bound it from below from two samples on any space with a bounded characteristic kernel. The kernel mean embeddings of all such trimmings of a law form a convex region, the regions of two laws first touch at $\alpha^\star$, and in every direction a region reaches as far as a trimmed mean. The difference of their closest points, the witness, selects the trimming. We fit a ramp of the witness on part of the data and bet on the rest, at each level of a grid. The bound is valid at every sample size. The cut points of the tested level carry most of its finite-sample gain over an untrimmed witness, while refitting the witness at that level makes it consistent, gives its rates and returns the trimming. When a function of the kernel's Hilbert space separates the parts of the two laws without counterpart, the bound is within order $(n\wedge m)^{-1/2}$ of $\alpha^\star$ on a grid of that mesh, which is minimax over such pairs. When these parts touch, a margin condition guarantees a polynomial rate for Sobolev kernels and a logarithmic rate for the Gaussian kernel. For the Laplace kernel on the line this guarantee is not sharp: the witness stays between its two cut points, and for densities that cross once, with a likelihood ratio bounded away from one off the crossing, the error on such a grid is again of that order up to logarithmic factors. No informative upper bound exists without assumptions. On the Right Heart Catheterization data, with confidence $0.95$, each arm must lose more than a fraction $0.35$ of its patients, if both lose the same fraction, before their covariate distributions can coincide.

papers.title: Notes for a seminar on vortex layer cascades
papers.abstract: After the seminars I recently gave at New York University, the University of Chicago, Princeton University and the University of Bonn and after having been asked by some people to publish these notes, I decided to upload them to arXiv. In recent years, the method of vortex layer cascades has successfully been applied to construct finite-time singularities in multiple fluid equations (3D Euler, Boussinesq, IPM, g-SQG...). In this talk, I will motivate and describe the method and sketch how it can be applied to the 2D Boussinesq and 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations. In both systems, the growth of the vorticity is driven by an accumulated hysteresis effect triggered by the cyclic deformation of the density layers, whose dynamics is governed by an infinite chain of degenerate pendula. Our work also settles the previously open question about global existence of classical solutions of the (forced) 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations.

papers.title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
papers.abstract:
Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(D\Phi) = 1) without topological folding (det(D\Phi) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox).
  We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(\Omega) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(\Omega). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations).
  We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(D\Phi)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.

papers.title: Localization and homogenization of anisotropic fractional energies
papers.abstract: We study the joint limit of localization ($s\uparrow1$) and periodic homogenization ($\varepsilon\downarrow0$) for anisotropic fractional energies with $p$-growth and oscillating kernels. We prove that the $\Gamma$-limit is governed by the single parameter $\theta=\lim\varepsilon^{p(1-s)}$, and that its density is the convex combination $\theta\mathcal{A}^* + (1-\theta)\bar{\mathcal{A}}$ of the homogenized and the averaged densities. This shows that the picture recently obtained for quadratic energies also holds for every $p$ and for anisotropic kernels, with no regularity in the oscillating variable; the approach is different, and is based on convex duality. A nonlocal version of the duality argument gives the limit as $s\uparrow 1$ for a fixed kernel under weak assumptions, correcting a previous proof by the authors.

papers.title: A fermionic framework for quantum machine learning benchmarks
papers.abstract: We present a framework for building and benchmarking scalable machine learning (ML) models based on simulating free-fermion systems. Our fermionic ML (FermiML) framework is (i) versatile enough to encompass kernel methods and neural networks, (ii) applicable to classification and regression, and (iii) scalable to real-world datasets. FermiML models are quantum circuits sharing the building blocks of most quantum ML (QML) models: (parameterized) qubit rotations and entangling gates. This allows us to build fermionic surrogates that mimic the architecture, and hence the quantum resources and inductive bias, of any QML model while remaining efficiently classically simulable. We thus benchmark QML models against close fermionic counterparts on equal footing and ascertain whether a purported QML gain truly stems from classically inaccessible resources or is an accidental side-effect. Across 31 configurations from five classification datasets, we benchmark quantum kitchen sinks (QKS), instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) and generic parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) models against fermionic surrogates. fQKS significantly outperforms QKS and is statistically indistinguishable from IQP and PQC; fPQC outperforms IQP and QKS and ties PQC in 28 configurations. We also introduce fermionic fidelity and Pfaffian covariance kernels for regression and establish QML baselines for this harder task. Finally, we introduce a fermionic energy-based classifier scalable to large text and image datasets, which outperforms prominent QML models on images, beats or closely trails them on text, and stays close to classical baselines throughout. Our results show that while performance depends sensitively on architecture, FermiML yields fermionic surrogates that challenge or outperform their unrestricted counterparts and fermionic QML models that match the scale of classical baselines on real-world datasets.

authors.name: Stefanos Kourtis
authors.institution: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

papers.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
papers.abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

papers.title: Airport-level runway-incursion rates normalized by movements: hierarchical shrinkage estimates, ranking uncertainty and severity for FAA-towered airports, FY2008-FY2024
papers.abstract: Runway incursions are one of ICAO's five high-risk occurrence categories, yet airport-level comparisons of incursion risk in the United States still rest on raw counts or on fixed-count thresholds that select on sampling noise. We assemble an airport-fiscal-year panel of 565 FAA-towered airports holding 27,079 runway-incursion records from the FAA Runway Safety database as held in the FlightFinder corpus (himaxym.com), normalized by tower operations from the FAA Terminal Area Forecast (ATADS/OPSNET actuals). A hierarchical negative-binomial model with log operations as an exposure offset, airport random effects, fiscal-year effects and traffic-mix covariates yields, for every airport, a shrinkage-adjusted rate per million operations, an exceedance probability relative to the national median, and a posterior rank with a 90% interval in the manner of Goldstein and Spiegelhalter. Severity (Category A-D) is modeled separately as an ordinal outcome, and empirical-Bayes and fully Bayesian shrinkage are compared. The crude national rate is 29.4 incursions per million operations (95% interval 29.1-29.8), with an index of dispersion of 8.61. Between-airport dispersion after exposure adjustment is sigma_u = 1.05: an airport one standard deviation above the mean carries 2.84 times the national rate. 199 of 565 airports exceed the national median with probability above 0.9, and the 90% rank interval at the median airport spans 134 positions, so much of the league table is statistically indistinguishable from its middle. Severity and frequency respond to different determinants: the airport-level rank correlation between them is -0.08 (90% interval -0.14 to -0.02), so a frequency ranking carries little information about where a severe outcome is likely. The results offer a reproducible, uncertainty-aware alternative to count thresholds for prioritizing runway-safety interventions.

papers.title: Dual-Pilot Design for OCDM Channel Estimation
papers.abstract: Channel acquisition in orthogonal chirp division multiplexing (OCDM) over doubly-dispersive channels incurs a large pilot overhead, since delay and Doppler jointly shift the symbols in the chirp domain and separating them requires repeated pilots, each protected against the complete coupled displacement. This letter proposes a dual-pulsone pilot design that reduces this overhead in two steps. First, a pulsone occupies fewer chirp-domain bins than alias-free Doppler estimation requires, deliberately allowing Doppler wrapping. Second, a phase-offset pulsone is placed within the same protected region to observe a complementary part of the displacement, further reducing the shared guard. The phase offset also resolves the wrapping ambiguity, enabling low-complexity delay-Doppler estimation. Simulations show competitive estimation and BER performance, with the lowest complexity and highest payload efficiency among the considered OCDM estimators.

papers.title: Interference-Free In-Symbol Pilots for High-Mobility DFT-s-OFDM Uplink
papers.abstract: The 5G New Radio (NR) uplink uses discrete Fourier transform spread orthogonal frequency-division multi- plexing (DFT-s-OFDM) for its low peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). Its demodulation reference signal (DMRS) occupies whole symbols, although channel estimation only needs channel samples. Since existing designs cannot place pilots inside a data symbol without interference on the data, or on both data and pilots, NR keeps whole DMRS symbols, which wastes spectral efficiency (SE), and adds more of them as the channel varies faster, lowering the SE further. We develop a technique that places pilots free of data interference inside the data symbols, for frequency-domain channel estimation in every symbol. Using the Zak transform, we show that leaving a set of equally spaced pre- DFT samples empty frees one column of the Zak grid of the DFT output. The data values of the pilot subcarriers are relocated into this column by adding a constant over a few subcarrier combs, which preserves the energy and keeps the NR DFT sizes. The receiver undoes it linearly with comb sums, without decisions or side information, and a symbol loses as few as one data sample beyond its pilots. Since the pilots raise the PAPR, we keep them few per symbol and hop their positions across symbols, so that a two-dimensional estimator over the slot resolves long delay spreads at high Doppler. On 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels, pilots in every symbol achieve a higher effective SE than all NR DMRS configurations from pedestrian to high- speed-train velocities, at a PAPR close to plain DFT-s-OFDM.

papers.title: Lower space bounds for polynomial-time quantum computation
papers.abstract:
We present new results on the minimal space requirements of problems solvable by polynomial-time quantum Turing machines. We define the notion of Monte Carlo space complexity (where the machine is allowed to give an incorrect output or exceed the designated space budget for every input with small nonzero probability) for quantum computation, and prove that for any computable nondecreasing space bound $s(n)\in \omega(1)$, there is a language that can be recognized in polynomial time by an $s(n)$-space QTM but not by any $O(1)$-space machine in that regime. We also demonstrate a sublogarithmic worst-case space hierarchy for polynomial-time quantum computation, proving that
  $\mathsf{BQTISP}(n^{O(1)},o(s_{i}(n)))\subsetneq \mathsf{BQTISP}(n^{O(1)},O(s_{i}(n)))$, where for each $i\ge0$, $s_{i}(n)=\left(\frac{\log n}{(\log \log n)^i}\right)$.

papers.title: The Commutant of the Adjoint Center Need Not Be the Center of the Dual
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a Banach lattice with ideal center $Z(X)$, and let $Z^*(X)=\{S^*:S\in Z(X)\}$ be the set of adjoints of central operators, acting on the dual $X^*$. The center $Z(X^*)$ of the dual is always contained in the commutant $(Z^*(X))^{\mathrm{com}}$ of $Z^*(X)$, and equality is known when $X$ has a topological order unit. It has been asserted that equality holds whenever $X$ has a topologically full center; the published proof of this assertion is incorrect, and the question has been recorded as open. We show that the assertion is false. For the Marcinkiewicz sequence space $m_\psi$, $\psi(t)=\log(1+t)$ (the sequence space underlying the Dixmier--Macaev ideal), which is Dedekind complete and therefore has a topologically full center, there is a bounded operator on the dual that commutes with every adjoint of a central operator but is not itself central; it maps one Dixmier trace onto another one disjoint from it. The construction rests on a general sufficient condition, proved with an invariant mean taking values in a Dedekind complete space $C(K)$ and the injectivity of $C(K)$. We also collect positive results and a norm-density criterion for equality. For every Orlicz space $L_\Phi$ we show that every operator in $(Z^*(L_\Phi))^{\mathrm{com}}$ is lower-triangular with respect to the decomposition of the dual into its order continuous and singular bands, with central diagonal entries, and, by a splitting lemma based on Young's inequality, that the off-diagonal entry vanishes. Hence equality holds for all Orlicz spaces and their duals, without any $\Delta_2$-condition.

papers.title: Do Layer Rankings Survive Silence Trimming? The Silence Shortcut in Frozen WavLM Representations for Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Layer-wise analyses of frozen self-supervised encoders are used to locate spoofing information in audio deepfake detection. On the ASVspoof 2019 logical access (LA) benchmark, bonafide recordings carry longer leading and trailing silence than spoofed ones, and detectors exploit this cue, the silence shortcut. This paper examines whether layer rankings for a frozen WavLM Base encoder survive the trimming of this silence. A small classifier is trained on each of the 12 layers with and without trimming and evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA and, zero-shot, on In-the-Wild, in all four train/test combinations, with speaker-level bootstrap intervals. Trimming at 40 dB raises the in-domain error at every layer and preserves the layer ranking only partly (Kendall's tau of 0.58 in domain, 0.73-0.76 on In-the-Wild). The best layer is unchanged at 40 dB, but on the evaluation set it moves from layer 5 to layer 6 at 15 dB and, with mean pooling, at 20 dB, thresholds at which trimming may also remove low-energy speech. At 40 dB, the equal error rate of a model trained with silence rises by 6.3-19.9 percentage points at every layer when only its test audio is trimmed. On In-the-Wild, the effect depends on the layer: at layers 3-5, trimming the test audio lowers the error only for models trained on trimmed audio, whereas at layers 6, 8, and 9 training on trimmed audio lowers it also on clean test audio. We quantify how zero padding alters WavLM features through group normalization, an effect that an attention mask does not fully undo.

papers.title: HyMTS: A Multiscale Tensor Factorization-Based Network for Hyperspectral Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) restoration has been explored using deep learning techniques recently. Because hyperspectral images have strong spectral and spatial redundancy, the underlying clean signal is usually represented in a low-dimensional spectral subspace and locally low-rank spatial structures. Existing methods primarily explore dense attention or feature mixing across spectral bands. In this work, we propose HyMTS, a hyperspectral restoration network with a backbone built on the Multi-scale Tensorial Summation (MTS) factorization operator. HyMTS provides a natural architectural mechanism for exploiting a low-rank prior, embedded directly in the network operator rather than imposed via an auxiliary loss or a constraint on the reconstructed output. Specifically, HyMTS stacks a unified block that couples factorized layers with input-adaptive layers, capturing both local and global dependencies across the spectral and spatial dimensions. Extensive experiments without auxiliary data on standard benchmarks for Gaussian and real-noise denoising and single-image super-resolution show that HyMTS efficiently achieves superior or comparable performance to various state-of-the-art approaches.

papers.title: Detecting Topological Phases Through Dynamics of Chiral Density in Momentum-space Lattices
papers.abstract: Momentum-space lattices offer a versatile platform for quantum simulation in particular emulating topological states of matter.In this work, we propose a spectroscopic protocol via utilizing the dynamics of the chiral operator to detect the topological properties of a momentum-space Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain. We show that the time evolution of the chiral density is directly linked to the local density of state (LDOS). By performing a Fourier transformation of that, we reconstruct both the LDOS and density of states of the system, enabling the unambiguous signature of zero-energy edge modes and the bulk-boundary correspondence. This dynamical approach provides a diagnostic tool for exploring topological phases in synthetic quantum matter.

papers.title: Capability and Interpretability of Transformers on Multi-task Recurrence
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely used in various language tasks, with limited understanding of their internal mechanisms. Motivated by the recurrent structure of many linguistic rules, we study the capability and interpretability of Transformers through a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups. These tasks range from executing a single fixed rule to identifying a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Through extensive experiments across different configurations, we find that switching specified rules is simpler than identifying latent rules for Transformers in general. We also identify how several key factors affect the generalization capability of Transformers, including the depth, width, and the algebraic structure of the linear recurrence. Curriculum training is extremely useful when the number of rules is large. With standard tools in mechanistic interpretability like linear probing and input patching, our study reveals how Transformers represent, identify, and execute multiple rules.

authors.name: Jiachen Hu
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Pinyan Lu
