authors.institution: Federal State Budgetary Institution of Science Federal Scientific Center "Vladikavkaz Scientific Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences"

papers.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

papers.title: FourStat: A Dual AutoEncoder Leveraging Frequency and Stationarity for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: While numerous studies have focused on multivariate time series anomaly detection, many existing methods perform poorly or are not directly applicable to univariate settings. We introduce FourStat, a dual-model framework for univariate time series anomaly detection that combines two complementary approaches. The Fourier Autoencoder (FAE) captures global patterns like seasonality through frequency-domain analysis, while the Stationary Autoencoder (SAE) focuses on local structures by enforcing statistical stationarity. We also propose a new evaluation metric called Perfect Point that assesses whether perfect F1-scores can be achieved directly from anomaly scores, eliminating thresholding subjectivity. Results demonstrate that FourStat outperforms existing baselines, particularly on challenging anomaly types, while the new metric provides clearer insights into model performance gaps and advantages.

papers.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

papers.title: The hot circumgalactic medium: implications of mixing and resolution at the disk-halo interface
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that microphysical processes at the disk--halo interface, typically unresolved in circumgalactic medium (CGM) simulations, strongly affect the thermodynamic structure and observational signatures of an inflowing hot ($\sim10^6\,{\rm K}$) CGM. If the hot gas is pulled through the interface faster than it can cool, e.g.\ by turbulent mixing with the ISM or fountain flows, the hot CGM approaches an isentropic state. If instead the interface is regulated by radiative cooling on the hot gas cooling time, the hot CGM develops an outward-increasing entropy profile akin to a classic cooling flow. The two regimes differ by a factor of $\sim\!10$ in the predicted hot gas density above the disk near the rotation axis, and consequently by a factor of $\sim100$ in the predicted X-ray emission measure. We show that an isentropic CGM is produced in idealized CGM simulations that fail to resolve the pc-scale disk--halo interface, as numerical mixing drives artificially rapid cooling at the interface. A similar isentropic structure is found along the rotation axis in FIRE zoom-in simulations of $z\sim0$ Milky-Way-mass galaxies, where the cooling layer is likewise unresolved, raising the possibility that numerical mixing contributes to the isentropic structure. In contrast, an outward-increasing entropy profile forms in our idealized simulations when we replace the unresolved interface with an inner boundary that enforces a slow inflow. This outward-increasing entropy profile is likely also present in the Milky Way hot CGM, inferred from comparing density estimates at $\sim100\,{\rm kpc}$ with the entropy of the eROSITA bubbles.

papers.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
papers.abstract: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.

papers.title: Temporal Soliton Waves in Modern Fiber Laser Systems
papers.abstract:
This chapter provides a comprehensive survey of temporal soliton-wave
  in modern fiber systems. Temporal soliton waves constitute a broad class of nonlinear localized structures in modern fiber laser systems, arising from different balances among dispersion, nonlinearity, gain, loss,
  spectral filtering, and various forms of cavity coupling. We review the underlying theory, basic experimental findings, and practical methods for the generation, real-time characterization, and active control of soliton families, with a particular focus on recent progress reported for mode-locked fiber-laser platforms. The families covered in the chapter include dissipative solitons, soliton molecules (bound states), and dispersion-managed solitons. For each species, we focus on the pulse energy, duration, stationary and breathing states, and emerging intelligent (machine-learning-assisted) control strategies.

authors.name: Shilong Liu
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: High-Performance Algorithms for Computing the V-BLAST Permutation
papers.abstract: We propose two novel and efficient algorithms for computing a column permutation called V-BLAST or an approximation of it. The V-BLAST column permutation is used in a QR factorization that is part of an integer/discrete least-squares solver. The overall solver is part of the receiver in advanced communication systems that transmit multiple symbols simultaneously. Two classes of efficient algorithms for computing the exact V-BLAST permutation have been proposed in the literature. The first, based on a sequence of Givens rotations, is unfortunately highly sequential. The other, based on a sequence of downdating operations on a pseudo-inverse, has a shorter critical path, but is unlikely to be numerically stable. The new algorithms that we propose are inspired by the similarity between V-BLAST and rank-revealing QR factorizations. Our first algorithm uses Householder reflections, is numerically stable, and has a short critical path. It is unable, however, to efficiently exploit cache memories. We rectify this with a randomized algorithm that computes an approximation to the V-BLAST permutation and has a short critical path and can effectively exploit cache memories. We prove approximation properties of the randomized algorithm and demonstrate experimentally that both algorithms are faster than existing ones, both when tested in isolation and when tested within an integer least-squares solver.

papers.title: One Take, Many Cameras: Audio-Grounded Shot Synthesis for Dialogue Re-Cinematography
papers.abstract: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.

papers.title: Optimal Signaling Mechanisms for One-round Matching Markets
papers.abstract:
Signaling mechanisms are used in various types of matching markets so that applicants may credibly signal interest in firms. They have been observed to improve outcomes in job markets and dating markets, and proven to improve outcomes in several stylized theoretical models.
  In this paper we develop optimal signaling mechanisms for a simple one-round matching market consisting of $n$ applicants and $n$ firms. We consider a much richer space of signals than have been used previously, in theory or practice, and also consider randomized signaling mechanisms, which have not been systematically studied.
  For each $k \geq 1$, we determine the optimal deterministic and randomized signaling mechanisms in which applicants signal $k$ firms. In the limit as $k\to \infty$, our deterministic mechanism guarantees that in expectation, $\approx 75.4504\%$ of the applicants receive job offers, and this is optimal. Likewise, for $k \to \infty$, our randomized mechanism guarantees that $\approx 78.197\%$ of the applicants receive offers, which is also optimal.
  The optimal $k$-signal randomized mechanism is non-constructive, and has a rather complex description. We describe some simple randomized signaling mechanisms whose efficiency surpasses that of the limiting optimal deterministic mechanism. Finally, we also discuss incentive-compatibility for the firms to follow the mechanism.

authors.name: Thomas P. Hayes
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
papers.abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.

papers.title: Emergent cloud patterns from stochastic jump models of parcel microphysics
papers.abstract: Warm clouds organize into bands, cells, and intricate wave networks, yet the dynamical mechanisms connecting these forms remain difficult to isolate. To bridge unresolved parcel microphysics and cloud organization, we formulate a spatial jump-process model of cloud-water and rain-water anomalies in an activated regime and analyze its mean-field closure. Eliminating fast supersaturation adjustment from droplet growth and vapor transport supplies a screened environmental kernel, which we couple to a cubic Stuart-Landau oscillatory law. Averaging over Poisson parcel episodes and closing third-order moments yields a pseudoparabolic Ginzburg--Landau equation (PGLE), whose mixed space--time derivative encodes dynamic inertia, slowing fine-scale relaxation. Unlike diffusive amplitude equations, the PGLE splits into a regularized nonlinear Schr\"odinger Hamiltonian sector and a pseudoparabolic Allen--Cahn gradient sector governed by a conserved Noether charge, alongside an open-system liquid-water budget separating conversion from vapor exchange, fallout, and triad-driven domain-mean oscillations. Exact stability criteria show how dynamic inertia and amplitude-dependent frequency shifts (twist) control modulational loss of synchrony and resonant cross-carrier sideband gain above a critical twist threshold. Numerical integrations show that increasing twist transforms undulatus-like bands into defect-rich asperitas-like waves via defect proliferation, while subcritical competition consolidates cellular patterns into rolls. Even without twist, random anomalies evolve into a persistent cellular exclusion scale and actinoform-like spiral arms, while 1D wave breakup reorganizes into a two-frequency combination-tone spectrum. The jump model identifies omitted fluctuation moments for calibration against large-eddy simulations.

papers.title: Sparse Additive Spanners and the Cost Spectra of Group Actions
papers.abstract: How sparse can a Cayley graph become if we retain all its vertices and allow distances to increase by at most a fixed additive constant? We study invariant random spanning subgraphs, measuring sparsity by the expected degree at a vertex. On the square grid, a random translate of a sparse mesh brings the mean degree arbitrarily close to two. If the choice must be made equivariantly from independent vertex labels, every edge is forced. In this expository note we follow these two answers through other groups. Geometry alone forces a positive gap on each non-elementary hyperbolic Cayley graph, while on one four-regular nilpotent Cayley graph the choice of action realizes every additive cost in $[1,2]$. The minimum of the action spectrum recovers the geometric cost. Open problems are presented in the end.

papers.title: Approximate MMS allocations for large number of agents
papers.abstract: We consider allocation of indivisible items to agents with non-negative additive valuations, under the maximin share (MMS) fairness benchmark. We prove that for every $\rho < 1$, there exists some $n_{\rho}$ such that every allocation instance with $n \ge n_{\rho}$ agents has a $\rho$-MMS allocation. This was explicitly stated as a conjecture in a recent paper of the authors, where it was shown to hold if the number of items is at most $(2 - \epsilon)n$ (and $n \ge n_{\rho, \epsilon}$). We build on some techniques from that earlier paper, including the construction of $\textit{ordinal MMS}$ allocations that give $n - O(\log^2 n)$ agents their full MMS. Among the new techniques that we introduce is the definition of $\textit{block-matchings}$ between the MMS partitions of two agents, and a proof that if the number of item types is small, then block-matchings of small width necessarily exist.

papers.title: Properties of the Sawin--Wood Model for Unramified Galois Groups of Global Fields
papers.abstract: We prove almost-sure finite generation and finite presentation in the pro-$|\Gamma|'$ $\Gamma$-category for the Sawin--Wood measure $\nu_{\Gamma,n,U}$, where $\Gamma$ is a non-trivial finite group, $n$ is coprime to $|\Gamma|$, and $U$ is a nonempty multiset of conjugacy classes of $\Gamma$. The $\Gamma$-generator rank of the random group $X$ has the sharp tail $\mathbf{P}(d_\Gamma(X) \geq r) = Ce^{-\kappa r^2-\zeta r}(1+O(e^{-\varepsilon r}))$, where $C>0$, $\kappa>0$, and $\zeta\in\mathbb{R}$ are explicit constants depending on $n$, $\Gamma$ and $U$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Almost surely, $X$ admits a presentation with the minimum number of $\Gamma$-generators, using at most $|U|$ more defining $\Gamma$-relations than generators. We also prove that every open subgroup of $X$ has finite abelianization almost surely under the assumption that for every complex representation of $\Gamma$ there is an element in $U$ that fixes a nonzero vector. Finally, we prove that $H_2(X,\widehat{\mathbb{Z}})=0$ almost surely when $n=1$, $\Gamma$ is cyclic, and $U$ contains only the conjugacy class of a generator of $\Gamma$ (with multiplicity one).

papers.title: Signatures of Kitaev quantum spin liquid states in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ revealed by nitrogen-vacancy spin-noise spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Bond-dependent magnetic interactions, strong spin-orbit coupling, and quantum fluctuations in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ make it an archetypical candidate for exotic Kitaev quantum spin liquid (QSL) states. While electronic transport, neutron scattering, optical and tunneling spectroscopies were used to probe global QSL signatures in large scale $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ samples, nanoscale evidence of local QSL behavior via a non-invasive experimental probe is still missing. Here, we use diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin-noise spectroscopy to probe QSL states in {\alpha}-RuCl3 nanoflakes with thicknesses ranging from 8 to 150 nm over a temperature range of 4.3-250 K. Our measurements reveal a pronounced decrease in the NV spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_{1}$) below ~100 K in proximity to the $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ flakes, indicating enhanced GHz-frequency magnetic fluctuations. This temperature scale is consistent with the energy scale associated with Kitaev interactions (~8 meV) and the emergence of low-energy fractionalized excitations. Below 50 K, thicker (> 90 nm) flakes exhibit a distinct bi-exponential $T_{1}$ decay, unlike the single-exponential behavior observed for off-flake and thinner (8 nm) flake measurements, suggesting an increasingly heterogeneous magnetic noise environment. These results establish NV spin-noise spectroscopy as a local, non-invasive probe of low-energy spin dynamics in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ nanoflakes and open a route to testing predicted noise signatures of fractionalized excitations in atomically thin QSL candidates.

authors.name: Xia Hong
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory on Integrated Optoelectronics

papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.

papers.title: A note on input-oblivious unambiguous hierarchies
papers.abstract:
Unambiguous hierarchies are defined similarly to the polynomial hierarchy; however, all witnesses must be unique. Their versions differ in the mode of using oracles. We consider input-oblivious unambiguous hierarchies built from the class OUP, in which all positive inputs of the same length have the same unique witness: the hierarchy OUH with language oracles and the hierarchy OUH$_\bullet$ with loose access to promise oracles, which is the input-oblivious version of the loose unambiguous hierarchy of Hirsch and Sokolov (IPL, 2015). We show that languages in OUH$_\bullet$ can be decided in deterministic polynomial time with an ONP oracle, and for languages in OUH oracle queries can be made nonadaptive.
  Moreover, languages in OUH can be decided in deterministic polynomial time with a tally NP oracle, and languages in OUH$_{\bullet}$ can be decided in P/OptP, that is, a subclass of P/poly where the advice is generated by a function that maximizes outputs of a nondeterministic machine on a unary input. We show that P/OptP can be characterized in terms of OGTD and OUGTD generator--tester--decoder classes recently considered by Hirsch and Volkovich (arXiv:cs.CC/2611.16096) and, in particular, is contained in their "ultimate" Karp--Lipton collapse class OUM.
  We also observe several other facts related to OUP: (1) the hierarchy defined by input-oblivious unambiguous dot-operators collapses, (2) in OUP computations, a single loose query to prOUP can be replaced by a query to OUP, (3) SOUP=OUP$\cap$coOUP, where SOUP is the same-witness class recently considered by Hirsch, Volkovich, and Williams (2026).

papers.title: The $\gamma = 1/2$ Problem: A Unified Viability Criterion for f(R) Gravity in the Solar System
papers.abstract: A novel framework for addressing both the accelerated expansion of the cosmos and the inflationary epoch involves modifying the Einstein-Hilbert action through a function $f(R)$. While these $f(R)$ gravity theories can, under certain conditions, replicate phenomena described by scalar-tensor theories, this is only viable if the associated scalar field can operate within the Solar System without violating stringent observational constraints. A significant challenge is that within this theoretical equivalence, the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ is fixed at $\gamma = 1/2$, a value that deviates substantially from the experimentally established result of $\gamma \approx 1$. Recent discussions have questioned the genuine equivalence between $f(R)$ gravity and scalar-tensor formulations. Furthermore, recent findings, independent of this equivalence, have demonstrated that the field equations for $1/R$ theory predict $\gamma = 1/2$ in a vacuum for spherical mass distributions. In this work, we extend these results to a broader class of $f(R)$ functions, aiming to delineate the specific conditions that lead to the prediction of $\gamma = 1/2$. This investigation provides a unified framework for identifying which classes of $f(R)$ gravity can satisfy Solar System constraints, deriving a general viability criterion that moves beyond previous case-by-case analyses. We derive a unified viability criterion that provides a necessary condition for any $f(R)$ theory to satisfy Solar System constraints, moving beyond case-by-case analyses toward a systematic classification framework.

authors.name: Jie Li
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Steiner porism and boundary value problems
papers.abstract:
The aim of this paper is to describe several interpretations of Steiner chains of circles in terms of certain boundary value problems and give a short review of related results. Our approach and discussion are motivated by the recent results on the geometry of Steiner porism based on an apparently novel analytic parametrization of poristic circles obtained by A.Diakvnishvili and the present author. We also mention a few feasible problems and generalizations suggested by the constructions and considerations presented in the paper.
  Keywords: Steiner chain of circles, Steiner porism, curvature, invariant moments of curvatures, boundary value problem, Riemann-Hilbert problem, Brylinski loop space, circle packing

papers.title: Exact nonstationary heat-excess statistics in the weakly asymmetric Kipnis--Marchioro--Presutti model
papers.abstract: Exact nonstationary large-deviation statistics remain scarce for interacting many-body systems. Here we employ the macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) to determine the complete long-time statistics of heat excess produced by an initially localized heat pulse in the weakly asymmetric Kipnis--Marchioro--Presutti model. We find a remarkable nonlocal canonical transformation which maps the weakly asymmetric MFT problem, including its initial and terminal conditions, onto the symmetric problem, previously solved exactly. The resulting rate function is an explicit nonlinear deformation of its symmetric counterpart. We also extend the solution to heat measured beyond an arbitrary observation point.

papers.title: Which Ellipses Are Outlines of a Given Ellipsoid? A Ratio Test with Unknown Focal Length
papers.abstract: When is an image ellipse the outline of a given ellipsoid with semi-axes $a <= b <= c? For a camera with square pixels, zero skew and known principal point, we show that it is an outline at focal length $f$ exactly when a cone ratio kappa(f), computed from two eigenvalues, is at most a/c; the middle semi-axis b plays no role. With f unknown, the admissible focal lengths form an interval; whether it is empty is decided by the smallest cone ratio over $f$, which, when attained, is obtained from an explicit quartic. The interval is bounded above only when the principal point is closer to the long axis of the ellipse than to its short axis. Thus one ellipse can rule out ellipsoids that are too round, never ones that are too elongated, and none if the principal point is unknown. Simulations and 45 Cassini images of Saturn's moons support the test.

papers.title: RenGen: Generating Images with as Many Tokens as the Scene Needs
papers.abstract: We present RenGen, a latent diffusion model that generates simple scenes from a few tokens and busy scenes from many, saving time and compute on simple scenes without losing realism. Most latent generators represent every image as a fixed grid of patch tokens, so a simple image costs as much to generate as a complex one. Prior methods that vary the token count through content-adaptive tokenization lose image quality as the count shrinks. RenGen instead trades scene complexity, rather than image quality, for fewer tokens. It does so by generating in the latent space of a pretrained region encoder, where each token represents one region of the image, and a decoder renders these region tokens back into pixels. Unlike patch tokens, region tokens cover areas of varying shape and position, so each token must capture both what its region contains and where it lies on the image canvas. We encode this spatial extent by adding positional embeddings to the encoder features before pooling, and we generate it by anchoring each token to a single randomly sampled point, from which the generator infers the region's shape, size, and content. At sampling time, the number of anchor points sets the trade-off between scene complexity and compute. On ImageNet $256{\times}256$, RenGen reaches a gFID of 1.34 with 88 tokens per image on average, the best among methods that vary their token count. It approaches the quality of RAEv2, a state-of-the-art patch-based model, at $2.5{\times}$ lower latency, advancing the Pareto frontier of generation quality versus compute. RenGen's gFID stays flat across scene complexity while latency varies by $2.4{\times}$ between simplest and busiest scenes, and its autoencoder reconstructs nearly as well as RAEv2 (rFID 0.32 vs. 0.30) with $2.9{\times}$ fewer tokens.

papers.title: Turnpike Estimates and Limiting Behavior for $N$-Player Differential Games under Displacement Monotonicity
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behavior of open-loop Nash equilibria of $N$-player stochastic differential games with nondegenerate idiosyncratic noise, under displacement monotonicity of the costs and joint strong convexity of the Lagrangians. We prove an exponential turnpike estimate: as the remaining horizon grows, the decoupling fields of the finite-horizon Pontryagin systems converge exponentially fast to the solution of a stationary Pontryagin system, which is unique in a natural stability class, and on bounded time intervals the equilibrium states and controls converge to those generated by this solution. The limiting control is a strong open-loop equilibrium of an associated ergodic $N$-player game, and the ergodic constant $\lambda^{i,N}$ of each player is the same at every such equilibrium. For the finite-horizon game, the law of the equilibrium state, at times away from the initial and terminal times, is exponentially close in the Wasserstein distance $W_2$ to the invariant measure of the limiting dynamics. Finally, the equilibrium cost of player $i$ on $[t,T]$ equals $(T-t)\lambda^{i,N}$ plus a uniquely determined corrector, up to an error exponentially small in $T-t$.

papers.title: Effect of humidity and phase transition on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of humidity on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows taking into account the effect of phase transitions on turbulent transport. We find that the coefficients of turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour decrease with increase the turbulent Damk\"{o}hler number (the ratio of turbulent time in the integral scale and phase transition time for condensation of water vapour), while the coefficients of the mutual turbulent diffusion that describe the turbulent cross effects increase with this parameter. For large turbulent Damk\"{o}hler number, the coefficient of turbulent diffusion of droplets is strongly depleted when the evaporation of droplets is much faster than the condensation of water vapour. The obtained theoretical relationships are potentially useful in modelling applications in the atmospheric turbulence.

papers.title: Knocked Off Course: Tracing Uncommanded Motion from Perception to Action in Embodied VLAs
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable simultaneous processing of egocentric video and textual target descriptions to produce action commands for embodied tracking platforms. However, these platforms rarely move exactly as commanded, in part due to unexpected environmental disturbances such as wind, unleveled terrain, and road bumps. Here we study how such models handle uncommanded egomotion. First, we explore performance across diverse disturbances by benchmarking three tracking VLAs on three datasets. We find that models differ in which environmental disturbances hurt them most, but all are sensitive to sudden target loss. Tracing egomotion from pixels to emitted actions, we identify two gaps. In representation, motion is reliably recovered through explicit relations between frames, but aggressive compression of past frames weakens small-motion readouts. In action, large rotations do reach the decision state, yet the decoded direction carries only a few percent of a mirrored rotation's effect on the turn. Targeting both gaps, we fine-tune one model, Uni-NaVid, on data amounting to just 1.7% of its original training set in a ladder of analysis-motivated variants. These gain 5-22 points after target-loss without degrading clean success; after a smooth loss, the best one improves success by 72% (relative), recovering 76% of its gap to clean. We also show that targeted fine-tuning improves recovery partly via a text-mediated action dependency, without new architecture, large-scale data collection or training from scratch.

papers.title: DOPER: Deep Object Pose Estimation Revisited
papers.abstract: We present DOPER, an RGB pose estimation framework that shares a visual backbone across object detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to recover the 6D pose of known objects through Perspective-n-Point. Starting from synthetic training, DOPER adapts to real observations using partial supervision while retaining synthetic keypoint labels. Calibrated multi-view observations provide geometric constraints for keypoint supervision. During inference, optional heatmap refinement fits a rigid pose directly to the predicted keypoint distributions, resolving ambiguous correspondences without depth input or a learned pose refiner. Starting from underspecified CAD models, DOPER progressively refines the object representation and pose estimator. Results on SPEED+ and SHIRT further demonstrate effective adaptation to illumination changes and accurate temporal pose estimation. Across the evaluated single-view and multi-view configurations, DOPER achieves state-of-the-art detection AP results on HANDAL, HOPEv2, HOT3D, and T-LESS while using only RGB and running in real time (35 Hz per object model on one GB300). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly learning detection and pose keypoints, with real observations and geometric constraints.

papers.title: The rotation period of the near-Earth comet (875163) 1998 SH2 and the limits of a single-apparition phase curve
papers.abstract: The near-Earth object (875163) 1998 SH2 was recently shown to be a weakly active comet: its 1998-2025 astrometry reveals a non-gravitational acceleration too large to be radiative in origin, and large-aperture imaging during its 2025 apparition revealed a faint tail (Farnocchia et al. 2026). No rotation period had been reported. We derive one from dense TTT2 photometry obtained on five nights of the same apparition: from 2392 calibrated measurements we find a synodic rotation period P = 6.970 +/- 0.020 h. The folded light curve is markedly bimodal (A2/A1 ~ 6.4) with a peak-to-peak amplitude of ~0.18 mag, implying a/b >~ 1.18. Combined with the published radar Doppler bandwidth, the period is consistent with an elongated body whose rotation the radar alone could not constrain. Over the narrow observed phase-angle range (3.7-9.3 deg) the IAU H,G and H,G1,G2 slope parameters are not physically constrained. The inter-night magnitude gradient, beta_app = 0.074 +/- 0.005 mag/deg, is steeper than the default G=0.15 and lies in the upper part of the Jupiter-family comet (JFC) distribution (median 0.046; Kokotanekova et al. 2017); because the object was weakly and increasingly active during the run, we treat this value as an upper limit to the intrinsic surface phase slope. Under the population prior of little or no opposition surge, as found in available JFC nucleus phase curves, the phase behaviour is best described by a linear law, giving a provisional H_Lum(1,1,0) ~ 20.9-21.0 over 3.7-9.3 deg in the Luminance band.

papers.title: A dedicated survey of fast-rotating near-Earth asteroids with the Two-meter Twin Telescope. II. Tumblers
papers.abstract: Fast rotation dominates the metre- to decametre-size near-Earth asteroid (NEA) population, but the incidence of non-principal-axis (NPA) rotation, or tumbling, in this regime is essentially unconstrained. We establish how common NPA rotation is among small, fast-rotating NEAs, how its prevalence varies with size, and what it implies for the internal structure and recent dynamical history of these bodies. We analysed the homogeneous high-cadence sample obtained with the Two-meter Twin Telescope at Teide Observatory and presented in the first paper of this series. Light curves showing coherent residual structure under a single-frequency Fourier model were refitted with a bivariate Fourier series in two independent frequencies, and dynamical modes were assigned from the normalised harmonic amplitude spectrum. We confirm 32 NPA rotators, 14 with both periods reliably resolved, with periods spanning 0.48-46.4 min and estimated diameters of 7-140 m. The most extreme object with both periods resolved, 2025 FB8 (shortest period $P_1 = 71$ s, estimated diameter $D \simeq 7$ m), is the fastest and smallest such tumbler characterised to date. Eight objects satisfy our harmonic quality criteria, and all eight are consistent with long-axis mode rotation. The tumbler fraction among fast rotators is 16.0 %, rising from 13.8 % at absolute magnitude $H < 26$ to 22.5 % at $H \geq 26$. Twenty-three of the 32 lie above the spin limit of a cohesionless rubble pile; none exceeds the lunar-regolith limit. Tumbling is common among small fast rotators, with no evidence that it becomes rarer towards the smallest sizes. Fast tumblers require modest cohesion but no monolithic interior, occupying the same structural domain as their principal-axis counterparts.

papers.title: The centre of mass of the primes and a reflection of Chebyshev's bias
papers.abstract: For $x\ge2$ we place a unit mass at $\log p$ for each prime $p\le x$, and let $D(x)$ be the distance from the centre of mass of this system to $\log x$; thus $D(p_n)=\log(p_n/G_n)$, where $G_n$ is the geometric mean of the first $n$ primes. Let $D_0(x)$ be the distance obtained when $\pi$ is replaced by $\mathrm{Li}(x)=\int_2^x dt/\log t$. We prove that $D(x)-D_0(x)\ll x^{\Theta-1+\varepsilon}$, where $\Theta$ is the supremum of the real parts of the zeros of $\zeta(s)$, and that the exponent cannot be lowered; in particular, the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to $\log(p_n/G_n)=D_0(p_n)+O_\varepsilon(p_n^{-1/2+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Under the Riemann hypothesis we prove a pointwise mirror theorem: for large $x$ the centre of mass lies to the left of its predicted position only when $\pi(x)<\mathrm{li}(x)-1.95\sqrt{x}/\log x$. Under the Riemann hypothesis and the linear independence hypothesis, the set of such $x$ has the same logarithmic density as the set on which $\pi(x)>\mathrm{li}(x)$, although for large $x$ the two sets are disjoint. We prove analogues for primes in arithmetic progressions, for the higher moments of the system, and, under a linear independence hypothesis, for $\mathbb{F}_q[T]$, where the biases of even and odd degrees are interchanged.

papers.title: Frequency-Conditioned Privacy Auditing of Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly fine-tuned on sensitive data, where the same person's information may appear multiple times across records. This can cause models to memorize sensitive information, but memorization does not necessarily mean that the information can be recovered. A more serious privacy risk arises when the model begins to reproduce that information during generation. In this paper, we study how often sensitive information must appear in the fine-tuning data before it becomes recoverable. Across four language models, we vary the frequency of email addresses and phone numbers from $1\times$ to $50\times$ and compare standard fine-tuning, gradient clipping, and differentially private training. We find that the number of repetitions required before sensitive information becomes recoverable varies substantially across models. Gradient clipping can delay extraction, but it does not consistently prevent leakage at high repetition. DP-SGD at $\varepsilon=5$ produces zero observed extraction through $50\times$ repetition across all four models under the attacks we test, although the utility cost varies by model. These findings characterize how observed extraction varies across sensitive-data frequencies, model families, and training mechanisms, and highlight substantial differences in extraction behavior across models. Code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: Trace-defined double covers of the $S_3$-involution graph of $PSL_2(2^n)$
papers.abstract: For $q=2^n\ge 4$, we construct a family of Deza double covers $\Gamma(q,\xi)$ of the $S_3$-involution graph of $PSL_2(q)$, parametrized by $\xi\in\mathbb F_q^*$. We show that each resulting cover is connected, arc-transitive and amply regular with parameters $(2(q^2-1),q,Tr(\xi),1)$, where $Tr$ denotes the absolute trace. We also show that the trace-one covers are antipodal of diameter $5$ and girth $3$, whereas the trace-zero covers are non-antipodal of diameter $3$ and girth $5$. For $q=4$, these cases yield the well-known icosidodecahedral and dodecadodecahedral graphs, respectively. Then we determine the distance distributions and full automorphism groups of the covers and prove that, for fixed $q$, two covers are isomorphic if and only if their defining parameters lie in the same Frobenius orbit. We also express the Ramanujan property of a cover in terms of the spectral norm of a signed adjacency matrix of the base graph.

authors.name: L. Yu. Tsiovkina
authors.institution: Ural Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Measuring Counterfactual Credit in a Replayable Wildfire-Suppression Benchmark
papers.abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, learned critics are usually evaluated by how well they predict the team's return. Yet predicting a team's return and assigning credit to individual actions are distinct tasks. To test credit directly, we introduce FLARE (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment), a stochastic wildfire suppression benchmark in which any moment of a fire can be replayed with different actions under the same random events. Replaying one step measures the immediate effect of each agent's suppression, which we call simulator credit and use for training. Replaying to the end of the episode measures the effect of each action, which we use for grading critics. In a comparison over eight seeds with multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), simulator credit reduces the interquartile mean burn score (each cell's burning time, capped and averaged over the map; lower is better) from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%. Learned credit from a centralized COMA-style critic does no better than the shared reward. Four trained critics predict the team's return well, yet the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay. The critics also give heterogeneous agents nearly identical action rankings. These results show that a good fit to the team's return is a weak test of a critic's credit.

papers.title: ECLIPSE: Embedding-Centered Foundation-Model Federated Knowledge Transfer for Data-Free Edge Intelligence
papers.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) are envisioned to become an integral component of intelligent federated edge networks because of their strong representation and generalization capabilities. However, their integration into resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive edge environments remains challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced in data-free settings, where no shared, public, or server-accessible reference dataset is available to establish a common reference space for aligning distributed knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose ECLIPSE, which is an embedding-centered FM-based federated knowledge transfer framework developed for data-free edge intelligence. ECLIPSE enables edge intelligence capitalizing on a server-hosted FM without sharing raw data, local models, or a public reference dataset. It establishes a shared embedding reference space through which edge devices encode their local task knowledge. Only the resulting embeddings are transmitted to the server for alignment and aggregation. Using the aggregated embeddings, the server constructs a task-aware surrogate dataset through an embedding-guided generative process. This surrogate dataset is then used to adapt the server-hosted FM to the downstream task. The adapted FM is subsequently distilled into a lightweight global model and distributed to the edge devices. This process allows edge devices to benefit from both distributed task knowledge and the generalization capabilities of the FM. Experimental results across diverse classification datasets show that ECLIPSE outperforms conventional Federated Learning (FL) and data-free Federated Knowledge-Transfer (FKT) baselines. It also achieves competitive performance compared with databased approaches. Furthermore, the framework remains robust under statistical and model heterogeneity across different data distributions and local architectures.

papers.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
papers.abstract: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

papers.title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.

papers.title: Gated Concept Adapters: Layer-Wise Concept Bottlenecks for Auditable Text Understanding
papers.abstract: Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.

papers.title: The Universal Frame Characterization of C*-algebras
papers.abstract: We prove that a C*-algebra A is a C*-algebra of compact operators if and only if every Hilbert A-module admits a frame. This answers affirmatively the question of Amini, Asadi, Elliott and Khosravi (2017), arising from the problem of Frank and Larson (2002)

papers.title: Improved Downward-Closed Delegation Bounds
papers.abstract:
We study delegated choice under a downward-closed feasibility constraint, where the principal and agent values of each item may be arbitrarily correlated but items are independent. We give a deterministic, agent-oblivious menu that guarantees the principal more than $29/70\approx0.41429$ of the expected offline optimum under every best response, including ties resolved against the principal. The menu depends only on the feasible family and the principal's value distributions, and verifies a proposal using only its items and their principal values. The previous best guarantee for downward-closed constraints was $0.1098$.
  Matroid constraints admit a guarantee of one half, which is tight already in rank one, but downward-closed constraints do not: a five-item knapsack instance bounds every deterministic menu by $500/1011$ of the optimum, and no rule with randomized acceptance, even one that knows the agent's utilities, can guarantee more than $30/61$. An explicit computer-assisted family of instances lowers the bound to $0.48105$ for all such rules.
  The guarantee is proved by contradiction. If every menu in a fixed family earns at most a $29/70$ fraction of the optimum, then a normalized instance satisfies a finite system of affine inequalities among the survival functions, stop-loss transforms and overshoot means of its clipped optima. An exact rational certificate shows that the system is infeasible. We also give a short analytic proof that a single threshold on the reported total value guarantees $3/10$.

papers.title: Sharp Casorati Inequalities for Pointwise Bi-Slant Riemannian Maps into Sasakian Space Forms
papers.abstract: We establish Casorati inequalities for pointwise bi-slant Riemannian maps into Sasakian space forms with the characteristic vector field tangent to the range. The Sasakian structure imposes specific conditions on the second fundamental form, leading to refined inequalities for the normalized horizontal scalar curvature that also account for O'Neill's tensor. For proper pointwise bi-slant maps, equality in the two principal inequalities is characterized by the vanishing of the second fundamental form on the orthogonal complement of the characteristic direction in the range. We also derive corresponding inequalities for pointwise semi-slant, hemi-slant, and slant Riemannian maps and construct examples attaining equality.

papers.title: Single-Photon Detectors for Optical Wireless Communications: A Tutorial
papers.abstract: Photon-counting receivers extend optical wireless communication (OWC) into regimes in which only a few detected photons are available per information bit, but the detector can no longer be treated as an interchangeable ideal counter. This tutorial develops a communication-oriented, port-to-bit framework for single-photon detection in indoor, terrestrial, airborne, space, underwater, non-line-of-sight, and integrated communication-and-sensing links. It compares SPADs, silicon photomultipliers, CMOS SPAD arrays, superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors, PMT/MCP-PMT receivers, upconversion detectors, and emerging technologies through photon-detection efficiency, timing, active area, dynamic range, spectral coverage, readout, cooling, and integration requirements. Beginning with the ideal Poisson channel, the tutorial then develops communication-level models for dead time, recovery, finite-pixel occupancy, saturation, background counts, afterpulsing, crosstalk, nonuniformity, and event loss. These models are connected to modulation, likelihood-based detection, synchronization, channel estimation, soft decoding, and detector-aware receiver processing, with numerical studies that compare algorithms under a common detector and detectors under a common algorithm. Finally, a unified link-budget and system co-design methodology is used to relate photons per bit, sensitivity, bandwidth, data rate, and link margin, and representative demonstrations are normalized to expose practical tradeoffs. The central conclusion is that useful photon efficiency is an end-to-end property of the optical front end, detector, readout, and digital receiver, rather than a detector metric in isolation.

papers.title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
papers.abstract: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.

authors.name: Quoc Phong Nguyen

papers.title: XMind: Thinking Twice via Cross-Memory Reasoning for LLM-Based Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind

papers.title: Exact Last-Iterate Bounds and Optimal Stepsizes for Proximal Stochastic Gradient Descent
papers.abstract: Proximal Stochastic Gradient Descent minimizes the sum of an $L$-smooth convex function $f$, known through unbiased stochastic gradients of bounded variance, and a nonsmooth convex function $R$, known through its proximity operator. We derive the exact worst-case value of the expected objective gap of its last iterate, for every predetermined stepsize schedule in a broad class, which contains all the schedules with stepsizes at most $3/(2L)$. This extends to the composite setting a recent result of Grimmer and Shen for the smooth case $R=0$. The value is the sum of an initial-error term and of one term per iteration, which is the price of the noise injected at this iteration, damped by the stepsizes that remain after it. The upper bound is proved with a simple potential, the Moreau envelope of the objective with a smoothing parameter proportional to the remaining stepsize sum, and it is attained by an explicit instance. The formula shows that a logarithmic factor is unavoidable with a constant stepsize, and it gives the exact price of the proximity operator, relative to the smooth case. It also makes the choice of the stepsizes a tractable optimization problem: for a uniform variance bound $\sigma^2$, the best schedule is unique, decreasing, and computed by a scalar search, and it is minimax optimal among all predetermined schedules, unless the noise level is low. Asymptotically, the minimax value $M_T$ after $T$ iterations satisfies $(D\sigma/M_T)^2=T+\log T+C_\star+o(1)$, where $D$ is a bound on the initial distance to a solution and $C_\star\approx1.768$ is a universal constant; unlike in the smooth case, $L$ plays no role at this order. This law is achieved by an explicit schedule, which is the optimal one when $f=0$.

papers.title: MargEmbed-Akan: Bridging Twi Questions and English Knowledge through Cross-Lingual Score Distillation
papers.abstract:
Most information sought online by Twi (Akan) speakers is written in English, making cross-lingual retrieval essential. We evaluate eight systems: BM25, five open embedding models, and two proprietary models (gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) on two Twi-English tasks. AfriQA contains 1,221 natively written Asante Twi questions that must retrieve their answering English Wikipedia passages. Bible translation retrieval requires a Twi passage to retrieve its English translation from 6,195 candidates.
  We introduce MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation. The frozen base model scores each English training question against its answer passage and seven hard negatives. The student learns to reproduce these scores from both an NLLB-200 Twi translation that passes a round-trip translation check and the original English question, preserving English behaviour. During training, passages are encoded by the frozen base model; at evaluation, MargEmbed-Akan encodes questions and passages.
  On AfriQA, base AfriE5 and gemini-embedding-001 both achieve 66.6 nDCG@10; EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large achieve 56.6, 51.3, and 53.4, respectively. MargEmbed-Akan achieves 71.5, outperforming gemini-embedding-001 by 4.9 points, its base model by 5.0, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by 18.1. Its largest gain is on Twi typed without E and O (+7.5 over gemini-embedding-001). English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, although both proprietary models score 1.5-2.2 points higher. On Bible translation retrieval, MargEmbed-Akan and gemini-embedding-001 are statistically tied on standard Twi (97.2 vs. 96.5 nDCG@10); MargEmbed-Akan performs better on diacritic-free Twi (92.7 vs. 84.9). No AfriQA data was used for training or model selection.

papers.title: Beyond Before-and-After Images: Evaluating Temporal Grounding in a Lightweight VLM for Disaster Assessment
papers.abstract: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the post-event image or on the prompt's temporal framing. We present a controlled diagnostic of temporal grounding and apply it to one lightweight VLM, InternVL3-2B, on DisasterM3: 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types, in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions. We compare post-only input, the true pre/post pair, the post image repeated twice, reversed image order, and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores $+0.5$ accuracy points above the repeated-post control (95\% paired bootstrap CI $[-0.2, +1.2]$), and reversing the order changes accuracy by $-0.2$ points ($[-0.8, +0.5]$). Under this protocol we therefore find no measurable benefit from the content of the true pre-event image and little sensitivity to temporal order. The model is not blind to the first image, however: the true pair scores $2.5$ points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event ($[+1.6, +3.4]$). State-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles. We outline temporal scene graphs as a testable next step, not a validated solution, and argue that temporal benchmarks for Earth observation should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not only how often they are right.

authors.name: Debabrata Ghosh

papers.title: Semirings Induced by Semilattices
papers.abstract: We investigate semirings induced by join-semilattice (meet-semilattices) with a degenerate multiplication on all the subset that excludes the multiplicative unity. The way those semirings are defined enables a big impact of the semilattices we start with on the associated semirings: many of their order-theoretic properties reflect in algebraic properties of the induced semirings. This enabled constructing examples of semirings with desired properties as well as providing counterexamples to wrong claims in old and recent papers/preprints. In particular, we construct families of examples of semirings induced by non-modular join-semilattices for which the lattice of subtractive ideals is non-modular disproving a claim of Henriksen who introduced this important class of ideals of semirings.

authors.name: Jawad Abuhlail
