On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.

authors.name: Zhang Enyan
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Training Lightweight Gaze Models without Target Gaze Annotation: What Makes a Good Teacher?
papers.abstract: Model-generated labels offer a scalable route to training lightweight vision models, but what makes a model a good teacher, and can we tell before training a student? We study this in gaze target estimation, where interactive robots need models that are both accurate and efficient. In a controlled comparison of eleven supervision conditions, we vary only the source of gaze-point labels, keeping the student, training protocol and 361k training samples fixed, across three video datasets, two student sizes and three seeds; every student is evaluated against human annotation. Three findings emerge. First, imperfect model-generated labels can replace human annotation: Gaze-LLE, never trained on the target datasets' gaze annotation, trains students that match annotation-trained ones on ViT-Tiny and are significantly more accurate on ViT-Small (average distance error 0.187 vs 0.196), and the ViT-Tiny student runs 32$\times$ faster than its teacher on a laptop CPU. Second, apparent competence can conceal unreliable supervision: given another person's face centre in the prompt, InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL return it on 93.4% and 81.1% of test samples, and a copy-the-coordinate baseline matches InternVL3's labels and students. Without that coordinate, both models fall far behind the specialist. Third, good teachers can be identified before training: validation label error ranks student test error (Spearman's $\rho = 0.91$), and ten annotated clips single out the two specialist teachers in 95% of draws. These findings give practical principles for assessing supervision, exposing shortcuts and selecting teachers for lightweight models.

papers.title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
papers.abstract: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

papers.title: What You See Is What You Certify: Concept-Based Certificates for Unseen Compositions
papers.abstract: Concept-based models justify a decision by concepts they claim to see, decoded through an explicit ontology. Yet concept predictions are known to leak label information, ignore locality, and be poorly grounded on new attribute combinations. A decision decoded from such concepts can satisfy the ontology and still be wrong, so we ask when it can serve as a certificate. On unseen combinations of familiar parts, a joint concept bottleneck model and a concept embedding model, trained as is standard, certify wrong classes 93-94% of the time despite a correct ontology (60% for a joint model trained only on visible parts and gated by a localizer). The joint model's part errors copy co-occurring values more often than chance (cross-concept shortcutting). Treating the ontology as an error-detecting code, we show that a certificate needs visible evidence excluding every rival, unseen parts reported as such, and rare misreads not driven by a shared shortcut. A minimal reference design, OCVE, reads each part from a local crop in its own forward pass. On unseen FunnyBirds classes, it certifies 52% of images at 0.4% risk, against 14% for mask-pooled features and 33% for full-image part readers (5.6% when trained and gated alike), at similar zero-shot accuracy. The best baselines, even calibrated or restricted to unseen classes, and a decoder counting only agreeing parts remain about 3-8 times riskier. On CUB, isolated region readers are more accurate than an attribute-prototype model (63.1% vs. 55.3%) and certify unseen species at about 6 points less risk than it and about 10 points less than features pooled in the same keypoint boxes. On real traffic signs, isolated readers lower certified risk from 99.8% to 67%, which is still far too high; most remaining errors are misread pictograms. On seen classes the ontology brings no gain over a fairly trained black box, and isolation costs accuracy.

papers.title: Bounds on the Distance of Subgradient Trajectories to the Optimal Set
papers.abstract: A subgradient method with a constant step size may reach a minimizer and subsequently move away from it. Thus, a bound on the best objective value does not characterize the remainder of the trajectory. In this manuscript, we first establish that the trajectory enters a near-optimal sublevel set in finitely many iterations. We then use the Hausdorff distance between this sublevel set and the optimal set to bound the distance of every subsequent iterate from the optimal set. For objectives with weak sharp minima, we derive a tighter bound and construct examples demonstrating that the bound is tight. Numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and illustrate when the bounds are conservative.

papers.title: Long-Range Hydrodynamic Communication in Active Matter
papers.abstract: Directed transport in active matter is typically achieved by introducing geometric asymmetry, such as ratchets or gears, that rectify the stochastic motion of active particles. Here we demonstrate a fundamentally different route in which persistent mechanical motion emerges without any geometric bias. A symmetric passive rotor placed at the center of a circular domain undergoes spontaneous unidirectional rotation driven solely by the hydrodynamic flow generated by a boundary-confined flocks of Marangoni swimmers, despite the absence of direct physical contact. While individual swimmers produce intermittent torque reversals arising from transient hydrodynamic backflow, increasing the size of the flock establishes coherent circulation that stabilizes the rotor dynamics. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reveals that the collectively generated flow transmits momentum over macroscopic distances, converting local active forcing into robust mechanical transport. Together with a minimal flow superposition model, our results identify the suppression of reverse-torque events as a collective signature of hydrodynamic coupling between active swimmers and a passive body, providing a contact-free mechanism for remote mechanical actuation in active matter.

papers.title: Marketing-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Models and Agents on Real-World Marketing Capabilities
papers.abstract: As frontier AI models and agents are deployed more broadly in the real world, marketing is emerging as one of their largest applications. Marketing teams use AI models to produce brand assets like website copy and social media posts, while consumers' agents autonomously discover products, research purchases, and navigate websites. However, evaluating marketing capability is difficult because unlike areas like software development, customer support, or legal review where ground truth is more objectively defined, marketing is subjective, and output quality is judged based on taste and brand. We introduce Marketing-Bench, the first open-source marketing benchmark, which pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative tasks (remediation), while keeping answers verifiable. Marketing-Bench tests five key pillars: factuality, consistency, coherence, structure, and brand voice, all crucial elements for good brand content on the web. We find that frontier models are far from solving the benchmark: the average model corrects only about half of the introduced issues (53.1%), whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. Even the strongest, GPT-6 Astra, reaches only 74.8%, with Claude Opus and Fable, Gemini Argon, and GPT-6 Sol falling well short. These findings suggest that marketing capabilities are less mature than adoption implies, and that principled evaluation should precede further scaling of usage. Marketing-Bench is a first step toward "frontier marketing models" with superhuman marketing performance.

authors.name: Sumanth Balaji
authors.institution: International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad

papers.title: Irreducibility, inertia and invertibility of the eccentricity matrices of unicyclic graphs
papers.abstract: The eccentricity matrix of a connected graph $G$, denoted by $\mathcal{E}(G)$, is obtained from the distance matrix of $G$ by keeping each entry that is the largest in its row or the largest in its column, and replacing all other entries by $0$. The eigenvalues of $\mathcal{E}(G)$ are called the $\mathcal{E}$-eigenvalues of $G$. In this article, we consider the eccentricity matrix of unicyclic graphs and study its various spectral properties. First, we give two sufficient conditions for the irreducibility of the eccentricity matrix of a connected graph, which generalize some previously known results. Then, we show that the eccentricity matrix of every unicyclic graph of girth $3$, $5$ or $7$ is irreducible and provide a unicyclic graph whose eccentricity matrix is reducible for every odd girth $g\ge 9$. On the other hand, we also provide a class of unicyclic graphs of odd girth, whose eccentricity matrices are always irreducible. Additionally, we find the inertia of eccentricity matrices of unicyclic graphs in which the trees attached to the cycle are nontrivial and have equal heights. Moreover, we characterize the graphs in this class whose E-eigenvalues are symmetric about the origin. Finally, we obtain necessary conditions for the invertibility of the eccentricity matrix of a unicyclic graph.

papers.title: Easing H0 tension with Constrained Cosmological Parameters in f(R,Lm) Gravity
papers.abstract: We constrain two f(R,Lm) gravity models formulated through power-law and exponential curvature--matter couplings to evaluate their late-time dynamics and capacity to alleviate the H0 tension. Using MCMC sampling within the Cobaya framework, we confront both models against Cosmic Chronometer, Pantheon+ Type Ia Supernovae, and DESI-DR2 Baryon Acoustic Oscillation data under uniform and local SH0ES Gaussian H0 priors, benchmarking performance against flat Lambda_CDM via Delta_AIC, Delta_BIC, and Delta_DIC. In the unanchored joint analysis, both extensions are statistically favored over Lambda_ CDM (Delta_BIC = -6.60 and -2.91, respectively) and drive a smooth transition to late-time acceleration at z_t between 0.62-0.67 for the power-law model and z_t between 0.56-0.60 for the exponential model. Relative to the unanchored LambdaCDM constraint of H0 = 68.24 \pm 0.39\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} which is around $4.3\sigma$ tension with SH0ES, the power-law model yields $H0 = 67.00 \pm 1.04\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ ($4.1\sigma$), whereas the exponential model modestly elevates H0 to $69.46 \pm 0.70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, easing the tension to $2.9\sigma$ without local calibration. Under the SH0ES prior, the power-law model exhibits dataset-dependent phantom excursions $q \to -1.21$, $\omega_{\mathrm{eff}} \to -1.14$ in $CC+H0$ and incurs a strong Bayesian penalty in the full joint fit Delta_BIC = +7.42. Conversely, the exponential model maintains strict quintessence-like stability, converging smoothly to the de Sitter attractor ($q \to -1$, $\omega_{\mathrm{eff}} \to -1$) while reducing the SH0ES discrepancy to $1.8\sigma$ ($H0 = 70.60 \pm 0.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$) with positive Akaike support (Delta_AIC = -4.29) and only a mild Bayesian complexity penalty (Delta_BIC = +1.17).

authors.name: Y. Kalpana Devi
authors.institution: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani

papers.title: Similarity classes of $5\times5$ matrices over local rings of length two
papers.abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative local principal ideal ring of length two whose residue field has arbitrary characteristic. Prasad, Singla and Spallone classified similarity classes in $M_n(R)$ for $n\leq4$ by using module extensions. We extend their classification to $n=5$. We determine explicit extension-orbit representatives and stabilizers for the partitions $(3,2)$, $(2,2,1)$ and $(2,1,1,1)$. We prove that every orbit contains exactly one of the listed representatives. Together with the known primary cases, these results give all similarity classes in $M_5(R)$ and their centralizers. We also determine representatives and stabilizers for the family $(m+1,1,1,1)$ for every $m\geq1$. When the residue field is finite, we obtain the sizes and total number of similarity classes.

authors.name: Gunja Sachdeva
authors.institution: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani

papers.title: Support2Sim: Visually Faithful Real2Sim with Stable Object Supports
papers.abstract: Reconstructing a scene for physics simulation requires recovering its spatial layout and the support relationships that govern its behavior. We present Support2Sim, a Real2Sim system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image. Our design objective is to maximize source fidelity, support realization, and stability within a practical time budget for scene generation. Support2Sim infers a support graph, which a contact-guided pose initializer uses to propose poses for objects with multiple supports. The initializer generates and ranks candidates by geometric fit and source-image agreement. A coarse-to-fine refiner allocates a fixed search budget across supported objects and evaluates pose updates with physics rollouts. After an accepted update, it searches from the new pose at a finer translation and rotation scale. We benchmark our method on 50 scenes spanning four datasets. Compared with the strongest baseline, Support2Sim improves source-mask IoU after 10 seconds by 21.4 pp, realizes 87.1% versus 73.2% of intended supports, and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm. See our project page at https://support2sim.github.io for more details.

papers.title: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification
papers.abstract: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs. Existing frameworks seek to improve verification efficiency through sensitive fingerprints: queries whose predictions are more likely to change under tampering than those of genuine inputs. We show that this sensitivity can also help dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively conceal tampering. We prove that excess sensitivity relative to genuine inputs lower-bounds statistical distinguishability. We evaluate five integrity verification frameworks across three model architectures, three datasets, and three adversarial knowledge settings. When the deployed framework is known, our fingerprint detectors achieve AUCs at least 0.989, and selective filtering makes all five frameworks require significantly larger estimated query budgets than genuine inputs, reversing their intended efficiency advantage. A query-efficiency advantage remains marginally in a small subset of evaluated settings with poor detection transfer. We further design verification methods under stronger concealment constraints but find that reduced detectability comes with losses in sensitivity or fingerprint-generation success. Our results expose a sensitivity-detectability tension and show that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient black-box verification against adaptive malicious providers.

papers.title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
papers.abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

papers.title: When "Neutral" Means Irrelevant: A Construct-Validity Audit of NormAd-ETI
papers.abstract: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way score measures. It combines two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. Separating them shows that when only a country is shown, applicability falls to near chance while conformity stays well above it, because the prompt withholds the rule a Neutral label depends on. Because one answer carries both decisions, the score follows the steadier conformity and hides the weaker applicability, and no single prompt recovers the two separately. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate them for frontier models but not for small open models, where the applicability judgment still tracks the hidden acceptability label. Adding a written rationale reduces that conflation without removing it. We recommend reporting the two results separately and measuring the conflation gap.

authors.name: Animesh Pathak
authors.institution: Centurion University of Technology and Management

papers.title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids
papers.abstract: Superfluids, in a spinning-down container with pinning centres, exhibit sudden collective migration of quantized vortices. The onset, progress, and termination of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we show that: 1) the first exodus of vortices occurs when a sector of the vortex array, having a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall; 2) driven by this exodus, the superfluid flow near the boundary continually decreases in strength and arrests the exit; and 3) the resultant depletion region has well-defined dimensions---governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, the container size, and the initial rotation rate---that limit the angular momentum transferred to the container. We conclude by discussing the relevance to pulsar glitches.

authors.name: Dipankar Bhattacharya
authors.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

papers.title: HiGS: A Hierarchical Architecture for Fast Differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes one screen tile the cell of partitioning, the cell of rasterization, and the unit of parallel work. Partitioning favors large tiles and rasterization small ones, and with one unit per tile the densest tiles set the frame time. We present Hierarchically Tiled Gaussian Splatting (HiGS), a unified architecture for rendering and reconstruction that gives each role its own granularity: Gaussians are partitioned over coarse macro-tiles, rasterized over the fine render tiles within them, and processed in bounded depth-sorted batches. A dense region issues more batches instead of one longer unit, so frame time follows the work in a view rather than its densest tile. The same batches carry reconstruction: compositing supplies the transmittance and color needed to differentiate each one independently, leaving optimizer memory traffic as the dominant training cost. We fuse the optimizer into the backward pass, halve the parameters and moments it stores and updates directly, and defer appearance updates outside the view. HiGS renders scenes faster than every published method we evaluate, by the widest margin on views with uneven load, and reconstructs them faster and in less memory, at equal image quality and with exact front-to-back alpha compositing.

authors.name: Rodolfo Lima
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte

papers.title: Reading Between the Layers: Where Representation Quality Lives, and What Geometry Reveals
papers.abstract: Representation quality in pretrained text foundation models is not concentrated at the final layer, yet practitioners routinely probe it there because layer selection without labels has remained an open problem. We present a large-scale empirical study of where layer quality lives across 25 models spanning four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets across classification, pair classification, semantic textual similarity, and multiple-choice question answering. Peak probing layers depend systematically on pretraining strategy and architecture: masked encoders peak in late-middle layers, sequence-to-sequence models shift their peak with task type, contrastive sentence encoders concentrate signal at the final layer under CLS and last-token readouts but peak early under mean pooling, and decoder-only models exhibit distinct phase structure tied to depth. We distill these findings into the Stable Geometry Index (SGI), a closed-form, fully label-free selector with no fitted coefficients combining power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior. Across 383 evaluation groups SGI improves over the last-layer baseline and lifts Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52, recovering 40% of the gap to the oracle without using any labels, and exceeds a supervised ELMo-style layer mix on the matched subset despite using strictly less information. Our ablations also reverse a common assumption in the spectral-decay literature: power-law fit quality is a stronger predictor of layer quality than the exponent's proximity to one.

authors.name: Arnesh Batra
authors.institution: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi

authors.name: Aniket Khandelwal
authors.institution: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi

authors.name: Arush Gumber
authors.institution: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi

authors.name: Kushagra Agrawal
authors.institution: Manav Rachna International Institute of Research and Studies

papers.title: A Sequential Quadratic Programming Perspective on Optimal Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between the iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator (iLQR), Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP), and Newton's method for optimal control problems. Using a unified Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) framework, we introduce Newton-LQR, a Riccati-based algorithm that solves for the exact Newton step the optimal control problem. Within this framework, we establish that iLQR is a principled modified SQP method rather than merely an approximation of DDP. We show that iLQR generates a descent direction, whereas the inclusion of dynamics Hessians in DDP and Newton-LQR may lead to indefinite quadratic subproblems and necessitate regularization. We further distinguish DDP and the proposed Newton-LQR algorithm through their treatment of costate information and second-order dynamics terms. Numerical experiments across six benchmark problems demonstrate that iLQR often exhibits superior convergence during the initial optimization phase, while Newton-LQR and DDP can exploit second-order information to accelerate convergence near a solution.

authors.name: Abhijeet
authors.institution: CSIR National Physical Laboratory of India

papers.title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
papers.abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Line bundles on regular semisimple Hessenberg varieties
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a connected simply-connected simple algebraic group over $\mathbb{C}$ and $B$ be a Borel subgroup of $G$. Let $Y$ be an irreducible regular semisimple Hessenberg variety in $G/B$. In this article, we give a necessary and sufficient condition for the natural restriction map $\mathrm{res}: \mathrm{Pic}(G/B)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Pic}(Y)$ of Picard groups induced by the inclusion $Y\subseteq G/B$ to be an isomorphism.

papers.title: An Inverse-Square Gain over Threshold Rounding at Bounded Degree: Reasonable Boolean 2-CSPs and Beyond
papers.abstract:
Bounding the number of constraints in which a variable occurs can improve the approximation ratio of semidefinite rounding. For weighted Max-Cut and Max-2-Lin(2) of degree $d$, the known gain over the worst-case ratio is $\Omega(1/(d\log d))$ (Buhai, Ghoshal, Huang, Kothari, Lee, Makarychev, and Makarychev, 2027). For binary Boolean CSPs satisfying a geometric condition, the algorithm of Ghoshal, Huang, Lee, Makarychev, and Makarychev (2026) achieves $a+\Omega(1/(d^4(\log d)^{7/2}))$, where $a$ is the expected fraction of the total weight satisfied by Gaussian rounding at fixed, bounded thresholds. For weighted Max 2-SAT, the same analysis gives a gain of $\Omega(1/(d^2\log d))$ over the worst-case ratio $\alpha_{\rm LLZ}\simeq0.94016567$.
  We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm with guarantee $a+\Omega(1/d^2)$ under a weaker geometric condition that holds for a strictly larger class of binary instances. For weighted Max 2-SAT we obtain the ratio $\alpha_{\rm LLZ}+\Omega(1/d^2)$. To improve a worst-case ratio, only the binary constraints close to equality in the baseline guarantee need to meet the new condition jointly. This gives an inverse-square gain for Max $\{1,2\}$-Horn-SAT and for positive binary disjunctions with unit clauses of either sign, each over its own sharp worst-case ratio (Brakensiek, Huang, and Zwick, 2024).

authors.name: Mrinalkanti Ghosh
authors.institution: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research

papers.title: Longitudinal Characterization of Personalized Hydration Dynamics Using a Facial-Video Digital Hydration Biomarker
papers.abstract:
Background. Hydration is often assessed at a single time point despite continuous changes in body water. A facial-video biomarker has tracked hydration-state transitions, but its longitudinal behavior is unclear.
  Objective. To assess within-person hydration score changes, individual differences in fluid response, and implications for personal calibration.
  Methods. Five adults completed water and electrolyte days with an identical 2.0 L fluid schedule, using facial videos every 30 minutes over 12 hours (250 videos). On a separate morning, each completed a 500 mL electrolyte challenge with baseline and four follow-up videos over 2 hours (25 videos). Analyses assessed trajectories, post-drink changes, variability, time at or above score 50, and exploratory effects of starting score and beverage day.
  Results. The first scan was the day's lowest on 7 of 10 days. Across 50 intakes, the mean post-drink change was +4.0 points, exceeding a shuffled-time comparison (p less than 0.001). For 21 intakes starting below 50, no subsequent score fell; the mean rise was +11.3 points versus +5.7 expected under permutation (p less than 0.001). Intakes starting at 50 or above showed no rise beyond chance. After 500 mL electrolytes, mean change over 2 hours was positive for all five participants, with peak increases of 7.2 to 22.6 points at 30 to 90 minutes. Despite identical fluid schedules, time at or above 50 ranged from 16% to 100%. The electrolyte day showed a greater mean increase from morning baseline than the water day (+7.7 points), although day order was fixed.
  Conclusion. Facial-video hydration scores showed longitudinal changes associated with drinking and marked individual differences. These exploratory findings support further research on personal calibration and hydration protocols in larger controlled studies.

authors.name: Yudara Kularathne
authors.institution: All India Institute of Medical Sciences

papers.title: LineEX: Data Extraction from Scientific Line Charts
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce LINEEX that extracts data from scientific line charts. We adapt existing vision transformers and pose detection methods and showcase significant performance gains over existing SOTA baselines. We also propose a new loss function and present its effectiveness against existing loss functions. In addition, we synthetically created the largest line chart dataset comprising 430K images. The code is available at https://github.com/Shiva-sankaran/LineEX.

papers.title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
papers.abstract: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

papers.title: MADlibs: Analyzing the Distribution of Generative Music
papers.abstract: What music can a text-to-music model actually make? The answer to this question has consequences for individual creators, communities, and musical culture more broadly. We introduce MADlibs, a framework to measure the expressive support of state-of-the-art music generators: the subset of musical behaviors they will actually produce across the space of prompts. We first develop strategies for generating musical prompts using natural language processing methods and existing caption corpora. Then, we use a set of MIR techniques to study the corresponding output spaces in terms of interpretable and qualitatively meaningful elements like key, beat, tempo, instrumentation, and dynamics. We find that text-to-music models are not interchangeable instruments for the same prompt space. Rather, each model has learned idiosyncratic properties that constrain the regime of music reachable via prompting it, for example, defaulting to certain tempi, failing to produce silences, or oversampling canonical band arrangements. Because users interact with these systems one prompt at a time, these biases are often invisible in practice yet cumulatively shape what AI-assisted music sounds like, risking the production of a new auditory monoculture hidden behind the promise of universal describability. We thus urge the MIR community to further study and responsibly steer population-level properties of music generation models.

authors.name: Matthew Keating
authors.institution: UC Irvine Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center

papers.title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

papers.title: DUST: Directional Uncertainty-aware and Scale-invariant Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Transfer learning seeks to improve efficiency in a target regression task by borrowing information from related external source dataset(s). Existing approaches achieve this by enforcing Euclidean proximity between the target and source regression parameters or, more recently, by encouraging their directional alignment through angle-based penalties. While such angle-based penalties mitigate the sensitivity of the transfer learning methods to the scale differences between source and target regression coefficients, they still rely on a point estimate of the source regression parameter and thus provide no direct mechanism to incorporate uncertainty in the source information. To that end, we propose a probabilistic framework for transfer learning that operates at the level of a \emph{scale-invariant directional distribution} of the source regression parameter estimate, rather than its point estimate, to enable robust, scale-invariant and uncertainty aware transfer under heterogeneous source information. Specifically, we project the sampling distribution of the source regression estimate onto the unit sphere, thereby extracting its scale-free directional distribution. Transfer from source to target is then induced through a novel \emph{angular cone prior} which shrinks the target regression parameter towards directions in which the source distribution assigns high probability, while allowing its magnitude to be learned exclusively from the target dataset. The proposed construction admits exact finite-sample characterizations of posterior angular concentration and posterior computation remains tractable via careful low-dimensional augmentation in the parameter space.

papers.title: A Piecewise-Linear Activation Function for Implicit Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Coordinate networks with ReLU activations perform poorly on implicit neural representation tasks, and the activations that address this, such as sinusoids and Gabor wavelets, all leave the piecewise-linear function class, so it remains unclear which property of ReLU is at fault. We introduce JaSIN, a family of bounded piecewise-linear activations that interpolates between ReLU and a piecewise-linear sinusoid without any the use of transcendental operation. Our results show that a bounded range improves image reconstruction PSNR on average by 0.06 dB, a single bump 3.29 dB, and centering that bump a further 3.64 dB. The oscillation count improves 6.30 dB more, raising ReLU from 24.0 to 37.3 dB on Kodak images, placing third over eleven activations, within 1.3 dB of the state-of-the-art, though beyond four oscillations the reconstruction collapses. Because an INR is fit on the grid on which it is evaluated, a unit whose pre-activations never reach the support of its activation is certifiably inactive over the entire domain; deleting such units is lossless without fine-tuning, removing up to 84% of parameters at zero loss in performance (dB) and decoding 3.2 times faster. Reference code and demos are available at https://github.com/jeovafarias/jasin.

papers.title: CEDVR: A virtual reality event display for CMS
papers.abstract: Collision event displays are widely used in high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, enabling researchers to visualize and debug raw and reconstructed event data, and to communicate aspects of individual events to broader audiences. Such event displays are typically viewed on a conventional two-dimensional computer screen. To enhance immersion and interactivity with CMS data, we have developed a virtual reality (VR) software package named CEDVR (for CMS Event Display in Virtual Reality) that uses widely-available VR headsets and hand controllers. This application provides an immersive detector-coordinate view and a novel, complementary LEGO-style view. CEDVR provides easy access to physics object properties and object filtering, and incorporates novel VR features for navigation and object selection. Compatible with consumer-grade Quest headsets, CEDVR is a useful visualization tool for CMS physicists, and contains built-in sample events that support educational and public outreach initiatives.

authors.name: Ethan Hsu
authors.institution: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center

papers.title: SlotFill: Repairing Lossy SoC Communication Traces for Post-Silicon Validation
papers.abstract: Post-silicon validation relies on traces of messages exchanged by SoC components, but trace buffers and monitors drop messages, often leaving no mark of what was lost. We present SlotFill, which puts each deleted message back in the right gap, with the right type and order. SlotFill gives every gap between the remaining messages a fixed number of slots, and a Transformer-based model fills each slot with a message or leaves it empty when nothing was deleted there, so the input never reveals how much was lost. The model also uses monitor fields (timestamps, transaction IDs, addresses) from surviving messages. On whole-program gem5 traces of 4- and 8-core systems (2.07 billion messages), SlotFill restores up to 97% of deleted messages exactly at 15% loss and up to 87% at 50% loss, and 76-83% at 15% loss when timestamps are coarse.

papers.title: Beyond Robust Algorithmic Recourse: Sharing the Burden of Validity through Model Multiplicity
papers.abstract: Algorithmic recourse provides actionable recommendations that enable individuals to achieve favourable outcomes. Implementing recourse for individuals requires significant time and effort, thus emphasizing robust recourse: recommendations that remain valid even under future model updates. While robustness preserves validity, we show it introduces systematic harms by constraining feasible recommendations to regions that disproportionately reflect majority behavior, reducing individual flexibility and amplifying disparities. Thus, non-robust recourse risks invalidation, whereas robust recourse creates a preference for high-density regions in the data that induces unfairness. However, this trade-off is driven by an implicit assumption that individuals alone should bear the burden of validity. We challenge this narrative and show that strategic model selection can help maintain validity while relaxing robustness requirements for individuals. By leveraging multiplicity, the existence of equally good yet competing models, system owners can share this burden with individuals, thus resolving the tension between validity and unfairness.

papers.title: Normal and Unitary Operators on Smooth Banach Spaces via the Duality Mapping
papers.abstract: This article extends the classical notions of normal and unitary operators from Hilbert spaces to smooth Banach spaces through the duality mapping. The class of normal operators introduced in this setting contains, as a special case, the self-adjoint operators on smooth Banach spaces defined via the duality mapping. We establish several characterisations of these operators and investigate their fundamental properties. In particular, we examine various spectral properties of normal operators on smooth Banach spaces. These results demonstrate that many fundamental aspects of the classical theory of normal and unitary operators on Hilbert spaces persist in the smooth Banach space setting.

papers.title: Boundary Representation-Driven Graph Transformer Modeling for Machining Operation Sequencing
papers.abstract: Machining process planning is inherently complex due to the interdependence between part geometry, machining operations, and evolving manufacturable states. Traditional approaches rely heavily on expert knowledge and rule-based systems, limiting scalability and automation. While recent machine learning methods have shown promise, most operate on simplified geometric representations, such as voxels or hand-crafted features, which fail to fully exploit the rich geometric and topological information encoded in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. In this work, we propose a graph transformer-based framework for geometry-to-sequence learning that directly predicts machining operation sequences from B-Rep design geometry. The proposed method constructs topology-aware graphs from B-Rep entities, where faces and their adjacencies are encoded as node and edge features capturing both geometric and relational information. A graph neural network encoder learns geometry-aware embeddings, which are then used to condition a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates machining operation sequences. This formulation enables the model to capture both operation-type prediction and process-level ordering constraints directly from design geometry, without requiring intermediate feature extraction or machining-state representations. Experiments on a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts demonstrate strong performance, achieving 95% accuracy for main operation prediction, 64% accuracy for sub-operation prediction, and 93% accuracy for sequence length prediction. Further analysis shows that the model effectively captures precedence relationships and geometry-dependent constraints inherent in machining processes. These results highlight the potential of B-Rep-driven graph learning for scalable and automated machining process planning.

papers.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.

papers.title: Mass gap for finite connections in supercritical percolation
papers.abstract:
We consider finite open clusters based at the origin in Bernoulli bond percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for $d\geq3$ at a supercritical value $p>p_c(d)$, whose maximal height in the direction of a unit vector $\pmb{\ell}$ lies in a fixed-width window at distance $u$. Conditioned on this event, we prove that, except with probability exponentially small in $u$, such a cluster is populated at positive density by renewal points. Here, a renewal point $w$ is the only vertex of the cluster in the fixed-width band immediately below the height hyperplane through $w$.
  The main technical estimate is that, under this conditioning, the absence of a renewal point is exponentially unlikely. From it we derive an exponential mass gap for the irreducible pieces delimited by successive renewal points, and from the mass gap the stated renewal abundance. The mass gap, together with the renewal decomposition and endpoint estimates established here, yields a sharp point-to-point Ornstein--Zernike asymptotic for finite connectivity, with its Gaussian-type power-law correction. The multiplicative prefactor in this asymptotic is positive and real-analytic, and the associated equidecay and Wulff boundaries are real-analytic and strictly convex.
  The principal innovation of the article is the use of a slide resampling that preserves the conditioned law. The slide acts by cutting the long finite connection at a given $\pmb{\ell}$-height and relocating the upper piece by a random shift. The mass gap is obtained by a delicate analysis of an iterated version of the slide operation along a positive density of attempted heights.

papers.title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
papers.abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.

papers.title: Revisiting TOI-2120 b: Updated mass and radius constraints on a sub-Neptune orbiting an M4 dwarf
papers.abstract: We present updated mass and radius measurements of TOI-2120 b, a short-period (5.80 days) planet orbiting a mid-M dwarf identified by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). TOI-2120 b was previously validated through transit photometry and high-resolution imaging, with a radius near the upper boundary of the radius valley around low-mass stars. We refined the planetary properties by combining archival TESS and ground-based photometry with new transit observations from the ARC 3.5m and Red Buttes Observatory (RBO) telescopes and new precision RV measurements obtained with the Habitable-zone Planet Finder (HPF) spectrograph. Our joint analysis yields a radius of $2.31\pm0.7$ Rearth, larger than previously reported. We also measure a planetary mass of $5.81^{+2.94}_{-2.69}$ Mearth at 2$\sigma$, corresponding to a bulk density of $2.62^{+1.37}_{-1.22}$ g cm$^{-3}$, positioning TOI-2120 b toward the water-rich region predicted by isocomposition models. Additional RV observations will be needed to further constrain its mass and composition.

authors.name: Scott A. Diddams
authors.institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology

papers.title: Fast Anatomy-Aware Diffeomorphic Augmentation for Brain MRI
papers.abstract: Data augmentation is essential for training deep learning models that are generalizable, particularly when training data are limited. In brain MRI, augmentation methods that synthesize anatomically diverse images without relying on large cohorts are particularly attractive, especially when training supervised models for scans with a specific resolution or MRI contrast. While conventional random nonlinear fields offer a simple means of achieving such diversity, they fail to capture the underlying spatial dependencies among morphological changes across brain regions. To address this limitation, we introduce BrainAug, an anatomy-aware augmentation framework that generates diverse, anatomically coordinated deformations without relying on population imaging data. BrainAug constructs an anatomical graph encoding spatial proximity and bilateral correspondence between brain regions, then incorporates these relationships into a probabilistic model designed to sample correlated regional volume changes. These sampled variations are translated into diffeomorphic transformations, enabling substantial structural changes while preserving anatomical topology. Combined with contrast-agnostic image synthesis, BrainAug generates training images with independently varying anatomy and appearance. Evaluations across eight brain MRI datasets demonstrate stronger segmentation generalization across diverse populations, while registration experiments show improved alignment under substantial morphological differences.

papers.title: A Correlative-Sparse Matrix Positivstellensatz under Pointwise Commutation
papers.abstract: The scalar Positivstellensatz adapted to correlative sparsity enables substantially smaller moment--SOS relaxations for sparse polynomial optimization. Its matrix counterpart, however, fails in general, even under the running intersection property and local Archimedean assumptions. In this paper, we establish a matrix Positivstellensatz under these assumptions and an additional pointwise commutation condition. Specifically, if a polynomial matrix admits a decomposition whose summands commute pairwise on the feasible set, then positive definiteness on this set implies membership in the sum of the local matrix quadratic modules. The proof uses central common lower envelopes to derive an integral inequality for positive matrix-valued clique measures with consistent separator marginals, without requiring these measures to admit a global extension. We apply this result to establish asymptotic convergence of the corresponding sparse moment--SOS hierarchy for polynomial matrix optimization. We also derive a criterion for finite convergence of moment relaxation and extraction of a global minimizer based on local flatness and consistency of the local representing matrix measures on overlapping variable blocks. Finally, we provide a sufficient construction of commuting decompositions through linear equations, using a reference polynomial matrix with a simple spectrum at some point.

papers.title: RankServe: Rank-Aware CPU-GPU Scheduling for Memory-Constrained MoE Serving
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity through sparse expert activation, but their large expert pools impose substantial memory requirements during inference. Low-rank compression reduces the memory footprint of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. However, the heterogeneous expert ranks create unequal storage, transfer, and execution costs. Under limited GPU memory, expert popularity and transfer cost alone cannot determine which experts are most valuable to retain. We present RankServe, a CPU-GPU serving system for compressed MoE checkpoints with fixed expert ranks. Its key insight is to value GPU residency against the cheaper nonresident path, CPU execution or weight transfer followed by GPU execution, under each expert's rank and token load. RankServe aggregates the resulting estimated savings over routing demand and prioritizes experts by savings per byte. It updates residency from recent routing history and selects miss paths using current token loads, allowing temporary GPU execution without cache admission. A variable-rank runtime executes heterogeneous factors through grouped matrix multiplications without common-rank padding. Implemented on vLLM, RankServe is evaluated on three MoE models against six serving systems on a single CPU-GPU platform. Across five batch sizes from 1 to 32, it achieves per-model geometric-mean speedups of $1.69$--$2.29\times$ in time to first token (TTFT) and $1.71$--$2.48\times$ in time per output token (TPOT), relative to the fastest baseline for each configuration and metric.

authors.name: Hengyi Zhu
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: KeyMemVLA: Subtask-Guided Key Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation requires vision-language-action (VLA) policies to infer task progress and recall evidence absent from current observations. Under a limited memory budget, the challenge is to retain history that resolves stage ambiguity and supports subsequent decisions. We present KeyMemVLA, a subtask-guided key memory framework based on progress indication and decision-evidence retention. A two-level annotation process selects subtasks satisfying either criterion and labels their final frames as keyframes to supervise online memory writes. A shared vision-language backbone jointly learns subtask, action, and keyframe prediction. At inference, the policy first predicts the current subtask from the instruction, visual context, and memory, then uses this semantic condition to predict actions and future memory-write positions. Actual observations are retained at the selected times during execution. We introduce KMBench to evaluate active memory retention for decisions across subtasks. Evaluations on RMBench-$M(n)$, RoboTwin-MeM, KMBench, and real-world manipulation tasks show higher average success rates than the compared baselines. Ablation studies and representation analysis support the roles of key memory and explicit task-progress semantics. These results highlight the value of coupling sparse key memory with online progress inference for history-dependent control.

authors.name: Tao Chen
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Sicheng Ma
authors.institution: Henan University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

authors.name: Yongen Zhao
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Benchmarking Protein Structure Tokenizers as Generation Targets for Language Models
papers.abstract: Discrete structure tokenizers are the standard way to give a language model access to protein three-dimensional structure, yet they are selected on how accurately they can be read, their reconstruction fidelity, while the property that governs generation is how well a model can write them. We measure this property, writability, directly: holding the base model, data, recipe and compute fixed, we swap only the tokenizer and train the same 9B model to emit structure tokens residue by residue, over eight tokenizers, four compute budgets and three evaluation sets (96 cells). At 2B tokens final writability runs from TM 0.662 down to 0.378 under identical conditions, with five of the eight arms clearing the TM 0.5 mark at which a fold is usually called correct and three falling short of it. Neither codebook size nor reconstruction ceiling explains where an arm lands; the best and worst both use 8192 codewords. What does explain the spread is local structure preservation of the code space. In DPLM-2 a one-bit codeword error costs 0.019 TM where a random codeword costs 0.347, and the trained model's own errors are correspondingly local, at 0.51 of the random Hamming expectation; FoldToken4 fails both tests at the same codebook size and is 0.13 TM less writable. Three controls discipline how such a benchmark may be read. A same-recipe rerun puts the noise floor at $\sigma=0.0067$ TM, which collapses an apparent six-way ranking into four tiers. A reference-free geometry panel turns out to be nearly orthogonal to TM (Pearson $-0.58$), with the worst arm by TM producing the most physically valid backbones. And two pre-registered interventions are null for a reason the mechanism measurements reveal: the quantity they target saturates at 1.5B tokens while TM is still rising. All 131 evaluation cells, including raw generated token streams, are released.

authors.name: Peicong Lin
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Jiayu Gu
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: An improved estimate for discrete $L^8$ restriction on the cubic curve
papers.abstract: We prove an improved estimate for discrete $L^8$ restriction on the cubic curve $(n,n^3)$. More precisely, for every $\varepsilon>0$, the following eighth moment estimate holds \[ \int_{[0,1]^2} \left|\sum_{n=1}^N b_n \exp(2\pi i(nx+n^3y))\right|^8 dxdy \ll_{\varepsilon} N^{1/2-1/47500+\varepsilon} \left(\sum_{n=1}^N |b_n|^2\right)^4. \]

papers.title: RoboDemo: Reconciling Demonstration Intent and Execution Progress for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

authors.name: Junjie Wang
authors.institution: Beijing Institute of Spacecraft Environment Engineering

papers.title: VC-OPD: Learning to See What Matters via Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.

authors.name: Peipei Yang
authors.institution: National Center for Nanoscience and Technology

papers.title: CriticJEPA: World Models Are Better Critics Than Optimizers
papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-directed planning by predicting action outcomes. Gradient-based planners optimize actions to lower predicted goal cost, but continued optimization can exploit prediction errors after execution stops improving. Comparing plans requires informative relative scores; improving them also requires reliable update directions. Exact-state execution reveals that a frozen hierarchical world model ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative. Effective planning pairs goal-directed candidates with predictions that distinguish their outcomes. We introduce CriticJEPA, which learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level. Forward selection forms a complete planner; short anchored updates refine candidates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation, CriticJEPA increases success at a fraction of the planning compute, transferring shared settings across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks while keeping every world-model weight fixed.

authors.name: Honglin Zhang
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Supramolecular Structure and Materials

authors.name: Fengli Xu
authors.institution: Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology

papers.title: Explicit KL Exponents for PLQ Functions on the Sphere
papers.abstract: Let $\phi$ be a proper piecewise linear-quadratic (PLQ) function whose domain meets the unit sphere $\mathcal{S}$. We prove that $f:=\phi+\delta_{\mathcal{S}}$, where $\delta_{\mathcal{S}}$ is the indicator function of $\mathcal{S}$, satisfies the Kurdyka--{\L}ojasiewicz (KL) property with exponent $3/4$ throughout its domain. This exponent is sharp even for the convex PLQ class. We characterize the smallest KL exponents of quadratics restricted to affine sections of $\mathcal{S}$, obtaining the values $0$, $1/2$, $2/3$, and $3/4$. A tangential projection identity shows that, at each point of ${\rm dom}\,f$, the maximum of the exponents from the relevant affine sections is admissible for $f$. When $\phi$ is piecewise affine (PA), each of these smallest exponents is $0$ or $1/2$. Thus $f$ satisfies the KL property with exponent $1/2$ throughout ${\rm dom}\,f$, and this exponent is sharp over the class of sphere-constrained PA functions. When ${\rm dom}\,\phi$ is a finite union of closed polyhedral cones, $f$ admits KL exponent $1/2$ for homogeneous quadratic pieces and exponent $0$ for nonnegative $\phi$ that is linear on each cone. For any convex polytope $C$ containing the origin, we use the KL exponent $0$ to show that the full-step manifold proximal point iterates for minimizing the support function of $C$ over $\mathcal{S}$ stabilize at a critical point in finitely many steps.

papers.title: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.

authors.name: Kun Wang
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Resolving the Hubble Tension at $0.1\sigma$ with Early Dark Energy: Key Role of the Highest-redshift Galaxies from JWST Observations
papers.abstract: We show that the Hubble tension can be resolved at the $0.1\sigma$ level within the early dark energy (EDE) framework, with the highest-redshift galaxies from the JWST observations playing a key role. By accounting for the reference cosmologies of the JWST ultraviolet luminosity function measurements and combining them with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, we obtain $H_0=72.76\pm1.00~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ in the axion EDE model, in excellent agreement with SH0ES at the $0.1\sigma$ level. We find that the enhanced galaxy abundances at $z=11$ and $12.5$ play a key role in driving this result. These observations favor stronger small-scale matter power, which can be accommodated by increasing the primordial scalar spectral index $n_{\rm s}$. Under the CMB constraints, the positive correlations among $n_{\rm s}$, $f_{\rm EDE}$, and $H_0$ lead to a higher inferred $H_0$. Allowing additional scale dependence in the primordial power spectrum through $\alpha_{\rm s}$ yields a positive running at more than $4\sigma$, further increasing $H_0$ to $73.75\pm1.04~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, with its value even exceeding the SH0ES measurement. These results reveal how high-redshift small-scale structure observations influence the inferred $H_0$ through the interplay between the primordial power spectrum and EDE parameter degeneracies.

papers.title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization
papers.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.

papers.title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor
papers.abstract: RL for LLMs often separates rollout generation from policy training. Although the two numerical engines share model parameters, they can induce different policies. This creates a challenge beyond correcting a known training-inference mismatch: during learner updates, the execution policy corresponding to the current parameters cannot be directly observed. We view this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor of its evolution. This perspective raises two fundamental questions: how can we estimate the execution policy's response to learner updates, and how much should we trust that estimate when optimizing the actual execution policy? We introduce Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (EPRO) to address these challenges. Starting from the observed rollout-time execution policy, we use training-policy changes to construct a differentiable predictor of the current execution policy, whose score yields Transported Score Centering (TSC). Our robust-improvement analysis reveals how prediction error limits the magnitude of reliably justified updates. For practical implementation, we introduce Policy Shift as an observable proxy for prediction risk and use Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates. Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

authors.name: Zhaoran Wang
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: PhysMend: Verification-Guided Program Refinement for Physics-Aware Video Generation
papers.abstract: Video generative models synthesize realistic scenes, yet their interactions often violate physics. A ball dropped onto sand should displace grains and settle into a crater, whereas a generated video may show it passing through the surface or leaving the sand flat. Post-hoc methods typically score generated videos with a vision-language model (VLM), but such scores offer limited guidance on which object or parameter to modify, and each correction costs another synthesis. Simulation-based pipelines instead run fixed stages before synthesis, so simulation errors reach the video. To address these limitations, we present PhysMend, a training-free framework for verification-guided program refinement. PhysMend describes the target event as an editable physical program of grounded objects, events, and required relations, paired with tunable execution parameters. Our key insight is to verify and repair the event on its simulated rollout and on the depth video that conditions the generator (depth control) rather than on generated videos, enabling quantitative violation measurement, targeted editing, and fast re-verification before synthesis. A hybrid verifier evaluates semantic event consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and visibility in the depth control. VLM judgments are confined to event semantics and cannot override failed physical measurements, which limits the impact of VLM hallucinations. Each failed check localizes the program fields eligible for repair, and its measured violation scales a bounded update of their parameters. Only accepted depth control reaches the generator, which runs once per input. Experiments on the commonly used benchmarks Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0 demonstrate substantial gains across different generator backbones; for example, PhysMend raises the overall Physics-IQ score of Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40.

authors.name: Meilong Xu
authors.institution: Ningxia Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences

papers.title: Sharp variational estimates for Schr\"odinger equation in higher dimensions
papers.abstract: We study strong $r$-variation estimates for the free Schr\"odinger equation on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq3$. Combining fractal and weighted restriction estimates with mixed space--time estimates, we determine the sharp Sobolev regularity, up to endpoints, in several ranges of the spatial exponent $p$ and the variation exponent $r$. In particular, our results give a sharp $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ variational extension of the Schr\"odinger maximal estimate of Du and Zhang [\emph{Ann. of Math.}, \textbf{189}, 837--861 (2019)].

authors.name: Tang Yongrui
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: Speculative Decoding for Semantic-ID-Based Generative Recommendations
papers.abstract:
Generative recommender systems with Semantic IDs (SIDs) represent each item as a short sequence of $L$ discrete tokens and use a sequence model to predict the next item's tokens from a user's history. Industry-scale deployments typically use these models to retrieve multiple candidates per request with constrained beam search. However, this incurs a fixed cost of $L$ sequential model calls per request, and accuracy degrades as the SID generator becomes less sharp, without a guarantee on how close the output is to the exact top-$K$. Production systems therefore cannot detect degraded retrieval for individual requests.
  We propose SIDECAR, which uses approximate draft candidates and a tree-attention pass to score the entire draft in a single model call, memory permitting. This pass bounds the probability of every unexplored SID prefix and certifies the exact top-$K$ if the draft contains them.
