  At a complex place, an admissible shift is simultaneously critical exactly when the two conjugate Levi weights after the shift occur in Kostant degrees summing to $\dim U$. With a common relative center, total degree balance at a regular admissible shift characterizes simultaneous criticality at every archimedean place. For split $E_6$ over $\mathbb Q$, a half-spin family yields Eisenstein cohomology classes in degrees $20$ and $21$, including a degree-$20$ class with nonzero restrictions to both associate boundary face types.

papers.title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

papers.title: Erd\H{o}s Distance Results for $k$-Degenerate Graphs with $m$ Edges
papers.abstract: The Erd\H{o}s distinct distances problem asks how many distinct distances $N$ points must determine. In the plane, Guth and Katz determined the optimal power of $N$. A natural generalization fixes a finite graph $G$ with $m$ edges and records, over all injective embeddings of $G$ into a finite point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, the vectors of edge-lengths realized; we write $\Delta_G^\circ(P)$ for this set of edge-distance vectors. Taking $G$ to be a single edge recovers the classical problem. In the plane, the exponent $|V(G)|-1$ is known up to an arbitrarily small loss for every connected graph. A graph is $k$-degenerate if its vertices can be ordered so that each has at most $k$ neighbors among those preceding it. We show that if $G$ is $k$-degenerate, then for every $d \ge \max(2k,3)$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, $|\Delta_G^\circ(P)| \gtrsim_{G,d,\varepsilon} N^{m/(d-1)-\varepsilon}$ for $|P|=N\ge |V(G)|$. For a connected graph with $m/(|V(G)|-1)>2(d-1)/d$, the exponent $m/(d-1)$ exceeds the spanning-tree exponent predicted by the pinned-distance conjecture. Our result is motivated by the threshold $\frac{d+k}{2}$ obtained by Borges, Foster, Ou, Palsson, and Romero Acosta for edge lengths of $k$-degenerate graphs in fractal sets. The proof combines a bisector-energy estimate for pinned $k$-stars with an entropy argument of Katz--Tardos type, applied along a construction order of $G$ and combined with an induction on the dimension.

papers.title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.

authors.name: Pratyay Banerjee
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Guwahati

papers.title: SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering
papers.abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.

authors.name: Pratyay Banerjee
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Guwahati

papers.title: A macroscopic-atom spectral theory of grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys
papers.abstract: Predicting grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys remains challenging because existing spectral approaches require alloy-specific atomistic calculations to resolve segregation-energy distributions and correlations across non-equivalent boundary sites. Here, we develop a transferable macroscopic-atom spectral theory that predicts the joint segregation behavior of multiple species from physically interpretable elemental descriptors. The theory is founded on the finding that local strain and bond deficit account for 91\% of the site-to-site co-variation of 40 solutes in a density-functional-theory (DFT) Al polycrystal. Linked to atomic size and surface enthalpy, these coordinates allow prediction of individual segregation spectra and their cross-species correlations, which determine whether species compete for or share grain-boundary sites. A closed-system formulation unifies host-element redistribution and dilute-solute segregation, couples metallic and light-element sublattices, and accounts for bulk compound formation and solute pairing. Calibrated using binary spectra only, the theory predicts unseen-host spectral means with a correlation coefficient of 0.81, outperforms embedded-atom spectra against DFT benchmarks, and ranks site competition across 870 solute pairs with a Spearman coefficient of 0.90. Without fitting to multicomponent observations, it reproduces 11 of 12 equilibrium Fe ternaries and 49 of 55 Mg ternaries. Predictions recorded before simulations of an 82,699-atom polycrystal identify site competition as the baseline behavior and metal-metalloid pair chemistry as a source of deviations requiring atomistic resolution. These results establish a physically grounded route to screening grain-boundary chemistry in multicomponent alloys, including steels and high-entropy alloys.

papers.title: One Release for All: Private Simple Linear Regression Via Improved Simplex Mapping
papers.abstract: We present a single-release extension of DP-RSS for private simple linear regression when both input and output are bounded in $[0,1]$. Rather than privately releasing several related sufficient-statistic estimates, we encode the required information in one unit-sensitivity vector and apply the Laplace mechanism once at the full privacy budget. The required least-squares sufficient statistics are then recovered by deterministic post-processing and used directly in an ordinary least-squares solve. We obtain variance reductions of $1.67$--$2.67\times$ relative to DP-RSS for several statistics. Experiments show that the benefit is most pronounced in the high-privacy regime, while the methods converge as privacy noise becomes negligible.

papers.title: XRL4T1D: A Post-hoc Explainability Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Type 1 Diabetes Management
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) requires lifelong insulin therapy, and reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automated dosing in the UVA/Padova simulator. However, the decisions of RL controllers remain difficult to interpret. We present XRL4T1D, a post-hoc explainability framework for evaluating pretrained insulin-dosing policies without retraining. Each policy uses 60 minutes of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and administered-insulin history, sampled every 5 minutes, to recommend insulin. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of CGM and insulin-history inputs and summarize insulin-history attributions over three 20-minute windows motivated by insulin-on-board. We assess whether these attributions correspond to policy-output sensitivity through targeted input replacement and compare temporal rankings with TimeSHAP. In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the normalized insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs. The highest-attribution insulin-history window is also the most output-sensitive in 115 of 120 patient-policy-scenario configurations, and KernelSHAP and TimeSHAP select the same top window in 111 of 120. Applying XRL4T1D to PPO and G2P2C across 20 virtual patients, we find that both controllers rely predominantly on CGM history, especially G2P2C. However, the distribution of insulin-history importance across recent, middle, and older windows varies by cohort, explainer, and analysis settings, without a consistent separation between controllers. Global feature-attribution rankings remain stable under the tested observation corruptions. These results show why attribution fidelity, temporal reproducibility, and controller-comparison robustness should be assessed separately.

papers.title: Schnyder Woods and the Chromatic Polynomial
papers.abstract: Let $\chi_G(q)$ be the chromatic polynomial of a graph $G$. Analogous to the classical results of Greene and Zaslavsky interpreting $(-1)^{n-1}\chi_G'(0)$ and $(-1)^n\chi_G'(1)$ as counting certain orientations of $G$, we show that if $G$ is a triangulation, $\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{n-1}\chi_G'(2)$ counts the number of Schnyder woods on a plane embedding of $G$. We also generalise this result to graphs obtained by removing certain edges of $G$.

papers.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
papers.abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
