papers.title: Burning the Bridge: Agentification and Domestic Value Added
papers.abstract: Firms that replace local work with foreign AI agents can produce more per paid hour while generating less income at home. We study this trade-off in a small open economy where exporters and local services both use agents. Once wages reach a reservation floor, extending agent use in local services lowers domestic income at unchanged foreign costs. Value added at constant prices and consumption also fall if suppliers capture enough of the saving. Exporters have an offset: adopting agents can expand production and earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for them. The difference is substantial. Using Brazilian accounts as a reference, a supplier bargaining share above about 0.15 is sufficient to make further local-service adoption reduce value added even at negligible foreign costs. The corresponding threshold in tradables is about 0.66. We derive separate export-growth requirements for preserving income and consumption and illustrate them using historical accounts for Brazil and Mexico. Cheaper agents ease the consumption requirement; lower export prices raise it. Over time, declining domestic capabilities can also make returning to local production more expensive, allowing suppliers to charge more at renewal.

papers.title: Black hole evaporation: From frontier physics to the classroom
papers.abstract: Half a century ago, Stephen Hawking discovered that black holes have a temperature, emit thermal radiation, and evaporate. Although Hawking temperature has been widely discussed in this journal, the evaporation process has received less attention. This work presents an accessible analysis of black hole evaporation, addressing the main questions raised by this phenomenon through intuitive ideas and heuristic calculations. It is shown that a problem situated at the frontier of physics can be reformulated in terms accessible for exploration in the classroom. In this sense, the article constitutes an educational resource that enables the integration of concepts from thermodynamics, relativity, and quantum mechanics within a meaningful learning context.

papers.title: Ranges of vector measures and copies of $c_0$
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a Banach space such that every weakly compact subset of $X$ is contained in the range of an $X$-valued countably additive vector measure defined on a $\sigma$-algebra. We prove that $X$ contains no isomorphic copy of $c_0$, thereby answering a question posed by R. Anantharaman and J. Diestel [Comment. Math. Prace Mat. 30 (1991), no. 2, 221--235]. In particular, every Banach lattice with this property is superreflexive.

papers.title: A source-based decomposition of thermal noise for mechanical system design
papers.abstract: Thermal noise limits the sensitivity of precision mechanical instruments. We present a thermal- noise formulation for lumped-element mechanical systems that writes the total displacement thermal noise at the readout as the sum of contributions from all dissipative elements. For each contribution, we separate the thermal force generated by the element from its transfer to the readout. This decomposition provides simple design rules for comparing contributions from elements in series and in parallel and identifying the dominant noise source. It applies to frequency-dependent dissipation and to elements at different steady temperatures under local thermal equilibrium. We use it to identify the frequency regimes in which parallel and series dissipation dilution reduce displacement thermal noise. We then use examples of a pendulum on a lossy support, a rotational flexure, and rigidly mounted lunar optics to show how support noise can dominate even when the support has little effect on the system dynamics. Finally, a feedback-controlled suspension illustrates how sensing and actuation noise can be included in the same displacement-noise budget.

papers.title: Typical-query energy figures mislead institutional AI electricity demand
papers.abstract: Institutions increasingly buy large language model services, yet we still often estimate electricity use as single Wh-per-query value. We present the Surrogate Large Language Energy Emulator (SULLEE), an open bottom-up model linking token geometry, serving hardware, and workflow structure to annual institutional electricity, with uncertainty propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. When an institution multiplies a single reported "typical" per-query energy figure by its count of visible user prompts our modelling implies that this compounds two separable shortfalls: a right-skewed task-energy distribution not represented by any single scalar, and workflow amplification of each visible prompt into additional agent and tool calls. Together these imply an underestimate of total inference electricity by a factor of approximately 3.4 under present-day observed use, rising to approximately 15 under a 2030 high-integration scenario. Using Australian public universities as a case study, we show how the top 10% of highest-energy requests contributes over half of modelled institution-level energy use. We quantify how institution-level electricity demand may increase across three AI integration scenarios of: 1) a continuation of estimated present-day 2026 usage; 2) a high-uptake present-day 2026 institution, and 3) a potential 2030 uptake scenario - based on present trends of generative AI tools and their uptake. For a representative Australian university, mean annual electricity demand for AI inference purposes is projected to increase from 17.3 MWh (with a 3.1-47.1 MWh uncertainty, within P05-P95 scenario quartile ranges) under the 2026 observed-use scenario to up to 287.4 MWh (41.5-830.7 MWh) by 2030.

papers.title: CosmoMap: Predicting Hot Gas Temperature and Density from Dark Matter with a Conditioned 3D U-Net
papers.abstract: Mock X-ray observations of hot gas in galaxy groups, clusters and the cosmic web require its temperature and density over large volumes and many cosmologies, for which hydrodynamical simulations are expensive. We present CosmoMap, a 3D U-Net FiLM-conditioned on cosmological and feedback parameters that predicts gas temperature $T$ and electron density $n_{\rm e}$ from dark matter density and velocity. On the CAMELS IllustrisTNG Latin hypercube, CosmoMap reaches $R^2 = 0.765$ for $\log T$ and $0.934$ for $\log n_{\rm e}$ at $z=0$, reducing the error of gradient-boosted trees by 22-23 per cent. Temperature is predicted best in the densest regions, mostly galaxy- and group-scale haloes ($R^2 = 0.88$), but the electron density of the brightest X-ray-emitting gas is biased low by $0.12$ dex. One model outperforms the baselines at every redshift up to $z=2$, and using inputs from gravity-only simulations costs little accuracy. The predictions reproduce scaling relations, surface brightness profile shapes and most of the cosmological information in the gas. They produce box-integrated luminosities with a median bias of $-0.16$ dex, sensitive at the $0.2$ dex level to the inference scheme unless batch normalisation is used. Training for per-voxel uncertainties with a heteroscedastic likelihood costs accuracy and lowers luminosities by a further $0.1$-$0.3$ dex; the composite-loss variant, CosmoMap-$\sigma$, provides uncertainties that are calibrated at 68 per cent after rescaling by predicted emissivity, except for the density of the brightest gas. Compact structures are smoothed: mock X-ray lightcones recover 89 per cent of the brightest tenth of sources but 28 per cent of all sources.

papers.title: An entropy-adjusted invariant likelihood for incidental parameters
papers.abstract: Incidental parameters can make maximum likelihood inconsistent in short panels. When they act through a known translation group, integration with respect to Haar measure eliminates them exactly and gives an invariant likelihood, whose score is shown to be the conditional expectation, given the maximal invariant, of the Neyman-orthogonalised score of every order. Under interactive fixed effects the orbit is an unknown factor space, and the invariant score for it has a drift equal to minus the derivative of the entropy of the retained contrasts. An entropy adjustment removes this drift and, at the true structural parameter, identifies the factor space uniquely when the loadings span it. The adjusted estimating equations are the gradient of a single criterion if and only if the entropy separates into an orbit term and an error-law term, as in scale and elliptical families; consistency then follows from a design condition, and in general from an equilibrium-identification condition, with asymptotic normality for fixed panel length. A boundary is derived for recovering a skewness sign discarded by a two-period invariant reduction. An application to Vietnamese rice farming rejects equal household-effect weights across survey waves and finds lower returns to scale.

papers.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
papers.abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

papers.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints
papers.abstract: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone's largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.

papers.title: Hardy and BMO spaces for the Laplacian with drift
papers.abstract: We study Hardy and BMO spaces associated with the Laplacian with drift. We define an atomic Hardy space $H^1$ whose atoms satisfy cancellation against constants and linear functions in directions perpendicular to the drift. We prove the John--Nirenberg inequality, Hardy--BMO duality, equivalence of finite and infinite atomic norms, and interpolation theorems. We show that the Riesz transforms and their adjoints are bounded from $H^1$ to $L^1$ and from $L^\infty$ to BMO. Moreover, we prove that the cancellation conditions are optimal, but the Riesz transforms do not characterize $H^1$. We also characterize the $L^p$ boundedness of their commutators, $1<p<\infty$, in terms of local BMO.

papers.title: The effects of closure parameter on the properties of kinetic range plasma turbulence
papers.abstract:
Simulations of plasmas such as the solar wind require an accurate representation of kinetic physics given the lack of frequent collisions. Fully kinetic treatments are computationally expensive and necessarily confine simulations to small domain sizes. A good compromise is to utilise higher-order fluid-moment models such as the 10-moment model.
  This model retains all physics up to the second moment, with the moment hierarchy closed by approximating the heat flux.
  One choice is to use a model for the divergence of the heat flux, $\partial_m q_{ijm} \approx v_t |k_0|(\mathbf{P}_{ij}-p\delta_{ij})$, with a free parameter $k_0$, called the ``closure parameter''. We study the effects of this closure parameter on the properties of turbulence, combined with artificial ion-electron mass ratios. We show that the heating of the two plasma species is affected by the choice of the closure parameter. For all combinations of closure parameters, the relative compressive and incompressive heating rates are affected even for realistic mass ratios. The effects are more prominent for lower mass ratios and diminish when approaching realistic mass ratios.

papers.title: Hidden Clues in WM-811K: Uncovering the Spatial Signals Behind Wafer Map Prediction
papers.abstract: WM-811K (also known as LSWMD) is a wafer map dataset first made publicly available in a 2015 paper by Wu et al. Convolutional neural networks have been used to achieve high classification accuracy on this dataset, yet it's not easy to decipher which features of the dataset are driving that performance. This study attempts to answer this specifically for WM-811K: how much of the predictive performance results from the wafer layout, the count of failed dies, their distance from the center and their exact 2-D location. After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. Therefore, high classification performance on this benchmark does not come only from learning the exact defect configuration.
papers.intro:
A typical semiconductor wafer is part of a lot. A lot has multiple wafers. A wafer has multiple dies (chips). Wafers are circular, whereas the dies placed on them are rectangular. A production lot is supposed to have 25 wafers, and in our copy, the median lot size was 24. The wafer maps are stored as rectangular 2D arrays and the additional pixels required for this padding are zeroes (background) [1, 2].

The main question we are trying to answer is how much incremental performance can be achieved by the count of failed chips, their approximate distance from the center, and the exact 2D arrangement on top of the wafer layout.

papers.title: Scoring Recovery-Time Agent Security: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions
papers.abstract: A timed-out tool write may be absent, committed, or still in flight. Evaluating an agent only on whether its goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions: auditing 12 supplied traces changes apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. We introduce an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording produces only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write is absent; a combined clarification produces 576/576. A further 1,584 episodes test stronger attacks and separate the effect definition from the recovery recipe with three rollouts per absent-state cell. Definition alone yields 276/288 valid recoveries; recipe alone yields 288/288. For Luna, malicious text is associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries under both original and definition-only wording, an availability signal limited by shared tasks and templates. The stronger attacks produce no attempted unauthorized or changed-key action and no unsafe effect. A trajectory audit finds six original-key retries after observing pending status: five denied and one deduplicated. Bounded checks distinguish atomic key enforcement from a delayed-commit race; stale negative reads also invalidate the evidence gate. A separate Claude Code program adds 720 successful episodes: 288 under the original attacks and 432 stronger-attack calibration episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5, with no observed proposal or effect deviations. The contribution is a measurement design and a diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, with no demonstrated general defense efficacy.
papers.intro:
An acknowledgement describes a request, not necessarily its external effect. A service can execute a write and lose the reply, reject it before execution, or continue after a client timeout. A retry can therefore complete missing work or produce an additional effect. Attacker-controlled recovery text can also change the requested destination, resource, operation key, or compensation action.

If the first send already committed, the requested invoice exists alongside an unauthorized send. Goal-presence scoring credits the task even though recovery caused harm. Conversely, when the first send is absent, declining every retry can preserve safety while leaving the task unfinished.

Our contribution is an executable measurement design that separates four objects: visible recovery instructions, hidden provider truth, proposed actions, and committed effects. We report a concrete scorer error in supplied model traces, task-wording sensitivity with an observed availability gap under malicious messages, and trajectory-level and bounded checks showing where provider guarantees determine control safety. Availability is measured separately from fulfillment of an unauthorized-action objective.

Unprotected attack results determine whether a runtime control can receive efficacy credit. A control receives no efficacy credit when the corresponding model proposes no harmful action. Completion is evaluated primarily in the absent state, where the recovering agent must create the requested effect. Existing and pending initial writes are evaluated for goal preservation and absence of harm. These distinctions make the null attack result interpretable without treating it as evidence of broad immunity.

papers.title: Bounds for the small Davenport constant of extraspecial groups of exponent three
papers.abstract: Let $E_s$ be the extraspecial group of order $3^{2s+1}$ and exponent three. We prove $4s+2r+2\le d(E_s\times C_3^r)\le 4s+2r+3$ for $s\ge1$ and $r\ge0$. For $s\ge2$, the degree in the polynomial proof is optimal among weights depending only on group-element multiplicities modulo three. For $s=2$, we reduce the question in all ranks to an abelian subset-sum problem with a fixed set of forbidden values in a $77$-dimensional space. We show that this set, together with zero, contains no $76$-dimensional subspace. The equality $d(E_2\times C_3^r)=2r+10$ in all ranks is not established here.

papers.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests
papers.abstract: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.
papers.intro:
Tool-using agents now compose file systems, databases, web APIs, and code interpreters at runtime. A chain can satisfy every local permission check and still produce an unauthorized end-to-end effect, such as reading a confidential document and sending a derived summary to an external endpoint. ChainCaps calls this permission laundering [1]. It attaches a sink-specific capability budget to each value and intersects budgets along the dataflow, so composition cannot restore authority that an earlier step removed. On 82 tasks, ChainCaps reduces attack success from 25–68% to 0–4.8% while preserving 96–100% benign completion, with 0.13 ms median proxy overhead.

In its manifest-quality sweep, expert manifests block 100% of attacks with 100% benign completion, while naive manifests block 27.3% of attacks and complete 50% of benign workflows. This establishes the importance of authoring, but not how component error translates into catalog risk. That distinction matters as tool surfaces grow. A production cloud MCP gateway, for example, evaluates tool retrieval over a catalog of up to 3,616 tools [5].

We therefore evaluate the catalog, as the fraction of authored catalogs in which a source-complete test finds at least one accepted exfiltration path (Section 2 states what this excludes). Figure 1 shows the gap between the two units in synthetic catalogs and in real MCP servers.

A fifteen-model pilot (twelve local, three frontier) puts a 200-tool catalog at about 5 decisions under policy-conditioned authoring (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2), against 60 under independence (Sections 4.3–4.5). • Real catalogs, measured errors. An HTTP-only test under-reports whenever errors land on other channels (Section 4.6).

papers.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.
papers.intro:
Adversarial trap corpora are the strongest available stress-test for a dense-embedding retriever. Unlike random-negative distractors—which are trivially rejected—a trap document BB differs from the correct answer AA by a small meaning-changing edit—often a single token (must vs. must not, 500 mg vs. 5000 mg, comprising vs. consisting of, increased vs. decreased), and a short multi-token edit in the legal corpus. Cosine similarity in the embedding space assigns near-identical scores to AA and BB, so BB routinely appears in the top-kk retrieved list for any query anchored on AA. In domains with regulatory or compliance stakes (legal contracts, medical treatment guidelines, patent claim scope, financial disclosures), a trap surfacing in top-10 is a silent operational failure—the retriever confidently returns a document that reverses the intended semantics of the query.

papers.title: CRAB-H: Task-Centric Certification for Healthcare Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CRAB H as a task-centric certification methodology for healthcare autonomous systems. CRAB H extends the ARC governance architecture by introducing the task as a first-class governance object, represented through Task Requirement Profiles TRP H. Each profile defines the cognitive capabilities, governance constraints, evidentiary requirements, and operational assumptions necessary for the safe execution of a specific healthcare activity. Rather than asking whether a robot achieves a sufficiently high benchmark score, CRAB H asks whether demonstrated capabilities satisfy the requirements of the task. Certification becomes a comparison between demonstrated capability and required capability. A reliability-gated assurance allocation mechanism routes cognitive dimensions that cannot be reproducibly evaluated to LEA operational requirements rather than discarding them. Governance integrity is preserved: unreliable dimensions are governed, not ignored. The Capability Margin is defined as the threshold-based conjunction of per-dimension compliance determinations, not as a subtracted scalar preserving non compensatory governance logic appropriate for safety-critical healthcare deployment

papers.title: Stacks of Parabolic Vector Bundles in the Geometric Langlands Program
papers.abstract: I define a locus inside stacks of parabolic vector bundles on smooth projective curves which is important for the construction of twisted Hecke eigensheaves in the ramified geometric Langlands program for $\mathrm{GL}_n$. I give an explicit description of this locus in the case of rank $3$ parabolic vector bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$ with parabolic structure at four points. This example involves partial flags in the level structure as well as a non-trivial twisted equivariance condition.

papers.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits
papers.abstract: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.

Our central claim is that destination authorization is not payload authorization. A guard can approve where a request goes while ignoring what it carries; a sandbox can deny the native route; and a host mediator can then reintroduce the same request on a path the sandbox does not govern. The result is not a defeated guard in isolation but a composition whose permitted channel delivers the effect. The same distinction applies to measurement: a decision log can record a block while an effect record shows delivery, and a frozen detector can miss a representation that later decoding recovers. We therefore follow each request from proposal through execution or host delivery to the resulting file and receipt.

We compare two intervention points in the agent’s action cycle. A proactive tool-call guard checks the model’s proposed tool name and arguments before the agent dispatches the call. A reactive runtime sandbox enforces restrictions when the dispatched tool attempts to access a file or network resource. Here, reactive refers to responding to an execution attempt rather than waiting for damage: a denied write or connection need never take effect. The checkpoints differ in both enforcement timing and available information. The guard inspects the proposed action; the sandbox constrains the resources that execution actually reaches.

A separate 80-run follow-up combines SafeAgents’ built-in scanner and local judge with OpenShell, including native and host-mediated delivery. The implementations operate at comparable intervention points but enforce different rules.

The prospective pilot identifies a failure in the composition: mediation restores legitimate uploads and reproduces the guard’s unchecked-payload disclosure. A complete-line check separates those pilot requests, but separate cohorts expose value-only and encoded disclosure outside its coverage. The boundary follow-up further demonstrates that the observer can miss recoverable disclosures and that identical task-success counts can conceal different benign refusals. These findings come from receipts and file hashes, using per-run canaries and fresh local sinks, independently of the controls’ decision logs.

papers.title: Off-the-Shelf Autonomous Agents for Game Playtesting
papers.abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.
papers.intro:
Developing a video game requires designers to craft various objectives for a player to interact with. These objectives can be logically correct and properly designed, but still impossible to play via normal means. A required midpoint of the objective could be spawned behind an impassable wall, an NPC could have required dialogue overwritten by another objective, a required object may be impossible to obtain, and so on. Determining if a quest is completable via normal means typically requires time from a human operator, which is expensive and pulls the operator away from other tasks they could be working on. [1, 2]

In this work, we present Buddy, an AI game solving agent we built to solve a 3D role-playing sandbox game. Buddy is capable of acting in many ways like a human player: it can observe its surroundings, navigate around the world, speak to NPCs, remember previous locations, and perform many other goal-oriented behaviors required to solve a role-playing game. Buddy is capable of completing the full multi-objective main quest of the game, autonomously operating for 45+ minutes, with no walkthrough or prior knowledge of what to do.

Our main contribution is our practical framework for constructing modular, autonomous game-solving agents. Buddy requires no additional model training, no custom harness, no trained input control policy, no game-specific training dataset, and no walkthrough. The only game-specific integration steps are observation and action tools, a Python runtime, and an in-engine executor. The other elements can easily be swapped out as harnesses and models improve. We design Buddy such that incorporating a similar system into a different, in-development game can easily and quickly be accomplished using strong, inexpensive, off-the-shelf components, for maximum flexibility and performance.

In this work we describe a two-loop system: first, we use Buddy to solve the task in multiple steps using a language model in the loop, in order to demonstrate that the objective can be completed; second, we have Buddy perform a postmortem analysis of its agent trace in order to create a single scripted hierarchical task network which solves the task. papers.title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
papers.abstract: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.
papers.intro:
I have worked in ASIC and SoC design verification for more than ten years, and much of that work runs on C++ models of RTL: reference models inside scoreboards, virtual platforms that boot firmware before silicon, and SystemC [1] models that run without a simulator license. Verilator [2] turns RTL into fast C++, and with --sc into a SystemC wrapper, but its output is a simulation engine that nobody is meant to read or edit. Readable models come from hand translation, from translators [3, 4, 5], and now from language models asked to translate between C++ and hardware languages [6, 7]. Some flows convert RTL to C or C++ only so that software tools can run on it, such as software verifiers [8] or fuzzers [9].

None of these models is checked against the RTL it came from, and their mistakes produce no warning. SystemVerilog sizes an expression from its context. C++ promotes small integer types to int and converts SystemC’s sc_uint<W> to a 64-bit integer. A translation of (a + b) >> 1 that does not truncate the sum keeps the carry, and a = b = 0xff gives 0xff instead of 0x7f. The two models agree on most inputs. A random regression on such a model can stay clean for a long time, because the difference needs both operands near the top of their range.

Translation validation [10, 11, 12] is the obvious way to do the second part: check each output of the translator against its input instead of proving the translator correct. This paper is the record of that. Section III describes the first check and the two models it passed, and the two rules I took from it. papers.title: A Sharp Lower Bound for the First Nonzero Steklov Eigenvalue of the Witten Laplacian on Weighted Surfaces with Nonnegative Bakry-Emery-Ricci Tensor
papers.abstract: We consider compact connected weighted surfaces with smooth boundary whose Bakry-Emery-Ricci tensor is nonnegative. We assume that the geodesic curvature of the boundary is bounded below in terms of the normal and tangential derivatives of the weight function. Under these assumptions, we prove a lower bound for the first nonzero Steklov eigenvalue of the Witten Laplacian, which is sharp in the sense that equality holds if and only if the surface is isometric to a Euclidean disk and the weight function is constant.

papers.title: Byte Patches versus BPE at Matched Data: A Matched-Twin Comparison at 350M Parameters
papers.abstract: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.
papers.intro:
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) and related subword tokenizers (Sennrich et al., 2016) are the default interface between raw text and modern language models. They compress frequent strings into atomic vocabulary items, reducing sequence length, but fragment spelling and morphology and make code whitespace brittle. A tokenizer is also a fixed, separately trained component: it is chosen before the language model, it is specific to the data it was fitted on, and the model cannot revise it.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) and related subword tokenizers (Sennrich et al., 2016) are the default interface between raw text and modern language models. They compress frequent strings into atomic vocabulary items, reducing sequence length, but fragment spelling and morphology and make code whitespace brittle. A tokenizer is also a fixed, separately trained component: it is chosen before the language model, it is specific to the data it was fitted on, and the model cannot revise it.

An alternative is to model bytes directly and recover efficiency with hierarchical structure. Operating on bytes removes the tokenizer and gives the model access to every character, at the price of much longer sequences. Hierarchical designs address that price by letting a large, expensive model operate on short sequences of coarse units (here, groups of four bytes) while a small model fills in the individual bytes. We study a MEGABYTE-style (Yu et al., 2023) variant: a patch-4 encoder, a global Transformer, and a two-layer causal byte decoder whose 64-byte attention window crosses patch boundaries (local64). The baseline is a decoder-only Transformer over an 8k byte-level BPE vocabulary (BPE-8k).

Hierarchical designs address that price by letting a large, expensive model operate on short sequences of coarse units (here, groups of four bytes) while a small model fills in the individual bytes. We study a MEGABYTE-style (Yu et al., 2023) variant: a patch-4 encoder, a global Transformer, and a two-layer causal byte decoder whose 64-byte attention window crosses patch boundaries (local64). The baseline is a decoder-only Transformer over an 8k byte-level BPE vocabulary (BPE-8k).

Claims in this area are easy to get wrong, because byte models and token models are scored in different units, see different amounts of context, and are trained with different sequence lengths. Recent work makes the same point from the tokenizer side. Controlled studies show that the choice of subword tokenizer changes downstream accuracy and cost (Ali et al., 2024; Schmidt et al., 2024; Meister, 2026), that the best vocabulary size depends on the compute budget (Tao et al., 2024), and that bits-per-byte (BPB), the usual cross-tokenizer metric, is itself not tokenizer-agnostic and can disagree with task accuracy (Schaeffer and Koyejo, 2026). These studies compare tokenizers with one another, mostly under a fixed token budget. At large scale, byte models with learned patches have been compared to tokenized models under FLOP control (Pagnoni et al., 2024). What is missing is a small, tightly matched answer to a simpler question: if the raw data, its order and the training recipe are held fixed, does a fixed-patch byte model keep up with a BPE twin, and which evaluation choices change the answer?

We therefore build the comparison around matched twins: two models of the same width and depth, trained on the same bytes in the same order with the same optimizer recipe, and then evaluated so that both score the same byte ranges with the same left context. Holding the budget in bytes rather than tokens matters here: under a token budget, the tokenizer with better compression sees more raw text, which confounds the architecture comparison.

Three design choices separate this work from the studies above (Table 1). (i) The unit of matching is the raw byte stream. Both models are trained on the same 101010^{10} bytes, in the same document order, with a learning-rate schedule keyed to bytes seen, so neither model gets more text or a different curriculum; the remaining compute difference is about 2%2\% and favors the byte model. (ii) The comparison removes the tokenizer instead of swapping it. Controlled tokenizer studies change which subword tokenizer a fixed model uses; we ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can do without one, at matched depth and width. (iii) Evaluation is treated as part of the result. We score both models on identical byte spans with identical left context, and we report how much the conclusion moves when that control is dropped. The size of that effect is the main warning of this paper: the same BPE-8k checkpoint scores 0.6000.600 bits per byte on code under matched spans but 0.8430.843 when it is asked to score 2048-byte windows past its trained context, which turns a clear BPE lead on code into an apparent byte-model win (Section 8, Table 9). This is a concrete, measured instance of the concern raised by Schaeffer and Koyejo (2026): cross-tokenizer BPB comparisons are only as meaningful as the evaluation protocol behind them.

papers.title: Quiet-Sun magnetic field configuration inferred from the ratio of longitudinal fields measured in the Fe I {\lambda}6301 and {\lambda}6302 {\AA} lines
papers.abstract: The estimate of the longitudinal magnetic field obtained from the Hinode spectropolarimeter data will be different if it is determined in different ways. In particular, the values obtained by the Center Of Gravity (COG) method for the Fe I $\lambda$ 6301 and 6302 $\AA$ lines do not coincide. Some of the differences are due to the different inaccuracies of the COG method for each of the two lines. However, some of the differences can be explained by the fact that the response functions of these lines to changes in the magnetic field are formed at different heights. This should be accompanied by a certain morphological structure of magnetic fields. It consists in the fact that most of the magnetic configurations of the quiet photosphere are similar to each other. To a rough approximation, their structure can be compared with the structure of a sunspot - there is a central region with the strongest field, close to vertical, and slopes - an analog of penumbra, where the field weakens and / or turns to horizontal. This turn occurs at the heights of the greatest response of the Fe I $\lambda$ 6301 and 6302 $\AA$ lines to changes in the magnetic field with a turn length of about tens of kilometers.
papers.intro:
A well-known problem is the discrepancy between magnetic field values obtained using different measurement methods. We illustrate these differences graphically (see Fig. 1), using the extensive data collected by the Hinode spectropolarimeter.

A well-known problem is the discrepancy between magnetic field values obtained using different measurement methods. We illustrate these differences graphically (see Fig. 1), using the extensive data collected by the Hinode spectropolarimeter.

First, let us compare the longitudinal field values in the quiet photosphere measured by the Milne–Eddington model-based inversion (ME inversion), which we will denote as BMEB_{\mathrm{ME}}, with the values obtained using the center of gravity (COG) method for the Stokes profiles I+V\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{V} and I−V\mathrm{I}-\mathrm{V}, which we will denote as BIVB_{\mathrm{IV}}; see Figs. 1(a) and 1(b) for the quiet photosphere, and 1(d) and 1(e) for the penumbra. It should be noted that when we discuss the magnetic field derived from ME inversion, we have both the field strength (measured in Gauss) and the magnetic flux density, which is obtained by multiplying the field strength by the filling factor and is measured in Gauss (or Maxwells per square centimeter). However, when we refer to the field measured by the COG method, it is always averaged over the observed region. That is, it is averaged over both the spectrograph aperture area and the height range within which the spectral lines are formed. For simplicity, we often call this quantity the field strength, but in essence, it represents the average magnetic flux density.

papers.title: Homothetic Copies of Polytopes and Binomial Barcodes
papers.abstract:
Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite full-dimensional configuration, and put $F_X(N)=\max_{S\subset\mathbb{R}^d, |S|=N}\#\{(\mathbf{v},\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,\infty):\mathbf{v}+\lambda X\subseteq S\}$. Elekes and Erd\H{o}s posed the problem of estimating $F_X(N)$. In this article, we determine its exact value when $X$ is the vertex set of a simplex. For several other classes of configurations, we obtain sharp asymptotic bounds and exact extremal values. We also introduce binomial barcodes for order polytopes and a recursive criterion for their effectiveness.
  In particular, if $X$ is the vertex set of the three-dimensional cube, then, for $n\ge 1$, $F_X(n^3)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^3=\left(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\right)^2$.

papers.title: New families of vertex-transitive quaternionic lattices in products of trees
papers.abstract: We describe infinite families of quaternionic arithmetic lattices in $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{T}_1)\times \cdots \times \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{T}_n)$ acting transitively on the vertices of the Cartesian product $\mathcal{T}_1\times \cdots \times \mathcal{T}_n$, where $\mathcal{T}_1,\dots, \mathcal{T}_n$ are regular trees. We present an algorithm to determine a presentation for each of these lattices. We also introduce a method for constructing such lattices that act regularly on the set of vertices. We illustrate our results with numerous explicit examples, including several families of known cases, as well as many new instances in arbitrary characteristic.

A BMW group is a subgroup Γ⩽Aut⁡(𝒯)×Aut⁡(𝒯′)\Gamma\leqslant\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{T})\times\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{T}^{\prime}) acting regularly (i.e. acting freely and transitively) on the vertices of 𝒯×𝒯′\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}^{\prime}, the Cartesian product of the trees. papers.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
papers.intro:
Small reasoning models often loop: they repeat “Wait, let me reconsider” until the token budget runs out. Pipis et al. [5] trace looping to errors in learning, and Liquid AI [6] report it in 22.9% of greedy Qwen3.5-4B completions. In Qwen3.5-0.8B [4] with thinking on, it is almost universal.

Sparks of Weight-Space Programming [1] let GPT-6 Astra read and edit this model’s weights in a Python session, with no gradients. Astra changed 64 columns of mlp.down_proj in layers 15 and 19: 131,072 weights, 0.015% of the model’s 873M. MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1%, and answers hitting the 32,768-token limit fell from 93% to 33%. The authors write that the edit “lets the model finish answers it could already work out”. A follow-up [3] reports a 29.45-point MATH-500 gain from an edit of 1,023 parameters.

Neither work compares against ordinary gradient training of an equally small set of weights, or against randomly placed edits. Without that baseline, it is unclear what a frontier model adds. We ask four questions: how small a gradient-found edit that stops the looping can be, and how much data it needs; what the edit is, mechanically; how it compares with the Astra edit under each edit’s own protocol; and whether the two edits can be combined.

Our contributions: • A cheap baseline. Sparse fine-tuning on the model’s own answers finds edits of 140 to 139,750 weights that take thinking-mode MATH-500 from 15.4% to 39.0–45.5%, in 2–9 minutes on one GPU. • Controls. At 1,398 weights, random positions fail (16.3%) while gradient-chosen ones work (42.9%). At 139,750 weights, about the size of the Astra edit, even random positions work (43.4%), so an edit of that size is not small for this behaviour. • A mechanism. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of layers 0, 1 and 2. In a model without bias terms, an edit to those channels is a constant vector in disguise: for an edit trained only there, adding three fixed vectors matches its accuracy. • A comparison. The Astra edit lives in other layers, points in a nearly orthogonal direction and depends on the input. Under its own 32k-token protocol it beats our edits (52.1% against 45.7%), but ours win at every budget up to 16k: our edit stops early, theirs needs room to think. • A combination. Adding our edit at half strength to the Astra edit gives 62.2% at 32k, above either edit alone (52.1% and 46.7%), with half the tokens of the Astra edit.
